title: They wallow in Trump gunk 24/7. They say it’s necessary | Media | The Guardian
description: Joanna Coles and Michael Wolff spend most of their days thinking about the president’s follies for their podcast, Inside Trump’s Head. Someone’s gotta do it
Author: Ed Pilkington
Headline: Joanna Coles and Michael Wolff spend most of their days thinking about the president’s follies for their podcast, Inside Trump’s Head. Someone’s gotta do it
Content: Joanna Cole and Michael Wolff photographed on 22 September 2026 at the Daily Beast office in New York City.View image in fullscreenJoanna Cole and Michael Wolff photographed on 22 September 2026 at the Daily Beast office in New York City.MediaThey wallow in Trump gunk 24/7. They say it’s necessaryJoanna Coles and Michael Wolff spend most of their days thinking about the president’s follies for their podcast, Inside Trump’s Head. Someone’s gotta do itEd Pilkingtonwith photographs by Dina LitovskySun 25 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 12.13 EDTShareFor a couple of journalists who spend such an inordinate amount of time sloshing around the putrid inner recesses of Donald Trump’s mind, they come across as remarkably chipper.Michael Wolff, chronicler of the 45th and 47th president, and Joanna Coles, chief creative and content officer of the Daily Beast, are just about to record the 168th episode of their runaway podcast,Inside Trump’s Head. Now in its 15th month, the thrice-weekly show is attracting an expanding audience as it digs down into Trump’s unique blend of megalomania, narcissism and insatiable lust for fame.We are sitting in Coles’s office on the fifth floor of the IAC building, the shiplike Frank Gehry structure in Manhattan where the Daily Beast is headquartered. Coles, dressed sharply as you would expect from a former mentor on Project Runway in snakeskin shoes, jeans and white jacket, is having her trademark shock of white hair groomed for camera.Wolff, who has styled himself more in the mould of a country gentleman in sumptuous brown corduroy suit (of which more later), seizes on the hair arranging to unleash his own trademark: the Wolff monologue.View image in fullscreenJoanna Coles: ‘We go deep into the dark matter inside Trump’s head.’“I don’t have any hair,” he laments. “I used to. You should see the author photo of my first book – I looked like a 70s porn star, heavy moustache and heavy hair. All gone now …”The pair are fond of ending each other’s sentences. And they bicker a lot, like those long-married couples in When Harry Met Sally. “Do be quiet!” Coles snaps at him in a mock schoolma’am’s voice. “She really was a kind of pest,” he snipes back, recalling the early days of their friendship.Underneath the crotchety patina, though, it’s clear they adore each other.In the fickle world of Trump-focused media, the Daily Beast’s podcast seems to be enjoying an enduring appeal. Since its launch in August 2025, its audience in audio form has tripled to 1.5m downloads a month, while it now exceeds 5m monthly full-episode viewson YouTube. The lion’s share of its supporters are in the US, but it also has a healthy following in Canada, the UK and Australia.Is Donald Trump winning his war against the media?Read morePart cod psychology, part celebrity gossip, part Shakespearean tragedy, the podcast leads us to places that more traditional Trump reporting rarely goes. The title is indicative. As Coles puts it, “we go deep into the dark matter inside Trump’s head”.The 168th episode, whose recording I attend, takes in Trump’s belligerent UN general assembly speech happening that day and his later fawning reception of China’s President Xi Jinping. But it is fair to say that fans of the podcast don’t come to it for geopolitical analysis.An average episode will delve into such matters as: the defenestration of senior women in his administration, including the short-lived press secretary Katie Zacharia and ambassador to Greece, Kimberly Guilfoyle; Trump’s weight (they call him the “all-you-can-eat president”); Melania’s mysterious disappearing act (Wolff and the first lady have form, having locked horns in a long-runninglegal dispute); and the outsized role of executive assistantNatalie Harp, whom Wolff flagged as an issue well before the White House correspondents’ pack.View image in fullscreenThe hosts of Inside Trump’s Head are fond of ending each other’s sentences.They have also tackled theportentous question: does the president wear diapers? “There was no odor that surrounded him,” Wolff revealed in one show, drawing on his olfactory reporting skills from when he trailed after Trump during the 2024 presidential campaign.There is no mincing of words in the pod, no on-the-one-hand-this-on-the-other-hand-that. Coles brings the sharpness of her Fleet Street training to bear in analysing Trump, as well as her skills as a forensic interviewer well-versed in the seamier side of celebrity lifestyles. Wolff can inject the observations of a book and magazine writer and the knowledge he gained from the extraordinary access given to him at the start of the era, when he was invited to spend weeks inside the first Trump White House.His language on the podcast is spicy. Wolff has variously described Trump on air as “that fat fucker” and a “fucking asshole”, while Coles likes to highlight what she is convinced is the president’s declining mental faculties.Trump’s top team returns fire with equal gusto. Steven Cheung, the White House communications director, has on umpteen occasions slammed Wolff as “a lying sack of shit” and a “fraud”, while Coles is a “retard” and a “blithering idiot”.Faced with such blowback, the duo are unapologetic about their choice of subjects or words, dismissing Cheung’s attacks as “performative”. “We talk how people talk, about their friends, about their bosses,” Coles says. “We are not trying to put a glass wall between us and politicians, we’re trying to understand them as people.”Trump has often claimed that he has made a fortune for the “fake news” media, and such bragging would appear fair comment when it comes to Inside Trump’s Head. Coles estimates that a third of the Daily Beast’s content and traffic is entirely dependent on him.As for Wolff, Trump has been a veritable cash cow. Accordingto Forbes, Wolff made $13m just in the first year of Fire and Fury. Will he say exactly how much he has profited from all four books?He hesitates, then says, “No.”Coles, true to form, finishes his sentence. “Well, you have made a lot of money,” she says. “There’s your 18th-century mansion in Amagansett.”View image in fullscreenMichael Wolff: ‘You can analyse Trump’s policies all you like, but what he is doing has nothing to do with policy.’“It’s 19th-century,” he retorts. “And it’s a farmhouse.”“What about your hand-sewn Savile Row suit, it’s Anderson & Sheppard isn’t it?” she presses, referring to that sumptuous brown corduroy affair he is sporting.Wolff silently concurs. A bespokeAnderson & Sheppardsuit, as worn by King Charles and Daniel Craig, can easily set you back $9,000.The podcast’s unashamed technique of examining Trump in the round, with all his personal flaws and foibles, is not without its critics. The New York Times columnist Frank Bruni last month wrote anopinion piecethat berated media outlets that focus on Trump’s appearance rather than on the damage he is doing to the world. Though he didn’t mention the podcast, Bruni did mention “cankles”, aDaily Beastfavourite.When I raise the Bruni argument – that what matters is Trump’s anti-democratic actions not his inner psychology – it sparks off another Wolff monologue.“Trump is the most unique politician anyone has come across,” he says. “He’s so unique no political reporter can cover him. That’s our conceit: to probe what the traditional media is not covering. They cover Trump as they would an ordinary politician, and his politics as an ordinary function of cause and effect. But Trump is completely outside of the familiar ecosystem of the presidency.”He’s only half done. “You can analyse Trump’s policies all you like, but what he is doing has nothing to do with policy. It has everything to do with himself, with his self-aggrandizement. To understand him, you have to look at his character, how this guy thinks, what are his fundamental motivations.”The seeds of Inside Trump’s Head can be traced back to the start of Wolff’s decade-long engagement with its subject. The two men had some contact in the early 2000s when Wolff was writing a media column for New York magazine, but it was not until May 2016 that he and Trump went head-to-head.In the course of an interview during Trump’s first White House bid, Wolff asked him why he was running for president. Trump replied: “To be the most famous man in the world.”Wolff recalls: “I thought at that moment, my God! This is going to be a trip.”View image in fullscreenColes and Wolff have been friends for 25 years, not without its intermittent spats. ‘I feud with a lot of people,’ Wolff concedes.Ever since that exchange Wolff has been on an epic voyage of discovery to get to the bottom of Trump’s bottomless desire for fame. “It’s not just a character flaw that he craves all this attention. It has become Trump’s strategy. ‘How do I stay the most famous person in the world?’ That is literally the question he asks himself when he wakes up every day.”Trump’s attention-seeking is one of the central themes of the four books that Wolff has written about him – starting with the bestseller Fire and Fury that took readers into the chaos of Trump 1.0, and most recently last year’s All or Nothing that marked his return to office. It is also what inspired Coles to create Inside Trump’s Head as part of her plan to reinvigorate the Daily Beast after Barry Diller, the billionaire chairof IAC,invited herand Ben Sherwood to take over its helm in 2024.Coles and Wolff have been friends for 25 years, after she left her West Yorkshire roots and relocated as a Guardian reporter from London to New York. It was Wolff who gave her a leg up into American media, helping her leave the Times of London to which she had defected and secure an editing job at New York magazine.Blurred lines: how Michael Wolff aspired to be part of elite circles he wrote aboutRead more(This seems a reasonable moment to make a full personal disclosure. I have been friends with Coles since we worked together in the Guardian newsroom in London in the 1990s. I have also known Wolff since I myself moved to New York for the Guardian in 2006, and I have on occasionwritten about him. Thelast time I did soI reported on the Trump-related interviews he conducted with Jeffrey Epstein, during which Wolff gave the convicted sex offender PR advice on how to handle the scandal spiraling around him. Wolff emailed me having read the piece. “Jesus, Ed, you’re a nitwit,” he said.)The Coles-Wolff friendship hasn’t always been easy. They’ve had intermittent feuds along the way, in which they have avoided speaking to each other for a couple of years, though neither can remember why. “I feud with a lot of people,” Wolff concedes.View image in fullscreenColes: ‘We are interested in people and power. Whatever comes next will be interesting, because Trump has blown off the doors and allowed us to see inside.’I wonder what price the two of them are paying for what they are doing. There are many journalists who have covered Trump for the past 10 years, myself included, who know only too well the toll it takes on one’s mental health, repeatedly grappling with his lies and darkness. But few have devoted themselves to the task as round-the-clock as they have. In one podcast, Wolff admits: “There are very few conversations I ever have that are not about Donald Trump.”What’s the collateral damage of all that wallowing in Trump gunk?“Good question,” Wolff says. “I would fall back on that, as a writer, to get this story, to get this character, is once in a lifetime. You have the opportunity to have a voice in history. You don’t walk away from this so readily.”“I’m British, so I don’t even think about my mental health,” Coles quips in that schoolma’am’s voice. She carries on: “We are at a pivotal moment for the global world order. Growing up in Europe, in the shadow of the second world war, you had tremendous confidence in America as an ally. All that is changing because of one man. I would feel depressed if I weren’t trying to understand this as much as I can.”View image in fullscreenWolff: ‘When [Trump] leaves, everyone is going to sigh with relief, even the Republicans.’With the midterm elections fast approaching, the tone and focus of the podcast is inevitably shifting towards Lame Duck Trump. Aren’t they worried that we are nearing the end of this extraordinary epoch, of the “government of one” as they like to frame it, and the journalistic riches it brings?Coles puts on a brave face. “We are interested in people and power. Whatever comes next will be interesting, because Trump has blown off the doors and allowed us to see inside the mechanics of power, and you can’t put the doors back on.”The last question I direct to Wolff. Having sacrificed (at great personal gain) 10 years of his life to Trump, can he see the US, the world, ever recovering from this trauma? Will we ever be post-Trump?“We’re going to get to the other side of this, yes,” he says, beginning his final monologue. “I absolutely believe that the unique Donald Trump will not come again. When he leaves, everyone is going to sigh with relief, even the Republicans.”He’s not done yet.“It’s a fascinating thing. Nobody, except his fanbase, likes this guy. I mean, Trump is a fat fuck, even to those closest to him.”Explore more on these topicsMediaUS politicsDonald TrumpTrump administrationPodcastsPodcastingDigital mediaShare

title: This City Is Ours review – the Liverpudlian gang drama is back … and the acting’s as terrific as ever | Television | The Guardian
description: Nefarious doings, tiny-headed henchmen and sockless villains – the mob saga is back. And it’s as lovable as it is bloody
Author: Sarah Dempster
Headline: Nefarious doings, tiny-headed henchmen and sockless villains – the mob saga is back. And it’s as lovable as it is bloody
Content: Fun in the sun … Michael (James Nelson-Joyce) in This City Is Ours.Photograph: James Stack/BBCView image in fullscreenFun in the sun … Michael (James Nelson-Joyce) in This City Is Ours.Photograph: James Stack/BBCTV reviewTelevisionReviewThis City Is Ours review – the Liverpudlian gang drama is back … and the acting’s as terrific as everNefarious doings, tiny-headed henchmen and sockless villains – the mob saga is back. And it’s as lovable as it is bloodySarah DempsterSun 25 Oct 2026 18.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJust when we thought we were out, they pull us back in. Seventeen months after it huffed off in its Toyota Omertà, This City is Ours is back for a second series of high-stakes gangland bastardry. Which means, all things being equal, or at least Liverpudlian, we can expect more of the following: convoluted drug deals conducted over congealing ragu; shouting; tiny-skulled henchmen with chests of astonishing bulbosity, as if someone had squeezed their legs like tubes of toothpaste and all the meat had been forced up to their armpits; beards. So yes, it’s back. Go tell it on the mountain. And bring a shovel while you’re at it. A shovel? Yes, a shovel. Now stop asking questions and start digging; this corpse won’t disappear by itself.“’Ee’s gone,” whimpers Cheryl (Saoirse-Monica Jackson), blinking weepily in the Marbella sunshine as troubled mobster Michael (James Nelson-Joyce) manoeuvres the decomposing remains of her late husband into a makeshift grave. And ‘ee has. Gone that is. Poor Davy (Stephen Walters). Shot by erratic kingpin Ronnie Phelan (Sean Bean) for leaking information about a drug deal, his life snuffed out like a heavily discounted Yankee Candle. Davy is now, alas, gravy.Michael, you may remember, took umbrage at the murder and, fearing for his position in the Phelan family’s crime empire, promptly plunged a kitchen knife into Ronnie’s pyjamas. Now here we are in series two, with the haunted, ferrety Michael attempting to “go straight” on the Costa del Carcass with only his conscience for company. But needs must and all that, and so we gather to clear up the crime scene with only Michael, Cheryl, Michael’s preoccupied wife, Diana (Hannah Onslow), and several thousand blowflies for company. Oh, and Felipe (Álvaro Morte), a sockless snarler who promptly kidnaps them all at gunpoint and locks them up in his swanky poolside lair (“I hem yor fokin’ host”).¿Por qué? Because he’s the younger brother of Ricardo – the cartel honcho who was, until he was run over at the end of the first series, the Phelans’ main supplier of cocaine and empty threats. Felipe wants to know who “fockin’ killed” his sibling and will not rest until he learns the “fockin’ truth!”Felipe looks like Craig Revel Horwood and is “strictly” surrounded by silent goons in black athleisurewear who stand with their legs so far apart they could be deployed as spirit levels. Good news for any unfinished shelving in the vicinity, but less encouraging for Cheryl and Diana, who learn they will be held captive by these lunks until Michael returns from “fockin’ Leeverpole” with the name of Ricardo’s murderer. Oh ño.The acting is, as always, terrific. Not least from Shaun “Endeavour” Evans as newcomer Ozzie Thompson, a sublimely chilly old lag who keeps asking questions about Ronnie while drifting around the Phelans like the Ghost of Bastards Past. And dear God, thetension. There’s a scene in a car wash that is so exquisitely palpitation-inducing it took me three attempts to get through the whole thing, and that was with a packet of digestives. (Frankly, the idea of approaching any of this without sufficient carbohydrates doesn’t bear thinking about.)This City is Ours is not The Gentlemen, with its preening toffs and their fists of dry-cured Ibérico ham. Nor is it MobLand with its showboating Oirish grifters. Nobody swaggers around Stephen Butchard’s mob saga in jeggings, or is hurled in slow-motion through a pub thick with whooping cockneys in flat caps. These tortured, blouson-wearing Liverpudlians are not, by any stretch of the imagination, “cool”. They are misguided dolts, mawkish bruisers or ambitious berks so flummoxed by the demands of everyday life that their chances of sustained gangland domination seem … slim. And so we get Michael fretting about his wife’s IVF injections and hapless, Ricardo-flattening Banksey (Mike Noble) reminding his teenage son to empty the cat’s litter tray. We get weary matriarch Elaine (Julie Graham) clearing her throat at Ronnie’s graveside while surrounded by wilting petrol-station daffodils and a heartbreakingly naff A3 photograph of her dead husband, his laughing face already bleached by the unforgiving Liverpool sun.Brief rays of tender, quotidian rubbishness that have the curious effect of making this ambitious crime drama as lovable as it is bloody. More power to its fockin’ elbow.This City Is Ours aired on BBC One and is on iPlayer now.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The joy of veg-maxxing: how to eat many, many more plants – without really trying | Health | The Guardian
description: A new report has found many crops are far less nutritious than they once were, so we need to eat more of them. Here is how to get your five portions of fruit and veg a day, easily and affordably – and potentially increase that to ten
Author: Lucy Knight
Headline: A new report has found many crops are far less nutritious than they once were, so we need to eat more of them. Here is how to get your five portions of fruit and veg a day, easily and affordably – and potentially increase that to ten
Content: Lucy Knight embarks on her veg-maxxing journey.Photograph: Hannah Cauhépé/The GuardianView image in fullscreenLucy Knight embarks on her veg-maxxing journey.Photograph: Hannah Cauhépé/The GuardianHealthThe joy of veg-maxxing: how to eat many, many more plants – without really tryingA new report has found many crops are far less nutritious than they once were, so we need to eat more of them. Here is how to get your five portions of fruit and veg a day, easily and affordably – and potentially increase that to tenLucy KnightSun 25 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen Eva Humphries first started working as a nutritionist, she met a client who had just found out he had high blood pressure and high cholesterol, and was on the verge of type 2 diabetes. He had no idea how to change his diet or lifestyle.The man broke down and cried for 45 minutes, leaving Humphries with “no idea of what to do”, she says. In the final 15 minutes of the session, scrambling for a quick but helpful message, she finally said: “When you look at a plate of food, can you just make half of it veg for me?”The client came back two months later and “the colour was back in his cheeks”, she says. He told her that adding the veg had “started to [make him] feel really good”.It’s a simple approach to eating more plants – and one we might all need to start emulating, sooner rather than later. Earlier this month,a new report found that, due to deteriorating soil quality, crops including carrots, apples and peas are now 20% to 50% less nutritious than they were in the 1960s. So should we be eating double the amount?When I was a child, the “five a day” mantra for fruit and veg was drummed into me and, as an adult, I thought I was doing OK. I’m vegetarian, which means that most of my meals revolve around plant-based foods; I subscribe to a vegetable delivery service from a local community farm; and I frequently snack on apples. I actuallydoeat my five a day, most of the time – and often exceed that.But even before these findings,there was research suggestingwe should aim for 10 portions of fruit and veg per day, instead of five, while some experts advocate for consuming30 different plants a week. Eating – and affordably sourcing – that kind of volume can feel overwhelming, and the news about declining nutritional value is potentially demotivating.View image in fullscreen‘Ultimately, the rule is: get the vegetables in’ … Lucy Knight, veg-maxxing at home.Photograph: Hannah Cauhépé/The GuardianWilliam Summers, senior associate at Deep Science Ventures, which published the new report alongside charity the Mark Leonard Trust, hopes the findings make farmers and policymakers consider and prioritise nutrient density. In the meantime, he doesn’t want people to imagine that there is no point in eating plants. His research has shown that “whole foods, across cereals, fruit and veg, have definitely got less nutrient dense. That’s a fact – but they’re still way, way better than eating ultra-processed foods.“There are certain vegetables that are known to be more nutrient dense and that’s tied to their genetics,” he adds. “Broadly, it’s leafy greens. So I’d say the more leafy greens you can get in your diet, the better.”According tolast year’s National Diet and Nutrition Survey,only 17% of UK adults get their five a day, which can include, fruit, vegetables, beans and pulses. So how can we consume more plants without really trying?A first step could be switching out meat for beans in meals you already make. Dr Shireen Kassam, visiting professor of plant-based nutrition at the University of Winchester, and executive director of Plant-BasedHealthProfessionals UK, suggests swapping a tofu curry for a chicken curry, or a lentil bolognese for one made with mince. Even if you don’t want to lose the meat completely, a “half and half” meat and lentil bolognese is a good way to sneak in vegetables without entirely changing the flavour, she says.Matt Beardmore, executive chef at the Italian restaurant Legare, also uses pasta sauces to pack in veg. At his restaurant, the focus is on taste, but at home, to get the maximum nutrition, he will double or triple the amount of sofrito (an onion, celery and carrot base for sauces) that he normally puts into a recipe. As the weather gets colder, Kassam and Beardmore both recommend soups as a way to use up any sad-looking leftovers in your vegetable drawer. With a soup such as minestrone, “you can just absolutely fill it with veg”, Beardmore says.His rule of thumb is “filling half my plate with veg” – which is what Humphries suggests, too. The approach she used with the unhappy client at the start of her career has become a guiding principle for the way she now works. “It’s this concept of: if we look at a plate visually, can we just shove a couple more pieces of veg on it, or maybe add some herbs or a handful of greens? I think we underestimate how far little practices like adding an extra portion of vegetables can go.”View image in fullscreenA green revolution?Photograph: Hannah Cauhépé/The GuardianThe next step, says Humphries, is to diversify your intake, to ensure you’re consuming as many different minerals and vitamins as possible. “We tend to get into a repertoire of eating broccoli and peppers and peas,” she says. One question she challenges her clients with is “when was the last time you’ve had watercress? Or, when was the last time you added a handful of fresh parsley on top of your food?” Fresh herbs are quite concentrated sources of nutrients, she says, so you don’t need to eat a lot to receive benefits. The idea is to get people thinking about easy ways to add new vegetables and other plants to the diet they already have.One plant we could be eating more in the UK is seaweed, says Humphries, particularly because it contains iodine, one of the minerals flagged by Deep Science Ventures as having been lost from our soils. “It’s got loads of iodine, iron, calcium and magnesium,” she says. “It’s one of those other plant foods that we don’t often think about.” You also don’t need a lot of seaweed in your diet to reap the benefits, so eating a bit of sushi, which often features a dried version called nori, will give you your fill. “I typically tend to use it in seasonings because it’s got quite a salty flavour,” says Humphries.The way we cook fruit and vegetables matters, too. “Typically, vitamins C and B tend to go from vegetables if you boil them,” says Humphries. “C is broken down by heat, and then a lot of the B-vitamins leach into the water.” On the other hand, certain vegetables actually improve when boiled: “Say, for example, iron in spinach. We can barely absorb any iron from raw spinach, but we can absorb it really well when it’s cooked or boiled”.Neither Humphries nor Kassam recommend getting over-worried about cooking methods, though – increasing your quantity of vegetables is the main thing. “For most people, the basic message remains the same: five a day is the minimum,” says Kassam. If you can manage more, that will serve your body well.To maximise the nutrients you absorb from the food you already eat, choose wholegrain varieties wherever you can – thereby “reducing the reliance on refined grains and going for brown rice, brown pasta”, Kassam says. One surprising thing that Kassam and Humphries tell me is that soaking beans and pulses before you cook them can also increase their bioavailability – which helps you to absorb more nutrients from them.Beans might be a great source of selenium and zinc, but it can be hard work for us to actually absorb those minerals if they haven’t been soaked for a long period or cooked very slowly, Humphries explains. This is because beans contain phytates, which are “anti-nutrients, and their main job is to bind minerals”, she says. “So when we eat beans or grains, we can’t fully absorb those minerals because they’re bound to these phytates. So the only way that we can get around it is to do things like soaking beans overnight. Because that tricks the plant into thinking that it’s about to sprout, and it releases the phytates.”View image in fullscreenKnight shopping for fruit and veg at Lewisham Market.Photograph: Hannah Cauhépé/The GuardianThis is great news if you’ve got the time and capacity to think ahead and prep your beans in advance – but the reality is that most of us buy beans in cans or jars. Most ready-to-eat beans in cans will have been boiled quickly, Humphries says – so while eating them is still good for you, you’re not maximising their nutritional content that way. For a convenient alternative, Humphries recommends the Bold Bean Co, which sells pre-soaked and slow-cooked beans in jars – but these are approximately four times the price of supermarket own-branded cans.The most nutritious option does often come with a cost, says Humphries, who says that she can’t afford to eat 100% organic produce, even though she would like to. Does choosing organic actually make a nutritional difference? “Our data on organic isn’t particularly brilliant,” she says. But she wants people to be aware that “when we metabolise pesticides or any kind of artificial chemicals that are left on our food, we use nutrients to detox it” – so there is actually a case for pesticide-free produce allowing us to retain more nutrients.If you can afford to buy organic and local, that’s great, says Humphries, “because we know that having a farmer down the road who really cares about supporting their local community is ultimately supporting more than nutritional wellbeing – it’s supporting our local economy. We also know that, when things are picked, they start losing nutrients fairly rapidly. So having access to fresher produce does have merit.”For this reason, if you are able to grow your own fruit, vegetables and herbs in your garden or on your windowsill, you are likely to catch more of the plants’ nutrients before they start degrading. That is probably “the one advantage”, nutrition-wise, that has been proven when it comes to homegrown v shop bought, according to Summers. “There isn’t a huge body of evidence, but from what there is, there doesn’t appear to be any reliable differences” other than “simply freshness”, he says. “The sooner you either eat or preserve it, the better.”View image in fullscreenA shortcut to feeling good … vegetables at Lewisham Market.Photograph: Hannah Cauhépé/The Guardian“Ultimately, as a nutritionist, my heart lies with: ‘get the vegetables in’” – in whatever way is affordable and manageable – says Humphries. While Kassam would recommend switching sugary snacks for fruits, nuts and crudités (the third one to pack in even more vegetables outside meals), “ultimately we have to recognise that unhealthy calories are cheaper than healthy calories”, she says. She points to the charity the Food Foundation’s most recentBroken Plate report, which showed that a fifth of UK households would need to spend 85% of their income on food to afford the government-recommended healthy diet, and that the price gap between healthier and less healthy food is now the widest it has been in over a decade.Because of this, Kassam says, “people don’t always make active choices: their choices are made in the food environment, what’s affordable, what’s familiar. We need to be representing healthier options in our supermarkets and incentivising those purchases.”There are ways to maximise your plant consumption slightly more cheaply: frozen vegetables still count, and sometimes even contain more nutrients than fresh ones. “There are cases where rapidly freezing veg will give better nutritional quality than fresh veg that has been sat around long enough to have time to degrade,” says Summers.“I tend to stash three to four different types of vegetables in my freezer,” Humphries says, so she’s always got a handful of spinach or peas to add to her meals.If you have room, keeping a store cupboard full of “tins of beans and wholegrains and things that are always going to make a nutritious meal” is also a good, and relatively cheap, way to ensure that you always have plant foods on hand, even if you haven’t got anything fresh in, says Kassam.But, she adds, any increase in fruit and vegetable intake is beneficial. “We’re not talking about being perfect.”Explore more on these topicsHealthVegetablesFoodFruitNutritionBeans, pulses and legumesSoupfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: As a young man, magazines were my window to the world. That wonder will be lost when all the shops have gone | John Harris | The Guardian
description: The closure of former WH Smith stores around the UK is sobering on many levels. The publications they sold were there to be perused, to broaden horizons, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: The closure of former WH Smith stores around the UK is sobering on many levels. The publications they sold were there to be perused, to broaden horizons, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Browsing magazines inside a WH Smith store in Bristol, 2007.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenBrowsing magazines inside a WH Smith store in Bristol, 2007.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyOpinionMagazinesAs a young man, magazines were my window to the world. That wonder will be lost when all the shops have goneJohn HarrisThe closure of former WH Smith stores around the UK is sobering on many levels. The publications they sold were there to be perused, to broaden horizonsSun 25 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 09.35 EDTShareTowards the end of the 1970s, the brief but spectacular career of those punk rockers and folk devils the Sex Pistols was followed by The Great Rock’n’Roll Swindle, a rather tawdry drama-documentary. It recast their rise and fall as a huge scam, summed up bya slogan on a T-shirtworn by their former manager Malcolm McLaren: “Cash from Chaos”.Back then, that motto was a neat representation of his personal brand of cultural mischief. But the culture always takes unexpected twists and turns – and 50 years on, an almost-identical maxim seems to be defining the fate of an increasing chunk of the British retail economy. While Andy Burnham pledgesto restore life to town centres, a private equity outfit is busy buying up national retail chains and then shutting down scores of their outlets, while seemingly operating in line with its boss’s most celebratedquotation: “Where there’s chaos, there’s opportunity.”Those words came from Jamie Constable, the owner of a set of businesses thatincludes Modella Capital, which specialises in“distressed investing”and“aggressive restructuring”. In 2024, Modella bought the craft supplies chain Hobbycraft – insisting on its“real commitment to bricks-and-mortar retail”, but thenshutting 18 shops and triggering 600 job losses, whileleaving redundancy costs to the taxpayer. Months later, it acquired the discount outlets branded as The Original Factory Shop, only for the entire chainto collapse. But its most ambitious move wasits recent purchaseof the 480 high-street shops that previously traded as WH Smith, rebranded by Modella as TG Jones (a completely made-up name, which it said would “keep that sense of afamily business”), and the rapidly announcedclosure of up to 150 of them.In September, 19 branchesbreathed their last, in such varied locations as Bath, Southend, Cardigan, Redhill and the Essex new town of Basildon. This month, the shuttersare permanently fallingin – among 23 places – Pinner, Truro, Inverness and Leek in Staffordshire. Thanks to their shortsighted folding into previous WH Smith premises, the closure plan will inevitably mean theloss of many local post offices: by early 2027, 70 will have gone. It will inevitably accelerate the decline of printed newspapers. But for me and many others, the key tragedy in this story is all about magazines, those gloriously tactile creations that played a crucial role in making many of us who we are.I say that as someone who fell in love with this form of publishing as a child, via a weekly educational magazine calledLook and Learn– stuffed, as I recall, with comic-strip versions of Dickens stories, and stuff about space exploration. By my early teens, I was an avid reader of Sounds, the Melody Maker and NME, the so-called weekly music papers that were really magazines whose ink came off on your fingers. Much to my amazement, between my 19th and 26th birthdays, I ended up successively working for all three – until, in 1995, I joined the now defunct company Emap Metro, which set enormous store by its mastery of glossy fortnightlies and monthlies.Some of these names may mean precious little to younger readers, but spark a Proustian rush among older ones: Q, Smash Hits,Select(which I edited for three years), Sky, the metal and hard rock title Kerrang!, Big,Neon, FHM. Most have now closed, but three of the old stable are still standing, under different ownership:Kerrang!, which mostly lives online; the film bible Empire; andMojo, the lovingly produced music magazine that I am thrilled to still write for.Thirty years ago, we all knew that there was no better medium for in-depth interviews, or high-end photography. The management constantly asked us who our intended reader was, and what the future was likely to entail. Even the smallest cover-lines were pored over, as if the mere mention of Placebo or DJ Shadow might attract scores of newbies. And though a lot of us didn’t listen, we were told to never, ever put our magazines in sealed plastic bags (which, in line with a longstanding convention, would contain “free gifts”), for fear of losing the kind of punter who liked to browse before they bought.And therein lies the TG Jones tragedy. The business has rightly acquired an utterly grim reputation, but is – or was – one reliable place to still find shelves full of printed content worthy of endless curiosity. And now? The culturally omnivorous twentysomething in Rickmansworth will no longer chance upon the latest edition of the cutting-edge music monthlythe Wire, and thereby be inducted into a world of esoteric electronica and contemporary avant-garde jazz. The student-age customer in Ormskirk tiring of production-line pop may know nothing of the more substantial music covered by Mojo’s excellent competitorUncut.Would-be radicals will be unable to browse the printed iteration ofTribune; film freaks may be completely unaware of the in-depth, art-house wonders ofSight and Sound. Publishers will fall over themselves to alert us to subscription offers, but for a lot of people, they will be prohibitively expensive.As George Orwell once put it, the UK is “a nation of stamp-collectors, pigeon-fanciers, amateur carpenters, coupon-snippers, darts-players, crossword-puzzle fans”. Products that reflect that enduring aspect of our national character are still at the core of magazine publishing, and why some titles still sell enviably: at the last count, for example,BBC Gardeners’ Worldsold a monthly average of 164,807 copies, while Country Living shifted 107,596. The broad women’s and fashion sector is also still here. It isn’t all over, by any means.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStill, one can easily imagine a Mark Zuckerberg-esque voice scoffing at all this as so much stone-age nonsense, and claiming that what printed magazines deliver can easily be either replicated or superseded on the internet. Experience often suggests otherwise: witness the fate of the once-independent online music magazine Pitchfork, bought out by the corporate publisher Condé Nast in 2015 andbizarrely foldedinto the workings of the men’s title GQ nine years later: a classic case of what we now know as enshittification. But there is an even bigger point here about how we now engage with the things we like and love, summarised in a forthcoming book titled Circulation: How Culture Moves in the Age of Algorithm by the Nashville-based US music insiderDavid Macias, with a foreword written byDan Clancy, the CEO of the livestreaming platform Twitch.His argument is about music, but its logic applies across the cultural, recreational and sporting board. “The algorithm is great at finding me new music in the limited style I listen to,” he writes. “But it is really bad at showing me something new and different. My listening has become homogeneous, even though I can pick any album ever created.” This is the tedious prospect that the demise of the magazine will only accelerate – so after the high-street chaos has died down, we could be faced with an awful silence, broken only by the leakage from headphones playing the same things over and over again. And to speak the language of the insatiable capitalist, where will anyone find money in that?John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsMagazinesOpinionConsumer magazinesNewspapers & magazinesWH SmithRetail industryMedia businesscommentShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’d rather live through something publicly than escape it privately’: Jack Antonoff on survivor’s guilt and still singing love songs after his breakup | Jack Antonoff | The Guardian
description: Whether he’s playing the role of soul-baring artist or starry producer, the Bleachers frontman strives to keep his integrity intact. He weighs in on Ed Sheeran, his love of working on ‘high-stakes’ albums and why he’s standing by the songs about his marriage
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Whether he’s playing the role of soul-baring artist or starry producer, the Bleachers frontman strives to keep his integrity intact. He weighs in on Ed Sheeran, his love of working on ‘high-stakes’ albums and why he’s standing by the songs about his marriage
Content: I’m with the band … Antonoff (second from right) with his band Bleachers.Photograph: Alex LockettView image in fullscreenI’m with the band … Antonoff (second from right) with his band Bleachers.Photograph: Alex LockettJack AntonoffInterview‘I’d rather live through something publicly than escape it privately’: Jack Antonoff on survivor’s guilt and still singing love songs after his breakupAlexis PetridisWhether he’s playing the role of soul-baring artist or starry producer, the Bleachers frontman strives to keep his integrity intact. He weighs in on Ed Sheeran, his love of working on ‘high-stakes’ albums and why he’s standing by the songs about his marriageSun 25 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 08.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSitting in the restaurant of a Denver hotel, in the middle of a US tour with his band Bleachers,Jack Antonoffshrugs. “There’s this intense need to figure me out,” he frowns, “and I don’t really know where it comes from, because I keepexplaining all of it.”He has a point. For the last 12 years, Bleachers have released a succession of albums packed with Antonoff’s strikingly personal and frank songs. Being strikingly personal and frank was the whole point. Antonoff had previously been guitarist in Fun, a pop-rock band who went supernova with their 2011 single We Are Young. Despite co-writing a song that sold 10m copies in the US alone, Antonoff says he “hated” the experience “because I wasn’t the leader, they weren’t my words, and I needed to write a song that if I fucking died tomorrow would be my life story”.He says he insisted his then-record label release said song I Wanna Get Better as Bleachers’ debut single “to let people know what they were in for”. It depicted Antonoff literally screaming in anguish, “losing my mind” with grief in the wake of his younger sister’s death, aged 13, from a brain tumour. You can tell it set the confessional tone of Bleachers’ oeuvre just by looking at some of their other song titles: I’m Ready to Move On, Everybody Lost Somebody, Stop Making This Hurt, Self-Respect, I Can’t Believe You’re Gone, We Should Talk.Their latest album, Everyone for Ten Minutes, offers his audience what you might call the Jack Antonoff origin story: there are songs about his teenage years spent traversing the US in his parents’ minivan, touring down-at-heel punk venues with an emo band called Outline, which by his own account was a pretty hair-raising experience (“Teenagers, in a van, drinking a lot, smoking pot, taking psychedelics, smoking what we thought was hash but turned out to be black opium,” he laughs, “I’m amazed we survived”), to which his parents only agreed because his sister’s illness meant “they could not give a fuck about anything that didn’t really matter. When something serious, existential is going on in your life, you get a little less stressed about a parking ticket or grades, you know?”double quotation markThere’s a difference between joyfully seizing the moment and something that’s predicated on anxietyIf Bleachers were the only thing that Jack Antonoff did, then it would all seem terribly straightforward. But, of course, they aren’t the whole story. Around the same time he started the band, he metTaylor Swiftat an awards ceremony, bonded over a mutual love of 80s synth duo Yazoo and embarked on a creative collaboration that ultimately led Antonoff to become perhaps the most in-demand pop producer on Earth: he’s worked not just on 11 Taylor Swift albums, but with Sabrina Carpenter, Lorde, Lana Del Rey, St Vincent, Kendrick Lamar and Gracie Abrams, among a host of others. He is in the vaunted position of being a blue-chip pop mega-producer who also makes soul-baring, Bruce Springsteen-influenced angst-rock, and insists neither activity takes precedence over the other in his career.“I’m in a very narrow group of people who truly do both, probably,” he nods. “Usually someone’s slumming it on one side: songwriters or performers who think they can produce a record but then have to really care about someone else’s work in a deep way, or producers who think: ‘Now it’s my turn!’ but don’t have that thing you can’t even describe that drew you to write your own songs and fucking sing them in front of people since you were a kid.”Indeed, for all his protestations that he’s really terribly straightforward, Jack Antonoff seems anything but. Rather, he seems like such a mass of complexities and contradictions that you sometimes get the impression he might be trying to puzzle them out himself, in front of you. He’s clearly very driven, but he worries his drive is bound up with “survivor’s guilt” over his sister’s death, “about not going for things or using my time when someone you love didn’t get time, which is not the best way to live – there’s a difference between joyfully seizing the moment and something that’s predicated on anxiety”.View image in fullscreenJack of all trades … Antonoff with (from left) Phoebe Bridgers, Julien Baker and Lucy Dacus of boygenius and Taylor Swift at the 2024 Grammy Awards.Photograph: Michael Buckner/Billboard/Getty ImagesHe decries the constant chatter of opinion on the internet: “I don’t give a fuck any more, it’s like, the very act of engaging negatively on the internet is inarguably such a fucking low-vibrational joke, and I think artists for too long over the past decade have read into it and there’s less than nothing there.” But equally he says he enjoys making “super high-stakes albums … helping to architect and guide something that everyone is going to have an opinion on, that people love to have the hottest opinions on”.He thinks his role in making some of the biggest records of the century so far is widely misconstrued as shadowy and machiavellian (“He’s annoyingly, inescapably, maddeningly everywhere…the designated steward of Tasteful Pop,” protested one piece on music website Pitchfork, which went on to accuse him of “musical manspreading” and suggest he had “extreme Main Character Energy”). “One of the great misconceptions of how it works in my world is that I write songs and hand them to, like, a pop star, which I’ve never done once in my life,” he says, but declines to discuss how it actually works because “it doesn’t really matter”. Besides he’s sick of people constantly trying to explain everything online. “You’re on your phone all the time beingexplainedsomething,” he says. “You’re being explained what’s happening in this country, you’re being explained how a train works, it’s like an information dump and it’s killing people’s imaginations. ‘Do you want to sound like Jack Antonoff? Here’s how he did it!’ It’s made me want to allow people to imagine the magic of it all.”Certainly, in the context of 21st-century pop, he’s a very odd fish. He is obviously someone who moves with enviable ease among the pop aristocracy: he apparently ended up working on Kendrick Lamar’s multiple Grammy-winning 2024 album GNX when he popped into the studio to visit a friend and “didn’t leave for three years”; Bruce Springsteen isn’t just an influence but a friend, collaborator with Bleachers and mentor (best advice thus delivered by The Boss: “Don’t live in the dream, let the dream live in you”). But Antonoff both looks noticeably more like someone who might have spent his teens playing gigs in anarchist book stores on drugs than someone who co-wrote, say, Sabrina Carpenter’s Please Please Please – close-cropped hair, tattered skate pants, Sonic Youth T-shirt – and often sounds more like a chippy indie outsider than someone who recently enjoyed chicken nuggets with caviar at Taylor Swift’s wedding.Certainly, he is more free with his opinions than you might expect from someone who operates at the top table of pop, a world where artists tend to have any capacity for controversy media-trained out of them. He’s currently engaged in a war of words with Live Nation over gig ticket prices (he is proud that Bleachers’ tickets are “as low as they can physically possibly be”). “Live Nation keep missing the point, because every time I say something, they’ll call my people and say: “Let’s have a meeting.’ You don’t get it, I don’t want to fucking talk to you people, I want to make it clear that I’m not fucking OK with you turning the most sacred thing into the world into some weird free-market piece of shit … the idea that if you’re rich, any ticket you want is yours at any time and if you’re not, you have to go through this demoralising online experience where you get whacked and kicked and fucked around.”View image in fullscreenWhen the Fun stops, stop … Antonoff (left) with Nate Ruess and Andrew Dost in his first major band.Photograph: Dave Hogan/Getty ImagesWhen I meet him, his social media channels are filled with abuse from commenters angry that a Jewish artist has made a point of saying “free Palestine” onstage at Bleachers shows: he points out that he was saying it long before the recent Ed Sheeran/Macklemore controversy blew up but says he has “felt way more emboldened to say it now, because it’s not in any way a strange, uncomfortable or controversial thing to say, it’s a deeply human thing to say. If you think it is [controversial] you’re lost in some other sauce that is so crazy. They’re going to let some fucking promoter tell me what I can say? Don’t book me. I’ll play for free outside. [Ed Sheeran] missed a massive, beautiful opportunity there: just cancel the whole fucking tour, then play for free outside each venue, raise a bunch of money, rather than let a fucking billionaire tell you what to do. The reason it’s not an anomaly or niche issue is because we all live in a world where billionaires are constantly telling us what to do. So stand the fuck up.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOf course you could argue that Antonoff has more freedom to be unguarded than the artists he works with. Bleachers enjoy a curious kind of success – their albums sell respectably rather than astronomically and they’ve never come “even close”, Antonoff points out, to having a huge crossover hit. Yet they are capable of filling out Madison Square Garden with an audience that Antonoff says aren’t there to see “that producer’s band”. His own celebrity is largely by proxy, thanks to the company he keeps in the recording studio – his 2023 wedding to actorMargaret Qualleytook place amid a scrum of fans and paparazzi, but that seemed to have less to do with the bride and groom than the fact that Taylor Swift was in attendance.Recently, the gossip pages have been alive, first with his former partnerLena Dunham’s memoir Famesick, which suggested that one of the reasons their romance floundered was because Antonoff was more invested in shepherding Lorde through her Difficult Second Album than their relationship, and latterly with news of his marriage’s collapse. That came as a surprise given that Bleachers had released an album thick with loving peans to Qualley and to marriage a matter of weeks before their split was announced: one of them, You and Forever, even came with a video starring the couple together.double quotation markThe deal I’ve made with my audience is I’m going to tell you honestly how I feel and I’m going to risk  standing behind itAntonoff thus currently finds himself on tour, singing songs about a relationship that’s now over. When I mention it, he first interrupts me – “Oh, I can imagine what you’re going to say: it’s bizarre” – then clarifies my point: “Songs which I wrote recently,” he nods. “I obviously was really worried about this specific thing, I sat long and hard with it and thought: ‘If I change the setlist …’ and in my gut there was a unanimous jury that said, ‘No, this is the deal. The deal I’ve made with my audience is that I’m going to tell you honestly how I feel and I’m going to risk at any moment having to stand behind it for fucking ever.’Fans and A-list stars gather for the wedding of Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce in New York – in picturesRead more“Anyone could relate to the terrible sadness and pain, but there’s a great power to it also,” he says. “It’s actually been really beautiful. I mean, for people to come together, to know what I write a song about, to know how that must feel for me now, to know what that song means to you as an audience member, to just hold it all and sort of celebrate. I don’t rewrite the past, I have no shame about the things I’ve said. My life has been dedicated to making it impossible for me to rewrite the past, because I’m standing there, singing about how I felt during the good times, so when the bad times hit I can’t look myself in the mirror and pretend that those times didn’t exist. I would rather live through something publicly than even escape it privately.”After we speak, on stage at Colorado’s Red Rocks Amphitheatre, there is indeed a fraught emotional charge to Bleachers’ performances of Dirty Wedding Dress and You and Forever. Antonoff follows the latter by playing I Wanna Get Better alone on acoustic guitar. The audience – who, as he promised, are an odd combination of twentysomething women, middle-aged couples and a smattering of grizzled Deadheads in tie-dye T-shirts, none of whom look as if they’re there to see Taylor Swift’s producer in the flesh – bellow along, so loudly that they’re in danger of drowning him out entirely. For a moment, in the spotlight, Jack Antonoff does not need figuring out.Bleachers aretouring the UK and Ireland, 23 November to 4 December; tour starts Kingston upon Thames. Their album Everyone for Ten Minutes is out now.Explore more on these topicsJack AntonoffPop and rockMargaret QualleyTaylor SwiftinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: This comedian jokes about deportation … but it is happening for real | Ireland | The Guardian
description: Despite job offers, Jaishree Malik has had visa renewal and extension requests delayed and denied, and she is not alone
Author: Rory Carroll
Headline: Despite job offers, Jaishree Malik has had visa renewal and extension requests delayed and denied, and she is not alone
Content: IrelandThis comedian jokes about deportation … but it is happening for realDespite job offers, Jaishree Malik has had visa renewal and extension requests delayed and denied, and she is not aloneRory CarrollIreland correspondent; photographs by Clodagh KilcoyneSun 25 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 13.28 EDTShareView image in fullscreenJaishree Malik, a former event organiser at Trinity College Dublin, has lost a year-long fight with Ireland’s Department of Foreign Affairs to renew her work visa and must now return to India.Photograph: Clodagh Kilcoyne/The GuardianJaishree Malik bounds on to the Cheeky Monkey comedy club stage and brandishes an envelope – it is a letter from the Irish government. Would the audience like to hear what’s in the letter?“Yeah,” the first rows reply. She repeats the question, prompting a louder response. “Yeah!”Malik extracts typed A4 pages and begins to read. “I wish to advise you that under section 3 of the immigration act 1999, the minister for justice, home affairs and migration is proposing to make a deportation order in your case.”A nervous laugh ripples across the audience, then there’s a pause. “Oh,” says someone.Malik beams. “Don’t worry, it’s not for you.” She resumes reading. “The reason for this is because you have remained in the state without permission […] you are therefore a person whose deportation would, in the minister’s opinion, be conducive to the common good.”For the audience in the basement of the International bar in central Dublin, the penny drops: the letter is real. Malik, 25, is facing deportation to her nativeIndia.“Did you know you were friends with a criminal?” she asks. “I’m sorry you had to find out this way.” She cracks a few more jokes, then: “In case you can’t tell, I’m fucking furious about this.” She concludes her set to whoops and applause.View image in fullscreenJaishree Malik holds her deportation papers, which she uses as part of her standup routine, during a set at the Cheeky Monkey comedy club.Photograph: Clodagh Kilcoyne/The GuardianView image in fullscreenJaishree Malik outside a pub in Dublin.Photograph: Clodagh Kilcoyne/The GuardianMalik is not being deported - she is leaving voluntarily - but she may be the only immigrant to turn her deportation order into comedy. Plenty of others share her anger at a system they say has become harsh and arbitrary.The Irish government has toughened border enforcement and rules on migration, asylum and naturalisation amid a housing shortage and strain on public services partly attributed to immigration. Placards at anti-immigration protests declare that“Ireland is full”.The justice minister, Jim O’Callaghan, has said the authorities wish to curb population growth that is seven times the EU average. Critics say the welcome mat has been withdrawn unfairly from deserving cases, including students from Gaza denied visas despite scholarship offers from Irish universities.Others, such as Malik, have had visa renewal and extension requests delayed and denied despite job offers. “It’s Kafkaesque. Why would I read The Trial? I’m living it,” she said in an interview, referencing the novel about a protagonist pitted against unreasoning bureaucracy.From Gurgaon, near Dehli, Malik moved toIrelandin 2022 on a student visa to pursue an M.Phil (Master of Philosophy) in literature at Trinity College Dublin. She had a job on campus during her studies advising prospective and current students. After graduating she obtained a visa that let her stay and work for two years through the Third Level Graduate Scheme and continued working at Trinity with international exchange students.She moved to another job in Trinity and applied to the department of justice to extend her visa, pending confirmation of a new one, but a delay in processing the application led to Malik losing that job in February and entering legal limbo. The department told her she had no right to work while the application was being processed.She submitted additional information to bolster her case and, while awaiting a ruling, subsisted on savings and channelled her anxiety at open mic comedy nights. Malik had dabbled in comedy at Trinity but never previously performed around the city.“Your best material comes when your life is falling apart. But the first time I was so scared. I was reading bits from my phone. It wasn’t landing very well, I didn’t know where to pause. But I got a lot of good feedback. All the comedians were absolutely lovely.”View image in fullscreenJaishree Malik performing a comedy set at the Cheeky Monkey comedy club in the basement of the International bar, Ireland.Malik refined her act and incorporated her exasperation when the department of public works offered a job that she could not accept because of the visa imbroglio. “It’s so absurd. I’m being offered a job by the government that I can’t take because of the government.”Some audiences think she is playing a character, she said. “They come up to me and say, ‘Oh, that’s so funny’. Then I explain and they’re like, ‘Oh wait, it’s actually real?’”Ivana Bacik, a legislator and leader of the Labour party, said Malik’s case reflected a hardening of immigration policy. “It’s impacting on lots of people and indeed lots of employers because they’re losing good people.”The department of justice was using “spurious reasons” to deny visas to Gaza students, said Bacik. “I believe there’s much more compassion and warmth towards inward migration among Irish communities and it’s not reflected in the ministry’s approach.”View image in fullscreenJaishree Malik on Grafton Street in Dublin.Photograph: Clodagh Kilcoyne/The GuardianA group that represents the Gaza students said the “breakdown” started this summer. “We were refused for documents we were never asked to provide, such as a bank statement and proof of intention to return,” it said in an emailed statement. “We were then told to appeal with original documents by post, and as you know, Gaza is destroyed and there is no postal service.” The students have taken test cases to Ireland’s high court.A department of justice spokesperson said he could not comment on the court cases but that screening and verification were integral to the immigration system and that there had been no change in policy towards Palestinian students. “Each visa application is assessed on its own merits.”For Malik, the battle to remain in Ireland ended with the deportation letter sent on 5 October. She will leave next month but continue performing until the end.“I am very angry but when I get up on stage and I make people laugh, it sort of disarms the anger and the political stuff. If I can go up there and make you laugh about something so powerful it makes it less powerful and it becomes the joke. That is the jester’s privilege.”Ireland is not immune to xenophobia andracismbut audiences have been supportive, said Malik. “I’m talking about visas, yes, but under this I am still a person. I’ve made a lot of Irish friends who are basically family and they’re all outraged on my behalf.”She has not fully absorbed the fact she must leave, she said. “I don’t think it’ll hit me until I’m on the plane.” She is bracing for “reverse culture shock” once back in India.In the meantime, Malik is preparing to shed her possessions, close her bank account and pack before heading in the early hours of 14 November to Dublin airport. “My flatmate drives and she’s offered to take me even though it’s a very inconvenient time. That’s a very good flatmate. Shout out to the flatmate.”Explore more on these topicsIrelandEuropeMigrationInternational studentsShare

title: Serbian leader Aleksandar Vučić ousted by student movement in seismic election | Serbia | The Guardian
description: Vučić’s 12-year reign looks to have been ended by record turnout of voters in election provoked by student-led protests
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Vučić’s 12-year reign looks to have been ended by record turnout of voters in election provoked by student-led protests
Content: Celebrations break out in Belgrade as Student List win elections by a landslideSerbiaSerbian leader Aleksandar Vučić ousted by student movement in seismic electionVučić’s 12-year reign looks to have been ended by record turnout of voters in election provoked by student-led protestsAshifa Kassam, and Ana Milosavljević in BelgradeSun 25 Oct 2026 19.42 EDTFirst published on Sun 25 Oct 2026 16.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe long-serving leader ofSerbia, Aleksandar Vučić, has conceded defeat, ushering in a seismic political shift after a historic election that saw ​the increasingly authoritarian leader pitted against a student-led movement that had spent two years protesting against his government.Vučić pointed to preliminary results that suggested voters had overwhelmingly backed the students, potentially giving them a majority in the country’s 250-seat parliament.“We still do not have final ⁠results,” Vučić told supporters at his party headquarters in Belgrade. “On the basis of a sample … it is clear ⁠that we have lost these ​elections, the Student ‌List has ‌won, they will have between 135 ‌and 140 seats and we will have 105.”View image in fullscreenIlija Srdanović, first on the electoral list ‘Student List – Students Win’, celebrates after the first results of the parliamentary election in Belgrade.Photograph: Đorđe Kojadinović/ReutersA representative sample by the ​CeSID-IPSPS pollsters suggested that the ​Student List’s candidate list will have ​138 deputies, while Vučić’s rightwing Serbian Progressive party (SNS) garnered 104 seats. The remaining seats ‌were likely to be shared ​between ethnic ​national minority parties, said the pollsters.As news broke that Vučić’s 12 years in power had come to an end, celebrations erupted on the streets of Belgrade and other cities.In the capital, Ivana, 43, was ecstatic. “This feels like New Year’s Eve to me, like three New Year’s Eves all at once, really,” she said. “We can finally breathe again.” She added that she was hoping for swift accountability for top members of the ousted regime, a key campaign pledge from the Student List.View image in fullscreenA person celebrating the election results hugs a police officer as the result of the Serbian election prompts street celebrations in Belgrade, Serbia.Photograph: Ana Milosavljevic/The GuardianOthers offered handshakes, high fives and hugs to police officers in the streets, while a chorus of honking horns rang out from passing cars.At the headquarters of the Student List, supporters chanted “Victory, victory!” as they applauded, cried and traded hugs. “Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard,” said Radomir Saičić, a professor at Belgrade University, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters. “Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future.”The scenes of joy came hours after arecord number of voters turned up to cast their ballot on Sunday. Across the country, long lines snaked out of polling stations, with some reporting wait times of up to two hours. By 7pm local time pollsters and monitors CeSID and Ipsos put the turnout at 67.6%, the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992.The high turnout, along with the estimated 150,000 peoplewho flockedto the students’ final pre-election rally last week in Belgrade, fuelled early speculation that the students may have rallied enough support to launch a new political era in the Balkan country.Serbian voters around the world queue to cast ballots in snap parliamentary electionIn the lead-up to the vote, opinion polls had varied wildly, with analysts pointing to the high degree of uncertainty at play as the candidates representing the grassroots student movement went up against Vučić’s SNS.The results were watched across the world as part of10 pivotal days of electionsacross the globe in which the authoritarian right is facing off against pro-democracy forces. The victory for the student-led movement in Serbia is also likely to reverberate across Europe, adding momentumto the youth and student proteststhat have rocked cities across the continent.View image in fullscreenA man, carrying his dog, leaves a polling station after casting his vote as people queue to vote during the parliamentary election in Belgrade.Photograph: Marko Đurica/ReutersAs people waited for the election results to come in, speculation had begun to swirl online about whether Vučić would seek to hold on to power regardless. His swift admission of defeat, however, was reminiscent of his ally,Viktor Orbán, in neighbouring Hungary six months ago, fuelling hopes of a democratic resurgence to central Europe.The high-stakes election in the EU-candidate country traces back to November 2024, when a concrete canopycollapsed at the Novi Sadrailway station, killing 16 people. The tragedy set off protests among students, snowballing into a broad anti-government movement as evidence suggested that slipshod construction, fraud and corruption were to blame for the roof collapse.As Vučić, theincreasingly authoritarian leaderwho has dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade, grappled with mounting pressure from the students, he resigned the presidency last month to gamble on snap elections.View image in fullscreenPeople in Belgrade celebrate Aleksandar Vučić’s defeat at the polls.Photograph: Armin Durgut/APThe students seized on the chance to transform the movement into political power. They announced a slate of 250 candidates for the 250-seat parliament, ranging from academics to athletes and farmers, as they called on voters to back their push to rebuild Serbia’s economy and restore its democracy.The campaign pitted them against the political monolith of Vučić’s SNS party, leaving them in an uphill battle against a ruling party that had taken over almost all of the broadcast channels and which wielded ministries and other state institutions as political tools.Vučić had repeatedly sought to undermine the students by accusing them of being stooges of foreign powers, a charge that the students have dismissed. As he pledged to increase pensions and public sector salaries, Vučić sought to present himself as a leader capable of walking the diplomatic tightrope between the country’s ties with the west, and Russia and China to steer Serbia through global uncertainties.Undaunted, the students took to the streets, staging rallies, turning up in the rural areas that had long been Vučić strongholds and going door-to-dooras they sought to pitch themselvesas the anti-establishment candidates and to rally voters behind their slogan of “Serbia or Mafia?”View image in fullscreenFormer Serbian basketball player Dejan Bodiroga, a candidate for the Student List, celebrates after Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat in Belgrade, Serbia.Photograph: Petr David Josek/APThe message was reiterated on Sunday as Dejan Bodiroga, a candidate on the Student List and the Euroleague Basketball president, cast his ballot in Belgrade.“Today, above all, Serbia is fighting for freedom and for the return of a country that has been hijacked,” Bodiroga told reporters. “Serbia is voting today to decide which direction it will take – towards the future or the past.”In the lead-up to Sunday’s vote, both international and local election monitors expressed concerns about detentions and reports of surveillance and cyber-attacks against activists.On Sunday, independent monitoring groups warned of recorded cases of photographing of ballots that suggested pressure on voters, attempted vote-buying and carousel voting.Among them was Raša Nedeljkov of the election monitory CRTA, who said that “a large number of irregularities continue to be recorded, while violent incidents outside polling stations are also becoming increasingly frequent”.Explore more on these topicsSerbiaEuropeProtestActivismnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cabinet ministers back Burnham’s call for debate on return to free movement with EU  | Labour | The Guardian
description: PM’s plea supported by Angela Rayner, Ed Miliband and business leaders, while some ‘red wall’ MPs voice concern
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: PM’s plea supported by Angela Rayner, Ed Miliband and business leaders, while some ‘red wall’ MPs voice concern
Content: Angela Rayner and Andy Burham in August. She has said his comments on the EU relationship are ‘just pragmatism’.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Pool AFP/APView image in fullscreenAngela Rayner and Andy Burham in August. She has said his comments on the EU relationship are ‘just pragmatism’.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Pool AFP/APLabourCabinet ministers back Burnham’s call for debate on return to free movement with EUPM’s plea supported by Angela Rayner, Ed Miliband and business leaders, while some ‘red wall’ MPs voice concernRowena MasonandJasper JollySun 25 Oct 2026 15.57 EDTFirst published on Sun 25 Oct 2026 09.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham’s call for the UK to consider a return to free movement with Europe has been backed by senior cabinet ministers but risked a rift with “red wall” Labour MPs, who say it could jeopardise Brexit-voting seats.The prime minister made his plea for an“honest discussion” about freedom of movementin an interview with the Sunday Times, making clear that staying out of it would no longer be a red line in talks with the EU.Burnham also revealed his belief that rejoining the single market and accepting free movement could be done without the need for another referendum, ifLabourput it in their manifesto. In contrast, he said fully rejoining would need another in-out poll.The prime minister said: “Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament. But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now].“Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”His remarks were supported by Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, as well as Stella Creasy, the chair of the Labour Movement for Europe. However,Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, is among those Labour MPs who have previously been more cautious about closer ties with Europe, while a number of backbenchers with heavily pro-Brexit seats in the north and Midlands are wary about reopening the arguments for free movement or rejoining the EU.Rayner told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg she would “like to have an honest conversation about what the trade-offs could be, and then put that to the people at a general election”, and Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow, said Burnham was right that the UK was “long overdue for a grownup conversation about what EU freedom of movement actually means”.View image in fullscreenStella Creasy said the UK was ‘long overdue for a grownup conversation about what EU freedom of movement means’.Photograph: Milo Chandler/AlamyA number of senior cabinet ministers are keen for the UK to form a much closer relationship with the EU to help boost growth, potentially involving a return to the single market and accepting free movement as a result. Those in favour of reopening the discussion includeEd Miliband, the foreign secretary.At a New Statesman event during the Labour party conference in September, however, Mahmood said rejoining the EU would not be a “simple, straightforward thing” and there were “quite hard trade-offs”, such as eliminating trade friction without “some of the burdens that also brings”.One senior minister under Keir Starmer said the reopening of the debate on free movement was “brave” given how divisive it had been in theBrexityears. “It’s a question of timing. Public opinion is of a place where you can start to have this debate,” he said. “Theresa May, Rishi Sunak, Keir Starmer: what they were all trying to do was get as close as possible without freedom of movement. There is now the a possibility of being brave and making the case on single market and free movement without going for rejoin.”Labour MPs with pro-Brexit seats have expressed scepticism about rejoining the bloc, including Jonathan Hinder, the MP for Pendle, who recently pressed the prime minister in parliament to rule out a return to free movement.One red wall MP said they thought debating free movement was the right thing to do but many colleagues in the north-east, especially in coastal areas, had begun to raise serious concerns. “These MPs are definitely raising the alarm,” they said. “Andy may have to work out if he can win without them, which is brutal but true.” Another Labour MP from a Brexit-voting area said it would “undoubtedly put seats at risk to Reform” but that Burnham was making an argument from a position of strength, having taken the party to higher poll ratings in recent weeks.Worries were brought up publicly on Sunday by Richard Walker, the Labour peer and executive chair of Iceland, who told Times Radio that restarting the debate would be a “dangerous precedent” and that opening the borders would not help the “1 million young people that are out of work”.In his party conference speech last month, Burnham fired the starting gun on the argument about rejoining the EU as one potential route, but his latest comments suggest he appears to be favouring the option that would avoid a referendum.Although Labour’s manifesto pledges no return to free movement and the single market, Burnham signalled it could still be up for discussion at next month’s EU summit.Burnham’s comments at the weekend drew an immediate response from the right of politics, with the Conservatives and Reform UK criticising the idea of reopening the debate. Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said the idea of reopening free movement was “another example of Burnham’s foot-in-mouth syndrome”.View image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch said Burnham ‘hasn’t thought this through or the implications’.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPANigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, called it a “total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch”.“He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty,” he added.Polling suggests voters in the UK are increasingly open to rejoining the EU or a single market arrangement involving free movement. The concept of free movement was that British and EU citizens could move more freely for jobs within the bloc, which also shared a single market for goods and services.Luke Tryl, a polling and focus groups expert at the More in Common thinktank, said on Sunday that people tended to be less concerned about free movement given years of high non-EU migration but would be more exercised about EU budget contributions or joining the euro.During the Brexit referendum, the topic was hotly debated, with the leave campaign arguing that the UK would be able to take control of its borders if it voted to exit the EU. However, in the years that followed, net migration rose to a peak of944,000 in the year ending March 2023under a new points-based system, up from330,000 before the Brexit vote.Burnham’s decision to open the debate on free movement was welcomed by some businesses, which have grown frustrated at the lack of progress on the issue, and on reducing the extra paperwork required to do business with EU customers since Brexit – both seen asobstacles to faster economic growth.The British Chambers of Commerce lobby group called for the Treasury to analyse the various economic options for different forms of EU-UK relationships.
