Most economic studies have concluded that a closer EU relationship would benefit the UK economy.William Bain, head of trade policy at the BCC, said the common understanding strategy agreed by Keir Starmer in May 2025 was “approaching the ceiling of what can be achieved”.This week’s budget is expected to underscore the damage to the economy from Brexit, including from a drop in net migration. The Resolution Foundation, a thinktank, said that if migration falls by 300,000 over the next five years it would translate to a hit to government tax revenues of £4.7bn in 2029-30, reducing chancellor John Healey’s room for manoeuvre.The Institute for Fiscal Studies, another thinktank, estimated that lower net migration estimates would reduce the chancellor’s “headroom” by between £1bn and £5bn by 2031-32, depending on how the government’s Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) chooses to model the expected reductions in population.The OBR has previously estimated that Brexit barriers to trade and free movement have caused a long-term hit of about 4% of UK output.Explore more on these topicsLabourAndy BurnhamAngela RaynerStella CreasyShabana MahmoodForeign policyBrexitnewsShareReuse this content

title: Two dead and 160,000 properties without power as Storm Boelo batters UK | UK weather | The Guardian
description: Man aged 60 and another in his 20s killed by falling trees in Scotland and London as Met Office reports gusts of up to 84mph
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Man aged 60 and another in his 20s killed by falling trees in Scotland and London as Met Office reports gusts of up to 84mph
Content: Waves crash over the promenade during Storm Boelo on Sunday in Largs, Scotland.Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWaves crash over the promenade during Storm Boelo on Sunday in Largs, Scotland.Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/Getty ImagesUK weatherTwo dead and 160,000 properties without power as Storm Boelo batters UKMan aged 60 and another in his 20s killed by falling trees in Scotland and London as Met Office reports gusts of up to 84mphHannah Al-OthmanandCharlie MoloneySun 25 Oct 2026 18.19 EDTFirst published on Sun 25 Oct 2026 06.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo people have been killed and more than 160,000 properties have been left without power as Storm Boelo continues to batter the UK.Two men, one aged 60 and the other in his 20s, were killed by falling trees on Sunday, police said. The 60-year-old died in south-westScotlandwhile the man in his 20s was killed in London.A spokesperson for Police Scotland said: “We were made aware of a 60-year-old man having been struck by a falling tree on a minor road at Mid Kelton at about 10.30am on Sunday, 25 October 2026.“The man was pronounced dead at the scene. There are no suspicious circumstances and a report will be submitted to the procurator fiscal in due course.”In London, the man was killed when a tree fell on to his car at 12.40pm as he drove through Mill Hill in the north of the city.Ch Insp Guy Ellwood said: “Our thoughts are with the loved ones of the young man who lost his life.”The adverse weather that arrived in northern parts of the UK on Saturday evening wasthe second named storm in as many days, afterStorm Austen brought strong windsto south-west England on Friday.The Met Office said wind speeds widely reached 60-70mph, affecting areas in an amber warning zone that came into force at 9pm on Saturday.The warning covered Scotland, parts ofNorthern Irelandand the far north of England, with gusts reaching more than 80mph in exposed coastal spots.The island of Tiree in the Inner Hebrides was hit by 82mph winds, according to the forecaster, while wind speeds reached 84mph in Argyll and Bute and 83mph in Snowdonia (Eryri).Approximately 53,000 homes in Scotland were still without power by 5pm on Sunday, according to updates from SP Energy Networks and Scottish and Southern Electricity Networks.Across Great Britain, 161,400 customers were without power, according to the Energy Networks Association (ENA).The Scottish government’s “resilience room” met to discuss the impact of the storm on Sunday afternoon, with ministers focusing on the outages and how they were being restored.Scotland’s first minister, John Swinney, met senior politicians, emergency agencies and forecasters to discuss the government’s response, amid warnings that similar conditions would return early next week.Storm Boelo causes severe flooding in town centre of Largs, ScotlandEngineers had restored power to 344,900 customers but 82,600 remained disconnected, the ENA said on Sunday morning. The figure included more than 30,000 homes across Scotland.The ENA said: “The networks have been focused on reconnecting customers this morning, though the continuing severe weather in some regions is limiting network engineers’ opportunities to safely start the work of restoring customers’ power today and access to certain areas remains difficult. Engineers are working around the clock to identify and fix faults.”Train travel was disrupted on Sunday. Network Rail Scotland shared an image of flooding from the tracks to the platform at one Glasgow station, and fallen trees above the lines near another. Speed restrictions were in place across Scotland and several sections of its railways were closed, the operator added.Network Rail shared images of a trampoline beneath a train and a shed by the tracks, and it reminded people living near rail lines to firmly secure objects in their gardens.Some flights were diverted from landing at Leeds Bradford airport and others were cancelled.The Met Office advised people in affected areas to secure loose items in gardens and to stay indoors as the storm posed a danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Met Office chief forecaster, Jason Kelly, said: “Storm Boelo will be felt across the UK this weekend, with the strongest winds and greatest potential for disruption in the north.“Amber warnings are in place across mainland Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north ofEngland, where gusts of 60-70mph are expected widely, with the potential for 80mph in exposed coastal locations.View image in fullscreenWaves at Gourock in western Scotland on Sunday.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PA“Strong winds will also affect other parts of the UK, with gusts of 50-60mph possible in places. Heavy rain will provide an additional hazard, particularly in the north, bringing the potential for further impacts. People should prepare for the potential for disruption, particularly to travel and power supplies.”Several events have been cancelled this weekend due to the inclement weather. Visit Liverpool said the River of Light event, featuring illuminated artworks, had been cancelled “in the interests of safety”, while London’s annual Diwali on the Square celebrations on Sunday were cancelled on the advice of independent health and safety experts.Edinburgh Castle was closed on Sunday because of the high winds and adverse weather, while the Fountains Abbey estate in North Yorkshire was also closed for the day, after its Fountains by Floodlight event on Saturday evening was cancelled.View image in fullscreenA road closure on the A78 near Skelmorlie in North Ayrshire after Storm Boelo passed through the area.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAThe Environment Agency had issued six warnings as of 1.45pm that flooding was expected for spots in northern parts of England, as well as 50 alerts stating flooding was possible. The Scottish Environment Protection Agency said 17 flood warnings and 11 flooding alerts were active as of the same time.Cumbria police said they had received a number of calls overnight to localised flooding and fallen trees blocking roads across the county, and urged motorists to drive with care while emergency services worked to clear the obstructions.The amber warning sits within wider yellow wind warnings, which cover parts of England farther south, as well as north Wales and the whole of Northern Ireland.Hundreds of homes were still without power in south-west England after Storm Austen hit the region on Friday, bringing 76mph winds to St Mary’s airport in the Isles of Scilly, with 74mph recorded at Aberporth in south Wales and 71mph at Culdrose in Cornwall.Stuart Wilson, from Transport Scotland, said “significant recovery work” was required before the network returned to normal.The Scottish social justice and housing secretary, Shirley-Anne Somerville, said on Sunday: “Disruption to travel is likely to continue into tomorrow and I strongly recommend people check official sources such as the Met Office, Traffic Scotland, transport operators and local authority channels before setting out.“While we expect some respite from the adverse weather during the day on Monday, there is a possibility of more severe weather conditions early on in the week and we urge everyone to continue to follow advice and heed any warnings.”Explore more on these topicsUK weatherScotlandNorthern IrelandNorth of EnglandEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to double spending on homelessness amid drive to end rough sleeping by Christmas | Homelessness | The Guardian
description: Downing Street will allocate a further £432m in this week’s budget, bringing total funding for finding a ‘lasting solution’ to nearly £900m
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Downing Street will allocate a further £432m in this week’s budget, bringing total funding for finding a ‘lasting solution’ to nearly £900m
Content: ‘Rough sleeping isn’t a fact of life,’ said Andy Burnham before a rough sleeping summit on Monday that will bring together business and charities.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Rough sleeping isn’t a fact of life,’ said Andy Burnham before a rough sleeping summit on Monday that will bring together business and charities.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianHomelessnessBurnham to double spending on homelessness amid drive to end rough sleeping by ChristmasDowning Street will allocate a further £432m in this week’s budget, bringing total funding for finding a ‘lasting solution’ to nearly £900mRowena MasonWhitehall editorSun 25 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham is to double spending on ending rough sleeping to almost £900m by the end of the current parliament, as he steps up efforts to get people off the streets by Christmas.The prime minister has pledged to offer every rough sleeper in England a safe route off the streets or wider support as a central part of his premiership.As he prepared for a Downing Street summit on ending rough sleeping on Monday, Burnham said the budget would bring a further £432m commitment to helping to tackle homelessness.The sum is on top of an initial £442m from Ministry ofHousing, Communities and Local Government budgets that will be allocated to the problem before March 2027.Speaking ahead of the meeting, which will bring together charities and businesses, Burnham said: “Rough sleeping isn’t a fact of life. It’s a thing governments either choose to accept or don’t.“Well, I don’t accept it. That’s why we’re doubling funding so that people aren’t just offered a safe route off the streets this winter but have that same support right through the rest of this parliament too.“But we can’t do it alone. If we’re going to end rough sleeping, we need every part of society behind us on this. So today we’re bringing together businesses, charities and local leaders in Downing Street to make sure this is a solution that lasts.”Andy Burnham calls on wider society to help end rough sleeping by ChristmasRead moreBurnham’s mission to end rough sleeping is already under way with just two months to go before his deadline. There are specialist outreach teams and new accommodation spaces operating in Coventry, and further provision is being rolled out in places including Plymouth and Camden over the coming weeks.The additional funding is being provided in an attempt to solve the problem of rough sleeping in the longer term. As mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham introduced schemes such as A Bed Every Night to offer emergency accommodation, but while the number of rough sleepers fell, it then began to increase again.Burnham has previously said this was because “we were the only place providing that level of support and, understandably, people then travelled to Greater Manchester to access that support”.He has said ending rough sleeping across the country will only be possible “if all areas are pulling in the same direction, and that’s what this funding is designed to achieve”.11:13Will Andy Burnham get rough sleepers off streets by Christmas? – The LatestThe prime minister’s rough sleeping summit on Monday will bring together businesses, charities, housing providers and local leaders as they attempt to create more lasting changes.Alongside the government, other organisations are making pledges towards solving the problem, with the National Housing Federation working with housing associations to identify at least 2,000 potential homes and bed spaces, including empty properties that could be brought back into use.Virgin Media O2 will provide practical digital support to frontline organisations, while the charities St Mungo’s and Haircuts4Homeless will work with L’Oréal on hair salons and wellbeing provision for those who have been sleeping rough.View image in fullscreenRayner, pictured with Burnham at a homeless accommodation centre in Newcastle this year, said ending rough sleeping was a ‘big ambition’.Photograph: Lauren Hurley/No 10 Downing StreetAngela Rayner, the housing secretary, said it was a “big ambition” and the government would “not back down from making sure everyone has the offer of a route off the streets this Christmas”.She said: “The first step is giving people a roof over their head and freedom from the nightly struggle to find somewhere safe to sleep. But Christmas is only the beginning and that’s why we will keep working together to tackle the root causes of homelessness and end rough sleeping for good.”The homelessness charity Shelter welcomed the announcement. Its acting CEO, Mairi MacRae, said the funding showed “the government understands that a safe home is not a privilege, it is a necessity”.However, the Conservatives dismissed the move, with Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, accusing the government of wanting to spend too much money on ending rough sleeping.Why are rough sleepers dying a stone’s throw from luxury waterfront houses in Victoria?Read more“Burnham is throwing another £432m at a problem he failed to solve in Greater Manchester,” she said. “UnderLabour, rough sleeping has hit record highs – yet their answer is always more taxpayers’ money and more empty promises.”Referring to the chancellor, Lam said: “[John] Healey must use his budget this week to cut taxes for working people, get the ballooning benefits bill under control, and stop pushing up energy prices. Instead of piling more costs on to hard-working people, Healey must focus on easing the cost of living and delivering real value for taxpayers’ money.”Explore more on these topicsHomelessnessAndy BurnhamAngela RaynerLabourBudget 2026HousingPovertynewsShareReuse this content

title: Macron accused of putting France’s right to protest at risk with ‘vandal’s law’ | France | The Guardian
description: Making innocent protesters liable for damage would be bad for rule of law and play into far-right hands, say opponents
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Making innocent protesters liable for damage would be bad for rule of law and play into far-right hands, say opponents
Content: A protester throws a projectile towards police after a demonstration against rising living costs in Paris on Saturday.Photograph: Thibault Camus/APView image in fullscreenA protester throws a projectile towards police after a demonstration against rising living costs in Paris on Saturday.Photograph: Thibault Camus/APFranceMacron accused of putting France’s right to protest at risk with ‘vandal’s law’Making innocent protesters liable for damage would be bad for rule of law and play into far-right hands, say opponentsAngelique Chrisafisin ParisSun 25 Oct 2026 15.57 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 16.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmmanuel Macronhas been accused by trade unions of trying to curb the fundamental French right to protest as the government fast-tracks a bill to make protesters pay for damage caused by vandalism at street demonstrations even if they did not directly cause it themselves.The French president, who leaves office next spring, has faced more than a month ofprotestsin which high-school students haveblockaded schoolsdemanding a response to teacher absences, repairs to decrepit buildings and changes to the university applications platform.Trade unions andgilets jaunes(yellow vest) anti-government protesters are now joiningsustained street demonstrationsin a growing social crisis over schools, as well as the cost of living and public services. Authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrating after France saw one of itsworst days of violence in yearsearlier this month when largely peaceful demonstrations were marred by looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings.The senate will this week debate the government’s proposed “vandals pay” law. The legislation would mean that a person protesting could be held liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage and vandalism even if they did not directly cause it themselves, if they were continuing to demonstrate nearby or as part of the same group as perpetrators. The bill also provides for greater use of drones over protests.Hundreds of thousands march across France in protests over schools and policingRead moreThe prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the bill, which was originally prepared in the wake ofviolent clashesafter Paris Saint-Germain’s victory over Arsenal in the football Champions League in May, was “absolutely essential” after looting and burning during recent demonstrations across France.The bill comes as the government struggles to contain the current crisis.Marine Le Pen, of the far-right, anti-immigration National Rally (RN), has seen her frontrunner status in next spring’s presidential election boosted as she seeks to reinforce her law-and-order credentials and back police.Le Pen, who has lodged an appeal to France’s highest court over herconviction for embezzlement of European parliament funds, launched her presidential campaign on Sunday at a rally in Orléans, promising to “bring back order to France”.The RN has claimed the “vandals pay” bill was originally its idea and Le Pen said she would ensure damage to property was paid for by rioters. Le Pen told a cheering crowd of more than 8,000 people at the rally: “Vandals will pay and if it takes their whole life to pay, then they will spend their whole life paying.”She said: “We are going to restore the rule of law. Who can claim that there is rule of law when hordes come to ransack and burn our buildings?”Éric Coquerel, fromJean-Luc Mélenchon’s radical left La France Insoumise, said on Sunday that the “vandals pay” law “would mean the end of street demonstrations” in France because people would not want to take the risk of being held responsible and made to pay up to €10,000 for vandalism they had not committed. The Communist senator Fabien Gay told the parliamentary TV channel Public Sénat: “No demonstration could take place again in our country.”In an open letter toLe Monde, leftwing trade unions and France’s Human Rights League wrote: “This unfair law, which is a serious attack on the freedom to demonstrate, should be abandoned, or risk a major step back for the rule of law.”At this weekend’s protests there was widespread anger at Macron forbanning non-union demonstrationsthat his government deemed “illegitimate” and for keeping all protesters away from city centres.Although Macron has not put in place a state of emergency, the government and local authorities have introduced limits on demonstrating, including bans on gatherings in front of schools and demonstrating in city centres, as well as curfews in some places and extended periods of police custody for the record number of people arrested.NFL shutters Paris fan experience as protests overshadow first France gameRead moreAt demonstrations this weekend, many said they had come out to defend the French right to protest in the street. Street protests in France, which are seen as a fundamental way for people to make themselves heard by a centralised state, have regularly been used to express criticism of changes to the law, frompension changestosame-sex marriage.Serge Slama, a professor of public law at Université Grenoble Alpes, told Telerama magazine: “Although a state of emergency has been ruled out [by Emmanuel Macron] at this point, we have seen a number of decrees bringing a wide restriction on public liberties.”He said this was “unprecedented” and would benefit the far right if they won elections next year, allowing them to put in place further crackdowns without changing the law.Lecornu will meet representatives of protesting high-schoolers on Monday as the government comes under pressure to respond to their demands with funding and school repairs in order to avoid further school blockades.Explore more on these topicsFranceProtestEmmanuel MacronMarine Le PenEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Four-year-old girl dies after falling from east London tower block | London | The Guardian
description: Police say the incident at an address in Barking is not believed to be suspicious
Author: Charlie Moloney
Headline: Police say the incident at an address in Barking is not believed to be suspicious
Content: The girl was taken to hospital but later died from her injuries.Photograph: Joshua Bratt/PAView image in fullscreenThe girl was taken to hospital but later died from her injuries.Photograph: Joshua Bratt/PALondonFour-year-old girl dies after falling from east London tower blockPolice say the incident at an address in Barking is not believed to be suspiciousCharlie MoloneySun 25 Oct 2026 15.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 15.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA four-year-old girl has died after falling from a tower block in eastLondon.She was injured after “falling from height” at an address in St Paul’s Road, Barking, on Saturday and died in hospital, the Metropolitan police said.The force said investigations were still being carried out but “at this time, the incident is not believed to be suspicious”.Officers were called on Saturday at 11am.A police spokesperson said: “Officers attended the scene alongside the London ambulance service, where emergency first aid was administered.“The girl, aged four, was taken to hospital but, very sadly, later died from her injuries. Our thoughts and deepest sympathies are with the child’s family and loved ones at this incredibly difficult time.“An investigation into the circumstances surrounding this tragic incident is ongoing. However, at this time, the incident is not believed to be suspicious.”A spokesperson for the London ambulance service said it sent ambulance crews, a clinical team manager, an incident response officer, an advanced paramedic practitioner and London’s air ambulance to the scene.“We treated a child at the scene before taking the patient to a London major trauma centre,” the ambulance spokesperson said.Anyone with information about the incident has been asked to contact police on 101.Explore more on these topicsLondonnewsShareReuse this content

title: Manchester United board hold crisis talks over Carrick’s future and Howe approach | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Michael Carrick’s job as manager is in the balance after Manchester United’s 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth, with Eddie Howe remaining the preferred candidate
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Michael Carrick’s job as manager is in the balance after Manchester United’s 3-0 defeat by Bournemouth, with Eddie Howe remaining the preferred candidate
Content: Michael Carrick said ‘it’s a tough situation, there’s no hiding from it’ after Manchester United’s defeat by Bournemouth.Photograph: Gary Oakley/EPAView image in fullscreenMichael Carrick said ‘it’s a tough situation, there’s no hiding from it’ after Manchester United’s defeat by Bournemouth.Photograph: Gary Oakley/EPAManchester UnitedManchester United board hold crisis talks over Carrick’s future and Howe approachJob in balance after 3-0 home defeat by BournemouthHowe is director of football Jason Wilcox’s top candidateJamie Jacksonat Old TraffordSun 25 Oct 2026 15.24 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 17.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleManchester United’s hierarchy are in crisis talks over whether or not to sack Michael Carrick as head coach after heoversaw another torrid defeat, against Bournemouth at Old ­Trafford on Sunday, that left his job in the balance.Carrick was defiant after the 3-0 humbling, insisting he was not expecting to be removed from his post. “I totally understand the situation,” Carrick said of his job prospects. “I’m not expecting anything in ­particular, to be honest. Carrying on as normal and I love this place.”Michael Carrick on the brink after Manchester United are humiliated by BournemouthRead moreBut the United executive are actively ­considering his dismissal, the ­Guardian understands, with the expectation at the club being that Carrick will be sacked.Eddie Howe remains the preferred candidate of Jason Wilcox, United’s director of football, should there be a change in the dugout, with the former Newcastle manager’s extensive Premier League experience placing him ahead of other potential ­targets.Howe would be less expensive to bring in than Unai Emery, another admired candidate, given that Aston Villa would demand about £20m in compensation for the ­Spaniard.Julian Nagelsmann, the former Germany and Bayern Munich head coach, is highly regarded by Christopher ­Vivell, United’s head of ­recruitment, but Wilcox’s view may hold more sway with Sir Jim ­Ratcliffe, who ­controls football policy at United. Antonio Conte is another who may be in the frame.Carrick, who left Bruno Fernandes out of his starting lineup – insisting before kick-off that he did so for football reasons and not because of thecaptain’s criticismof his ­tactics after the midweek ­Champions League defeat at Como – said: “I’ll always do what I feel is going to be the best for the football club, ­whatever decision is made on anything really. So that’s kind of it. I’m not expecting anything either way.“It’s a tough situation, there’s no hiding from it. What it looks like and what’s next I really don’t know. I will always do my best for the football club and I won’t change that now. I love what I do and I feel the responsibility – we’ll have to wait and see.”United endured a sixth defeat in 12 games in all competitions after Rayan, Marcus Tavernier and ­Evanilson scored for Marco Rose’s side. They have won only once in the league this season and sit in 16th. Their last win was on 10 September, against Sabah in the Champions League.The club cannot announce a sacking until they inform the New York Stock Exchange, which is closed at weekends. When Ruben Amorim was sacked in January, the decision was taken on the Sunday night after the coach’s explosive press conference following a draw at Leeds, but was not announced until the next day.Carrick made a point of ­applauding the home supporters at the end of the match, pumping his hand to his chest as he walked past a supportive Stretford End. As soon as he disappeared down the tunnel, boos met Fernandes, who was following the manager, alongside other United players.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“It wasn’t a farewell from me,” ­Carrick said. “I’m feeling it for my players, they’re going through a tough spell. Some of it we can help, some of it the situation unravels and the boys are feeling it at the moment. Mixed emotions for the supporters to respond in that way.“To have that connection with the supporters, it’s mixed emotions, it’ll take a bit of time to digest but I certainly appreciate their support. The situation is where we are and we haven’t had results or performances that have been good enough.”On his decision to omit Fernandes, who was an unused substitute, ­Carrick said: “There’s always times when you’re trying to make decisions that are to change the course of play and made a difference, but those are the decisions we made today.”Harry Maguire, United’s captain in Fernandes’ absence, insisted that the squad were “fully behind” ­Carrick. He said: “Coming into the team last season he turned things around and got Champions League football this season.As individuals, we’re not ­playing well enough. We have to look at ­ourselves and find something within ourselves to bring more to the team. That’s every player that I’m talking about. When things aren’t going your way you have to do the basics well.”Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedMichael CarrickEddie HoweBournemouthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Has Healey’s military-style budget secrecy really played out so differently to past budgets? | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: Chancellor was said to be worried about market-sensitive leaks, yet significant policies have been heavily trailed in the media
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Chancellor was said to be worried about market-sensitive leaks, yet significant policies have been heavily trailed in the media
Content: The chancellor, John Healey – photographed here meeting British personnel in Estonia while he was defence secretary – is said to have deployed ‘military-style protocols’ to prevent leaks of his budget.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenThe chancellor, John Healey – photographed here meeting British personnel in Estonia while he was defence secretary – is said to have deployed ‘military-style protocols’ to prevent leaks of his budget.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Budget 2026AnalysisHas Healey’s military-style budget secrecy really played out so differently to past budgets?Rowena MasonWhitehall editorChancellor was said to be worried about market-sensitive leaks, yet significant policies have been heavily trailed in the mediaSun 25 Oct 2026 15.35 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 16.14 EDTShareThe public has been told repeatedly thatJohn Healeyis so concerned about budget leaks that he has set up defence-style “compartmentalisation” to prevent the Treasury’s financial secrets escaping.The macho military analogies began in mid-August when Healey was said by the Telegraph to be “on a war footing” to stop the drip of information that he believed had beleaguered Rachel Reeves.The Financial Times added that “military-style protocols” were being deployed, while the Spectator was excited about the use of “classified computer systems” and the i newspaper described a process where officials could sign in to only their parts of the document and could not access the sections they were not working on.This weekend, the Observer reported that Healey was “flabbergasted” by the lack of security around financial information when he became chancellor and “it was so different to how we did things in the MoD”.The chancellor is known to have been worried that market-sensitive leaks cost Britain billions in the run-up to the last government’s budgets. But has this time around been so different after all?Despite the heightened “security” around Wednesday’sbudget, many of its announcements have been leaked already from a clear mixture of authorised and unauthorised sources.It emerged well in advance that there will be ahigher tax on banks– a deeply market-sensitive policy – and apackage of energy supportfor the most vulnerable.View image in fullscreenIt has already emerged that the budget will include an energy support package for the most vulnerable.Photograph: Libby Welch/AlamyThere will also be billions of pounds in extra defence spending, directed towards the British Business Bank and National Wealth Fund, as well as a £1bn crackdown on online VAT sales, with big retailers such as Amazon, eBay and Temu to be responsible for collecting what is due from smaller merchants selling on their platforms.On top of that, there have been stories indicating the level of headroom the chancellor will be looking at – in the region of £15bn – known in the political trade as “pitch rolling” to avoid alarming the markets or the public.The Treasury and No 10 have also undertaken their traditional stream of embargoed announcements by press release in the days before the fiscal event, such as a new£1.5bn borrowing facility for local authoritiesand £1bn for social housing, as they seek to build a sense of action and momentum about what the government is trying to achieve.Former Treasury advisers believe the rigamarole around budget security is partly designed to deter civil servants and gossiping MPs from thinking they can embark on unauthorised chatter before a policy is ready.View image in fullscreenFormer Treasury advisers think the rigamarole is partly designed to deter Westminster gossips.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianBut they also say it is unhelpful for the chancellor to produce a hermetically sealed budget, which could cause a backlash over surprise measures – in the markets, the media, among the government’s own MPs and the wider public.It is often the less-trailed policies that have tended to go wrong, from George Osborne’s pasty tax in 2012 to Philip Hammond’s surprise national insurance hike for the self-employed in 2017 that had to be abandoned within seven days after a furore among Conservative MPs about breaking their manifesto promise.Aides say there is a balance to be struck – and it’s not always a good idea to hoard information until budget day. “If everything is kept tight, then you end up surprising people. And that’s called a Liz Truss situation,” says one former strategist from the Tory years.View image in fullscreenLiz Truss resigned as prime minister in 2022 after her government’s mini-budget crashed the markets.Photograph: Alberto Pezzali/APHealey has been shutting down speculation about various tax rises, from higher capital gains tax on certain assets to lowering the mansion tax on properties worth more than £1.5m – showing he has begun to see the virtue in expectation management and limiting surprises on the big day.There may still be a few fiscal “rabbits out of the hat” on the day, as Healey seeks to combine a “steady-as-she-goes” budget with some eye-catching measures designed to show the public that the government is on their side.But if the Treasury really has aimed for military levels of secrecy around its budget, theMinistry of Defencemight have something to worry about.Explore more on these topicsBudget 2026John HealeyTax and spendingBanks and building societiesEnergy billsDefence policyMinistry of DefenceanalysisShareReuse this content

title: How cocaine conquered the UK: in pubs, festivals and workplaces the drug has become an everyday habit  | Drugs | The Guardian
description: Previously considered a middle-class drug, price drops have made cocaine more widely available, and created a new set of problems
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: Previously considered a middle-class drug, price drops have made cocaine more widely available, and created a new set of problems
Content: COCAINE PARTIES copyComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCOCAINE PARTIES copyComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesDrugsHow cocaine conquered the UK: in pubs, festivals and workplaces the drug has become an everyday habitPreviously considered a middle-class drug, price drops have made cocaine more widely available, and created a new set of problemsCocaine-linked crimes on the rise in Britain as consumption surgesAgeing users and record deaths – the data behind Britain’s £9.8bn-a-year cocaine habitRobyn VinterSun 25 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 10.35 EDTShareLisa* is watching Scissor Sisters at a festival in the Lake District, a can of cider in hand, dancing along to the music on a sunny afternoon.The 30-year-old has a few days off from her job as a veterinary nurse in Gateshead, where she lives with her fiance. She loves going to festivals, especially as “I love meeting new people,” she says.She is confident and makes friends at the festival very easily. The reason for that? “I’m on a bit of coke,” she says.It is a crime largely hidden in plain sight – and one many people would barely consider a crime. However, it could land her a maximum sentence of seven years in prison, though for a first offence it is more likely to be a police caution. But she’s unlikely to be caught, especially at a festival, where over the course of the weekend numerous people admit to the Guardian to taking cocaine – or trying to get hold of it – and are seen openly taking it.By many estimates, use of the class A drug is soaring. Wastewater analysis suggests people in England consumed 123,000kg of cocaine in 2024-25, a rise of 26% since 2021. That’s equivalent to roughly 2.5bn lines of cocaine, at an estimated street value of almost £10bn.Cocaine and crimeCocaine is a powerful and addictive stimulant that causes euphoria, overconfidence, restlessness and paranoia. A Guardian investigation has found a 10% rise in recorded crimes where the drug was mentioned since 2019.Research from wastewater samples in 2022 carried out by Imperial College London and released earlier this year found that cocaine use spiked during major sporting and music events, heatwaves and bank holidays.View image in fullscreenA Guardian investigation has found a 10% rise in recorded crimes where the drug was mentioned since 2019.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesIts reputation as a middle-class drug still stands, though it has become more available across different demographics, as prices have dropped year-on-year and reached “historically low levels” last year. That wider use brings wider problems.Cocaine was thought to have been a major factor in the 2021 widespread disorder at Wembley stadium during the Euro 2020 final, when thousands of ticketless fans breached safety barriers to get access to the ground. Lady Casey’s independent review later that year found that “excessive consumption of alcohol and cocaine” were fuels of a “febrile atmosphere”.More than half of fans who responded to a survey in the aftermath of the incident said they had seen open drug use at Wembley stadium or on the way from the station.“People were taking cocaine in front of us [and] my sons cried for most of the game,” one person quoted in the report said. A safety official was quoted as saying: “Drug usage was noticeable. It took four or five stewards to try and hold someone down – more than the number it usually takes when fans are drunk.”It has also become a drug of choice for the far right.Cocaine was a factor in the 2024 summer riots when some of the perpetrators of violence were found to be in possession of it or have taken it before the riots erupted. Two rioters also later pleaded guilty to selling it. Open cocaine use was also seen at the Unite the Kingdom rally, a far-right anti-immigration protest in London last year.The party drugBut cocaine was – and still is – a party drug, popular at nightclubs, student house parties, middle-class dinner parties and now in the pub.At a West Ham pub in east London, a pub manager explains she cleans cocaine residue off surfaces in the toilets most mornings. It is a pub for people who live and work in the area and for West Ham fans who are regulars on match days.“It is just staggering the amount and the accessibility of it,” she says.“It seems to be so blended with the concept of a night or even a day out for a lot of people ... It has been very normalised [and it’s] just a thing that you can quite blatantly and overtly do.”She says the ubiquity of cocaine has become “significantly worse” over the past five years.While other drugs are more obvious – they have a strong smell or leave their users visibly intoxicated or even incapacitated – cocaine can be harder to spot, which is a problem for publicans.There can be telltale signs though, she says, such as when a punter appears to be getting agitated, leaves the pub and then comes back some time later, going straight to the toilets. “I’ve had real idiots, and they’ve been very blatant, and it’s been easy to kick them out.”The manager believes people often take cocaine in an effort to “sober up” so they can continue drinking, “which obviously does not actually work but a lot of people believe it does”.“Now you’ve got the impaired judgment from alcohol but you’ve also got the alertness from cocaine. That for me is a really big problem because that’s when you get potentially very volatile behaviour. That’s probably the point that I would call the most dangerous, both in terms of people behaving erratically, but also because they don’t realise how drunk they are. They are – at that point – a danger to themselves in terms of me having to call an ambulance or something.”View image in fullscreenCocaine was – and still is – a party drug, popular at nightclubs, student house parties, middle-class dinner parties and now in the pub.Photograph: Everynight Images/AlamyCocaine use becomes particularly obvious when punters get into fights. “I had a 60-something-year-old man beat up a 70-something-year-old man in the toilet, knock his teeth out, because he said that the other guy had allegedly called him a cunt,” she says. “Now I understand that there are egos involved and that people can be volatile – and there’s all kinds of silly petty rivalries going back decades amongst some of the customers – but you’re not telling me that’s a normal reaction.”She says she has spent years working in hospitality, managing different venues, and she thinks the problems that come from cocaine use can be seen in both cheap chains and expensive country gastropubs.“But technically none of us can talk about it because none of us can admit that drug-taking takes place on our premises,” she says. “Everyone’s scared of losing their licence.”Coping mechanismWhat wastewater analysis cannot reveal is whether more people are taking cocaine, or more is being taken by those who are habitual users, or both.For some people, cocaine is simply a part of life, something taken every day, even while at work.The first time Will* took cocaine was at about the age of 15. “I remember it being stimulating, like I felt kind of chatty. I felt a lot of my social anxiety-based inhibitions fade away and, in the space of that, I was really confident and felt kind of unstoppable, in a sense.”Things quickly escalated to him dealing the drug. “I was a 16-year-old with like half a fucking kilo of cocaine in my bedroom.”He began selling to friends and friends of friends, though he admits he was an “atypical” dealer. He was from a relatively wealthy family in Essex, surrounded by teenagers with a lot of disposable income.“That would pay for my usage of it,” he says, earning as much as £7,000 in a weekend.“But then over the last like 20 years, it has developed much more into a coping mechanism,” the 37-year-old says.A carpenter in TV and film, he has used it to help with long hours, being the first on set and the last to leave. It is so common among his colleagues that he says parts of the industry “basically run themselves on cocaine”.He has “successfully hidden it from professional relationships so easily” and says people he interacted with at work would have no idea he was taking coke in the workplace.“It can really seem like a good idea but it ultimately isn’t. [It’s fine] until you realise that you’ve built the physical dependency and then you go a day without it and you’re like dragging yourself through mud.”At one point he counted up and realised he had spent £35,000 in one year on cocaine. He says: “I was like, oh my god, that’s a lot of money.”He has managed to cut down on his use substantially, from “spending thousands of pounds a week doing cocaine every single day to someone who’s spending maybe £120 to £180 a weekend”. But even still, he thinks he will probably never stop taking it.“I’m trying to be in control of it as opposed to being fully sober, because I don’t really see myself as someone who is ever gonna be fully sober.”*Lisa’s name has been changed. Will spoke to the Guardian on the condition of anonymity. His name has also been changed.Explore more on these topicsDrugsShare

title: This is how we do it: ‘Our fertility doctor told us we were having too much sex’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Ines and Ross shared a high sex drive, but things calmed down a bit after their daughter was born
Author: Olivia Ladanyi
Headline: Ines and Ross shared a high sex drive, but things calmed down a bit after their daughter was born
Content: Illustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Ryan Gillett/The GuardianThis is how we do itLife and styleThis is how we do it: ‘Our fertility doctor told us we were having too much sex’Ines and Ross shared a high sex drive, but things calmed down a bit after their daughter was bornHow do you do it? Share the story of your sex life, anonymouslyAs told toOlivia LadanyiSun 25 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleInes, 40double quotation markOur desire hasn’t diminished, but I’m content with a cuddly, loving shag these daysRoss and I had been dating for four months when I asked if he wanted children. I’d memorised a script, but I was so anxious I was visibly shaking as I asked him. It felt so vulnerable, and what if he said no? I’d have to end the relationship.That year, I went through three rounds of egg freezing after being told myanti-Müllerian hormonelevels were so low I might never be able to have a baby. I met Ross just before starting the first round, but I didn’t tell him because I didn’t want to scare him off. It also played on my mind that Ross was 28 and I was 36.double quotation markI’d never been with anyone who had as high a sex drive as me beforeAfter Ross reassured me he did want children, he hugged me and said: “This is inappropriate, but I have a boner.” He called it a romance boner.Two months later, he referred to “our kids” in conversation.Six months after that, we decided to start trying. The fertility doctor told us we were having too much sex. Apparently having sex every other day gives the sperm time to properly develop, but we’d been doing it four or five times a day: once before work, when we got home from work, before dinner and again before bed. I’d never been with anyone whose sex drive was as high as mine.After we miscarried our first child, sex became less about experimentation and more about comfort. And now we have a 10-month-old daughter, we just don’t have the energy to do it like we used to. Rather than four times a day, we have sex four times a week, and it’s more vanilla. But our desire hasn’t diminished, and I’m content with a cuddly, loving shag these days. We still hold hands and touch feet while we sleep.Although there are some days when we joke that we’re more like workmates now we’re a team getting things done, we’re just as close as we always have been – it’s just a different kind of closeness.Seeing how wonderful he is with our daughter has made me love him even more. I say to her: “I picked your dad wisely.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionShare your experienceIf you’re keen to talk to us about your sex lives you can get in touch by filling in the form below. It is very important that both sexual partners are happy to participate.Please share your story if you are 18 or over, anonymously if you wish. For more information please see ourterms of serviceandprivacy policy.Tell us hereYour responses, which can be anonymous, are secure as the form is encrypted and only the Guardian has access to your contributions. We will only use the data you provide us for the purpose of the feature and we will delete any personal data when we no longer require it for this purpose. For alternative ways to get in touch securely please see ourtips guide.First name of partner oneFirst name of partner twoLength of relationshipContact number or email address of partner onePlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Contact number or email address of partner twoPlease include your country's area code if outside of the UK.Do both parties agree to being contacted by a journalist from the Guardian?YesBy submitting your response, you are agreeing to share your details with us for this feature.SubmitShow moreRoss, 31double quotation markIt became a game to make Ines orgasm as many times as possible – I get a lot of pleasure from her pleasureOn our first date, Ines made a joke about being older, but it wasn’t an issue for me. We were just two people who were very compatible and had a lot of common interests. But the age gap probably sped up the process of having a child. When Ines told me she had frozen her eggs and I was welcome to leave if that wasn’t what I wanted, I gave her a big hug and said I’d love to stay.On our second date, I baked Ines a red velvet cake and she opened the door in a bathrobe. The sex was amazing – the best I’d ever had. I came more than 10 times that night. It became a game to make Ines orgasm as many times as possible – I get a lot of pleasure from her pleasure. Although her drive was higher than mine at the start, mine increased to match hers because the sex was so good.double quotation markWe’re often too tired and it feels too weird to have sex with the baby in the room, so we have to be more sneakyThis is how we do it: ‘My mistress has complete control over me and makes me so happy’Read moreAlthough we were too sad to have sex after the miscarriage, we were still very open to each other. We got married soon after, which was a helpful distraction, and slowly our sex life returned to normal. When we first had sex after our daughter was born, we took it slowly because I was afraid of hurting Ines. Now we’re parents, we don’t have time for two-hour oral sex. It has gone from a marathon to a sprint, but it’s always very intimate. We’re often too tired, and it feels too weird to have sex with the baby in the room, so we have to be more sneaky, making the most of the time when she’s asleep.I stopped initiating sex to take the pressure off Ines; so she doesn’t feel as if she’s letting me down by not wanting sex. Looking after our daughter is our priority. Although we love sex, we don’t owe it to each other. I’ve made it clear that, despite letting Ines take the lead, I still desire her. There’s intimacy outside sex too – dancing in the kitchen to our wedding song, or taking the baby out when one of us needs a rest.Names have been changedExplore more on these topicsLife and styleThis is how we do itSexRelationshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A Course Called Ireland review – why did Bill Murray ever agree to this Irish golf show? | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: The Hollywood star is so grumpy in this new travelogue it’s like he wishes he wasn’t there. Think sulky car journeys, strained encounters and the sense of a TV series imploding
Author: Sarah Dempster
Headline: The Hollywood star is so grumpy in this new travelogue it’s like he wishes he wasn’t there. Think sulky car journeys, strained encounters and the sense of a TV series imploding
Content: Largely uncommunicative … Bill Murray in A Course Called Ireland.Photograph: BBC/Stellify MediaView image in fullscreenLargely uncommunicative … Bill Murray in A Course Called Ireland.Photograph: BBC/Stellify MediaTV reviewTelevision & radioReviewA Course Called Ireland review – why did Bill Murray ever agree to this Irish golf show?The Hollywood star is so grumpy in this new travelogue it’s like he wishes he wasn’t there. Think sulky car journeys, strained encounters and the sense of a TV series implodingSarah DempsterSun 25 Oct 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 18.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleACourse Called Ireland is a new documentary in whichBill Murraygolfs his way around the “Emerald Isle” while reflecting on everything from his great-grandmother to worms. The heart leaps. Bill Murray? The same Bill Murray whose genius for wounded obnoxiousness was so beautifully deployed in Groundhog Day and Lost in Translation? Yes, the same Bill Murray.A montage of coming attractions does little to dampen the ardour. Here is the 76-year-old actor teeing off amid the gasp-inducing greenery of County Kerry. Here he is squinting at the “hardworking Irish worms” that stripe the fairways of coastal Cork. And here he is saying “hah-hah” in a variety of other golf-adjacent locations while surrounded by locals whose body language suggests that they, too, are in the process of saying, or at least thinking, “hah-hah”. We ready our jaws for the cavalcade of bittersweet guffaws that will inevitably follow.But what’s this? A shadow has fallen across the opening moments of episode one and from a darkened doorway steps a pensioner in a quilted raincoat. This is Margaret, a small Irishwoman who bumps into Murray (“You were in the Ghostbusters!”) during his visit to the harbour town of Cobh and, for reasons that presumably involved the phrases “local colour” and “cheaper than hiring a professional”, is subsequently employed to narrate the first episode. Can Margaret’s chuckling befuddlement compensate for her inexperience? No, she’s terrible. Still, she is here now so we may as well let her get on with it. “This series is not about golf,” she shouts over footage of a golf course. “And it’s not really about Bill Murray,” she adds over footage of Murray.Whatisit about, Margaret? It’s “about the Irish”, she says, uncertainly. “Sort of.” And it is about the Irish. Sort of. But it’s not what the series isreallyabout. A Course Called Ireland is really about what happens when a TV production implodes like a machine-gunned meringue because it has hired a celebrity who doesn’t want to do what he has been hired to do. It is also about what happens when producers, sensing calamity, allow said celebrity’s seeming waywardness to dictate the tone of the production, then get frustrated with the results and overcompensate with an effortful “quirkiness” and a soundtrack of theme-pub fiddles so hysterical it appears for ever on the brink of Riverdancing itself off the nearest cliff.The awfulness begins in County Cork, with a largely uncommunicative Murray driving around various golf courses and pubs with his friend – and author of the book on which this six-part travelogue is based – Tom Coyne. Murray doesn’t want to do what the producers want him to do. This includes discussing the history of Irish storytelling (“It’s not the fucking Bill Murray show”) and walking up a staircase (“No”). I assume these huffs have been left in the edit as an explanation/excuse for the subsequent arse-over-tittery. “Look what we’ve had to put up with!” is the subtext, a cry for help that would be more stirring had anyone from the production company bothered to type the words “Bill Murray reputation for prickliness” into Google before they signed him. But no. And so we must endure innumerable near-silent car journeys, golf-course longueurs, strained encounters with local eccentrics and Margaret’s increasingly desperate efforts to pretend everything’s tickety-boo (“just try to enjoy yourselves!”), all of which is punctuated by the eyerolls of a man who gives the impression of wishing to be anywhere else.There are brief flickers of respite. Murray is thoughtful re his Irish heritage (his great-grandmother moved from Ireland to Chicago in the 1850s) and charmingly droll with well-wishers. But then the producer asks for his thoughts on, say, Irish poetry, and the bowtie stops spinning and the shutters come down at the chuckle factory.Why did Murray agree to it, I wonder? The Guinness? The worms? I fear the answer – along with the point of this extraordinarily irritating series – may have been “lost in translation”.A Course Called Ireland is on iPlayer nowExplore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV reviewBill MurrayreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Stephen Fry: ‘Sherlock Holmes altered the course of my whole life’ | Arthur Conan Doyle | The Guardian
description: Nearly a hundred years after Arthur Conan Doyle’s last Sherlock Holmes story, the writer and broadcaster unravels the mystery of the detective’s enduring appeal
Author: Stephen Fry
Headline: Nearly a hundred years after Arthur Conan Doyle’s last Sherlock Holmes story, the writer and broadcaster unravels the mystery of the detective’s enduring appeal
Content: Stephen Fry in Sherlock Holmes: A Game of Shadows.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyView image in fullscreenStephen Fry in Sherlock Holmes: A Game of Shadows.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyArthur Conan DoyleStephen Fry: ‘Sherlock Holmes altered the course of my whole life’Nearly a hundred years after Arthur Conan Doyle’s last Sherlock Holmes story, the writer and broadcaster unravels the mystery of the detective’s enduring appealStephen FrySun 25 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 14.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has become quite the fashion for contemporary writers to have a go at reinventing past classics. We’ve seen it done with imperishable literary heroes like Bond, Jeeves, Poirot and Winnie-the-Pooh. This is a relatively new phenomenon. But not in the case ofSherlock Holmes, where the practice is almost as old as the man himself.Sherlock Holmes was the conception ofArthur Conan Doyle, a Scottish doctor down on his luck who had turned his hand to fiction to make up for a worrying lack of success in attracting patients to his surgery. Conan Doyle could never have guessed that the first Sherlock Holmes story he wrote, A Study in Scarlet, published in the 1887 issue of Beeton’s Christmas Annual, would in a few years propel him and the characters he created to literary fame. The personalities and characteristics of Holmes and Watson became as familiar to late Victorians as their own friends and families. The readership was worldwide and spread across all ages and classes.Conan Doyle himself – frustrated by the burdensome discomfort of what he felt had become something of a millstone around his neck – killed off his creation by having Holmes apparently plummet to his death in Switzerland’s Reichenbach Falls, pulling his arch-enemy Moriarty down with him into the roaring cataract. The public outcry was swift and over­whelming. Grown men and women wept openly, black armbands were adopted, and a host of angry readers wrote abusive letters to Conan Doyle’s publishers, to the Strand magazine and to Conan Doyle himself. He grudgingly bowed to public pressure and unearthed a story set before Holmes’s plunge into the abyss – The Hound of the Baskervilles. But only after the clamour still refused to subside did he at last bring his hero back to life in The Return ofSherlockHolmes, presaging a new stream of short stories and a full-length novel, The Valley of Fear. He was to continue writing Sherlock Holmes adventures right up until 1927, although he never set a story later than the eve of the first world war.During his lifetime, stage productions (he collaborated on the first himself) and silent films were produced, and after his death in 1930 the great post-Conan Doyle Holmesian caravan began to rumble into full life.View image in fullscreenJeremy Brett as the famed detective in the ITV series Sherlock Holmes.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyNow, you should know that the Sherlock Holmes body of work written by Arthur Conan Doyle himself is called by Sherlockians “the Canon” (coincidentally and happily an anagram of Conan). The Canon comprises four full-length novels and five collections of short stories.In all, 60 canonical stories. How many have been written since? I don’t believe it is possible to count. I know I have written one myself. Conan Doyle’s son Adrian Conan Doyle, along with the great Golden Age mystery writer John Dickson Carr, wrote a collection of new stories under the title The Exploits of Sherlock Holmes. After that, the stampede was on, in all media, of course. The Hollywood films starring Basil Rathbone as Holmes and Nigel Bruce as Watson began in 1939 with the canonical The Hound of the Baskervilles, but soon began to move the pair into all kinds of modern settings. By the 1940s, they were doing their bit for the homeland by pitting themselves against the Nazis. The Conan Doyle Estate was open to allowing and authorising such variations, which soon became an established and legitimised part of the whole Sherlock Holmes enterprise. Between 2014 and 2023 Holmes emerged from copyright and entered the public domain.Most Sherlockians I have come across will, like me, cite Jeremy Brett as their favourite Holmes, but one feels there will always be a new kind of Sherlock for every age. I had the honour of playing Sherlock’s brother Mycroft in Guy Ritchie’s Sherlock Holmes: A Game of Shadows, with Robert Downey Jr and Jude Law as Holmes and Watson, and the pleasure of reading the entire Canon for Audible. Along with the publication of my own Holmes pastiche, these were the completion of some kind of a lifelong dream. The closing of a very strange circle.I can say without the slightest fear of exaggeration that Sherlock Holmes altered and determined the whole course of my life. Let me explain.I had been entranced by the Sherlock Holmes stories from the earliest age. I read and reread the entire corpus of stories avidly and before long I had joined, as their youngest member to date, the august Sherlock Holmes Society of London. This eccentrically aristocratic institution had Lord Gore-Booth as chair and the Marquess of Donegal as editor of its magazine, the Sherlock Holmes Journal. I managed to get permission from my housemaster to leave school one weekend, travel by train to London and attend a society meeting, at which I was scheduled to read a paper. The subject of my disquisition? Well, I had noticed with excitement one day the parallels between Sherlock Holmes’s description of Professor James Moriarty (“He is extremely tall and thin, his forehead domes out in a white curve, and his two eyes are deeply sunken in his head”) and TS Eliot’s description of Macavity the Mystery Cat (“his eyes are sunken in. His brow is deeply lined with thought, his head is highly domed”). The society was being very kind in letting me address them on this topic: any fool could see that Eliot had based his Macavity entirely on Moriarty, it was hardly news. I thought I had discovered a great literary secret. At any rate, the event went well, but the sequel did not.double quotation markHe was surely the first caped crusader, for all that his cape was constructed of good tweedI stayed in London, sitting in cinemas from dawn till midnight and watching any number of films. By the time I came to and hopped on a train back to school, a full three days later than had been agreed and sanctioned, I found that I had been officially declared missing. My parents and the police were informed, and the hunt was on. The fat was truly in the fire, my number finally up. The school expelled me. That expulsion led to other expulsions and disasters, which culminated in my landing in prison; I shan’t go into too much detail: Moab Is My Washpot, the first volume of my autobiography, is also happily still in print, and the full story can be read there.View image in fullscreenA poster for the 1939 film of The Hound of the Baskervilles, starring Basil Rathbone and Nigel Bruce.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyAnyway, all these ructions finally got me thinking straight and determining to change my ways and try for Cambridge, the university on which I had always set my heart. I did get there, where I met my friend Hugh Laurie and found myself set on the course of writing and performing which has filled my life ever since. None of which could have happened without that Sherlock Holmes Society evening and its cascade of consequences back in the early 70s.But I still haven’t quite addressed the most pertinent question.Why? Why do these characters – Holmes, Watson, Mrs Hudson and Mycroft (along with that hapless cast of professional bunglers, sceptics and sincere admirers from Scotland Yard) – seem to attract reinvention and retelling so much more than any other fictional creations? And why the Game? How did that arise? The Game, I should explain, is what Sherlockians call the tradition of Holmesian scholarship that makes the very serious and straight-faced assumption that Holmes and Watson were real and that they actually did live at 221B Baker Street and that everything Watson writes about (although he makes plenty of mistakes in consistency and continuity) truly did historically happen.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMartin Freeman as Doctor John Watson, left, with Benedict Cumberbatch in the eponymous role of BBC TV’s Sherlock.Photograph: Robert Viglasky/BBC/HartswoodBut I repeat:why? This doesn’t happen with Poirot, Father Brown or Lord Peter Wimsey. What’s so special about the denizens of Baker Street?Well, one can begin by making the surely undeniable statement that Sherlock Holmes is one of the most fully realised and enduring fictional characters ever created. Very quickly, his complex and rounded personality, the details of his intellect, his manners, his dress, his habits, his appetites, techniques and methods combined to create a place for him in the public consciousness of a kind that had never before been experienced in literature.Holmes’s world is also vivid and tangible. Everyone who has read even a handful of stories will have their own clear picture of the Baker Street rooms, the fireplace, the test tubes, the violin case, the pipe rack, the fog at the window … we all have our images, reaffirmed or modified by countless films and television adaptations certainly, but unmistakably real. So real, indeed, that even as the stories were still being written and published, tens of thousands around the world behaved as if Holmes and Watson truly lived and breathed. From as far as Japan and South America came letters addressed to 221B Baker Street begging for Holmes’s assistance. Some even wrote to Buckingham Palace and Downing Street to urge the king and prime minister to award Sherlock Holmes a knighthood.But there is, I think, another reason for the astonishing connection that Holmes made with the public on his arrival and that he continues to make in all the multiplicity of his incarnations today. And that is need. The world needed him in 1887 and the world needs him now.View image in fullscreenDónal Finn as Moriarty (left) and Hero Fiennes Tiffin as Holmes in Young Sherlock.Photograph: Daniel Smith/PrimeWith the great rise in literacy from the middle of the 19th century onwards, it perhaps seems inevitable that a new kind of fiction should arise that tried to solve the puzzle of the lately arrived Big City – most especially the biggest by far in the world, London. The daunting size of the metropolis was something quite new in human history. Society was transforming itself from a knowable hierarchy into a bewildering network. It could be seen structurally as like a great web, interlinked and complex, mastered only by those sensitive enough to understand, touch, feel and identify every node and every twitch on the filament. In fact, by a Sherlock Holmes.And after Holmes, of course, ten thousand more detectives sprang up, all with their own USPs, their own special ways of clearing up mystery and caging the monsters. But so, too, did a strange breed of 20th-century heroes who offered a similar promise of bringing light and order to the darkness and chaos of modernity, but in their case without bothering to think much. I mean, of course, the comic book and film superheroes. Our infantile side (and there was never an age in our history that so encouraged and coddled our inner child as the present) seems to have embraced magic, flying, invisibility, X-ray vision and all kinds of impossible superpowers. It seems to me fair to suggest that Superman and Batman, unlikely as it may seem, follow in the great detective’s footsteps and owe him their being. He was surely the first caped crusader, for all that his cape was constructed of good tweed. They, like him, answered a need.‘If you try to fix Holmes, you’ll get your arse handed to you’: do we really need another Sherlock remake?Read moreWhy so many have moved from valuing the real and achievable powers that Holmes exhibits – achieved through his own self-training, study and practice – to valuing imaginary, unearned, randomly achieved magical superpowers is another question. But fortunately the appetite for Holmes and real deductive talent is undiminished, too. We can have both kinds of hero, after all. On television alone, for every Superman and Deadpool, there has always been – as well as a new Sherlock for each new generation – a Columbo, a Monk or a Ludwig reaffirming the power of the Sherlockian method and re‑establishing the primacy of mind over mayhem. Holmes’s cigar ash, footprints and almost invisible telltale particles are the forerunners of the crime lab’s mitochondrial DNA, epithelial particles and microfibres, and his magnifying glass gives way to today’s scanning electron microscope. But the principles are quite unchanged. Which is why he is the presiding spirit behind every CSI operative and why the modern Scotland Yard criminal database (the Home Office Large Major Enquiry System) has initials that spell out the name HOLMES.Like London and the wider human world, the world of Holmes and Watson is a work in progress, capable of being modernised and made over in countless ways, but always, underneath it all, entirely its noble and magnificent self.Sherlock, a collection of new stories with an introduction by Stephen Fry, is published by Simon & Schuster.
