title: Adultery review – a risible tale of middle-aged car sex, rat poo and rickety furniture | Television | The Guardian
description: Romola Garai and Dominic Cooper are far too good for this by-the-numbers tale of two people having an affair. It is a clattering bag of cliches
Author: Lucy Mangan
Headline: Romola Garai and Dominic Cooper are far too good for this by-the-numbers tale of two people having an affair. It is a clattering bag of cliches
Content: Giving it everything … Shelley Conn and Romola Garai in Adultery on ITVX.Photograph: Ben Blackall/ITVView image in fullscreenGiving it everything … Shelley Conn and Romola Garai in Adultery on ITVX.Photograph: Ben Blackall/ITVTV reviewTelevisionReviewAdultery review – a risible tale of middle-aged car sex, rat poo and rickety furnitureRomola Garai and Dominic Cooper are far too good for this by-the-numbers tale of two people having an affair. It is a clattering bag of clichesLucy ManganSun 25 Oct 2026 18.05 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 18.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHere are a few valuable life lessons to be gathered from the new six-part series Adultery, which is about adultery.One, don’t bother.Two, if you do bother, don’t do it with the father of your son’s girlfriend or the mother of your daughter’s boyfriend.Three, if you do mess around with the father of your son’s girlfriend or the mother of your daughter’s boyfriend, make sure nobody’s got anyone saved in their phone under the moniker “Dickhead Dave”. Because he is not going to help matters.But Beth (Romola Garai, far too good for this by-the-numbers effort from Danny Brocklehurst) is a bored, beleaguered fortysomething mother of two who has recently lost the personal-trainer business she was passionate about. She is also mourning the loss of her best friend whose husband is facing an assault charge. And Tom (Dominic Cooper, ditto) is a fortysomething father and GP, married to charity fundraiser Hannah (Shelley Conn) who has been struggling with her mental health for a bit. So when Beth comes along, he is helpless before her. They look at each other like two equally stunned halibut, first in a hospital waiting room (they meet when she knocks him off his bike and injures his wrist, the one he uses for foreshadowing), then across a garden party at Tom’s posh home (where Beth – who I should mention is Lancastrian so, you know, darling – trails her fingers reverentially across books! About art! On a shelf! And dreams of a life of getting banged on higher thread counts), and then in his GP surgery before Beth launches herself at him and gets the party started.Soon they are having sex in cars until Beth remembers her dead best friend kindly left her a house in her will and they could probably prang more comfortably there. Which they do, until disaster strikes! No, that one’s been averted. I hope there isn’t another one coming down the … Oh! This one’s worse. Dave. Such a dickhead.They have to drive to Tom’s cottage in the Lake District instead. “I’m going to scatter my dead friend’s ashes!” Beth tells her family. “I’m going to clear out the rat poo,” Tom tells Hannah. But the urn and bleach go equally unemptied as the pair opt to go at it on a dangerously rickety hall table instead. I’m not sure if it’s a neighbour we see disappearing behind a fence at one point or a crew member hiding from the increasing embarrassment of seeing people boggle at a bookshelf because they’ve got Northern accents and deliver lines like “Do you ever worry that our best days are behind us?” and “Depression’s for the middle classes, isn’t it?”Meanwhile, the kids are having a much better time, mainly because they still think sex is a novelty and aren’t trying to have it with anyone but each other. Their idea of a thrill is to bunk off school and go to Blackpool for the day. While their adulterous parents get it on in the surgery for the first time, Ollie and Jess are riding the rollercoaster. Diagnosis: metaphor. As the sun sets, Jess celebrates their perfect day: “I don’t want things to ever change!” “They won’t,” Ollie assures her. Prognosis: terminal.‘I’ve hit my midlife sexpot era!’ Romola Garai on marital misery, cheating … and sex scenes in carsRead moreAdultery, in short, is a clattering bag of cliches delivered by ciphers, despite a host of good actors giving it everything they can. Everywhere you look there are unconvincing people doing unconvincing things. Yes, you think, Dave may well be a dickhead, but would he really take one look at his ex-wife lying in her coffin in the chapel of rest and say “I’ve been inside that body” to Beth? No. Or, if you were about to swim in an isolated lake in the Lake District on a dirty weekend away, would you do it in a swimming costume and trunks? No. Or, if you were a doctor who’d injured your wrist would you not be able to fashion a sling that actually supports it? Yes. Or, would a neurotic like Hannah, who demands a four-way action plan be forged among the parents when Jess is told off for imitating Ollie by cheeking a teacher, really be unbothered about finding out they take edibles together? No.It all adds up to people it is impossible to believe in or care about. The plot is slight. The attempts at class commentary or the problems of mating in middle-aged captivity are like iron rivets being sledgehammered into a balsa wood miniature. There are great central performances, especially from Garai and Conn, and occasional glimpses of what might have been. But like sex on a rickety table in a rat-shat cottage, Adultery remains hardly worth the effort.Adultery is on ITVX now.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewRomola GaraiDominic CooperreviewsShareReuse this content

title: Is having urine the color of Mountain Dew normal? | Well actually | The Guardian
description: A Trump administration doctor says neon yellow urine is normal because of diets consisting entirely of meat and fermented foods. Here’s what experts say
Author: Keren Landman
Headline: A Trump administration doctor says neon yellow urine is normal because of diets consisting entirely of meat and fermented foods. Here’s what experts say
Content: You may have seen charts that indicate what color and shade urine ‘should’ be, but ‘considered imprecise’. Experts don’t rely on them for serious purposes such as managing kidney diseasePhotograph: Anna Efetova/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenYou may have seen charts that indicate what color and shade urine ‘should’ be, but ‘considered imprecise’. Experts don’t rely on them for serious purposes such as managing kidney diseasePhotograph: Anna Efetova/Getty ImagesCall the doctorWell actuallyIs having urine the color of Mountain Dew normal?A Trump administration doctor says neon yellow urine is normal because of diets consisting entirely of meat and fermented foods. Here’s what experts sayKeren LandmanSun 25 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 12.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdoctor who advises several Trump cabinet members on their dietsrhapsodizedthis summerabout having urine the color of Mountain Dew, thanks to a diet consisting entirely of meat and fermented foods.What you consume does determine what you see in the toilet. But should urine be neon yellow – or some other hue? Here’s what you need to know.What color should urine be?Urine is normally a shade of yellow owing to a pigment called urobilin, which your gut bacteria produce. The more diluted it is by extra fluid intake, the lighter its shade – so urine is typically darker in the morning or when you’re dehydrated.Are you taking supplements correctly? Here’s a guide on their dosage limitsRead moreYou may have seen charts that indicate what color and shade urine “should” be, but “they are considered imprecise” and experts don’t rely on them for serious purposes such as managing kidney disease, says Suzanne Watnick, a nephrologist at the University of Washington. Urine’s darkness or lightness loosely corresponds with hydration status, but for most people, it’s best to rely on your sense of thirst rather than what’s in the toilet to determine when to drink water.That said, in people who need to stay highly hydrated, urine shade can be a helpful hydration indicator. For example, people prone to kidney stones should aim for very pale urine, Watnick says.What factors can affect your urine’s appearance?Your kidneys constantly filter blood to removeexcess water and waste products, which trickle down to the bladder to get peed out as urine. These organs’ goal is to ensure your blood consistently has exactly the right balance of fluid, minerals, salts and acid.“Your kidneys are really smart,” says Sharon Moe, a nephrologist at Indiana University School of Medicine. As long as they’re healthy, you can’t really override their settings. For instance, if you consume more water-soluble nutrients than you need, anything “extra” ends up in the toilet. This includes the by-products your body makes when it breaks down food and medicines, as well as the majority of any vitamins and supplements you might be taking.Some of these compounds won’t visibly change urine – for instance, digesting a lot of beef is likely to turn urine more acidic but not change its color, says Watnick. But some canchange the colorof urine or make it exceptionally bright. B vitamins (like riboflavin) can turn it fluorescent yellow, rhubarb a reddish-brown, and beets a festive pink.Anything but the usual yellow – including Mountain-Dew-adjacent hues – may signal your body is consuming something it can’t use. “If you get super fluorescent or super red, you’re eating too much of something or taking too many supplements,” says Moe.What should you do if your urine changes unexpectedly?For most healthy people, urine color changes are rarely an emergency. Notable exceptions include people with kidney disease, or if the color change is accompanied by other concerning symptoms like new pain, a new rash or severe leg swelling. These types of changes might signify a medical problem – get it checked out.Otherwise, to troubleshoot a strange new urine hue, first stop any supplements you’re taking, says Moe. If it doesn’t go back to normal, cut out brightly colored foods next.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toWell ActuallyPractical advice, expert insights and answers to your questions about how to live a good lifeEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAdditionally, look over your medication list. If you recently started a new drug, ask your clinician whether it could cause urine color changes. But don’t stop taking any prescribed medicines before that conversation, as urinary changes are an expected and harmless side-effect of some drugs.What urine changes can signify health problems?If your urine is red or brown, you haven’t had any red flag symptoms, and the color persists after you’ve ruled out any recent dietary or medication changes, get checked out.Bleeding in the kidneys, the bladder or the urinary tract can also turn it red or brown, and your clinician can assess that with a simple urine test. (In people who menstruate, it can occasionally be challenging to determine where blood in the toilet is coming from. Talk to your clinician if you’re not sure.)Foamy urine can mean protein is leaking from your kidneys – a few bubbles aren’t worrying, but you should be concerned if you see anything that looks “like a beer head in the toilet”, says Moe.Odor, frequency and transparency are also important. A sweet or foul smell, peeing much more or less than usual, and cloudy urine are all reasons to get checked.Although urine changes can occasionally herald kidney problems, most kidney disease is invisible;37 million US adultshave chronic kidney disease, but only one in 10 of them is aware. Moe says the best prevention is keeping your blood pressure in a healthy range and eating lots of fruits and vegetables, with meat in moderation. “Thecarnivore dietis not a healthy diet,” she says.Explore more on these topicsWell actuallyCall the doctorDiets and dietingHealthNutritionTrump administrationfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lights out: the island that goes dark to save young seabirds – in pictures | Oceans | The Guardian
description: Every autumn, Corvo Island in the Azores turns off its public lighting for a few key days to help fledgling Cory’s shearwaters as they attempt to fly to the ocean guided by the stars
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Every autumn, Corvo Island in the Azores turns off its public lighting for a few key days to help fledgling Cory’s shearwaters as they attempt to fly to the ocean guided by the stars
Content: After three months in the nest, young Cory’s shearwaters on Corvo are ready to take wingEvery autumn, Corvo Island in the Azores turns off its public lighting for a few key days to help fledgling Cory’s shearwaters as they attempt to fly to the ocean guided by the starsByAndrea D ZanengaSupported byAbout this contentSun 25 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 08.10 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOnce a year, Corvo, the smallest and most northerly island of Portugal’s Azores archipelago, goes dark. Since 2019, the island’s 450 or so inhabitants have chosen toswitch off the lights every autumn for five nightsto tackle the disastrous effects of artificial light on Cory’s shearwaters, a seabird endemic to the Atlantic Ocean.It began in 1991 when the community noticed huge numbers of deaths among young shearwaters.The juveniles spend three months in their nests before attempting their first flight to the ocean, orienting themselves by the stars.View image in fullscreenA newborn Cory’s shearwater chickUnfortunately, many are fatally confused by the artificial glow of streetlights, and end up crashing into Vila do Corvo’s narrow streets.Local people began rescuing them at night, roaming through the village in the dark. This inspired other communities, and in 1995, the Azorean government launched the “SOSCagarro” [shearwaters] campaignto include the other eight islands.In subsequent years, the Portuguese Society for the Study ofBirds(SPEA) joined the project, helping it grow.View image in fullscreenAt nearly 2am, dedicated young volunteers remain engaged in their work, helping with the recovered birdsView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenLeonardo Xavier is one of the young volunteers who helps to capture the disoriented birds around the village, top left. Top right, the webbed foot of a Cory’s shearwater. Rui Pimentel, left, is Corvo’s forest ranger, and on the frontline of Cory’s shearwater conservation. Cats, right, are the main predators of Cory’s shearwater chicks. The SPEA team has installed ultrasonic devices around nests to deter attacksI discovered the initiative on my second trip to Corvo, in June 2024. I knew of the Cory’s shearwater because I had travelled to the Azores before and had the chance to observe them in the open sea.But it was not until I saw a campaign sticker in a shop on the island that I found out about the blackout. When it was explained to me, I decided to come back and document it.The bird that changed Ecuador: how a chance discovery of a rare species helped to save many moreRead moreTo me, the message of this story is that there is always hope, especially when we involve future generations and teach them to care about our planet and its beauty.Today, Corvo is still the only island that performs a full blackout of public illumination to help the birds find their way to the ocean without interference from artificial lights.View image in fullscreenA long exposure photograph of Vila do Corvo during the blackout, with only security lights on. People do not have to turn off their household lights, but many choose to do so. The island of Flores can be seen in the distanceView image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenTania Pipa, left, a marine biologist from SPEA, checks each artificial and natural Cory’s shearwater nest on the island. A native of São Miguel Island, the largest of the Azores, she travels to Corvo every year to check on the birds. ‘To me, the day I don’t hear Cory’s shearwaters in the Azores, it will certainly not be the Azores,’ she says. Right, a Cory’s shearwater in its artificial nestThe island sinks into darkness and the stars can be seen clearly; the birds begin their journeys, hoping to find their way to the ocean, while people walk through Vila do Corvo, the only village on the island, to find and rescue any fallen birds.Those rescued will be placed in cardboard boxes overnight to recover, and released the next day from a cliff close to the ocean, giving them a second chance to reach the water, their new home.The campaign says more than 30,000 Cory’s shearwater fledglings have beenrescued in the Azores since 2015– about 6,000 of them on Corvo alone.This collective effort is a powerful example of howreducing light pollution can restore ecological balance. It demonstrates that small changes can significantly affect biodiversity.How can an action like this inspire global reflection? This intentional blackout is not just an act of conservation but a step towards developing the ability to coexist with nature without disrupting its rhythms.View image in fullscreenThe night sky above Caldeirão, the volcanic crater that shapes the island of CorvoFind moreage of extinction coverage here, and follow the biodiversity reportersRebecca Ratcliffe,Phoebe WestonandPatrick Greenfieldin the Guardian app for more nature coverage.Explore more on these topicsThe age of extinctionOceansBirdsWildlifeAnimalsConservationPortugalfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Don’t call me ‘mumsy’ – the contempt behind that word makes me livid | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett | The Guardian
description: It means to be drab, homely or old-fashioned – ‘motherly’, essentially. Why can’t we have some respect for mothers, instead of deriding them, asks Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Headline: It means to be drab, homely or old-fashioned – ‘motherly’, essentially. Why can’t we have some respect for mothers, instead of deriding them, asks Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Content: ‘Mumsy’ is essentially saying mums can never be stylish again.Photograph: Juice Images/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Mumsy’ is essentially saying mums can never be stylish again.Photograph: Juice Images/AlamyOpinionParents and parentingDon’t call me ‘mumsy’ – the contempt behind that word makes me lividRhiannon Lucy CosslettIt means to be drab, homely or old-fashioned – ‘motherly’, essentially. Why can’t we have some respect for mothers, instead of deriding them?Sun 25 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 07.15 EDTShareArecentnewspaper headline– “Sorry Radley! These dated handbag brands will make you look mumsy – here’s where stylish A-listers and Royals are shopping instead” – reminded me of a word I despise: “mumsy”.My list of words that make me want to throw things is varied and long, but “mumsy” is near the top. The quality of being mumsy means to be drab, homely or old-fashioned, essentially “motherly”. Something about the casual misogynistic contempt it carries makes me livid. So livid I might even use “that voice”. You know. The scary mum voice that turns misbehaving children in supermarkets into stone.“Mumsy” crops up in fashion coverage, which in autumn is unduly focused on the new school-run “style rules”.Articlesabout how to look chic at theschool gateand short-form videos about “what the cool mums are wearing” add to this feeling that the last thing you, as a mother, would want to appear as is what you actually are: someone’s mum.Of course, it’s understandable, and totally normal, to not want to be entirely defined by your reproductive status. Few of us want our entire identities to be “mother”. I still remember the shock I felt when a health professional first referred to me as “Mum” instead of by my name. It can feel as though you have ceased to be a person in society’s eyes. Add to that the fact your body’s changed because you’ve made and birthed a whole human being, and that you are now responsible for that other human being’s every want and need, drastically limiting the time you have to attend to personal style and grooming, and it can feel hard to know who you are now.These conflicting feelings are never a reason to deride mothers in general, though, or to act like “I’m not a regular mom, I’m a cool mom”. There’s a reason Amy Poehler’scomic Mean Girls catchphrasehas proved so legendary. There’s something inherently ridiculous about working to deny something that you so irrevocably are and will always be. The harsh reality that dawns on you as you transition from not-mother to mother is that you are for ever changed. You can try to dress it up all you want, but the fact is that you’re someone’s mum now.View image in fullscreenAmy Poehler in Mean Girls (2015).New theories ofmatrescencetell us that this change is a lot more complicated than suddenly wearing really naff jeans, although you might be doing that too (or be simply too sleep-deprived to give a toss that you’re wearing really naff jeans. Or using the word “naff”, which is probably also mumsy). The concept of mumsy changes according to the era you are living in. In the 1990s, all the mums wore high-waisted Levi’s 501s, which we even came to call “mum jeans”. This came to be co-opted by fashion brands, albeit using the slightly less mumsy sounding “mom”. I wouldn’t have been caught dead in mum jeans. What am I wearing now, as I type this? That’s right, a pair of vintage 501s. It all comes back round eventually. The teenagers I pass on the school run every morning would never.I look at how their baggy jeans are soaking up the puddles and pigeon piss all the way up to their knees and am not nostalgic. This must have been the sort of zen that my own mum felt; I feel confident in my personal style. That doesn’t mean that fear of mumsiness doesn’t try to stalk us all regardless. The anxiety around this question is palpable on forums such as Mumsnet: what shape of jeans should we be wearing now? Are coloured trainers fashionable?I’m not going to pretend that I don’t care at all, but I would think less of someone who uses the word “mumsy” about other women. I will never forget, long before I had a child myself, one writer I know saying of another that her work was “a bit mumsy”. The writer in question wrote brilliantly and hilariously about parenthood, and also about a lot of other things. I found the way that “mumsy” was used to reduce and deride her intelligence and the quality of her work deeply unpalatable. I also recall an editor saying that she hated seeing the word “mum” in print. I suppose she preferred the more literary sounding “my mother”, which has its place but, let’s be honest, it’s not how most of us speak.It made me realise that it isn’t just fashion, then, that is resistant to mumsiness but culture more generally, and that’s only going to change when mothers and the work they do are afforded the respect they deserve. As it stands, to become a mother is to not only be confronted with biological reality and structural sexism, but to somehow navigate this without dressing, writing or sounding too much like a mother. Perhaps, like the fashion writer Frankie Graddon, whoseSubstack’s strap lineis: “I’ve had a baby, not a style crisis”, the solution is to simply be “Mum-ish”. Whatever. You can prise my 501s from my cold, dead hands.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Your boss might be an idiot – and 12 other things you need to know about work | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: British teenagers are stressing about jobs (or the lack of them). Here is my advice, from owning your mistakes to the importance of biscuits, writes Emma Beddington
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: British teenagers are stressing about jobs (or the lack of them). Here is my advice, from owning your mistakes to the importance of biscuits, writes Emma Beddington
Content: Even jobs you hate can teach you something.Photograph: PeopleImages/Getty Images/iStockphotoView image in fullscreenEven jobs you hate can teach you something.Photograph: PeopleImages/Getty Images/iStockphotoOpinionJob huntingYour boss might be an idiot – and 12 other things you need to know about workEmma BeddingtonBritish teenagers are stressing about jobs (or the lack of them). Here is my advice, from owning your mistakes to the importance of biscuitsSun 25 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 10.08 EDTShareYoung people want to know more about the world of work.A survey of 2,000 13- to 18-year-olds for BBC Radio 5 Livefound that they wanted to learn about applying for jobs (42%), managing stress (39%) and developing their communication skills (38%).It’s sensible stuff – dispiritingly so. Shouldn’t they bedrinking BuzzBallzat bus stops? If someone had asked 13-year-old me what I wanted to know about work, I would have stared blankly, or asked: “What job will let me touch Mark Shaw (of obscure 80s band Then Jerico)?” Look at whattheir French peers are up to!I asked a French friend what she thought kids needed to know about work and she said (imagine her taking a drag on a Gauloise; she wasn’t, but still): “Nothing matters, nothing is real, hierarchy is a social construct. Burn it all down.” But in mustn’t-grumble Britain, with itsnearly 1 million Neets, teens aren’t rioting – they’re worrying about work experience, CVs and LinkedIn. The least we can do is try to help, so I asked what people think kids should know about exchanging labour for money and these things came up again and again:Anyone who tells you “do something you love and you’ll never work a day in your life” is a cliche-sodden bullshitter. “Do something you love and see your relationship to that thing shift, become ambivalent, maybe even curdle” is more accurate. Most people don’t keep a pure, unsullied passion for the thing they spend 40-plus hours a week doing. “All jobs get boring, even if you’reMick Jagger,” as a friend says.You don’t need to know what you want to do yet. Try things out: even jobs you hate are illuminating, and it’s almost always better to do something than nothing. Working somewhere poisonously unethical is the exception.Your colleagues make more difference – good or bad – to the quality of your life than the work itself. You can’t do much about it, but cherish the nice ones.You never know who the really important people at work will be. There’s usually someone who makes you want to bang your head against a wall until you pass out, but one day they might be the only thing standing between you and disaster – treat them (and everyone else) accordingly.Equally, just because someone is in charge, it doesn’t mean they aren’t an idiot.The best advice on complaining to others about your colleagues (or bosses) is don’t, but we’re only human. Take a tip from someone with two scarring, unforgettable “replied instead of forwarding an email” professional experiences to her name, and always triple check you’re sending the bitchy message to the right person.Speaking of mistakes, you’ll make them. Own up immediately, because the longer you leave it, the harder and scarier it gets. Most people respect and appreciate an honest admission of fault; anyone who doesn’t is an idiot.Most difficult work situations are improved by a packet of biscuits (unless you work in a biscuit factory).Speak up when you don’t understand, and don’t pretend you’re on top of a job when you’re not. Bad managers make this feel almost impossible, but try not to let yourself get steamrollered.So much is forgivable if you’re enthusiastic and cheerful. I say this as someone who is naturally neither, but I’ve seen how winning these qualities are even in people who are, in all other ways, basically unemployable.You’ll probably lose your job at some point and it will feel like a shameful, personal rejection and the end of the world. It isn’t.“Shit on company time,” says a wise acquaintance. That’s her pithy way of explaining you can start believing work is so important you can’t spare time for basic bodily needs. Work is neverthatimportant (unless you’re doing brain surgery, which you probably aren’t at 16). You’re a human first and an employee second; you have time for a sandwichanda loo break.Finally, perhaps the most important tip of all from the same wise woman: “Never tell anyone your living grandparent status – you’ve got at least four days off for funerals that way.” Hope that helps, kids.Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Cutting ‘red tape’ is nothing but a red herring – and arguably counterproductive | Heather Stewart | The Guardian
description: Blaming a moribund economy on too many rules is a hackneyed neoliberal trope – UK plc needs smarter regulation, not less regulation
Author: Heather Stewart
Headline: Blaming a moribund economy on too many rules is a hackneyed neoliberal trope – UK plc needs smarter regulation, not less regulation
Content: ‘When it comes to the labour market, Labour has unashamedly adopted a pro-regulation stance.’Illustration: Guardian Design TeamView image in fullscreen‘When it comes to the labour market, Labour has unashamedly adopted a pro-regulation stance.’Illustration: Guardian Design TeamEconomics viewpointEconomicsCutting ‘red tape’ is nothing but a red herring – and arguably counterproductiveHeather StewartBlaming a moribund economy on too many rules is a hackneyed neoliberal trope – UK plc needs smarter regulation, not less regulationSun 25 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTShareBefore becoming prime minister, Andy Burnham pledged to “end 40 years of neoliberalism”. But as he prepares for his first budget on Wednesday, his government is yet to let go of one of its most tedious cliches: red tape.In the run-up to the chancellor John Healey’s high-stakes Commons address, the government issued a press release last week promising his plans would include measures to “slash the red tape choking firms”.Named after the tape once used to tie up government bills, and popularised by the historian Thomas Carlyle, the phrase is straight from the neoliberal playbook and has long outlived its usefulness.Getting the interfering state out of the way of the wealth creators was a trope of Thatcher and Reaganite economics, and on this side of the pond it has been repeated ad nauseam by every government since.Thatcher unleashed the City with her “big bang” deregulation drive, and her successor John Major was enthusiastic about “hacking back the jungle of red tape”. It was the man he appointed for the job – Michael Heseltine – who coined what has become the most hackneyed description of this particular approach: the “bonfire of red tape”.WithLabourback in power, Gordon Brown celebrated a light-tough regulatory regime for the UK’s hard-driving financial sector – until the Treasury had to bail out the banks after the 2008 financial crisis.Boris Johnson wanted to unfetter Britain’s businesses from “Brussels bureaucracy” and waffled on during the Brexit campaign about bendy bananas. Yet, after Brexit, business groups said their members would rather comply with longstanding EU standards in many areas than adopt an entirely new UK regime. And bananas are no more or less bendy than before.Rachel Reeves had a more unpleasantly graphic way of making a similar point, referring to regulation as a“boot on the neck”of British business.There is nothing wrong with ensuring the interaction between business and the state is smooth. But even during the early years of neoliberalism, the free market good, regulation bad dichotomy was always unhelpful, for several reasons.First, good regulation – a robust competition regime, for example – is essential to make markets work well. And even most enthusiasts for a laissez-faire approach would acknowledge the need for some basic quality standards – for food and medicines, for example.When it comes to the labour market, Labour has unashamedly adopted a pro-regulation stance. ItsEmployment Rights Actis the most significant increase in workers’ rights in a generation – but it inevitably, and deliberately, increases the rules firms must follow.That is to the benefit, ministers rightly argue, of low-paid employees trapped in insecure work. But a bonfire of red tape it is not. Labour posing as a champion of deregulation will seem unconvincing, given that context.Second, and ironically, the march of neoliberalism itself is a reason regulation has mushroomed in recent decades. As the Labour MP Yuan Yangargued in a recent lecturefor the journal Renewal, as the state retreated from providing important services, watchdog institutions to oversee the private sector became necessary.As she put it: “The neoliberal illusion, that privatisation liberated markets from state interference, obscures the reality that the state already significantly controls our privatised utilities, but through a maze of arm’s length regulatory agencies which operate outside democratic influence.”For the water sector, privatised in 1989, these include Ofwat, which sets bills (with the Competition and Markets Authority acting as an appeals body in the event of a dispute); the Drinking Water Inspectorate; the Environment Agency; and the Consumer Council for Water.Yet, as Yang points out, none are responsible for drawing up a coherent plan for the sector as a whole. “Everyone knows how this story ends: with our rivers polluted and our water infrastructure dangerously lacking.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHacking away at the regulatory thicket fails to deal with the structural features of the economy that make the rules necessary in the first place.Mat Lawrence, the director of the thinktank Common Wealth and author of The Productive State, a policy paper influential among those close to Burnham, calls this “the regulatory state”. He cites affordable housing targets for private developers as another example of regulation taking the place of stuff the state once did itself.The third reason the endless red tape discourse is unhelpful is one raised by Mike Clancy, the general secretary of the Prospect union, which represents workers at many of the regulators.He has urged the government to lay off these often not lavishly paid staff, who are trying to do their jobs with stretched resources. “Regulators continue to be labelled as ‘blockers’ despite the vital work they do keeping us safe and protecting our natural environment,” he said.Prospect has been urging the government to ditch a promise to “cut the administrative burden” of regulation by 25% by the end of the parliament, arguing it is arbitrary and potentially counterproductive.Finally, we would all benefit from some over-mighty businesses being reined in by regulation, not least the tech firms, which insouciantly concede that their AI agents have been busting through safety controls andmay be about to start spawning spontaneously.Embracing the tired idea that red tape is “choking” business is hardly likely to help the government make the case for the more stringent approach that is clearly necessary.As it happens, Bonfire Night is almost upon us. If Burnham really wants to embrace a different approach to the economy, he could start by consigning the phrase “red tape” to the flames.Explore more on these topicsEconomicsEconomics viewpointRegulatorsEconomic policyPrivatisationJohn HealeyLabourcommentShareReuse this content

title: Matthew McConaughey has read all his bad reviews – and I applaud him | Polly Hudson | The Guardian
description: The Hollywood actor revealed he once read two-decades’ worth of pans in one fell swoop, during two days in the desert. It’s the kind of preposterous self-flagellation we can all learn from and enjoy, writes Polly Hudson
Author: Polly Hudson
Headline: The Hollywood actor revealed he once read two-decades’ worth of pans in one fell swoop, during two days in the desert. It’s the kind of preposterous self-flagellation we can all learn from and enjoy, writes Polly Hudson
Content: ‘They said WHAT??’ … Matthew McConaughey in True Detective.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘They said WHAT??’ … Matthew McConaughey in True Detective.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyOpinionMatthew McConaugheyMatthew McConaughey has read all his bad reviews – and I applaud himPolly HudsonThe Hollywood actor revealed he once read two-decades’ worth of pans in one fell swoop, during two days in the desert. It’s the kind of preposterous self-flagellation we can all learn from and enjoySun 25 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 13.57 EDTShareTo assume makes an ass out of you and me, but as sweeping generalisations go, this seems fairly uncontroversial: nobody likes hearing themselves being criticised. Obviously there are exceptions to the rule – no kink shaming here – but most people aren’t fans.Which is why a recent admission from Matthew McConaughey is unusual. The Hollywood actorrevealed that he oncespent two days in the desert reading 20 years’ worth of negative reviews about himself.I love everything about this. Each detail is perfect: the setting, the duration of the pursuit and the period spanned by the reviews, the narcissistic/anti-narcissistic intent, the ridiculousness, the pretension, the commitment.“I read every one,” McConaughey saidon the podcast Build or Break, while wearing tinted sunglasses inside and the sort of hat last seen on The Only Way Is Essex. “I sat with them – I spent two days looking. It was hard.”The mental image this conjures up is a gift – nay, payback. This is why McConaughey is paid the big bucks; why, as the world burns, we need celebrities more than ever. Thinking about a 56-year-old tortured artist-millionaire, hunkered down in a barren landscape, nobly forcing himself to pore over his harshest critiques, is a wonderful distraction from proper news. It’s like a ludicrous minibreak from reality.There are a few gaps we’ll have to fill in ourselves. When McConaughey says he “collected 20 years” of slatings and “went away to the desert for a weekend and took them all in this thick book”, do we imagine him sitting by the printer with his Pritt Stick, constructing his burn book with his own fair hands? Or is it more likely that this endeavour fell to an assistant in his employ? (In which case, talk about a fool’s errand.) Did McConaughey’s wife and kids join him on the multi-day desert jaunt and, if so, how was his 48-hour absence explained? “Sorry darling, Daddy can’t play Uno, he’s wallowing in painful self-reflection.”In summary: this column will definitely not feature in any of his handmade tomes of the future. Ten out of 10, Mr McConaughey, no notes. And thank you.Polly Hudson is a freelance writerDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: The hill I will die on: The email sign-off is archaic – it needs to go. No regards, Tom | Tom Gill | The Guardian
description: The torture of the inbox is made insufferably worse by the dated cliches at the beginning and end, says journalist Tom Gill
Author: Tom Gill
Headline: The torture of the inbox is made insufferably worse by the dated cliches at the beginning and end, says journalist Tom Gill
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/GettyThe hill I will die onEmailThe hill I will die on: The email sign-off is archaic – it needs to go. No regards, TomTom GillThe torture of the inbox is made insufferably worse by the dated cliches at the beginning and end. Enough!Sun 25 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 11.42 EDTShareIf email were a person, it would be an adult dressed in a teenager’s clothes, desperately trying to stay relevant. Despitebeing 55 years oldand having been surpassed by numerous developments in communication technologies, its functionality remains largely the same as when it was first widely adopted. Unfortunately, so does the etiquette surrounding it.Whereas other forms of communication have long since dispensed with unnecessary textual tassels, email communication styles still lean closer to telegram than a text. Since I last checked, almost no one relishes receiving a new email – unless it’s informing you of a significant cash windfall that means you can, in fact, now quit your job and stop using it altogether. Yet, for some reason, many people start their responses with “Thank you for your email!” I would put this forward as one of the least convincing sentences in the English language.At the other end of the page is one of the most common yet totally unnecessary habits of the digital age: the email signoff. For those who haven’t yet realised, I’m here to tell you that you don’t need to sign your name at the end of an email – I can already see it’s from you. I know your name. Outlook has gone to extraordinary lengths to tell me your name. It’s in my inbox, the “from” field and the thread, and I probably begrudgingly addressed my last email directly to you.And then there is whatever form of final flourish you see fit to precede that with. To me, the whole concept of “regards” – kind, best or otherwise – is archaic and overly formal, not far from sealing the whole thing with a wax stamp and dispatching it via horse. But worse are the new ways of signing things off. “In solidarity”, “Keep dreaming” and the ultimate Covid-era classic: “hope you’re staying positive and testing negative”. This reaches its logical conclusion with the use of “KR” as a signoff. We have begun to admit that we don’t actually feel enough “kind regards” to type the words any more – and yet, the convention rolls on.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hill I will die on: Forget potholes – the true indicator of societal decline is the ropey shoelace | Coco KhanRead moreThat’s to say nothing of email signatures, which now routinely exceed the length of the emails they are attached to. Name, job title, mobile number, office number, LinkedIn profile, logo, environmental disclaimer, confidentiality notice, statement about working hours and a quote from Maya Angelou. All appended to an email saying: “Running 5 mins late!”However, I appreciate that we must retain some means of expressing digital distaste, such is the harsh reality of the world of work. Therefore, the only use of the word “regards” I will permit is the one placed at the end of an email to communicate blunt and absolute hostility towards the recipient.With absolutely no regards,TomTom Gill is a freelance journalist and consultant from London, based in MelbourneExplore more on these topicsEmailThe hill I will die onSocial etiquetteComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Oxford Street’s pedestrianisation: cities should be designed around people, not cars | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: The transformation of Europe’s busiest shopping street should be a case study in making cities greener, less congested and more inviting places to live
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: The transformation of Europe’s busiest shopping street should be a case study in making cities greener, less congested and more inviting places to live
Content: Shoppers during a special Christmas pedestrianisation of Oxford Street in 2007.Photograph: Fiona Hanson/PAView image in fullscreenShoppers during a special Christmas pedestrianisation of Oxford Street in 2007.Photograph: Fiona Hanson/PAOpinionEnvironmentThe Guardian view on Oxford Street’s pedestrianisation: cities should be designed around people, not carsEditorialThe transformation of Europe’s busiest shopping street should be a case study in making cities greener, less congested and more inviting places to liveSun 25 Oct 2026 13.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 13.32 EDTShareSadiq Khan has beentrying to pedestrianiseOxford Street since he first became the mayor of London in 2016. On Monday, after numerous setbacks, his plan will finally come to fruition. The busiest stretch of the nation’s famous shopping street will be closed to traffic in a scheme designed to improve the area and make it more attractive to pedestrians. It should be an emblematic case study in making cities greener, less congested, more inviting places to live and visit.The Greater London Authority hopes it will rejuvenate a high street fallen on hard times. Since the pandemic, the number of vacant shops on Oxford Street hasmore than quadrupled. It estimates that the scheme will generate£82m of value a year in the areaby increasing footfall and encouraging visitors to linger. This impact remains to be seen, butresearchfrom other cities suggests that shops experience higher sales once an area is pedestrianised. Given the prime minister’s focus on rejuvenating British high streets, whosedilapidationis correlated with support for Reform UK, he should be watching with interest.View image in fullscreenSadiq Khan.Photograph: Victoria Jones/PAThe benefits of pedestrianisation are far greater than increased shopping. Domestic transport remains thelargest contributorto greenhouse-gas emissions in Britain. This sector’s emissions have fallenmore slowlythan others largely because too many people still rely on cars. Mr Khan’s city is an outlier:59% of all journeysin Britain were made by car in 2024, while in London carsaccounted for 34%. This is hardly surprising when the Treasury spendstwice as muchon London’s transport system as it does on other regions in England, and the capital’sbus faresare cheaper. In Leeds, which has no mass-transit system,nearly halfof people drive to work. Car use cannot be reduced without simultaneously improving public transport.The critics of pedestrianisation – includingWestminster council– suggest it merely displaces traffic elsewhere. But the evidence on this is more nuanced. Onestudyfrom the University of the West of England suggests the closure of strategic roads causes some traffic to disappear permanently, as people switch to public transport or walk. Low-traffic neighbourhoods (LTNs), the pedestrianisation schemes that were rushed through in the capital during Covid-19 and have since been introduced inManchesterandBirmingham, were fiercely criticised for causing a buildup of road traffic elsewhere. Yetone studyof 46 LTNs in London suggested their impact on traffic elsewhere was minimal.Car-free areas should be accompanied by other policies that reduce pollution on surrounding roads, such as the low-emissions zones introduced in London and Oxford. Mr Khan was criticised by the then leader of the opposition,Keir Starmer, for the expansion of Ulez in 2023, and also sufferedracial abuse. He has since been vindicated by research from Imperial College suggesting Ulez hassignificantly improvedthe health of primary school children in the capital, whose lung growth had been stunted by pollution.That Transport for London estimates the pedestrianisation of Oxford Street will have only aminimal impacton nitrogen dioxide emissions, which were already decreasing as a result of Ulez, is testimony to the policy’s success. In 2014, Oxford Street had the highest concentration of nitrogen dioxide pollution in the world. Its pedestrianisationshould be an inspiration to other cities to embrace policies that work for people, not cars.Explore more on these topicsEnvironmentOpinionPedestrianisationLondonSadiq KhanPollutionChildrenAir pollutioneditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on adult education: learning should be for all ages | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Teenagers and young adults are not the only people in need of new skills and a sense of purpose
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Teenagers and young adults are not the only people in need of new skills and a sense of purpose
Content: ‘The MPs’ report makes a persuasive case that an overall vision for adult education has been missing for a long time.’Photograph: Bill Cheyrou/Alamy‘The MPs’ report makes a persuasive case that an overall vision for adult education has been missing for a long time.’Photograph: Bill Cheyrou/AlamyOpinionEducationThe Guardian view on adult education: learning should be for all agesEditorialTeenagers and young adults are not the only people in need of new skills and a sense of purposeSun 25 Oct 2026 13.30 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 13.33 EDTShareThe neglect of adults was, David Blunkett said in arecent interview, his biggest regret about education policy under New Labour. Spending on classroom-based adult learning in England has fallen steadily, from a high point of more than £5bn in 2003-04, to less than £2bn last year. We should not expect two decades of decline to be reversed quickly. But the upcomingreport from Alan Milburnon young people who are not in education, employment or training is widely expected to result in a boost for colleges, as well as apprenticeship changes so thatmore are offered to new recruitsrather than existing staff.A timelyreport from MPsaims to ensure that older learners are included in these reforms. The all-party group for further education recognises the need to tackle the low level of labour market participation among young adults, which is particularly pronounced insmaller towns and cities. But the MPs take a longer view of the current system’s failings. Their report makes a persuasive case that an overall vision for adult education has been missing for a long time.Economic and employment outcomes are important. If people are being trained in construction or IT or social care, their ability to find work afterwards matters. But adult education has a broader purpose that is harder to measure. Acquiring new skills, the MPs point out, can be a first step on a longer journey – a way to “begin to imagine different futures”. Learning can contribute to health and wellbeing, as well as income and productivity. One of the consistent themes from research was the importance of relationships – highlighting the role of education as a social glue, and of classrooms as a potential source of the people skills that employers want.View image in fullscreenAlan Milburn.Photograph: Teri Pengilley/The GuardianIt is right for ministers to prioritise help for young adults who have yet to find their feet. But mid-career adults facing redundancy, or aiming to come off benefits, or to transition out of manual roles due to declining health, also need support. And while the promised modularalternative to maths and English GCSEsshould be useful to future cohorts, the low literacy level of up to 8 million older people must also be addressed. In some areas, English language lesson providers urgently need more resources to meet demand. So does prison education, which has faced damaging cuts.Adult education is not helped by the complicated administrative and funding arrangements that sit behind it. Overall responsibility for skills, including the £3.3bn apprenticeship budget, was transferred to the Department for Work and Pensions last year. But the Department of Education retains a role in further education, while the division of powers between Whitehall and the mayor-led regions isexpected to be clarifiedin the budget.This report proposes an England-wide minimum standard, which could then be developed by local partnerships. The lack of incentives for employers to invest in training is among the most serious problems at the moment. Uncompetitive pay is another, which makes recruitment of qualified instructors difficult. Careers advice is yet another gap.Given these interlinked shortcomings, the proposed “renaissance” in adult education sounds optimistic. But at a time when the benefits of social and economic participation are being vigorously advocated, MPs are right to resist overly narrow prescriptions, and to champion the freedom to learn at any age.Explore more on these topicsEducationOpinionAdult literacyFurther educationHigher educationMature studentsEmployabilityCollegeseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: Cutting welfare to pay for work support is all wrong | Youth unemployment | The Guardian
description: Letters: Priya Sahni-Nicholas on a proposal by Alan Milburn to help those not in education, employment or training. Plus letters from Ruth Lister and Alan Coppin
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Priya Sahni-Nicholas on a proposal by Alan Milburn to help those not in education, employment or training. Plus letters from Ruth Lister and Alan Coppin
Content: ‘Framing welfare as something that plunges young people into a life on benefits ignores the fact that nearly half of Neets do not claim benefits.’Photograph: Iryna Melnyk/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Framing welfare as something that plunges young people into a life on benefits ignores the fact that nearly half of Neets do not claim benefits.’Photograph: Iryna Melnyk/Getty ImagesYouth unemploymentLettersCutting welfare to pay for work support is all wrongPriya Sahni-Nicholason a proposal by Alan Milburn to help those not in education, employment or training. Plus letters fromRuth ListerandAlan CoppinSun 25 Oct 2026 13.14 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 13.16 EDTShareAlan Milburn correctly identifies that the nation’s 1 million young people not in education, employment, or training (Neet) represent a crisis of “youth detachment” deeply intertwined with mental ill health (Cut benefits to fund work support for young people, says Neet review author Alan Milburn, 18 October).However, his proposal to cut welfare benefits to fund employment support both misdiagnoses the problem and points to a solution that will worsen it.Framing welfare as something that is “plunging far too many young people into a life on benefits” ignores the fact that nearly half of Neet young people do not claim benefits.The modern social security system is experienced as a regime of surveillance and scrutiny rather than a safety net. Paternalistic approaches that treat structural disadvantage as a personal failure actively drive vulnerable young people away from public institutions. Squeezing benefit safety nets further will deepen inequality, increase mistrust and worsen the problem, not alleviate it.Rather than robbing Peter to pay Paul, we need the government to invest directly in reducing inequality. Creating the conditions for young people to thrive requires a fairer economic model that eradicates poverty and tackles gross disparities in income, wealth and power.Health and employment support funding must come from progressive taxation on extreme wealth and corporate profits, not from threatening to withdraw support and further impoverishing already underresourced and vulnerable people.We need government action that actively reduces inequality and builds security, giving every young person the structural foundation required to live a good life.Priya Sahni-NicholasCo-executive director, Equality TrustThank you, Frances Ryan, for the call to arms in defence of our social security system (The right’s scrounger rhetoric dominates the benefits debate. Labour must fight back – and win, 16 October). But while it’s true that the right’s attack has been largely focused on disabled people’s benefits, the underlying hostility to social security and those reliant on it runs wider and deeper.Fuelled by false claims that spending is out of control, the calls for cuts are relentless. And any attempt to start repairing the damage wreaked by the previous government’s cuts and restrictions – for instance, through the recent abolition of the two-child limit – are vilified with the kind of rhetoric she warns against. Cutting benefits to promote jobseeking is a false economy, as research suggests that impoverished people are ill-placed to seek and gain employment, and the costs are likely to fall elsewhere, including on the NHS.The fightback needs to emphasise that social security, adequately financed, is both an essential weapon in combating poverty (including child poverty) and, as the name suggests, a key element in any strategy to promote the financial security of a wider population at a time of widespread insecurity.Ruth ListerLabour, House of LordsYour article (Who exactly will be affected by the UK review of benefits for young people?, 20 October) again uses the term “Neets”. When I chaired the young people’s social inclusion charity Cities in Schools, we recognised that a new name was needed. Interbrand gave us Include, free of charge, with a modern logo: a lowercase “i” with a jagged line running through it, positive yet honest about the challenges our young people faced. The name mattered. It shaped how those young people saw themselves, and how others saw them.Neet does the opposite. It defines young people by what they are not: in education, employment or training. Surely a government with all the resources at its command can find a less negative, less stigmatising term for the young people we need to help build a future.Alan CoppinBourne End, BuckinghamshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Plague risks in Russia and a dangerous delay on WHO pandemic agreement | Infectious diseases | The Guardian
description: Letters: Responding to an editorial on a potential plague outbreak, Dr Darren Mann deplores delays to the agreement, while Kent Buse says Britain could do more
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Responding to an editorial on a potential plague outbreak, Dr Darren Mann deplores delays to the agreement, while Kent Buse says Britain could do more
Content: The Irkutsk anti-plague research institute, where an employee died on 2 October of a mysterious illness.Photograph: Smirnov Vladimir/Anadolu/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Irkutsk anti-plague research institute, where an employee died on 2 October of a mysterious illness.Photograph: Smirnov Vladimir/Anadolu/Getty ImagesInfectious diseasesLettersPlague risks in Russia and a dangerous delay on WHO pandemic agreementResponding to an editorial on a potential plague outbreak,Dr Darren Manndeplores delays to the agreement, whileKent Busesays Britain could do moreSun 25 Oct 2026 13.13 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 13.15 EDTShareYour editorial on the silence from Siberia after a worker died at a plague research institute there is right that the lack of information is the real worry (The Guardian view on plague in Russia: what is most worrying is the lack of information, 18 October). But the deeper failure is not Russian. It is that, six years after Covid, we still have no agreed system for sharing pathogens, or for sharing what is made from them.I spent three decades in Hong Kong, through bird flu, Sars and Covid, working on outbreak surveillance and sample-sharing between Hong Kong and the UK. It is also where this territorial argument began. In June 1894, two bacteriologists arrived to investigate the plague. Kitasato Shibasaburō was given lab space and immediate access to the bodies. Alexandre Yersin was refused access to the dead, and worked from a straw hut, having to appeal to the governor for his share of cadavers. Access to the material was allocated by favour, not by need. The organism carries the name of the man who was shut out:Yersinia pestis.The pathogen access and benefit-sharing annexe to the World Health Organization pandemic agreement is the same argument in modern dress, and it has stalled on the same point. Poorer countries are asked to detect and share dangerous pathogens quickly. In return, they want a binding guarantee of what follows: 20% of real-time production of vaccines and treatments, half donated and half sold at cost. Inarticle 13, the global supply chain and logistics network provides for a more equitable distribution of personal protective equipment. Richer countries prefer all that sharing to stay voluntary. The agreement cannot open for signature until this is settled, and it has now beendeferred to 2027.All pandemics start with a rumour. The next pandemic is likely to be something we have never seen before, and whoever first holds the samples will not be us. If we cannot agree what they get in return, we should not be surprised when they are slow to hand them over.Dr Darren MannFormer medical director, Cabinet Office Covid-19 PPE taskforceYour editorial on plague in Russia is right that the system is fraying, but wrong to treat Moscow’s silence as an aberration. It is the predictable product of rules that member states built without teeth. The InternationalHealthRegulations oblige governments to notify the WHO within 24 hours, yet provide no verification, no sanctions and no independent monitoring. States mark their own homework through annual self-assessments. The amendments in force since last September add an implementation committee that is, by design, consultative only. Member states, Britain included, chose this. They then starved the WHO of assessed funding, leaving it dependent on the goodwill of the governments it is meant to hold to account.Britain accepted the amended regulations in July 2025 and, with the United States gone, is among the WHO’s largest government funders. Ministers should raise Russia’s non-reporting formally within the WHO rather than leave Washington to make the only public request. The UK should table proposals for independent verification and a public compliance register when the pandemic agreement’s pathogen-sharing annex returns to the assembly, due by May 2027. And it should volunteer for the WHO’s Universal Health and Preparedness Review, a peer review that only 11 countries have joined and Britain has not. A government cannot demand transparency it declines to practise. The recent UN declaration on pandemics will mean little unless the governments that signed it are held to account.Kent BuseCo-CEO, Global 50/50Have an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: On dementia, we need to tell it how it is | Dementia | The Guardian
description: Letter: David Lee responds to a letter questioning the use of language about people with dementia
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: David Lee responds to a letter questioning the use of language about people with dementia
Content: ‘In all the care homes I have been into, people with dementia weren’t “living well with dementia”; they were suffering.’Photograph: Image Source/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘In all the care homes I have been into, people with dementia weren’t “living well with dementia”; they were suffering.’Photograph: Image Source/AlamyDementiaLettersOn dementia, we need to tell it how it isDavid Leeresponds to a letter questioning the use of language about people with dementiaSun 25 Oct 2026 13.12 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 13.14 EDTShareSally Byers takes Polly Toynbee to task (Letters, 19 October) for using what she considers to be “deeply troubling language” about people with dementia, in particular the phrases “glazed stares or sleeping mouths agape” and “that terrible human vacancy” in Toynbee’s article (In Liverpool I saw the tough choices Louise Casey faces on social care – starting with who will pay?, 13 October).I looked at the Dementia Engagement and Empowerment Projectlanguage guidefor journalists highlighted in the letter. It gives a list of words and descriptions to avoid, including “dementia sufferer”, and lists alternative phrases to be used as “person/people with dementia”, “person/people living with dementia” or “person/people living well with dementia”.I disagree. Toynbee described what she saw and wrote it, and her words had impact. In all the care homes I have been into to see elderly relatives, people with dementia weren’t “living well with dementia”; they were suffering. So why can’t we all tell it how it is rather than pretending otherwise?David LeeStaveley, CumbriaHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Tech firms should pay the creators whose work they use | Technology | The Guardian
description: Letter: It could raise up to £300m a year, providing UK creators with additional income, write Barbara Hayes, Tayyiba Nasser, Christian Zimmermann and Paul Seheult
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: It could raise up to £300m a year, providing UK creators with additional income, write Barbara Hayes, Tayyiba Nasser, Christian Zimmermann and Paul Seheult
Content: ‘It is creators’ work that attracts people to technology, sustains their engagement and drives innovation.’ An anti-AI protest in New York last week.Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPAView image in fullscreen‘It is creators’ work that attracts people to technology, sustains their engagement and drives innovation.’ An anti-AI protest in New York last week.Photograph: Olga Fedorova/EPATechnologyLettersTech firms should pay the creators whose work they useIt could raise up to £300m a year, providing UK creators with additional income, writeBarbara Hayes,Tayyiba Nasser,Christian ZimmermannandPaul SeheultSun 25 Oct 2026 13.11 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 13.13 EDTShareAnthropic’s proposal (AI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’, 19 October) raises an important question: who should benefit from technological progress? Before pledging money for the public good, AI companies such as Anthropic should first pay the creators whose work they use.Device manufacturers have a separate responsibility under the same principle: creators should share in the value their work generates.Smartphones, computers and other devices enable creative work to be copied and stored, yet UK creators receive no private-copying payments, unlike their counterparts in more than 40 other countries.The proposedSmart Fundwould require manufacturers and importers to make modest contributions on devices used to copy or store creative work. It could raise up to £300m a year, providing creators with additional income and supporting skills, cultural programmes and affordable workspaces.For creators on persistently low and falling incomes, these payments would make a tangible difference. Visual artists’ median annual earnings are just £12,500 – 47% lower in real terms than in 2010. Authors earn a median of only £7,000 from writing, down from £11,300, according to surveys published in 2022 and 2018 respectively. Audiovisual performers report median annual earnings from performingof £17,500. Yet it is creators’ work that attracts people to technology, sustains their engagement and drives innovation. Those creators should share in the value their work helps generate, so they can continue creating and powering that cycle. The government should turn this principle into action by introducing the Smart Fund.Barbara HayesChief executive, Authors’ Licensing and Collecting Society (ALCS)Tayyiba NasserChief executive, British Equity Collecting Society (BECS)Christian ZimmermannChief executive, Design and Artists Copyright Society (DACS)Paul SeheultChief executive, PICSELExplore more on these topicsTechnologyAnthropicIntellectual propertyArts fundingArtArts policyTechnology sectorlettersShareReuse this content

title: Fernandes gamble leaves Carrick to carry the can for United’s institutional failures | Premier League | The Guardian
description: Leaving out his captain was doomed to fail but so are the club under the current leadership and the fans at Old Trafford know that all too well
Author: Will Unwin
Headline: Leaving out his captain was doomed to fail but so are the club under the current leadership and the fans at Old Trafford know that all too well
Content: Bruno Fernandes’ non-appearance was a source of intrigue throughout the match.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAView image in fullscreenBruno Fernandes’ non-appearance was a source of intrigue throughout the match.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAPremier LeagueAnalysisFernandes gamble leaves Carrick to carry the can for United’s institutional failuresWill Unwinat Old TraffordLeaving out his captain was doomed to fail but so are the club under the current leadership and the fans at Old Trafford know that all too wellSun 25 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 15.25 EDTShareDropping your captain, who has held the team together for most of the past five years, is a bold move from a man whose job is on the line. It was very much a make-or-break decision fromMichael Carrickto leave out Bruno Fernandes against Bournemouth. It did not work and Carrick knew the consequences if it failed and will probably pay the price for it, but he should not be alone.Carrick said the decision to drop the Portuguese playmaker was purely based on football reasons but criticising his manager afterthe desperate defeat to Comocannot have helped. Clearly Carrick disagreed with his captain’scomments on the lack of pressingin the Champions League fixture. It was somewhat telling that Lisandro Martínez kept his placedespite pointing outthe director of football, Jason Wilcox, was a hindrance to the club the previous week.Michael Carrick on the brink after Manchester United are humiliated by BournemouthRead moreFernandes has been a long way from his best this season, with three goals and one assist in the Premier League,all in one game against Ipswich. It would have been justifiable to give someone else an opportunity in the No 10 role, especially when the squad contains far too many of those. But then, no one at United is in form, so keeping an angry Fernandes in position may have made more sense. United have won almost half the Premier League fixtures Fernandes has started since he joined in 2020, and less than a third when he is absent.Some question Fernandes’ attitudebased on his complaints when things are not going right, but that is his way of showing he cares. He may not be a leader in the Bryan Robson or Roy Keane mould but is certainly the one who sets the example, shown by a banner in the Stretford End depicting the two former captains and Eric Cantona alongside the word “STANDARDS”. Those have dipped here. This is a mid-table team, made worse by a lack of desire.Everything was pedestrian in thought and execution. One promising attack lost momentum and United decided the most sensible course of action was to pass the ball all the way back to Senne Lammens, resulting in deserved boos. It felt like a moment that indicated Carrick’s days were coming to an end.Hypotheticals are pointless, as was Youri Tielemans, Fernandes’ replacement. The central midfielder has not impressed sincejoining from Aston Villa in the summerand the extra responsibility for an experienced player did not spur him on. He was ponderous in midfield, repeatedly losing the ball as he struggled to cope with the pace of the game against a Bournemouth team eager to press and hunt in pairs. The No 10 is supposed to be a creative influence in the final third but the Belgian was a lost boy against men.View image in fullscreenThe Stretford End made it clear with their banner what they think is missing at Manchester United.Photograph: Simon Stacpoole/Offside/Getty ImagesA poorly defended first goal resulted in the inevitable cutting by the cameras to a sullen Fernandes sunk into his seat on the bench. It was a goal that summed up the mood at Old Trafford, Rayan was left in space to volley home at the back post after Ayden Heaven needlessly gave away a free-kick. He looked miserable and the majority inside the ground felt exactly the same.United lack pace across the pitch so require someone in key areas to speed up play, but Tielemans is not capable of doing so. His main influence on the match was getting booked in the first half, which all but confirmed his exit at the break. It was telling that Carrick turned to Matheus Cunha to take over the duties behind the labouring Bryan Mbeumo in the desperate hope he could spark his team into life.Carrick has been left with an unbalanced squad, lacking quality in key areas. It would be hard to suggest on Sunday’s viewing that United were the Champions League team andBournemouth in the Europa League. The Cherries can boast a wealth of smart recruitment, acquiring the likes of Adrien Truffert and Rayan – two players who would walk into the United team – for half a Harry Maguire.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe shambles of the third goal was on Lammens and Maguire, the former for running out too fast and the latter for not knowing how to run fast. Evanilson nipped in and flashed in the definitive game-ender. It sent Fernandes back to the bench with the expression of a man who had sipped sour milk. The final insult came when Carrick sent on the academy graduate Shea Lacey and left his captain to brood.View image in fullscreenManchester United fans have been venting their anger at the club’s hierarchy for some time.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianIt is not solely one bottle; the whole dairy has curdled. Carrick can take some of the blame; the Glazers, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, Wilcox and Omar Berradashould receive more. United are not fit for purpose and the supporters’ ire was largely aimed at the directors’ box, demanding the owners sell up and go home, with slightly less savoury language. The Old Trafford faithful know where the fault lies, offering more creativity than any of their team with a fine repertoire of chants against the hierarchy, most pointedly at Wilcox, whose signings left Carrick in trouble before the season started.Carrick had his name chanted, the full-time boos not for him. The manager – for now – did a lap of honour, cheered by the fans who jeered the players. Another era is nearing an end and finding reasons to be optimistic would be a greater waste of time than playing up front for United. Change will almost certainly come but it will not be enough.Explore more on these topicsPremier LeagueManchester UnitedMichael CarrickJim RatcliffeThe Glazer familyanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Kimi Antonelli storms to US F1 GP victory but is made to wait for title glory | Formula One 2026 | The Guardian
description: The 20-year-old championship leader won from Charles Leclerc and Max Verstappen and should become F1’s youngest world champion next week in Mexico
Author: Giles Richards
Headline: The 20-year-old championship leader won from Charles Leclerc and Max Verstappen and should become F1’s youngest world champion next week in Mexico
Content: Kimi Antonelli celebrates with the trophy on the podium after winning the US GP.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersView image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli celebrates with the trophy on the podium after winning the US GP.Photograph: Mike Segar/ReutersFormula One 2026Kimi Antonelli storms to US F1 GP victory but is made to wait for title gloryChampionship leader wins from Leclerc and Verstappen20-year-old should win title in next race in MexicoGiles Richardsat the Circuit of the AmericasSun 25 Oct 2026 18.21 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 19.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith a calm assurance that belies his tender years,Kimi Antonellidelivered another masterclass at the US Grand Prix, ensuring that while he could not quite seal the Formula One world championship in the Texas sunshine, it is a coronation that is surely only delayed for a week. The 20-year-old has made it almost a formality that he will seal the deal at the next round in Mexico.Antonelli’s dominant victory in Austin at the Circuit of the Americas, with a controlled and composed drive to beat the Ferrari ofCharles Leclercinto second place and the Red Bull of Max Verstappen into third, was described by the Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff as “one small step” towards the title in what has been a season of giant leaps for the Italian.Kimi Antonelli looks forward to drivers’ title after victory in US Grand PrixRead moreThose leaps were exemplified by Antonelli’s run in Austin where he did everything required of him,taking poleand converting it to a dominant race win, his ninth of the season. “The race of a champion who isn’t the champion yet,” was Wolff’s accurate assessment.Quick GuideUS GP resultsShow1Kimi Antonelli🇮🇹Mercedes1:35:16.650 –25pts2Charles Leclerc🇲🇨Ferrari+13.078 –18pts3Max Verstappen🇳🇱Red Bull+17.485 –15pts4Lewis Hamilton🇬🇧Ferrari+18.515 –12pts5Lando Norris🇬🇧McLaren+30.521 –10pts6Isack Hadjar🇫🇷Red Bull+34.373 –8pts7Oscar Piastri🇦🇺McLaren+52.674 –6pts8George Russell🇬🇧Mercedes+54.303 –4pts9Liam Lawson🇳🇿Red Bull+79.183 –2pts10Pierre Gasly🇫🇷Alpine+87.516–1pt11Nico Hülkenberg🇩🇪Audi+94.945s12Arvid Lindblad🇬🇧Racing Bulls+1 lap13Gabriel Bortoleto🇧🇷Audi+1 lap14Esteban Ocon🇫🇷Haas+1 lap15Lance Stroll🇨🇦Aston Martin+1 lap16Fernando Alonso🇪🇸Aston Martin+1 lap17Alexander Albon🇹🇭Williams+1 lap18Carlos Sainz🇪🇸Williams+1 lap19Sergio Pérez🇲🇽Cadillac+1 lapNCValtteri Bottas🇫🇮Cadillac+1 lapNCFranco Colapinto🇦🇷AlpineDNFNCOliver Bearman🇬🇧HaasDNFWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.However, while it was a perfect weekend for the Italian, it was not quite enough to claim the title in Texas. With his teammate George Russell finishing in eighth place andLewis Hamiltonin fourth for Ferrari, the fight remains alive but only just and Antonelli is now in position to finish the job next weekend in Mexico City.Antonelli leads Russell by 123 points and Hamilton by 124. With nine wins, the Italian cannot be caught on countback and needs to be only 100 ahead after the Mexican GP. Any finish in front of Russell and Hamilton, or ninth or better regardless of where his two rivals finish, will be enough for him to become the youngest driver to claim the sport’s crown and the first Italian to do so since Alberto Ascari in 1953. The joy when Antonelli climbed from the car was palpable as he allowed himself the chance to acknowledge the feeling that he really is now world champion-elect.View image in fullscreenKimi Antonelli doused himself in the winner’s champagne and knows ninth or better in Mexico will suffice for him to be world champion.Photograph: Jerome Miron/Imagn Images/ReutersIt was not a thrilling victory in what was something of a stately affair, but again Antonelli had its measure and was all but untouchable in a race enlivened really only by a split strategy.The Mercedes of Antonelli and Russell opted for a one-stop strategy over the two-stop choice ofRed Bulland Ferrari, and the former proved to be the right call. Antonelli led from the off and after putting in a long first stint while his rivals dashed in for new boots, he emerged able to regain the lead without having to stop again.The strategy split made the procession at least open to debate for the mid-period until it became clear that the one-stop option was the quicker. The late phase did see some feisty passing by Verstappen, who took advantage of his fresher rubber to hustle through the field, as in his wake did Leclerc, who was equally brave and ultimately took second place.
