TheMoVe Yaoundé project, launched in January 2024, includes a four-year urban renewal plan for the city centre, with about 1,000 sq metres (10,800 sq ft) of green space planned, including tree-lined avenues.In September, the council published a call for tenders that included landscaping works, new parks, tree-lined avenues and permeable paving.But until the green spaces promised under MoVe Yaoundé take shape, the work of preserving what is left falls to people such as Nonga. “If we don’t know what we’re losing, we can’t defend it,” she says.The Guardian contacted the Yaoundé urban council about the loss of Essos park and the authorisation of the private car park. The council referred the questions to the official in charge of the MoVe Yaoundé project, who did not respond to requests for comment.This article is published in collaboration withEgab.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentAccess to green spaceUrbanisationTrees and forestsGardensGreen citiesCameroonfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Policy U-turn could stall Britain’s take-up of electric vehicles | Electric, hybrid and low-emission cars | The Guardian
description: The 2030 target for 80% of new cars to have zero emissions could be cut to as low as half
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The 2030 target for 80% of new cars to have zero emissions could be cut to as low as half
Content: Analyst Jess Ralston said weakening emissions targets would not solve the problems for manufacturers, who are already facing intensified competition from China.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAView image in fullscreenAnalyst Jess Ralston said weakening emissions targets would not solve the problems for manufacturers, who are already facing intensified competition from China.Photograph: Gareth Fuller/PAElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsAnalysisPolicy U-turn could stall Britain’s take-up of electric vehiclesFiona Harvey and Jasper JollyThe 2030 target for 80% of new cars to have zero emissions could be cut to as low as halfSun 25 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 08.01 EDTShareElectric cars make people happy. More than nine in 10 EV drivers – 94% in a recent poll – are saving money, and a similar number would stick with electric for their next purchase, and recommend them to family and friends. Sales are soaring: more than half of the new cars sold in the UK last month were electric, if hybrids are taken into account, and about 28% of new car sales overall were electric only.This is hardly surprising, given that soaring petrol and diesel costs have pushed up the price of a full tank to about £120. EV drivers are paying about 2.4p a mile.Why then is the government considering a major U-turn on electric vehicle policy that, if followed through, could stall the take-up of EVs, help to close off a route to lower living costs, and dent the UK’s ability to meet its carbon targets?Andy Burnham, the prime minister, wrote in the Guardian this week that he would push ahead with the target of reachingnet zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050. Despite the go-ahead for the Jackdaw gasfield this week, sources in government also hinted to the Guardian that another large project, the Rosebank oilfield, west of Shetland, wasless likely to be greenlighted.However, analysis from the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit (ECIU) thinktank, seen by the Guardian, shows that the looming decision on the future of electric vehicles could also have a major impact on net zero and carbon budgets, though it has received far less attention.Under the zero emissions vehicle mandate, all new cars and vans sold from 2035 must be fully electric, with interim targets for 80% of new cars and 70% of new vans to be ZEVs by 2030.The end goal of 2035 is likely to remain, but under a consultation that ended on Friday,the 2030 targets could be weakenedto 70% or even as low as 50% of new cars. Taken with previous watering down of the policy to allow more sales of hybrid cars – which use both electric and combustion engines – that change would lead to emissions greater than burning all the gas in the Jackdaw field, according to the ECIU.If the mandate were cut more drastically to require only 50% of sales to be EVs by 2030, this could mean an additional 147 megatonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, which would equate to about 58% of the likely emissions from burning the oil produced by the Rosebank field.Jess Ralston, an analyst at the ECIU, said weakening the target would not solve the problems for manufacturers, who are already facing intensified competition from China as increasing numbers of people opt for EVs. It would also not benefit the public because EVs can be £1,750 a year cheaper to run, and potentially more with oil prices rising.“With climate concern high among the public afterextreme heat and persisting drought, and public support for net zero up above two-thirds, a decision to U-turn could look very odd,” Ralston said. “Ministers have talked about getting families off the fossil fuel rollercoaster – this would be the opposite, locking in higher driving costs, more air pollution and higher carbon emissions.”Burnham faces a further complication: in 2024, the EU imposed tariffs on Chinese EVs, and now wants to limit public subsidies to vehicles made in Europe, under pressure from European carmakers. If Burnham wants closer integration with the EU, and more favourable trade terms, he may be forced to slapmatching tariffs on Chinese importsto the UK. This would raise the cost of EVs in the UK and cut off one route to lower living costs.If fully implemented as originally planned, the ZEV mandate could be the largest single carbon-saving measure the government has yet proposed, according to previous research. But afterintensive lobbying from carmakers for a weakening, Labour MPs are deeply divided.Car manufacturers in the UK have been slow to retool their plants to EVs, and some have pursued hybrid vehicles instead. Many analysts consider hybrids, which combine a polluting petrol engine and a smaller battery, a technological dead end. By contrast, China has rapidly ramped up its EV manufacturing, and now dominates the global market, producing about three-quarters of all EVs. Sales of EVs have soared, now making up about a quarter of all new car sales around the world.Some Labour MPs in constituencies with car plants side with the manufacturers, while others argue that with petrol prices soaring and unlikely to abate, EVs are a way to lower the cost of living and get Britain off the fossil fuel hook.Chris Hinchliff, Labour MP for North East Hertfordshire, told the Guardian: “Weakening the EV target would be another nail in the coffin of a livable future.”Barry Gardiner, Labour MP for Brent West and former environment minister, said a U-turn would hurt forward-looking companies and favour laggards. “Watering down the mandate means that good companies, who moved straight away to comply, feel they have been unfairly burdened with additional costs while their lazy competitors have sneaked an advantage,” he said. “Government flip-flops are a huge problem for business. State the regulation clearly and then stick to it. Business will then adapt and do what it does best because it knows it has a level playing field.”A government spokesperson said: “We are reviewing the ZEV mandate to ensure it continues to support British industry and investment, and no decisions have been taken. Crucially, the end goal has not changed – we will phase out all new petrol and diesel cars by 2030 and be fully zero emission by 2035, and remain committed to our legally binding net zero targets.”Consumer research showsthe 2 million people currently driving EVsin the UK tend to like them: polling by the Electric Vehicle Association found 94% of EV drivers reported they were saving money compared with petrol or diesel cars. A similar number would stay electric for their next car, and recommend an EV to friends or family.Explore more on these topicsElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsGreenhouse gas emissionsMotoringanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Two children’s laureates to give royalties to Sally Rooney after her UK sales halted | Sally Rooney | The Guardian
description: Irish and Welsh authors Chris Haughton and Nicola Davies show solidarity after Rooney’s support for Palestine Action
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Irish and Welsh authors Chris Haughton and Nicola Davies show solidarity after Rooney’s support for Palestine Action
Content: The bestselling author is unable to receive royalties from UK sales because of her public support for the direct action group.Photograph: Martina Bocchio/Awakening/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe bestselling author is unable to receive royalties from UK sales because of her public support for the direct action group.Photograph: Martina Bocchio/Awakening/AlamySally RooneyTwo children’s laureates to give royalties to Sally Rooney after her UK sales haltedIrish and Welsh authors Chris Haughton and Nicola Davies show solidarity after Rooney’s support for Palestine ActionHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentSun 25 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 11.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe children’s laureates for Ireland and Wales are donating royalties from their works to Sally Rooney in a show of solidarity after she wasforced to stop selling booksin the UK because of her support for Palestine Action.Chris Haughton, Ireland’s children’s literature laureate, said he also wanted to demonstrate the “absurdity” of the bestselling author being unable to receive royalties from her own UK sales because of her public support for the direct action group.Haughton, whose books have sold millions worldwide, said: “I really want to express my full support for Sally Rooney. As someone who is in the UK a lot of the time, I can’t do what she has done, but I can support her instead of supportingPalestine Action.View image in fullscreenChris Haughton.Photograph: Kirstine Bowen“As authors, we need to be focused on freedom of expression, this is everything we’re about, and this is just showing solidarity with an author who has bravely spoken out.“The entire situation is just a farce. SendingSally Rooneythe money adds another level of absurdity to this absurd situation, it’s making a mockery of the law.”Haughton said he has twice been arrested for holding placards allegedly supporting Palestine Action, which became the first direct action group to beproscribed under the UK Terrorism Actin July last year, placing it in the same category as the likes of al-Qaida and Boko Haram. His alleged offence carries a maximum sentence of six months in prison.After the ban was introduced, Rooney, whose books include Normal People and Conversations with Friends, said she woulduse proceeds from her sales to support Palestine Action. Providing money one knows or has reasonable cause to suspect will or may be used for terrorism carries a maximum jail term of 14 years.Nicola Davies, the children’s laureate forWalesand author of The Day War Came, about a child refugee from war, said: “I can’t say that I am standing up for the children of Wales if I allow the children of Gaza to be murdered and mutilated without comment.“Gaza is smaller than the Welsh county of Flintshire, and it’s as if all Wales’s children were concentrated there and being bombed. So I support Sally Rooney in the stand she’s taken, and when my half-year royalties arrive shortly, I will donate to her the royalties from my book The Day War Came, whose sales have been boosted by the conflicts in Ukraine and Palestine.”View image in fullscreenNicola Davies.Photograph: Bronac McNeill/BronacMcNeillHaughton, who will be donating royalties from his UK book sales, said: “Palestine Action are the only organisation – or the most effective organisation – in the UK that that has had some success in stopping arms going to a genocide. I’m very sure that I will be on the right side of history.”Asked at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday whether he would review the ban on Palestine Action in light of Rooney’s situation, Andy Burnham said proscription “followed a rigorous and evidence-based process that came before this house, endorsed by parliament”.He said he would not comment further given that the supreme court is due to hear alegal challenge to the banon 4 and 5 November. The challenge is on the basis that the ban interferes disproportionately with the rights to freedom of expression and protest.Explore more on these topicsSally RooneyPalestine ActionIrelandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Interest rates unlikely to reach 4.75% by next summer, say City economists | Interest rates | The Guardian
description: Experts say Bank of England unlikely to increase rates by full percentage point – and could lower them by end of 2027
Author: Graeme Wearden
Headline: Experts say Bank of England unlikely to increase rates by full percentage point – and could lower them by end of 2027
Content: The Bank of England on Threadneedle Street, London. The monetary policy committee is expected to raise rates to 4% next month.Photograph: Corey Rudy/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe Bank of England on Threadneedle Street, London. The monetary policy committee is expected to raise rates to 4% next month.Photograph: Corey Rudy/ReutersInterest ratesInterest rates unlikely to reach 4.75% by next summer, say City economistsExperts say Bank of England  unlikely to increase rates by full percentage point – and could lower them by end of 2027Graeme WeardenSun 25 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 11.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFinancial markets are wrong to predict theBank of Englandwill raise UK interest rates by a full percentage point or more by next summer, City economists believe.According to market-implied interest rate expectations, the Bank is likely to raise interest rates at least four times over the next year, lifting the bank rate from3.75% todayto 4.75% by the end of July, and possibly to 5% – meaning five rises – by December 2027.But a number of City experts believe such a sharp tightening cycle is unlikely, given there is little sign thatthe rise in energy costsis pushing up other prices sharply.“If you look at the swaps market, and you look at what’s priced in for the Bank of England, you’ve got four rate hikes and then no cuts ever. And I think you’d be hard-pressed to find anybody that really agrees with that,” said James Smith, a developed markets economist at the Dutch bank ING.“By next spring, I think they [the Bank] could be sounding the all clear, and by the end of next year they could be cutting rates again,” Smith told a briefing in the City last week.Market-implied interest rates are calculated from the prices of a range of financial instruments, including derivatives such as “swaps”, to establish where traders think interest rates will be in future.Economists cite several reasons why market-implied interest rates expectations are high. One is that these expectations have been closely correlated with oil prices since the Iran war began.The higher oil prices have risen, the more rate increases have been priced in. An investor could be right that interest rates won’t rise as far as markets think, but if oil prices keep increasing in the meantime, they would face mark-to-market losses and potentially margin calls.“It can get pretty painful, so a lot of traders are quite reluctant to take this risk until there’s greater certainty about energy supply and the extent of inflation this winter,” said Smith.Many traders got burnt at the start of the current Middle East crisis, when most were positioned for further rate cuts this year, he said.Sanjay Raja, the chief UK economist at Deutsche Bank, also doubts that the Bank will raise rates as fast as the market pricing suggests.“I do not believe that any mainstream forecaster thinks the Bank of England will hike to 5% by the end of next year with the information set we have today,” Raja said. “It’s not to say it won’t happen. But based on current projections, it seems less likely.”He has calculated that a lot of the forecast interest rate rises is actually “baked-in risk premia” – where investors require an extra return to protect them from uncertainty or instability.“Once we strip that out, we have estimated that there is only really ~50bps [half a percentage point] of hikes pencilled in,” he said.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDeutsche Bank’s base case is for the Bank of England to take the bank rate to 4.25% by next February and then hold rates there until the end of 2027.The Bank of England is widely expected to raise interest rates to 4% at its next meeting, on 5 November, afterUK inflation rose further above its target in September to 3.5%.Last month Goldman Sachs said its probability-weighted forecast path for the bank rate remained “notably below market pricing”, although it does expect the Bank to raise rates to 4% next month.Morgan Stanley’s base case is for rises in November and February, with rates on hold thereafter. But in a new research note, it suggests there could be additional pressure to raise interest rates if the Low Pay Commission recommends a larger increase in the national living wage than expected.OxfordEconomics, a consultancy, also thinks the UK rate-raising cycle will be much less pronounced than what is currently priced into financial markets.“We forecast the [Bank’s] monetary policy committee will raise interest rates by 25bps [a quarter of a percentage point] at its November and February meetings, taking the bank rate to 4.25%. This is significantly below the peak in money market expectations, which currently point to the bank rate peaking between 4.75% and 5%,” they told clients last week.Even Huw Pill, the Bank’s hawkish chief economist, has suggested market expectations are running too hot. He told an International Monetary Fund meeting in Bangkok this month he was sceptical that the Bank would need to raise interest rates four times over the next year.Explore more on these topicsInterest ratesBank of EnglandEconomicsInflationnewsShareReuse this content

title: All aboard the TrainTok trend: spotters and staff boost rail content online | TikTok | The Guardian
description: Number of videos about British trains doubles in three months as creators find audiences interested in workings of railways
Author: George Francis Lee
Headline: Number of videos about British trains doubles in three months as creators find audiences interested in workings of railways
Content: Nathan Pinnock-James: ‘TikTok has really opened the door to really niche, specific topics coming on to your “for you” page.’Photograph: @networknathan InstagramView image in fullscreenNathan Pinnock-James: ‘TikTok has really opened the door to really niche, specific topics coming on to your “for you” page.’Photograph: @networknathan InstagramTikTokAll aboard the TrainTok trend: spotters and staff boost rail content onlineNumber of videos about British trains doubles in three months as creators find audiences interested in workings of railwaysGeorge Francis LeeSun 25 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThey are not just gathered at the end of your local train station platform any more. Now they are on your social media platforms too.Trainspotters have played a part in more than doubling the number of videos about British trains onTikTokin the last three months. According to the platform, the rise in rail content is also down to more people seeking information on cheap tickets, facts about the London Underground and tales from train staff.Posts tagged with #UKTrains have increased by 247% over recent months. The trend has even led to train staff moonlighting as content creators. Shamal Cain, who goes by the handle Tube Bellingham, is aTransportfor London employee who shares advice for commuters across the capital.According to Cain, scrollers are keen to learn more about topics they know little about but that affect their daily lives. “I realised how many people use London transport but don’t actually know a lot of information about it,” he said.Cain said many commuters were not fully aware of the TfL journey planner or how to avoid penalty fares from not tapping in and out. After noticing the gap, he thought: “Why don’t I just record giving information on what I do?”He said: “A majority of people commute through TfL. I think because a lot of people are doing that on a daily basis, they’re very engaged with information.”When Cain joined TikTok, direct messages came in fast, with followers asking him about alternative routes when services were down or for advice on getting a job with TfL.The popularity of train content has also risen thanks to enthusiast rail influencers such as Nathan Pinnock-James, who makes educational transport videos.“Since I started posting on TikTok, there’s been a lot of people that have the context of what a train is, how to use a train, but may not have noticed certain aspects of it,” said Pinnock-James, AKA Network Nathan. “They’re like: ‘Oh, wow! That’s quite shocking!’”He said obscure hobbies thrived on the app. “TikTok has really opened the door to really niche, specific topics coming on to your ‘for you’ page. It’s allowed people to find things that they didn’t know were interesting to them.”The 24-year-old said he found an audience online by creating videos about the best trainspotting locations, station openings, and explainers on how the shape of train wheels make DLR carriages wobble.Yazmin How, the head of emerging communities at TikTok UK, said: “It’s inspiring to see such a wide variety of creators, whether it’s professional train drivers, tube historians, young enthusiasts or comedy creators, using short-form video to make transport content entertaining and accessible to everyone.“The growth we’re seeing in #traintok reflects a real appetite among our UK community for authentic, educational storytelling that connects people, turning everyday travel into a shared community interest.”View image in fullscreenFrancis Bourgeois found popularity on TikTok in 2021.Photograph: Alex Lake/The ObserverShort video content about trains, sometimes called TrainTok, has been a growing part of the social media app for years. The media personalityFrancis Bourgeoisfound popularity on TikTok in 2021 after his videos of him reacting to British locomotives went viral.While human creators are jumping onboard, AI-generated videos – including clips that show high-speed trains and passengers falling out of tube carriages – are also contributing to the growth. In late 2025, TikTok revealed thatmore than 1bn videos that included AIwere hosted on its application.The company said its content operations team “works closely with creators and publishers to support the flow of high-quality content in the TikTok ecosystem”.TikTok, which announced the increase in train content during an annual trend report at its UK headquarters, said there was a growing interest in niche topics across its platform.It said searches about history in the UK had gone up by 50% in the last six months, and posts about the National Trust had doubled during the same period.How said: “The rise of train content on TikTok shows that even a niche passion can build highly engaged communities.”Explore more on these topicsTikTokSocial mediaRail transportTransportnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Why would I leave?’: Middlesbrough pushes back against ‘hardest place to grow up’ label | Middlesbrough | The Guardian
description: Teesside town has come out worst in children’s commissioner’s report, but residents say such rankings are demoralising and counterproductive
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: Teesside town has come out worst in children’s commissioner’s report, but residents say such rankings are demoralising and counterproductive
Content: Schoolchildren outside Middlesbrough town hall.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenSchoolchildren outside Middlesbrough town hall.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianMiddlesbrough‘Why would I leave?’: Middlesbrough pushes back against ‘hardest place to grow up’ labelTeesside town has come out worst in children’s commissioner’s report, but residents say such rankings are demoralising and counterproductiveMark BrownNorth of England correspondentSun 25 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“It’s disappointing, it’s just another kicking,” said a youth worker after the town in which they work was labelled as the hardest place in which to be a child inEngland.“It suggests our children are living unhappy lives,” said a teacher, who described her pupils as joyful.A clearly riled Chris Cooke, the mayor ofMiddlesbrough, said: “We get told a lot by people outside this place what we are. We know what we are. There is another side.”They were all reacting to a report published this week by the children’s commissioner, Rachel de Souza, titledThe Childhood Lottery, in which shedeclaredchildhood to be in “a state of emergency”.Youth services in parts of England in state of emergency, children’s commissioner saysRead moreThe report drew on a “landmark dataset” that “brings together 162 measures of children’s lives to build a comprehensive picture of the areas in England where it is the hardest to grow up”. The metrics included everything from child poverty to exclusion rates to poor air quality. And at the bottom was Middlesbrough.The Guardian visited the town this week and spoke to children and professionals about growing up there. No one denied there were many challenges, but equally no one thought the label was helpful.At a busy, buzzy youth club in the residential suburb of Coulby Newham, children aged 10 and up were making papier-mache Halloween decorations, cooking, playing table tennis and, outside on a strikingly mild October evening, getting ready to play dodge ball. “You’d think they were playing professionally,” said one volunteer.View image in fullscreenChildren at a club run by the Linx Youth Project in Coulby Newham, Middlesbrough.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianHannah*, 15, said her life was good but she knew it was not the same for others. “I love living in Middlesbrough. I love Albert Park and the Dorman Museum. I love going to the football. I love coming to youth club and making friends,” she said.A boy looked confused when asked if it was hard being a child in Middlesbrough. “I’m going to be here the rest of my life,” he said. “Why would I leave?”His friend let the side down by declaring: “I’m going to a hot country when I’m older … Hawaii. Or Zanzibar. Middlesbrough is too cold and scruffy.”Wayne Mason, a former soldier who is chief executive ofLinx Youth Project, which runs the club, said of the report: “We are disappointed. What it’s doing is attaching yet another label to Middlesbrough and its young people, and we already have many, many labels. It’s disappointing … all this negativity attached to the town.”View image in fullscreenWayne Mason, the Linx Youth Project chief executive.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianHe and the project’s deputy, Eilís Sexton, were at the club but could not stay long as the local Rotary club was about to give them a much-needed and much-appreciated cheque.Sexton was worried about the message the report sent out. “I’ve been thinking about young people who want to start their own families and how it’s going to make them feel, knowing that their child is going to have the ‘most difficult upbringing’ in the country? It is quite demoralising for them,” she said.She was born and raised in the area and studied at Teesside University. “I did move out of Middlesbrough for six months and I hated it,” she said.View image in fullscreenEilís Sexton, who says the report is ‘quite demoralising’.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianNeither of them disputed the statistics but they said there was another side. “Pride is the overriding thing that we see with the young people,” Mason said. “We know youngsters living in some of the most deprived areas of Middlesbrough, of which there are many, who don’t want to leave. They don’t want to leave because this is their home.“We always talk about deprivation and poverty and crime, but we don’t talk about community.”The report comes weeks after a collision on the A66 in which a car with five young people inside crashed into a police car carrying two police constables, killing the occupants of both vehicles.Some subsequent media portrayals painted a picture of an urban dystopia where gangs were in charge, but residents said the reality wasdifferent.It would have been hard for children to avoid media coverage about the deaths. Hannah said she had been past where it happened and burst into tears.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA sculpture in Middlesbrough’s Central Square.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianIn Middlesbrough town centre there is a huge open square and thecontemporary art gallery Mima, currently hosting the Turner prize. Next door is the town’s oppressive 1970s-built magistrates court building. Opposite is the grand Victorian town hall where Cooke, the elected Labour mayor, has his office.When it comes to the subject of it being hard to grow up in Middlesbrough, Cooke is better equipped than most to talk about it. He grew up in a violent family. His father took his own life when he was a teenager, and his mother’s mental health spiralled. He said that as a young boy he felt he had to be in charge of everything because he was terrified of being separated from his sister.Cooke had periods of not going to school and ended up in care. “I bounced around the system. People struggled to take me because I was quite difficult. I think that’s the polite version. What wouldn’t have helped me during any of that time is someone telling me that my life was difficult or that my life would get harder or that this place wouldn’t let me achieve the things I wanted to.”View image in fullscreenChris Cooke in his office at the town hall.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianHe said he remembered applying for jobs as an apprentice and being told not to include his TS6 postcode for fear of being judged. He not only included it, he made it bigger, he said. “This is why I’m angry. I don’t need people characterising Middlesbrough when we already know the challenges.”The fact that Cooke came out the other side was, he said, because of “beautiful” foster carers and other people around him. Middlesbrough is one of 16 councils in England that spendmore than 80%of their core funding on social care. Cooke said he was passionate about spending on youth services, reeling off a list of initiatives that included a fund to ensure there were youth clubs in every Middlesbrough postcode.View image in fullscreenPupils in a lesson at Newport primary school.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianA 15-minute walk from the town hall is Newport primary school, where the headteacher, Patricia Maxwell, showed the Guardian around. It has a particularly well-stocked, well-used library – Middlesbrough’sreading for pleasure statsare way over the national average.Maxwell had read the commissioner’s report. “It wasn’t telling me anything anything I didn’t already know,” she said. “But also it wasn’t telling people about all the positives that our children grow up with in Middlesbrough.”Stacey Carlisle, the school’s deputy head, agreed. “It just suggests that those children are living really quite unhappy lives, and that is not the case for our children,” she said. “They’re joyous and joyful, our children. Yes, there might be challenges at home for some, but it’s the same in affluent areas as well.”View image in fullscreenHeadteacher Patricia Maxwell: ‘We want our children to reach their full potential.’Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianBoth teachers said they would not want to work anywhere but Middlesbrough. “We’d like to do more,” Maxwell said. “We want our children to reach their full potential and to thrive and flourish and become the doctors or whatever it is that they want to be in the future.“But what we don’t want is them to feel labelled and told that they can’t go on and achieve those things. Just because you’re living in a challenging environment does not mean that that defines you.”*Name has been changedExplore more on these topicsMiddlesbroughChildrenYoung peopleNorth of EnglandEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Emirati diplomat who helped deliver aid to Gaza enters UN secretary general race  | United Nations | The Guardian
description: Lana Nusseibeh has Palestine’s endorsement but faces criticism over UAE’s human rights record and alleged funding of the RSF in Sudan
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Lana Nusseibeh has Palestine’s endorsement but faces criticism over UAE’s human rights record and alleged funding of the RSF in Sudan
Content: The UAE ambassador to the UN, Lana Nusseibeh, who has entered the race to succeed the current secretary general, António Guterres.Photograph: Amr Alfiky/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe UAE ambassador to the UN, Lana Nusseibeh, who has entered the race to succeed the current secretary general, António Guterres.Photograph: Amr Alfiky/ReutersUnited NationsEmirati diplomat who helped deliver aid to Gaza enters UN secretary general raceLana Nusseibeh has Palestine’s endorsement but faces criticism over UAE’s record on human rights and SudanPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorSun 25 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 15.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Emirati diplomat who as UAE ambassador to the UN helped secure the delivery of humanitarian aid to Gaza has entered the race as a late contender to succeedAntónio Guterresas the world body’s secretary general.Lana Nusseibeh, who is of Palestinian heritage, is widely noted for her advocacy of the Palestinian cause and the two-state solution and has won the endorsement of the state ofPalestine.She is however facing criticism over the UAE’s contested role in arming the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan, a group that has been accused of genocide by two successive US administrations.Nusseibeh, 48, has been one of the leading UAE diplomats denying reports that the UAE supplied weapons to RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo in defiance of a UN arms sales ban.A grouping of Latin American and Caribbean states, CELAC, has also sent a letter of objection to the security council, claiming her late entry came just as a consensus was emerging behind their region holding the UN top job.Fears mount that next UN chief will downgrade climate actionRead moreNusseibeh, who was educated at Cambridge University, was born in 1978 in Abu Dhabi, where her father, Zaki, had emigrated after the Arab-Israeli 1967 war made it difficult for him to return to his birthplace, Jerusalem.She is the niece of Sari Nusseibeh, a distinguished Palestinian intellectual and author of a widely admired book on Palestine, Once Upon a Country.She has justified her late – but widely predicted – entry into the race on the grounds that the UN security council appears to be close to deadlock on the six remaining candidates in the race, with no one as yet able to establish a clear lead after six rounds of voting, the latest on 16 October.The latest straw poll – the first in which it was revealed whether any of the five permanent members of the 15-strong UN security council objected to a candidate – ended with Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica holding the lead spot.But Grynspan faced objections from two unidentified permanent security council members, making it harder for her to claim she is a breakaway consensus candidate. She has support from nine security council members and objections from five. Guterres is due to stand down at the end of the yearOther candidates include: the Argentine diplomat Rafael Grossi; the UN envoy from Guyana, Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett; Olara Otunnu, a distinguished veteran Ugandan diplomat; and Ecuador’s former foreign minister María Fernanda Espinosa. Two previously declared candidates have pulled out.In her vision statement, Nusseibeh said: “At the heart of the UN sits a wager: that states will give up a little today to gain a great deal together over time.“States have not stopped needing to partner with one another, but they no longer trust that cooperation will yield sufficient returns. Rebuilding that trust, with faster, more certain, and more realistic results, is the work of the UN.”Brett McGurk, who served in the Biden administration as a top national security adviser, backed Nusseibeh for her work onGaza.“How did UAE become the largest global provider of humanitarian aid to Gaza, according to UN data? Because of Lana Nussaibeh – a diplomat who knows everyone and works with them … she would be an inspired choice for this impossible job,” he said.Cuts force World Food Programme to end support for half a million Palestinians in GazaRead moreNickolay Mladenov, the Bulgarian diplomat who heads Donald Trump’s Gaza Board of Peace, said Nusseibeh “has always understood that the UN works when someone is willing to systematically build the bridges nobody else wants to build”.He added: “In the Security Council [as UAE representative] she did that quietly and consistently and with great professionalism. She now has the chance to take that same spirit and ethos to the UN secretariat.”But there is a fierce backlash from human rights activists who point to the UAE’s domestic human rights record and its alleged funding of the RSF in Sudan, the group responsible for killing thousands, including in the capture of El Fasher in October last year.A January 2024 report by the UN panel of experts described allegations from sources in Chad and Darfur – including those of arms being smuggled into the RSF from the UAE – as credible.One of the strongest attacks on Nusseibeh’s candidacy has been mounted by Kenneth Roth, the former executive director of Human Rights Watch, over her denials of UAE provision of any “military, logistical, financial or political support to any faction in Sudan”. The UAE says it supports the formation of a civilian-led government in Sudan.Explore more on these topicsUnited NationsAntónio GuterresUnited Arab EmiratesMiddle East and north AfricaGazaPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Exiled opposition leader María Corina Machado returns to Venezuela | Venezuela | The Guardian
description: Nobel peace prize winner’s return after almost a year in exile is unlikely to please interim president Delcy Rodríguez
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Nobel peace prize winner’s return after almost a year in exile is unlikely to please interim president Delcy Rodríguez
Content: Upon her return after almost a year in exile, María Corina Machado attended mass in Barquisimeto.Photograph: Vente Venezuela Press/ReutersView image in fullscreenUpon her return after almost a year in exile, María Corina Machado attended mass in Barquisimeto.Photograph: Vente Venezuela Press/ReutersVenezuelaExiled opposition leader María Corina Machado returns to VenezuelaNobel peace prize winner’s return after almost a year in exile is unlikely to please interim president Delcy RodríguezTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroSun 25 Oct 2026 15.56 EDTFirst published on Sun 25 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Venezuelan opposition leader,María Corina Machado, has announced she has returned to Venezuela almost a year after she left the country to receive the Nobel peace prize.“I’m here. With you,” she wrote on X on Sunday lunchtime.Her close ally Edmundo González, who is in exile, confirmed her arrival. “Venezuela! I am thrilled to announce to you that our leader, my dear María Corina, is on Venezuelan soil,” he posted on social media.“Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!” he said, adding that he too would soon return.It was not immediately clear how Machado, 59, had managed to return to Venezuela but footage on social media showed she was in Barquisimeto, the capital of Lara state, which is about 220 miles west of the capital, Caracas.Images showed her surrounded by supporters holding mobile phones in the Sanctuary of the Divine Shepherdess church.View image in fullscreenMachado at the Sanctuary of the Divine Shepherdess in Barquisimeto.Photograph: Jose Miguel Alarcon/EPAFootage posted on social mediaby her close ally Pedro Urruchurtu showed hundreds of supporters gathered outside the church to greet her, shouting: “Freedom! Freedom! Freedom!”TheTrump administrationhad reportedly opposed Machado’s return, believing her presence would complicate the cosy relationship it has struck up with the interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, since abducting her former boss, Nicolás Maduro, in January.Nicolás Maduro tells New York court new torture allegations are ‘false’Read moreMachado and Rodríguez are political arch-rivals.Machado slipped out of Venezuela last December – a few weeks before Maduro’s capture – and in recent months has reportedly made more than half a dozen failed attempts to return home, including after the devastating earthquake that hit the northern coast in June.View image in fullscreenMachado is surrounded by supporters in Barquisimeto on Sunday.Photograph: Jesus Hernandez/APAfter Maduro was seized, many had expected Donald Trump to give Machado his blessing to take power. Her movement is widely believed to have beaten Maduro in the 2024 presidential election, but he refused to hand over power.Instead the US president embraced Rodríguez, Maduro’s vice-president, who now governs a country widely seen as a US protectorate.Machado has repeatedly heaped praise on Trump for launching the operation to remove Maduro, and gave him her 2025 Nobel peace prize medal, which she had been awarded for her peaceful challenge to Venezuela’s authoritarian government.‘It’s utter surrealism’: Venezuela’s Chavistas lament government’s embrace of TrumpRead moreAsked by reporters on Sunday about her return, Trump said: “I don’t know anything about it, but I think she’s a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel prize, so how can I say anything else?“I hope she’s safe. She’s a very nice woman. But we’re doing very well in Venezuela.”The US secretary of state​, Marco Rubio, claimed credit for creating the conditions that allowed Machado’s safe return after 10 months in exile.Her return “is the direct result of the U​S​-supported reconciliation talks which has already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile”, he said.From Barquisimeto, Machado headed east through the ​state of Yaracuy towards Caracas in a convoy of vehicles.Images released by aidesshow her reaching out from a car’s sunroof towards dozens of supporters who had gathered at the roadside to see her.Members of Venezuela’s government have long hinted that Machado would be arrested if she tried to return as a result of her years-long struggle for political change. But there was no sign of the security services bothering her on Sunday as she moved towards the capital, perhaps suggesting Washington had sanctioned her return and instructed Rodríguez’s government not to react.Machado has called for fresh presidential elections to be held by July 2027, but it is unclear whether the Trump administration supports that timeline given the lucrative partnership it has struck up with Rodríguez.Trump announced what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history” with Venezuela in August, subsequently describing the agreement as the spoils of January’s brief “war”.Explore more on these topicsVenezuelaMaría Corina MachadoAmericasDelcy RodríguezUS foreign policyNicolás MaduroTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Portuguese police with dogs and batons dismantle housing protest camps | Portugal | The Guardian
description: More than 30 people arrested as officers clear at least 100 tents in central Lisbon and about 50 in Porto
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: More than 30 people arrested as officers clear at least 100 tents in central Lisbon and about 50 in Porto
Content: A police officer in riot gear removes a tent from the protest camp in Lisbon’s Rossio Square.Photograph: José Sena Goulão/EPAView image in fullscreenA police officer in riot gear removes a tent from the protest camp in Lisbon’s Rossio Square.Photograph: José Sena Goulão/EPAPortugalPortuguese police with dogs and batons dismantle housing protest campsMore than 30 people arrested as officers clear at least 100 tents in central Lisbon and about 50 in PortoAshifa Kassamand agenciesSun 25 Oct 2026 11.32 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 11.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice inPortugalhave dismantled housing protest camps in Lisbon and Porto, baton-charging campaigners in the early hours of Sunday and arresting more than 30 people.The raids were the latest incident in days of clashes between police and campaigners who – inspired bysimilar campsin Spain – had sought to pitch tents in central squares to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis.Dozens of officers, some with dogs, moved shortly after 2am on Sunday to clear out the more than 100 tents that had sprung up in Lisbon’s Rossio Square. Police said they had also taken down a smaller camp of about 50 tents in Porto’s Dom João I Square.The camp in the heart of Lisbon had been set up after thousands of people marched along one of the Portuguese capital’s main thoroughfares to rail against housing prices that have soared past average incomes in the country.Police described their actions on Sunday as proportionate and said they had earlier urged people to leave the camps of their own accord. The operations in the two cities led to the arrests of 31 people for disobedience and 171 structures were removed, police said on social media. Eleven people were injured, including three police officers.View image in fullscreenRiot police arrest a woman in Lisbon.Photograph: José Sena Goulão/EPAReuters reported that 25 people detained in Lisbon had been released with orders to appear in court on Monday.The group Casa Para Viver (A Home to Live In) contested the police figures, saying the raids had left more than 20 people injured as police moved into the camps with batons, dogs and rubber bullets.“Choosing the early morning to deploy police dogs and fire rubber bullets at people who were sleeping or peacefully protesting is a political decision,” the group said in a statement as it called for further protests on Wednesday. “It shows that this government would rather crack down on those who speak out against the housing crisis than solve the crisis itself.”Fabian Figueiredo, an MP with the Left Bloc, described the police action as a “wound that had been inflicted” on the country’s democracy. “Fighting for a home is a right. So is peaceful protest. The constitution guarantees both,” he said on social media. “Let’s keep going – for the sake of our future.”The housing protest camps in Portugal trace back to early October when campaigners began pitching tents in Porto, prompting police toclearthem out. Similar actions soon began sprouting up in Lisbon, leading todozens of arrestsand reports of injuries as police repeatedly clashed with campaigners.As European citiesgrapple with a waveof discontent, much of the focus in Spain and Portugal has been on housing costs that have priced many local people out of the market.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHouse prices in Portugal havemore than doubledsince 2017, while those seeking to rent have struggled with prices that have nearly doubled, fuelling one of Europe’smost acute home affordability crises.Residents have long told ofbearing the bruntof a market that has surged as a result of liberalisation, the issuing of so-called golden visas, digital nomad schemes and the proliferation of short-term rentals.Campaigners have called on the centre-right government to scrap proposed legislation that would make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases. The legislation recently passed a first parliamentary reading.In Spain, the sprawling housing camp in the centre of Madridmarked its fourth week on Saturday, becoming one of the most tangible symbols of a widespread protest movement that hasled to early general electionson 29 November.With contributions from Reuters and Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsPortugalProtestEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: US south-west braces for more storms after enduring days of rain and flooding | US weather | The Guardian
description: More inclement weather forecast in rain-soaked Four Corners region after evacuations and rescues last week
Author: Coral Murphy Marcos
Headline: More inclement weather forecast in rain-soaked Four Corners region after evacuations and rescues last week
Content: People traverse a cordoned-off street as floodwaters from the San Juan River rise in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, on Friday.Photograph: Emilija Jefremova/ReutersView image in fullscreenPeople traverse a cordoned-off street as floodwaters from the San Juan River rise in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, on Friday.Photograph: Emilija Jefremova/ReutersUS weatherUS south-west braces for more storms after enduring days of rain and floodingMore inclement weather forecast in rain-soaked Four Corners region after evacuations and rescues last weekCoral Murphy Marcosand agenciesSun 25 Oct 2026 15.02 EDTFirst published on Sun 25 Oct 2026 13.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnother round of heavy showers and thunderstorms were expected to hit the south-west US on Sunday after the region endured days of rain that forced evacuations, water rescues and multi-million-dollar damage.The National Weather Serviceissueda flood watch for much of the Four Corners – the meeting point of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah – even as local officials forecast further receding of swollen rivers that surged since rains picked up on Wednesday.About 4ft (1 meter) of water flooded the home of Shane Ferrari, the sheriff of San Juan county,New Mexico. He said the area’s situation was stable on Sunday, but he and other residents were trying to clean up and deal with damage.The New Mexico governor, Michelle Lujan Grisham, said in a statement on Saturday that law enforcement had reported hundreds of water rescues between the cities of Farmington and Bloomfield.View image in fullscreenFlooding in the Gould Wash drainage watercourse in Hurricane, Utah, on Thursday.Photograph: Landon Christensen/AP“Families in Bloomfield and Farmington spent the night on rooftops watching the river flood their homes, and our national guard and state police crews have been bringing them to safety,” said Lujan Grisham. “Right now, our focus is saving lives. If you’re told to evacuate, go. Once the water recedes, the state will do everything in its power to help San Juan county families rebuild.”“No deaths have been reported,” she added.The San Juan River in Farmington on Friday ran 2 ft above its previousrecordset in 1909.San Juan county spokesperson Devin Neeley said the county did not have official numbers on damage to homes or the number of people evacuated, but he was not aware of any loss of life.View image in fullscreenPickup trucks are submerged along Highway 160 in South Fork, Colorado, on Friday.Photograph: South Fork Fire Rescue/APNeeley said the flood waters were receding but left mud and silt, much of which has been contaminated with sewage because of failures at waste plants. There were still power outages affecting multiple areas, and it would probably be a few days until residents got their power back on.“It’s a pretty active disaster zone,” he said. “We’re not on the downswing by any means.”The flooding is just the latest from two months of on-and-off heavy rain caused by tropical moisture coming ashore from the Pacific. After months of drought, other recent deadly flooding struck theGrand Canyonand areas of New Mexico.New Mexico has been hit with back-to-back weather events this weekend. A tornado struck Santa Fe on Saturday, damaging at least eight houses, including to roof collapses, according to astatementby the city of Santa Fe. No injuries were reported.Explore more on these topicsUS weatherFloodingNew MexicoColoradoArizonaUtahExtreme weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘You can’t bring in robots’: the leather firm handmaking everything from wallets to cigar cases | Manufacturing sector | The Guardian
description: In the third article in a series on high-end British manufacturing, we visit the Ettinger factory in Walsall
Author: Sarah Butler
Headline: In the third article in a series on high-end British manufacturing, we visit the Ettinger factory in Walsall
Content: Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenComposite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesManufacturing sector‘You can’t bring in robots’: the leather firm handmaking everything from wallets to cigar casesIn the third article in a series on high-end British manufacturing, we visit the Ettinger factory in Walsall‘Our town is making jeans again’: reviving jobs and skills in WalesFrom feathers to pet portraits, Rolls-Royce rides high on custom crazeSarah ButlerSun 25 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“It is all down to attention to detail and everything we do is based around that.”Gary Billingham is demonstrating how the 28 pieces which make up an Ettinger wallet are cut from leather using a hydraulic press by the small team at one of Walsall’s last remaining leather goods factories. The edges of the pieces are thinned down so they are ready to be turned, glued and stitched together by hand.Billingham has been at the factory near Birmingham since the 1980s, when “there were three pages in the Yellow Pages” business directory listing leather factories in theWest Midlandstown. “They were everywhere. It has gone from that to about five factories. It is more like a cottage industry.”View image in fullscreenGary Billingham, factory manager at Ettinger, a family-owned luxury leather goods maker based in Walsall.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianAbout 20 people, mostly women, work carefully and precisely in Ettinger’s factory – a site of leather goods production since the 1890s – with a handful more doing work from home.Robert Ettinger, the company’s chief executive, says the vast majority of its manufacturing process has to be done by hand. “You can’t bring in robots.”He still owns the British brand founded in 1934 by his father, who turned to selling and manufacturing leather goods in the UK after fleeing Nazi Germany via Paris and a stint in the film industry.Ettinger began making wallets and sourcing leather items, and today the company supplies a range of luxury goods to wealthy customers, including King Charles and Queen Camilla whose royal warrants they hold.The company’s bestseller is still a wallet, but they also sell leather pill containers, cigar cases, picture frames and various accoutrements for dog owners, from treat cases to dog-waste bag holders, all of which can be personalised with initials.View image in fullscreenRobert Ettinger, son of the leatherware maker’s founder, in the Ettinger showroom in London.Photograph: Sean Smith/The GuardianThe brand sits in a niche between the big label luxury and high street with a British hand-crafted leather tote bag for just under £800 compared with more than £2,000 charged by a big swinger such as Louis Vuitton.An array of machines resembling pastry-cutters are used to punch out leather shapes that are then glued by hand with a brush to build up each item with trims and linings.The tiny seams around the leather edges are thinned down with a shaving machine, known as a skiver, and turned inward before being stitched with a sewing machine. Each piece is then carefully checked and trimmed using a scalpel and sharp scissors before being polished and wrapped in tissue paper.View image in fullscreenAll manner of leather goods are made at Ettinger, from pill containers to cigar cases, bags and various accoutrements for dog owners.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianGerry Ettinger, the founder, began by using an array of manufacturers before buying his original factory at the heart of London’s leather-working trade in Clerkenwell near the Smithfield meat market in the 1950s.Robert Ettinger says: “When I was a kid, there were dozens and dozens of small factories, making leather goods, and they all specialised. One made suitcases, and one made handbags, and one made wallets.”As the area gentrified in the 1990s, the Ettingers decided to move and bought out one of their suppliers, James Homer in Walsall, established in 1890. It was then mostly making corporate promotional leather goods. Staff were trained up and new machinery brought in to make the high standard of goods expected by Ettinger’s new international clientele led by the Japanese.Walsall has been a centre of leather-working from the middle ages. It was focused on saddle-making with more than 100 firms operating in the town by the end of the 19th century.As the use of horses in everyday life declined, the factories began expanding into making other leather goods, ranging from bicycle saddles, car upholstery and furnishings to bags, gloves and purses.The industry thrived during the first world war when there was high demand for military saddle wear but began to suffer in the 1950s as it faced competition from abroad and from human-made alternatives to leather.Still, by 1970 there were about 50 leather goods manufacturers in Walsall, and the town produced around half of the British-made fancy leather goods, according to the Wolverhampton Heritage and History Society.View image in fullscreenProducts for dog lovers, such as keyrings, are popular.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianTracy, expertly glueing and building Ettinger’s elaborate cigar cases before they are sewn, has been at the company for 15 years and working in the leather industry since she left school 40 years ago.“When we were that age it was all leather work. You could walk out of one job and into another on the same day,” she says.That history is recognised in street names and the local Saddlers Centre shopping mall and there is a leather skills training centre which offers courses in bridle making.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionLauner, whose customers included the late Queen Elizabeth II, J&E Sedgwick, the bridle maker, and small leather goods firm E Hulme, founded in the 1920s, continue to make leather goods near Ettinger’s factory. However, all employ only small numbers of people and the local industry is a shadow of its former self.Even Walsall’s leather museum, housed in a former factory that dates back to the 1880s, is now closed amid disputed plans to move it to a modern city centre site.View image in fullscreenLeather sewn at an industrial sewing machine.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianThat reflects a rapid decline in the leather goods manufacturing industry across the UK with just 7,000 people employed in it today compared with 37,000 30 years ago.Ettinger itself had to cut its staff numbers by about seven after the Covid pandemic hit trade.Robert Ettinger says he never really considered shifting production overseas, despite most of his customers coming from outside the UK.“We might have made more profit, but then we would also have much more competition because when you’ve got 50 companies bringing in a purse from the far east, then it’s all about price.”He says the gambit is now paying off as a younger generation increasingly appreciates British craft, with online sales up 30% on last year and UK sales up by a fifth, with shoppers aged from their early 20s.“A lot of younger people are now thinking that they want something that will last, that won’t go out of fashion in three months’ time. Yes, it costs more, but it lasts for 15 or 20 years, and can be repaired. I’ve just repaired my wallet which is 17 years old.View image in fullscreenThe Ettinger brand.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The Guardian“Our products are affordable luxury. A purse or wallet for £200 or £300, it’s the price of some trainers and they’re not made in the UK. So it’s not out of reach of most people.”Still, expanding production in the UK might be tricky. Billingham says it is hard to find and train new staff. Even those who attend Walsall’s Leather Skills Centre are more likely to go into making car upholstery or saddles.“We are all getting old now, that’s a problem, we are from 40s to 60s. If you find someone working for somebody else you take them,” says Billingham.“To take five to 10 people on would be great but the reality is they are not there.”View image in fullscreenBlue leather being guided through a sewing machine at Ettinger’s workshop.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianRobert Ettinger says the UK should look at how young people are trained into the trade in mainland Europe, where he was sent by his father to serve an apprenticeship.“They spend a few years really learning a trade, everything from making leather goods, to being a chimney sweep, or a butcher, or baker. When you pass all the apprenticeship exams, you then go on to do more and become a master, a Meister. We don’t have that here. So, it’s harder for us to take on younger people.”He is optimistic things could change. “People might go into jobs which they don’t really enjoy or get bored of doing, and then they join us, and, you know, it’s like a family in our factory.”Explore more on these topicsManufacturing sectorLuxury goods sectorWalsallCraftVocational educationWest MidlandsApprenticeshipsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Nationwide to slash 275 jobs in latest round of cuts since takeover of Virgin Money | Nationwide | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Bosses tell staff cuts part of effort to ‘simplify’ operations and ‘remove duplication’ across wider workforce
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Exclusive: Bosses tell staff cuts part of effort to ‘simplify’ operations and ‘remove duplication’ across wider workforce
Content: Nationwide said no customer-facing staff would be affected. The cuts are to fall across its retail division and are on top of the 600 job losses announced in June.Photograph: PhotoEdit/AlamyView image in fullscreenNationwide said no customer-facing staff would be affected. The cuts are to fall across its retail division and are on top of the 600 job losses announced in June.Photograph: PhotoEdit/AlamyNationwideNationwide to slash 275 jobs in latest round of cuts since takeover of Virgin MoneyExclusive: Bosses tell staff cuts part of effort to ‘simplify’ operations and ‘remove duplication’ across wider workforceKalyeena MakortoffandMark SweneySun 25 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 11.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNationwide building society is slashing another 275 jobs in the latest round of cuts since bank bosses pushed through a £2.9bntakeover of Virgin Money.Bosses made the announcement to staff on Wednesday, saying it was part of efforts to simplify the bank’s operations and “remove duplication” after absorbing thousands of staff in to the group’s wider workforce.The cuts are to fall across its retail division, including those working on mortgages, as well as in HR, the chief operating officer’s office, customer operations, communications and finance.Nationwide said no customer-facing staff would be affected, which appears to be in line with its pledge to keep its 700 branches open until at least 2030.It follows closely behind the last round of job losses, which wereannounced in June and affected 600 staff.Commenting on the latest cuts, a spokesperson for the lender said: “As we integrate Virgin Money into Nationwide, we’re making a limited number of changes. No customer-facing colleagues are at risk and we’re supporting those affected, including through retraining and redeployment.”The Virgin Money takeover was a boon for the building society sector when it was first announced two years ago, having marked a rare moment when a member-owned lender – traditionally focused on mortgages and savings – was snapping up a commercial high street bank. However, the move also proved controversial, with Nationwide havingrefused to give members a vote on the deal.Virgin Money had more than 7,000 staff around the time Nationwide formalised its takeover in late 2024, when the building society had about 18,000 of its own employees, accordingto its 2025 annual report. Its total workforce now sits at roughly 27,000 today.Executives had confirmed back in 2024 thatthere would be “limited workforce changes”to deal with overlapping roles but that they would undergo a formal review of its employee base in the years that followed.A Nationwide spokesperson stressed that the cuts were not linked to any growing use of AI.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOn Thursday, Barclays revealed it wascutting 5,000 jobs as part of cost-saving plansdriven by advances in AI, illustrating the real-life fallout linked to the rapidly evolving technology.Nationwide is to release its half-year financial results on 19 November.Explore more on these topicsNationwideJob lossesBanks and building societiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Volkswagen to build $4bn Audi SUV factory in US despite job cuts at home | Volkswagen (VW) | The Guardian
description: VW investment, creating 4,500 jobs in Georgia, comes amid Trump’s damaging tariffs, intense Chinese competition and costly shift towards EVs
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: VW investment, creating 4,500 jobs in Georgia, comes amid Trump’s damaging tariffs, intense Chinese competition and costly shift towards EVs
Content: Audi’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a rally on Saturday to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia.Photograph: Friso Gentsch/EPAView image in fullscreenAudi’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a rally on Saturday to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia.Photograph: Friso Gentsch/EPAVolkswagen (VW)Volkswagen to build $4bn Audi SUV factory in US despite job cuts at homeVW investment, creating 4,500 jobs in Georgia, comes amid Trump’s damaging tariffs, intense Chinese competition and costly shift towards EVsJasper Jollyand agenciesSun 25 Oct 2026 09.43 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 11.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAudi has said it will spend $4bn (£3bn) to build its first factory in the US, as its parent company, Volkswagen, struggles with the impact of steep tariffs imposed by Donald Trump.The German brand’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a campaign rally on Saturday night to announce the factory in Macon,Georgia, in an unusual move by a big European brand just days before the US midterm elections.The Republican party under Trump is trying to retain control of both houses of Congress, butit is polling poorlyas it struggles withhigher fuel prices caused by Trump’s war on Iran, as well as his trade war against some of the US’s biggest trading partners.Volkswagen to cut further 50,000 jobs as it ends row with union over revival planRead moreTrump has long tried to convince voters that his tariffs are helping to increase the number of manufacturing jobs in the US, and has seized on any new factory investments. However, US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year.Audi, Volkswagen’s most important premium brand, hassuffered from Trump’s 15% tariffs on importsfrom the EU as well as the president’s efforts to cut sales of battery electric vehicles in favour of petrol cars.It said it aims to build 200,000 SUVs at the new US factory, creating 4,500 jobs. The factory will build the Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, shifting some production from Bratislava in Slovakia.Volkswagen has said Trump’s tariffs cost it up to €5bn(£4.2bn)a year, before the impact of lower sales. The German manufacturer this month said it was still struggling with “continued high pressure from import tariffs”. The carmaker was also forced to shift some production of its cheapest cars, such as the Jetta saloon and Taos SUV, from Mexico to the US.The new factory may add to tensions in Germany, where Volkswagen has started tocut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the job losses on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as the tariffs and a need to invest heavily in the shift to EVs for markets other than the US.Döllner said he accepted the invitation to speak at Trump’s rally out of respect for the US.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We are planning to bring our ⁠biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” he said at the event. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.”Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, told investors in July that “US tariffs create a significant burden and restrict international trade”.However, the group has said there is still demand in the US for Audi’s large petrol SUVs, and it is planning its largest-ever SUV, the Q9, with the American market in mind. Large petrol-powered SUVs have played abig role in global carbon emissions.Explore more on these topicsVolkswagen (VW)Automotive industryGermanyUS economyTrump administrationTrump tariffsEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m not someone who has sex to music. I like uncomfortable silence’: Katherine Ryan’s honest playlist | Katherine Ryan | The Guardian
description: The comedian unashamedly loves the Spice Girls’ Wannabe and cries to Boyz II Men, but which novelty song changed her life?
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The comedian unashamedly loves the Spice Girls’ Wannabe and cries to Boyz II Men, but which novelty song changed her life?
Content: Katherine Ryan … ‘If I like a song, I just like it. I have no shame’Photograph: Suki Dhanda/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKatherine Ryan … ‘If I like a song, I just like it. I have no shame’Photograph: Suki Dhanda/The GuardianHonest playlistKatherine Ryan‘I’m not someone who has sex to music. I like uncomfortable silence’: Katherine Ryan’s honest playlistThe comedian unashamedly loves the Spice Girls’ Wannabe and cries to Boyz II Men, but which novelty song changed her life?As told toRich PelleySun 25 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song I fell in love withMy mother would sing and dance and cook and clean in the kitchen, as many 80s moms did, to divas like Madonna and Paula Abdul. Material Girl made me think: “This is who I want to be.”The first single I boughtI bought three records at the same time – Jagged Little Pill by Alanis Morissette, a Sheryl Crow single and Waterfalls by TLC – from Sam the Record Man in Sarnia, Ontario, with money I’d saved up from doing chores around the house. My uncle was always trying to influence me with Canadian music, and he wasn’t wrong for doing so.The song I do at karaokeProbably Son of a Preacher Man. Although I think karaoke is the best way to let many people know straight away that you are an attention-seeking alcoholic, so I do try to stay away from it.The song I inexplicably know every lyric toGive me a wine, and somehow I know all the words to the entire score of Hamilton, even though I’ve only seen it twice. [Sings Satisfied] “I’m a girl in a world in which my only job is to marry rich. My father has no sons, so I’m the one who has to social climb for one. I’m the oldest and the wittiest and the gossip in New York City is insidious.”The best song to play at a partyAnything early-2000s hip-hop or R&B, like Gasolina by Daddy Yankee.The song I can no longer listen toWhat I Am by Will.i.am with Sesame Street. It makes me cry because he’s giving positive affirmations to young kids about being strong and being the best version of yourself. I can’t even get through it because it makes me so sad. I start worrying that these kids need Sesame Street and Will.i.am to tell them that they’re special.The song I secretly like, but tell everyone I hateIf I like a song, I just like it. Every Spice Girls song – I have no shame. I don’t need to be a music snob. I would crank up Wannabe any time, anywhere.The best song to have sex toI’m not someone who has sex to music. I like uncomfortable silence. But if I had to choose, Let Me Love You by Mario.The song that changed my lifeThe Chanukah Song and Ode to My Car by Adam Sandler. I would have been about 11 or 12, and it was the first time I thought: “Oh, wait a minute. These can be funny and make music. You can make trauma a little bit funny, or at least be trauma-adjacent. You can make darker subjects funny.” I listened to his album over and over.The song that gets me up in the morningCurrently, I’m So Happy by Ms Rachel because we have so many small children. It has a really great message. I really love what’s available for kids now.The song that makes me cryWater Runs Dry by Boyz II Men. I wanted to use it in The Duchess. It’s meant to be about a romantic partner, but whenever I heard it I thought of my daughter growing up. It’s about two people not communicating properly any more and wanting to get back to where they started, and I thought about that relationship changing as she got older.The song I want played at my funeralThong Song by Sisqó.Katherine Ryan has partnered with meal-subscription service Gousto.
