title: TV tonight: a horny drama stuffed with sex in a car, toilet and … city farm  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Adultery is a moreish series starring Romola Garai and Dominic Cooper. Plus, hit gang thriller This City Is Ours is back. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Adultery is a moreish series starring Romola Garai and Dominic Cooper. Plus, hit gang thriller This City Is Ours is back. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Risky Business … Romola Garai and Dominic Cooper in Adultery on ITV1.Photograph: Thomas Wood/ITVView image in fullscreenRisky Business … Romola Garai and Dominic Cooper in Adultery on ITV1.Photograph: Thomas Wood/ITVTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: a horny drama stuffed with sex in a car, toilet and … city farmAdultery is a moreish series starring Romola Garai and Dominic Cooper. Plus, hit gang thriller This City Is Ours is back. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Phil Harrison,Graeme Virtue,Jack SealeandEllen E JonesSun 25 Oct 2026 02.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 02.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdultery9pm, ITV1“Attraction plus obstacle equals excitement.” This is the risky life motto that bored, put-upon personal trainer Beth (Romola Garai) takes to heart after her best mate unexpectedly dies. Wife to a useless husband and mother to an ungrateful son, it doesn’t take much for handsome doctor Tom (Dominic Cooper) to catch her eye. But Tom also happens to be the married father of Beth’s son’s new girlfriend. Created and written by Bafta winner Danny Brocklehurst (Shameless, Brassic), the addictive drama follows a steamy, sex-packed affair over six episodes – and the fallout from it. While the opener remains pretty PG, we’re promised trysts in cars, toilets … and a city farm.Hollie RichardsonKevin McCloud’s Listed Britain7pm, Channel 4This exploration of Britain’s listed buildings acts as a polemic, too: why do the buildings we choose to preserve nod towards power and grandeur? Kevin McCloud visits a few (including the Palace of Westminster, Hereford Cathedral and Chatsworth House) but also wonders why many apparently humbler buildings, including pubs, aren’t protected.Phil HarrisonThis City Is Ours9pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenHoliday from hell … This City Is Ours on BBC One.Photograph: BBC/Left Bank Pictures/James StackThe hit Liverpool gang drama remains on top form in its second series. Picking up where it left off, Michael (the brilliant James Nelson-Joyce) and Diana (Hannah Onslow) are enjoying the quiet life in Spain, when a Colombian cartel member intrudes with questions about his brother Ricardo. Back in Liverpool, a tense dinner party, an even more tense car wash and an unexpected face from the past stir trouble among the gang.HRMortimer & Whitehouse: Gone Fishing9pm, BBC TwoSeries nine of the laid-back angling odyssey gets off to a bittersweet start as it features the final appearance of loyal terrier Ted, who passed away earlier this year. As ever, he threatens to steal the show, frolicking around Paul on the banks of the Ribble in Lancashire and nosing his way into Bob’s hotpot.Graeme VirtueApocalypse9pm, Channel 4The doomy but silly reality experiment concludes, with its two rival groups of survivors having reached some sort of accord. While that’s jeopardised by someone running their mouth during a shared feast, the exploration of new territory offers a big clue about how to end the experiment by securing evacuation.Jack SealeA Course Called Ireland9.30pm, BBC TwoBill Murray is buying sweets in Cork when Margaret stops to ask for his autograph: “Do you still do the acting now or anything?” She narrates this rather lovely series following the Hollywood star around Ireland as he reconnects to his ancestors on a golf tour with journalist and friend Tom Coyne. After being mistaken for another Hollywood actor, he plays his first golf in Kinsale.HRFilm choiceThe Boston Strangler,10.10pm, Talking Pictures TVView image in fullscreenCreepy and kooky … Tony Curtis with Henry Fonda in The Boston Strangler.Photograph: RONALD GRANTTony Curtis turns up halfway through, playing against type as the now DNA-linked killer, Albert DeSalvo. The real stars, though, are the dogged detectives of Boston PD, featuring a host of reassuringly craggy-faced character actors such as George Kennedy and Murray Hamilton, and headed up by John S Bottomly (Henry Fonda). They run down seemingly every creep and kook in eastern Massachusetts before eventually landing on their man. Director Richard Fleischer’s use of split-screen adds to both the pacing and the period feel.Ellen E JonesLive sportInternational One-Day Cricket: Pakistan v England, 7.30am, Sky Sports Main EventHarry Brook captains England in their third Tri-Series match in Lahore. England v Sri Lanka is on Thu at 8am.Premier League Football: Man United v BournemouthSun, 12.30pm, Sky Sports Main EventSunderland v Leeds is at 4.25pm.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lara Croft is 30! We look at the video game icon’s biggest blunders | Games | The Guardian
description: We all know the highlights of the tomb raider’s storied career – but what about the lowlights? We dig deep to unearth the archaeologist’s less glorious moments
Author: Ellie Gibson
Headline: We all know the highlights of the tomb raider’s storied career – but what about the lowlights? We dig deep to unearth the archaeologist’s less glorious moments
Content: Thirty years of kicking ass … Lara Croft in Tomb Raider IV-VI Remastered, 2025.Photograph: AspyrView image in fullscreenThirty years of kicking ass … Lara Croft in Tomb Raider IV-VI Remastered, 2025.Photograph: AspyrGamesLara Croft is 30! We look at the video game icon’s biggest blundersWe all know the highlights of the tomb raider’s storied career – but what about the lowlights? We dig deep to unearth the archaeologist’s less glorious momentsEllie GibsonSun 25 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHappy birthday, Lara! This month marks 30 years since Ms Croft first swan-dived into our lives with her unique blend of athletic prowess, archaeological expertise and giant knockers. More than 100 million Tomb Raider games have been sold since. We all remember the good times: the bold design and sheer playability of the original titles; the establishment of Lara as a 90s icon, embodying both lads’ mag culture and girl power; the way she made games cool, even appearing on the cover of the Face. We’ve had blockbuster movies, big budget reboots, andshiny reissues. And who could forget the time we got topowerwash her house?But no one gets to 30 without a few skeletons in the closet – or in Lara’s case, butlers in the freezer. So here’s a look at the darker parts of her past.Lara Croft, corporate shillView image in fullscreenLara Croft sells Lucozade in 1999.Photograph: Core DesignLara’s image has been used to hawk a multitude of products over the years, from cereal and soft drinks to reasonably priced Spanish hatchbacks. Low points include the 1999 promo for a German women’s magazine in which Lara tells us what she really, really wants isn’t the Dagger of Xian or the MacGuffin of Atlantis, but abig meringuey wedding dress.See also the weirdDreamcast advertwhere Lara talks about the console as if it’s a jar of anti-ageing moisturiser. This led an entire generation of women to try reducing the appearance of fine lines by rubbing Sega hardware on their faces. Because she’s worth it? Let’s hope the money was.Murdered by her makersView image in fullscreenOne last adventure … Tomb Raider: Chronicles.Photograph: Eidos InteractiveBack in 1996, no one predicted how successful this quiet game about a posh archaeologist made by a small team in Derby would be. But once publisher Eidos realised it was in possession of a goose that laid golden eggs, it launched an intensive battery farming operation. Core Design was forced to churn out a newTomb Raidertitle every year.Four games in, the developers had had enough. In 1999 they decided to bury Lara under a collapsing pyramid at the end of The Last Revelation. News of her demise was tucked away towards the end of the design document, the Core team having taken a punt that their publisher overlords wouldn’t bother reading that far.They were correct. The Eidos execs were furious when they learned of Lara’s fate, but it was too late to change the game’s ending. Instead they put pressure on Core to find a narrative workaround so they could squeeze out one last PS1 adventure. The result was Tomb Raider: Chronicles, which begins with a memorial service for Lara and continues in a series of flashbacks. It isrubbish.Lara’s emo periodView image in fullscreenEmo Lara Croft with the reviled Kurtis Trent... Tomb Raider: Angel of DarknessPhotograph: Core DesignLara’s first PS2 outing, The Angel of Darkness, was released in 2003. It was aiming for mature and edgy, but landed slap bang in the middle of dull and depressing.The game missed the point of what players loved about Tomb Raider – the thrill of exploring exotic locations and abandoned temples. No one asked to wander around a gloomy version of Paris that could pass for Croydon, talking to sex workers and pawn shop owners while dressed in double denim.It didn’t help that the game was full of bugs and had awful controls. A terrible new strength mechanic forced the player to build up Lara’s muscle before she could perform previously simple tasks, like moving a crate.To top it all off, a secondary protagonist was introduced: tiresome edgelord Kurtis Trent, whose toxic masculinity ruined the party for everyone. Which brings us to…Terrible sidekicksView image in fullscreenAbsolute liability … Jonah Maiava and Lara Croft in the TV series Tomb Raider: The Legend of Lara Croft, 2024.Photograph: COURTESY OF NETFLIXAnother key appeal of the original Tomb Raiders was the feeling of being a solo adventurer exploring a strange world, never knowing when the eerie silence would be shattered by the snarl of a hungry wolf. No one ever wished Lara was accompanied by a bloke in a padded gilet saying: “Hey, I wonder if that rusty key we found will fit in this rusty lock?”But when Crystal Dynamics took over from Core in the 00s, they decided Lara needed some annoying sidekicks. The worst offender is Jonah, who makes his debut in the 2013 reboot. Not only is he feckless and mansplainy, he actively creates work for Lara by being an absolute liability. Over the course of their adventures he gets trapped, tortured, stabbed, kidnapped, knocked unconscious, shipwrecked, buried in an avalanche, caught in a tsunami, falsely declared dead, and almost killed in a plane crash. Ironically, the only calamity that doesn’t befall Jonah is being swallowed by a whale. A shame.Big screen blundersNone of the Tomb Raider films are stellar – although many middle-aged women have a soft spot for the first Angelina Jolie outing, in which our hero dispatches an army of goons without having to leave the house, or even get out of her pyjamas.The follow-up, The Cradle of Life, is absolute twaddle.Philip Frenchcalled it “repetitive and curiously inert”. The BBC’sNev Piercewent further: “Incoherent, dumb and stupefyingly bland … It’s as though theywantedto make a terrible film.”Pierce went on to describe Lara as a “pumped-up Judith Chalmers”, which points to a missed casting opportunity – who wouldn’t want to watch the affable host of Wish You Were Here…? scale Angkor Wat with a grappling hook?View image in fullscreenAbsolute twaddle … Angelina Jolie in Lara Croft: Tomb Raider – The Cradle of Life, 2003.Photograph: REUTERSPlayboy problemAlthough Chalmers never got the chance, plenty of other women were cast in the role of real-life Lara over the years. They included model Nell McAndrew, who donned the turquoise tank top to promote Tomb Raider III.Things went tits up when she also appeared in Playboy magazine, the game’s logo proudly displayed on the cover alongside the words: “LARA CROFT NUDE.”Core Design sued, unhappy that the video game character they had endowed with comically enormous breasts was being sexualised. They won – a judge orderedstickers be applied to 20,000 copies of the magazine, covering up the offending logo. It is not known how badly this affected sales among the Playboy readers eager to catch an illicit glimpse of unlicensed intellectual property.Reboot controversyView image in fullscreenLara Croft having a bad time in 2013’s Tomb Raider reboot.Photograph: Crystal Dynamics/Square-EnixThe 2013 Tomb Raider reboot was solid and polished. However, its creators failed to understand Lara’s appeal as a strong, enigmatic main character, particularly for female gamers.Art director Brian Horton talked about wanting to make players “care for” Lara. He said her torturous experiences and ripped clothing would show “beauty and vulnerability”, suggesting this was “sexy in its own way”.The controversy really kicked off after a trailer was released showing a man pinning Lara against a wall and groping her. Executive producer Ron Rosenberg said the sexual assault would make players want to “protect” the game’s protagonist, and “root for her in a way you wouldn’t root for a male character”. This focus on the male gaze and demotion of Lara to damsel in distress represented a staggering failure to read the room, and to notice there were women in it.Thirty years of hurt?There’s no doubt that Lara has endured some dark times over the last three decades. In fact, she’s had it harder than any other veteran video game character. No one ever suggested Solid Snake would have more appeal if he sported a gigantic pair of testicles, or insisted on giving Mario daddy issues. (Although, as annoying sidekicks go, Sonic the Hedgehog’s mate Tails gives Jonah a run for his gold rings.)Yet here she is, still standing, withanother adventure arriving next year. Perhaps this one will tell Lara’s true origin story: how she rose to prominence not because of her prominent chest, or past traumas, but because she was the cool, enigmatic star of a bloody great game.Lara Croft remains a leading icon of gaming culture, despite the repeated failure of sexist developers and unimaginative marketing teams to understand her power. As someone born after she was created might say, that’s why Lara Croft is the GOAT – not just the greatest of all tomb raiders, but the greatest of all time.Explore more on these topicsGamesLara Croft: Tomb RaiderTomb RaiderfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Derren Brown turns into Nostradamus – and I predict you’ll submit to one gasp-inducing stunt after another | Magic | The Guardian
description: Prophecies are impossibly fulfilled by the superstar who takes his cue from the legendary French seer in his show Only Human
Author: Brian Logan
Headline: Prophecies are impossibly fulfilled by the superstar who takes his cue from the legendary French seer in his show Only Human
Content: Be astonished … Derren Brown and volunteers in Only Human at the Apollo.Photograph: Pamela RaithView image in fullscreenBe astonished … Derren Brown and volunteers in Only Human at the Apollo.Photograph: Pamela RaithMagicReviewDerren Brown turns into Nostradamus – and I predict you’ll submit to one gasp-inducing stunt after anotherApollo theatre, LondonProphecies are impossibly fulfilled by the superstar who takes his cue from the legendary French seer in his show Only HumanBrian LoganSun 25 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDo we have free will – or are the words I am about to write, the four stars twinkling atop this review, pre-ordained? That’s the stuffDerren Brownconjures with in his new show Only Human, which takes its inspiration from Nostradamus’s ability to foresee the future. Nostradamus used divination techniques – and so Brown engineers a stunt in which his audience, en masse, dowse a waterway in the building next door. Nostradamus had a near-death experience – and so, in one remarkable sequence, Brown orchestrates something similar for a hypnotised member of his crowd.This of course is territory Brownhas always made his own: strip away the free will rhetoric and Nostradamus folderol, and artful dodger Derren stands revealed, doing the same mentalism and mesmerism tricks as ever. By the interval (and acknowledging that we’ve been spoiled by his jaw-dropping back catalogue), this current collection of stunts doesn’t feel all that high-powered. Predicting an audience member’s yes/no answers to a series of questions is amazing, yes, but low stakes. And that water divination set-piece misfires: only one of his three selected dowsers is up to the task, and the venue’s seating is too cramped for the mass mobility the routine requires.The Snowman gets a hi-tech rebuild – with help from Raging Bull and a ‘Hot Santa’Read moreAct two raises the bar. First there’s a routine which – not to give anything away – is extraordinary and disconcerting in equal measure. The all-enveloping theatrics of the sequence (video, booming sound, whiplash set changes) are so giddying, one loses sight of the point it’s trying to prove. But there’s no denying it gives the gig lift-off, into a stratosphere of one gasp-inducing stunt after another. There’s a mind-reading number involving photos that audience members submit at the interval, followed by a reveal showing how prophecies made in the show’s first half have now, quite impossibly, been fulfilled.You can grasp at explanations for that, or for the closing coup involving a bowl of Smarties and a 16th-century augury. Or – we have no free will, after all – you can submit to Brown’s powers and be astonished.At theApollo theatre, London, until 30 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsMagicDerren BrownWest EndTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘There’s nothing interesting about me – and no interest in me’: how Larry David’s new biography nearly didn’t happen | Television | The Guardian
description: He point-blank refused, begged the author not to talk to people who knew him … and eventually relented. Making the first authorised biography of the Seinfeld and Curb creator was no mean feat
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: He point-blank refused, begged the author not to talk to people who knew him … and eventually relented. Making the first authorised biography of the Seinfeld and Curb creator was no mean feat
Content: ‘Oh Jesus, if we must’ … David wasn’t exactly convinced he was the ideal subject for a book at first.Photograph: Amanda Edwards/WireImageView image in fullscreen‘Oh Jesus, if we must’ … David wasn’t exactly convinced he was the ideal subject for a book at first.Photograph: Amanda Edwards/WireImageTelevision‘There’s nothing interesting about me – and no interest in me’: how Larry David’s new biography nearly didn’t happenHe point-blank refused, begged the author not to talk to people who knew him … and eventually relented. Making the first authorised biography of the Seinfeld and Curb creator was no mean featDarren RichmanSun 25 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmperor of Nothing: The Making ofLarry Davidmight be the most begrudgingly authorised biography ever written. The story of how author Blake J Harris convinced the comedy titan to “tolerate” him begins, of all places, at Fox News.It was 2020 and Harris’s second book, The History of the Future: Oculus, Facebook, and the Revolution That Swept Virtual Reality, had been published the previous year. Palmer Luckey, the Oculus founder, was “fired for being a Trump supporter” and Harris, anything but a Trump fan, simply reported the facts. Speaking on the phone from his home in Colorado, he explains: “My book ended up doing well because I was all over rightwing media, as they loved having me on. I was the liberal journalist who exposed the truth about how conservatives were treated in Silicon Valley.”Glenn Beck was one of several rightwing commentators who gave Harris a television platform that helped his book to succeed. He even asked if the author would consider writing his biography. Harris politely declined but started to ponder whether there was a public figure he would like to spend years of his life researching and writing about. One day, while taking a shower, he started to think about the way Seinfeld andCurb Your Enthusiasmhad shaped his sense of humour, formative years, his entire worldview. Harris had an epiphany – he would write about the man behind them, Larry David.View image in fullscreenLarry David talks to Jerry Seinfeld on set while filming Seinfeld’s last episode.Photograph: David Hume Kennerly/Getty ImagesHarris had written a lengthy piece for ESPN to mark the finale, at the end of 2015, of The League, a sitcom written and directed by Jeff Schaffer. Schaffer was aSeinfeldwriter who would become David’s chief collaborator as Curb Your Enthusiasmwore on. Schaffer liked Harris’s proposal because he felt there should be a biography of his mentor, arguably the most significant comedy writer in American television history. He was also aware that his boss would be reticent given David was the man whom comedy writer Alan Zweibel once described as: “The only person I know who has buyer’s remorsebeforehe buys something.”Emails flew back and forth in August 2020, with the potential subject informing the potential author that this was a bad idea. In one, reproduced in the prologue of Emperor of Nothing, the subtext is clear – curb your enthusiasm: “There are far better ways to spend your time. There’s nothing interesting about me and there’s no interest in me. That’s not being modest. It’s the truth. So why the book? My parents are dead, so now we’re only left with my kids and my wife to read it. I don’t think three books is making it to the bestsellers’ list. Surely there are better subjects that would welcome a biography.”Harris was not deterred. He enlisted David’s friends and explained to his hero that this would not be a conventional biography, but rather David as “the protagonist in an ensemble story”. Eventually, to appease his friends in a way his Curb Your Enthusiasm alter ego rarely would, David sent Harris a five-word email: “Oh Jesus. If we must.”View image in fullscreenLarry David and Barack Obama pictured together for HBO sketch miniseries, Life, Larry, and the Pursuit of Unhappiness.Photograph: HBOWhen Harris was eventually introduced to his idol, he had what he considers one of the greatest ideas of his life: a ploy George Costanza (the scheming Seinfeld character modelled on David) could be proud of. He decided to focus on a shared interest: “I really wanted to make a good impression with Larry and show him I’m someone he can just shoot the shit with … I’m not a typical stiff journalist who’s going to make his life difficult … So, I suggested for that first conversation … the only topic I want to talk about is the New York Yankees.”(David is a lifelong fan.)Steering clear of the work in that initial chat proved an inspired move, even if, six years on, David recently told Harris: “I agreed to do the book, but I immediately regretted it.” Those regrets will be his alone: what started with a conversation about baseball is a 576-page tome that captures the spirit of the comedy great in ways that suggest Harris understands the Davidian shtick so well that this is the closest we will get to a Larry David memoir. Take the story of David’s birth, which reads as a glorious tribute to the late Richard Lewis, his best friend and collaborator: “On 29 June 1947, at Brooklyn Jewish hospital, a remarkable little boy was brought into the world. This boy – who’d prove to be special in so many ways – would by the age of thirty become one of the most influential comedians of his era. Three days later, at that same hospital, another little boy was born. That boy’s name was Larry David.”View image in fullscreenLarry David in Curb Your Enthusiasm.Photograph: HBOThe author spoke to friends, family, colleagues and neighbours as he attempted to forensically trace a journey that began in Brooklyn, encompassed years of struggle on the standup circuit and would ultimately produce two of the greatest television comedies in the history of the medium. Few people manage to produce a work of such quality once; to do it twice is almost unprecedented.The book is especially compelling when covering David’s lean years (a period that stretched into his early 40s). It explains how he found himself picking out potential spots in the street for when he would inevitably become homeless, despite being viewed as the “comedian’s comedian” by his peers. His talent was never in doubt, only his temperament. Harris is skilled at drawing parallels between the art and the life, just as Seinfeld and Curbwere at their best when blending fact and fiction. We learn about our hero giggling uncontrollably at a piano recital when confronted with a Pez dispenser, quitting his job at Saturday Night Livein a fit of pique on a Friday only to walk back in the following Monday as though nothing had happened, and taking part in a masturbation contest. All this would become material during the Seinfeld years: Jerry ruins George’s girlfriend’s recital by making Elaine laugh with Pez; George screams at his boss and storms out, then acts as though nothing has happened when he realises the financial implications; and The Contest, in which the four main actors have a wager to determine who can go the longest without indulging in onanism, won David an Emmy. In 2009, The Contest was No 1 in TV Guide’s Top 100 Episodes of All Time.View image in fullscreenLarry David in 1981.Photograph: ABC Photo Archives/Disney General Entertainment Content/Getty ImagesIndeed, every funny life experience in those early years would invariably find its way into a David sitcom. The urgency of the writing and our awareness of the greatness to come ensures Harris’s biography rattles along like a thriller, but one which, rather than heading inexorably towards a crime scene, instead leads to some of the greatest art of the past century. Harris reassured David, who was afraid of looking egotistical, that he “could hide in his own biography”, due to it including interviews with people other than himself. When he heard Harris was talking to friends and collaborators, David urged him not to “bother them”. Sarah Silverman allayed the biographer’s fears: “That’s so Larry. What he doesn’t realise is what a joy it is for us to speak to you about him.”Harris describes his subject as the “idealised version of the artist we all wish we were”, a man far more concerned with artistic integrity than financial gain. In the 1980s, long before the fame and fortune, Larry wrote a screenplay entitled Prognosis: Negative. His manager sold the script and was thrilled when she secured a hefty payday for a rewrite. In an unprecedented move, the struggling comic asked for the fee to be negotiated down from $35,000 to $5,000 because he thought the material was good and had no wish to make wholesale changes.Through Harris’s biography, we learn that this strange combination of unerring belief in his own ability on the one hand and low self-esteem on the other has defined the career of the comic genius. During his standup days, he would routinely open with the following esoteric bit: “You seem like a very good audience tonight. I’m wondering, may I use thetuform with you people? Because I feel very close to you. Do you mind if I jump into thetuform?”By David’s own admission, it got nothing “60 to 70% of the time”. When Seinfeld asked his future collaborator why he persisted in opening with a routine that rarely worked, the answer was unequivocal: “I think that’s funny! And if that’s not funny, why am I even doing standup? What’s the point?” Typically defiant, he extended it: “You know, Caesar used thetuform even after Brutus stabbed him.” Thus, Seinfeld got an early glimpse of a man who would not be cowed by outside interference.Harris was grateful that David largely chose not to interfere with his manuscript. His only real notes were asking for sections to be toned down where he appeared “too nice”, especially in relation to his daughters (“What father doesn’t love his daughters?”). He did, however, witness one trademark David rant when he was invited to appear as a background actor in the Curb finale, a story he is delighted to relay over the phone.View image in fullscreenLarry David in Curb Your Enthusiasm season nine.Photograph: HBOHarris and Ken David, Larry’s older brother, were sitting at a table in the background while Larry and Richard Lewis improvised an argument. The pair of extras were instructed to mouth their words, but not speak audibly. Larry’s sibling, however, appeared not to have got the memo and audibly started trying to talk sports with Harris. Harris tells me: “In the middle of the take, Larry seamlessly turned from yelling at Richard Lewis to yelling at his brother and telling him he was supposed to be quiet and that he was ruining the take.”As an early Curb tagline made clear: “Just because he’s made it, doesn’t mean he’s got it made.” David, it seems, will never stop shouting. Emperor of Nothing perfectly captures the evolution of an artist – even as the man steadfastly refuses to change.Emperor of Nothing: The Making of Larry David by Blake J Harris is published by HarperCollins (£22). title: Zadie Smith tells Dua Lipa inequality has made culture clashes feel ‘existential’ | Books | The Guardian
description: Novelist says demise of Britain’s ‘incredible’ welfare system and housing struggles have led to deeper divisions
Author: Ella Creamer
Headline: Novelist says demise of Britain’s ‘incredible’ welfare system and housing struggles have led to deeper divisions
Content: Dua Lipa interviews Zadie Smith during the London literature festival at the Southbank Centre, London.Photograph: Pete Woodhead/PAView image in fullscreenDua Lipa interviews Zadie Smith during the London literature festival at the Southbank Centre, London.Photograph: Pete Woodhead/PABooksZadie Smith tells Dua Lipa inequality has made culture clashes feel ‘existential’Novelist says demise of Britain’s ‘incredible’ welfare system and housing struggles have led to deeper divisionsElla CreamerSun 25 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 14.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe novelistZadie Smithhas said that inequality has made culture clashes feel “existential”, adding that it has become “natural to look to your left and think ‘who the fuck are you?’”In an interview withDua Lipaas part of the Southbank Centre’s London literature festival, Smith argued that the demise of Britain’s “incredible, historic” welfare system has led to greater divisions.The pair discussed Smith’s debut novel,White Teeth, which was published in 2000 and primarily set in the last three decades of the 20th century.Asked by Lipa about how attitudes towards multiculturalism have changed since the 80s and 90s, and the current “dividing line” on immigration in UK politics, Smith pointed to increased inequality and unemployment.“When you’re living in basically decent housing, when you hurt yourself you know you can go to hospital and be treated just like the rich kid down the road – then the differences [with others] become interesting, sometimes annoying, but not existential,” said the novelist.“Now, they’re existential. When you can’t get a job, when there’s no housing, when your schools are falling apart, when the hospitals are falling apart – now it feels existential.”White Teeth traces the stories of three families – the Joneses, the Iqbals and the Chalfens – and is set in Kilburn and Willesden in north-west London, where Smith grew up. The writer praised her state education, saying it has stood her “in incredibly good stead” throughout her life. “I can talk to anyone. The posh kids up the hill? Not so much.“Now, when you look at my neighbourhood, the same schools, the same situations – everything is harder, everybody is poorer, everybody is struggling more,” she continued. “It becomes very, very natural to look to your left and think ‘who the fuck are you?’ That is an economic and structural question.”Smith encouraged developing “a nostalgia for the left”. While “you don’t want the LGBTQ+ politics of the 80s, you don’t want the racial prejudice” depicted in White Teeth, “do you want the healthcare and the schools and the education? I think you do. So it’s about looking back and seeing what was of value – and what was [of] value to me was a social democracy that basically functioned, and might function again if people cared about it, wanted it, believed it could happen again.”On the writing process for White Teeth – which she began when she was 21 and was published when she was 24 – Smith said that she finished the acclaimed novel in the aftermath of being broken up with and moving back in with her mum.“Everybody else was out clubbing, I was like, ‘I’m fucking stuck in this room, finishing a novel,’” she said. But Valentine’s Day was approaching, and “all my girlfriends were like ‘we gotta go out, go on the pull’.” She ended up finishing it on 14 February and then “literally ran straight out to the club” – so the ending of the novel is “a chaos”, she said, adding that this is “why young people shouldn’t write novels”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSince White Teeth, Smith has written five novels – The Autograph Man, On Beauty, NW, Swing Time and The Fraud – along with short stories and nonfiction. Her most recent book was the essay collection Dead and Alive.Lipa and Smith also discussed facing criticism for their works, with Lipa saying that “learning to live with reviews – bad reviews, good reviews” was “one of the hardest things for me to learn to deal with”. Smith said that literary criticism is “absolutely essential” because it “helps develop taste”.“I’m very interested in criticism,” added Smith. “Even if it’s a bad review of me, if it’s well written, if it’s intelligent … I quite love ‘takedowns’.”London literature festival runs until 1 November, with speakers selected by Lipa including Patti Smith, Malorie Blackman and Hisham Matar. Lipa runs a book club, Service95, through which she interviews authors on a monthly basis.Explore more on these topicsBooksZadie SmithDua LipaSouthbank CentreWhite TeethLiterary festivalsClass issuesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Readers reply: will there ever again be a band as big as the Beatles or the Stones? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on subjects ranging from trivial flights of fancy to profound scientific and philosophical concepts
Content: The Rolling Stones’ first official photoshoot, in 1963.Photograph: Mark and Colleen Hayward/RedfernsView image in fullscreenThe Rolling Stones’ first official photoshoot, in 1963.Photograph: Mark and Colleen Hayward/RedfernsNotes and queriesLife and styleReaders reply: will there ever again be a band as big as the Beatles or the Stones?The long-running series in which readers answer other readers’ questions on a wide variety of subjectsThis week’s question:with governments asking us to stockpile, could our experience of watching disaster films help us in a real emergency?Sun 25 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 10.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe 2020s have seen many individual pop artists make it big: Taylor Swift, Ed Sheeran, Sabrina Carpenter, Harry Styles. But the charts are not full of bands the way they used to be. Is the era of the all-conquering group that puts its stamp on popular culture (Abba, the Rolling Stones, the Beatles) over, never to return?Dominique Perrault, CannesSend new questions tonq@theguardian.com.Readers replyOasis.ThirdhandlukeMaybe not, but Oasis fandom is giving it a damn good try.dfic1999I’m not sure how best to measure the “cultural significance” of bands. If you go on pure sales then you’d have to include bands like the Eagles, and I doubt many in the UK would call them culturally significant – just as we might not consider the cultural significance of country music. Maybe the amount of breakthrough into everyday news? I think we know as much about the relationship between the Gallaghers as we did about Lennon and McCartney. Famous marriages help – Chris Martin and Gwyneth Paltrow? The Oasis/Blur rivalry was hyped up as the next Stones/Beatles. Ozzy was always in the news. Influence on other bands? The Beatles will top this, but it is generational – many people say that they only joined a band because of the Sex Pistols. Some say the Smiths, some Joy Division/New Order.DukeApricotThe question is about bands rather than popular music as such, but at the moment it’s more like the undercurrent of singer-songwriters of the 60s and 70s. Taylor Swift, for instance, is probably as big as the Beatles – she’s on the news pages, not just the music pages – but bands? No.jno50No, I don’t think so. The Beatles were propelled into the limelight by the surge of the baby boomers, plus a wealth of practical experience playing live gigs at fairgrounds, in Hamburg and at the Cavern Club in Liverpool. Above all, they had musical talent, and spent days in the recording studio to perfect their numbers. I cannot see another band coming along with anywhere near the same experience, talent and presence.DrBlamm0I agree. All of that was enabled by vast numbers of people paying to see live music, then paying for albums. There was an enormous amount of money flowing into the music industry, enabling artists to get started, experiment and flourish. But now, how much money do people spend on music? Free Spotify, and the occasional £80 to see a band that’s already extremely famous (most of which is eaten up by the costs of the actual tour)? The grassroots venues are closing and nobody’s buying music. That’s not the audience’s fault, by the way. It’s the music industry’s, for treating the product like it has no value, and allowing it to be given away for free.Alex42Bands are a fairly short-lived phenomenon. Before the 1960s, there were very few bands in the charts. It was mainly individual artists (occasionally with a named backing group) and vocal groups. It first started to change with instrumental groups like the Shadows and the Ventures, which led on to bands in which the vocalist(s) was an integral element. Chart-wise, they’ve been declining for most of this century, and I suspect one of the reasons is that the industry has always found bands annoying – they split up, argue about creative control. Boy/girl bands and individuals are much easier to manage.alexitoWill there ever again be an all-conquering composer of concertos, or of musical theatre, or an all-conquering trumpet jazz band? No, those are bygone eras and are no longer relevant to most listeners, and neither are the Beatles. They were all big, they came, changed everything, then went and nobody born subsequently listens any more. Music always moves onwards, and the present explosions of creativity of solo vocalists and electronic producers could not have been possible in earlier eras. Something else will replace those too.Randomusername222I wonder whether the arrival of streaming has diversified music-listening to the point where nobody can dominate. Even in the 80s, a hit song would be everywhere. Now I can happily live in a highly diversified bubble listening to Etta James, Leftfield, St Vincent and Ambrose & his Orchestra back to back, and honestly say I wouldn’t recognise any Taylor Swift song.TobermoryNightlifeThe internet has scattered our focus so much. The Beatles were able to put their stamp on the music, TV shows and films that everyone listened to or saw. We don’t have a monoculture that would allow a band as big as the Beatles again. Who even is the biggest gen Z band? Geese?tomtheintrigued_09BTS, if we are counting the whole world, not simply the west.WhenIsTheEpiphanyGlad somebody has a sense of humour.Waigu_Daji8Interestingly, the Beatles and the Stones are still in theTop 100 album charts. As they are every week. People, including a lot of young people, I suspect, seem quite happy to get their “band music” today from the likes of the Beatles, Stones, Fleetwood Mac, Abba, Oasis and Queen.PeterNewcastleI wonder if it’s that far fewer people are able to play instruments. When I was little, all the schools I went to had an orchestra and music lessons. Nowadays, it seems to be nowhere near as common. Bands like the Beatles and Led Zeppelin were phenomenal musicians, and part of the reason for that is that they came from a culture where a lot of people played instruments, and encouraged each other to get better and better.Alex42The music scene is very different now than it was when the Stones and the Beatles were dominant. Where are the radio stations where a disc jockey, to use a quaint and archaic term, might expose a person to a new song? Or the local venues featuring live music that gave musicians a chance to play to people in real time, and an analog world where the notes being played were the ones an audience heard? Streamed music sounds different to how it does live or on vinyl or disc. People are accustomed to a much more manipulated sound, Auto-Tuned and bass-heavy and often sampled. In a heavily curated musical world, there are fewer opportunities to be gobsmacked by a song out of the blue, seek out the musician’s work and then buy a ticket to their show in a venue that has room for hundreds not thousands.GrannieSalThe question seems to mix two ideas: chart dominance and cultural impact. How are we to cleanly compare the cultural impact of Taylor Swift and the Beatles? Björk and Britney Spears? Could we say that Bryan Adams or Wet Wet Wet echoed down the years, or that Ed Sheeran has had more cultural impact merely by virtue of charting for twice as long as Michael Jackson? Did Christmas No 1s about sausage rolls really offer the most incisive post-austerity commentary on the state of the world? Understanding the cultural impact of music and musicians requires careful ethnographic study. We might use quantitative data such as sales figures to refute or support our observations and analysis, and that will always be caveated by the limitations of comparing, say, chart compilation methods and music reproduction technology in the 1960s with those prevalent today.DorkaliciousNo. Once, enough income was generated to pay 20 musicians, the band leader, the greasy-fingered promoters and the bus driver from the sales of a bit of sheet music, a fair few shellac records, and admission tickets.Then came amplification and put the kibosh on all that. There was enough income generated to pay four or five musicians, the greasy-fingered promoters, the greasy-fingered A&R hangers-on and the bus drivers, roadies, and the helicopter pilots, from a tiny amount of sheet music, an enormous amount of vinyl records, bedroom wall posters, tour T-shirts, and admission tickets.Then came the internet and put the kibosh on all that. Now there’s enough income generated from streaming, and admission tickets to pay one musician, a heap of special effects, AI backing music, anti-ageing holograms, greasy-fingered promoters, greasy-fingered online platform owners, event managers, security consultants, concert technologists, psychologists, therapists, bus drivers, and private jet pilots.Every era has its music, every era has its format. You could, with a job in a factory, easily afford a ticket to go and see a band who wrote songs about the life you were familiar with, because the people in the band were the kind of people you grew up with. Now? There is all the noise of pushing, moulding, promoting, marketing, and selling auto-songs by people who perform in their underwear – that’s the big stuff. It’s clear there are loads of local bands, and more than enough for the mid-range circuit, but there are no young, original, giant bands any more, not as we know them, Jim? Jim?bricklayersoptionDon’t you just mean: a band as big as the Beatles? The Stones have lasted but were never as big. Abba wasn’t a band, just a vocal group with a couple of players.WoollyAphidJust what I was going to say. The Rolling Stones were nowhere near the Beatles. Led Zeppelin sold a lot of records, but their cultural impact was close to zero.MFowkeLed Zeppelin’s tracks are regularly sampled by hip-hop and electronic musicians today, which I guess is some kind of cultural impact?Randomusername222Yes, some kind of impact – close to zero. The Beatles changed the world.MFowkeThe whole genre of heavy metal. You might sneer, but it is certainly culturally significant.DukeApricotExplore more on these topicsLife and styleNotes and queriesPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Natasha Bedingfield looks back: ‘I had hits in the US that weren’t released in England. It was like being banished’ | Family | The Guardian
description: The singer-songwriter on her unconventional education, her brother Daniel, and her quest to write a classic like Purple Rain
Author: Harriet Gibsone
Headline: The singer-songwriter on her unconventional education, her brother Daniel, and her quest to write a classic like Purple Rain
Content: FlashbackFamilyNatasha Bedingfield looks back: ‘I had hits in the US that weren’t released in England. It was like being banished’The singer-songwriter on her unconventional education, her brother Daniel, and her quest to write a classic like Purple RainHarriet GibsoneSun 25 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleNatasha Bedingfield wearing a bright-red tracksuit, standing in a garden in 1984 and recreating the image in 2026Natasha Bedingfield in 1984 and 2026. Later photograph: Simon Webb. Styling: Andie Redman. Hair and makeup: Lisa Laudat at The Wall Group. Archive photograph: courtesy of Natasha BedingfieldBorn in London in 1981, Natasha Bedingfield is a singer and songwriter. Her 2004 debut album, Unwritten, sold more than 2.3m copies and featured the No 1 single These Words. She has released three further albums, scoring UK Top 10 hits and success in the US with Pocketful of Sunshine. Nearly two decades after it was released, her single Unwritten became a viral TikTok hit in 2021. Her new single, Dot Dot Dot, is out now.This was takenat HillyFields park in south-east London.I’m dressed in a sweet little tracksuit. I was a cute kid: I sucked my thumb until I was 11 and I had a sheepskin that I sniffed. But if anyone actually said I was cute, I’d reply: “No, I’m not!” I wanted to be taken seriously. That word made me think that nobody was listening to what I had to say.My parents come from New Zealand, and when they had my brotherDanielthey emigrated to England where they then had me and my two younger siblings. We lived in the inner city, so our backyard was a saviour. Together we were a pack and would spend all day making forts and watching frogs in the pond. We didn’t have much money, but I was rich in love.I come from a family of big thinkers. My parents are social workers and raised us to believe that everyone is equal. We were taught that you should talk to everyone, as you never know when you could be standing in front of an angel. Mum and Dad wanted each of us to learn in our own way, outside of a system, so I was home-schooled from 11 until 16. Back then it was a rebellious thing to do, but I loved self-study. I am overwhelmed by loudness, so the fact I didn’t have to learn in a full class of students worked for me. It’s ironic, really, considering my profession, but too much noise makes me shut down. Is that a neurodiversity thing? Probably.As well as my parents’ outside-the-box approach, another big influence on my childhood was church. Every week we would go to a Jamaican church, one that really encouraged kids to get into music. I loved the culture there – as well as singing, we had a strong community of people of all ages.double quotation markI still feel so alive when I am making songs. It’s that buzz of expressing an emotion that everyone feelsWhen I was 18, I started travelling on the tube and doing late-night writing sessions with producers. My brother was the more obvious musician in the family. Daniel would be at home, saying things like, “Everyone be quiet – I’m recording!” Whereas I was more private – writing but keeping it to myself. Why? Some friendly acquaintances – family, friends – warned me that it might be hard to have two Bedingfields in the industry. “It’s very rare that it would happen for both of you,” they’d say. So I decided to get on with it quietly. In the end I said to my brother: “I know this is your thing, but it’s actually my thing, too. And I’m not trying to take over from you.” He, of course, supported me entirely.Around the same time, I started studying psychology at university. I found the whole process stressful – I often felt dizzy, and struggled to learn all of the names and dates. My dad ended up saying: “We all know that you’re a singer-songwriter – that is what you should be doing.” He was the one who encouraged me to leave university and I will be for ever grateful.When I started out, my label told me that I was a pop artist.But I wasn’t Britney. I didn’t even know what pop meant at the time, because I wasn’t keeping an eye on the charts, I didn’t listen to the radio. Even as a teenager I never had boybands on my wall. I was a fan of Coldplay, Björk, India Arie and Stevie Wonder. I didn’t want to mime, or pole dance. I was just trying to be authentic. The only time I did learn a dance routine was for the video for Single. I did a few moves, then felt weird. They wanted to make me sexy, but the whole thing looked forced. It was frustrating. Female artists often get boiled down to how we look and it takes away from the substance of what we’re actually saying.I wrote Unwritten for my younger brother. It started as a poem, and then I tried to make it into a song with other writers, but they wanted to take a different approach, to do the whole blond bombshell pop type of thing. Then I met Danielle Brisebois [from New Radicals] and together we clicked and made Unwritten. The whole process felt simple. I wasn’t showing off vocally. I was just singing to my brother. I didn’t think about whether it would be a hit.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAfter the success of my first album,I started taking myself less seriously in my lyrics. I’d grown into my humour, which is where a song like I Wanna Have Your Babies comes from. The track was restricted by BBC Radio 2 as they thought it was encouraging young people to have kids. But, really, it was meant to make people laugh as it was about the thoughts you never say out loud when you are dating someone new. In the end, my label sent me to the US – a way to test out my career without other parts of the world watching. They essentially geo-blocked me. I had hits in the US, but they were not released in England. I even sang at the White House for Obama, and my mum couldn’t watch it. It was a bit like being banished. The only bonus was that being a Briton in the US meant I could get away with certain things. Because I taught myself to read, there were some words I knew how to write but not say out loud. In my song These Words, I use the word hyperbole. A word I had never said out loud before. I sang it wrong for a long time, but told the Americans that was how you pronounced it in England.Rapper and actor Eve looks back: ‘I was the only girl in the boardroom in major label meetings – that Philly girl had to come out’Read moreAfter that I left my label and had a 10-year period where I was doing a lot of corporate shows and touring. I got married, had a baby and kept on songwriting. I wrote with some Swedish songwriters, but the songs didn’t show much growth. Then around the pandemic, people started making up dances to Unwritten. It went viral and I started having a resurgence. Some friends called and said: “Natasha, you have to become part of the conversation.” I didn’t get it at first. I thought TikTok was just a dance app and I didn’t want to dance. But once I saw the videos I realised it was a creative place to be. I’ve embraced the song’s new life ever since.My goal now is to write my Purple Rain.I haven’t written my best songs yet and I want a timeless classic. Getting older doesn’t threaten me – artists like Tina Turner had careers that took off when they were my age. I find that so inspiring, as so often it’s, like, women are written off when they reach a certain age.I still feel so alive when I am making songs. It’s that buzz of expressing an emotion that everyone feels, but is hard to articulate without music. I don’t get excited about the things other people do – I don’t like going to Disneyland or holiday resorts. Even on my birthday I would rather be in a recording studio, making songs and geeking out about a triple entendre, than at a party. I don’t think that will ever change.Explore more on these topicsFamilyFlashbackPhotographyPop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make mushroom stroganoff – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: An age-old Russian favourite, rich and full of flavour, in nine easy steps
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: An age-old Russian favourite, rich and full of flavour, in nine easy steps
Content: Who needs meat? Felicity Cloake’s mushroom stroganoff.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food Styling: Flossy McAslanView image in fullscreenWho needs meat? Felicity Cloake’s mushroom stroganoff.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food Styling: Flossy McAslanFelicity Cloake's masterclassFoodHow to make mushroom stroganoff – recipeAn age-old Russian favourite, rich and full of flavour, in nine easy stepsFelicity CloakeSun 25 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStroganoff is a richly savoury dish of sautéed beef in soured cream named after a 19th-century count (though no one seems quite sure exactly which one). But it was only as recently as the 20th century that this age-old Russian favourite was gussied up with onions and mushrooms. Here, it has evolved again to eschew the meat altogether – and you may be surprised how little you miss it.Prep15 minCook40 minServes415g dried porcini2 large onions50g butterSalt and black pepperFreshly grated nutmeg, or ground allspice300g white or chestnut button mushrooms4 field mushrooms250ml soured cream, preferablyśmietana(see step 7)1 tbsp Polishsarepska, or English mustardA squeeze of lemon(optional)Chopped chives or dill, to finish1 A note on the fatDon’t be tempted to reduce the amount of butter in this dish – stroganoff shouldneverbe low-fat – but do feel free to substitute a plant-based alternative, or a good rapeseed or olive oil and a plant-based creme fraiche, though you may also need to add a spritz of lemon juice to taste at the end.2 Prep the vegView image in fullscreenPut the dried porcini in a heatproof bowl, pour over 200ml just-boiled water and leave to soak while you get everything else ready. Peel and thinly slice the onions. Put a wide frying pan on a medium-low heat, add half (25g) the butter and leave to melt.3 Fry the onionsView image in fullscreenFry the onions, along with a pinch of salt and a good grating of nutmeg or allspice, in the melted butter, stirring regularly to ensure they don’t burn, until soft, golden and sweet. Meanwhile, briefly rinse the button mushrooms, if necessary, or brush any dirt off them. If they’re small, leave them whole, and cut into halves or quarters if large.4 Fry the button mushroomsView image in fullscreenScoop the softened onions into a bowl, leaving as much butter as possible behind in the pan. Turn up the heat to medium-high, then saute the button mushrooms in the residual butter until softened and well browned. Scrape the cooked mushrooms into the fried onion bowl.5 Dry-fry the field mushroomsBrush the field mushrooms, then trim and cut into roughly 1½cm-thick slices. Put the pan back on a medium-high heat and, once it’s hot, add the sliced mushrooms and give them a very light sprinkling of salt. Cook, turning occasionally, for eight to 10 minutes, until their liquid has evaporated and the sound from the pan is a sizzle rather than a hiss.View image in fullscreen6 Add butter and fry againAdd the remaining 25g butter to the now dry mushroom pan, then keep frying, turning so the mushroom slices cook evenly on both sides, for roughly seven to 10 minutes, until they’re a glossy, rich and golden brown. Scoop the sliced mushrooms into a second bowl. (The dish can be prepared ahead up to this point.)7 Finish the sauce baseView image in fullscreenAdd the porcini soaking liquid (fine-strained, if need be, to remove any grit) to the pan, scrape the base to deglaze, then gradually whisk in the soured cream – ideally, go for Polishśmietana, which often has a slightly higher fat content than much UK soured cream and is thus less likely to curdle. Stir in the mustard (again, Polish brands are ideal) and heat very gently.8 Add the fried onion mixView image in fullscreenReturn the fried onions and button mushrooms to the pan. Finely chop the drained soaked porcini and stir them in, too. Leave to simmer very gently for 10 minutes (if the mix curdles, it will look less than appetising, but rest assured it will still be perfectly safe to eat), then stir in the fried field mushrooms towards the end.9 Season and serveSeason to taste with salt, black pepper and some more nutmeg or allspice, if you like, and add a spritz of lemon juice if it needs it. Serve hot, but not bubbling, topped with finely chopped chives or dill and paired with steamed rice or mashed or sauteed potatoes, or even wide egg noodles, as stroganoff is commonly enjoyed in the US.Explore more on these topicsFoodFelicity Cloake's masterclassVegetablesVegetarian food and drinkStewEastern European food and drinkMain coursefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Outlier, Glasgow G1: ‘This kind of carefully orchestrated can’t-be-arsedness is really quite magical’ – restaurant review | Restaurants | The Guardian
description: You cannot fake fabulous by simply buying in cool crockery and a freezer full of someone else’s pastry
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: You cannot fake fabulous by simply buying in cool crockery and a freezer full of someone else’s pastry
Content: Outlier, Glasgow: ‘Intensely likeable.’Photograph: Stephen Lister/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOutlier, Glasgow: ‘Intensely likeable.’Photograph: Stephen Lister/The GuardianGrace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsReviewOutlier, Glasgow G1: ‘This kind of carefully orchestrated can’t-be-arsedness is really quite magical’ – restaurant reviewYou cannot fake fabulous by simply buying in cool crockery and a freezer full of someone else’s pastryGrace DentSun 25 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 07.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn my misspent youth, I’d head to Glasgow to watch the likes ofFields of the NephilimandHawkwindat theBarrowland Boardroom, drink snakebite and buy posters from the touts on Gallowgate to Blu-Tack to my bedroom wall and tear holes in my mother’s woodchip wallpaper. Today, however, I’m here to visitOutlier, a bakery/restaurant/art space that serves warm bread, sticky treats and porchetta with beetroot and plum caponata. It’s on London Road just minutes from the Barrowland, and I’ve wound up here thanks only to a complete stranger on Buchanan Street who wrote down its name on the back of an old receipt and pressed it into my hand. She implored me to try the green jasmine rice pudding, the fresh sourdough and the chocolate and hazelnut babka. We used to do this type of inter-human face-to-face contact thing a lot back in the 1980s, before the internet ruined life.View image in fullscreenOutlier’s ‘clodhopping’ fried chicken thigh in a milk bun.Outlier originally opened back in 2022, after Steven Turner, who had previously run various arts venues, applied to turn the building into a space for artists with a kitchen attached. What we have now is a fairly sparse but charming space, tiled a bit like an old swimming baths in places, in mustards and dark, glossy browns. There are pale, unvarnished wooden tables, speckled stoneware plates, green, pressed-glass tumblers and prices handwritten on scraps of coloured card. When it all comes together, this kind of carefully orchestrated can’t-be-arsedness is really quite magical, and from the outset I found Outlier intensely likable.We perch in a window seat, perusing an actively dreamy brunch menu: blood peach panzanella with Isle of Wight tomatoes, Toulouse sausage with braised Umbrian lentils, or celery soup with Highland blue cheese. Even so, it is the cake counter that has proper main-character energy here. Just after opening at 11am, it is piled high with those babka buns, apple crumble and custard cakes, and bright, jubilant strawberry pastries. The bakers work behind that counter on long tables, and a queue snakes through the space and back out of the door. Outlier’s playlist is cheery and knowing – classic ska, Squeeze’s back catalogue – and it just can’t fail to keep things buoyant. Thirty-five years may have passed since I last hung out meaningfully in this postcode, but the place still feels vibrantly alive.View image in fullscreen‘Like a pixie swimming pool’: Outlier’s green jasmine rice pudding.A plate of warm house sourdough comes with a generously large serving of cured sea trout with bronze fennel, sharp horseradish creme fraiche and summer pickles dyed into a hot-pink, Barbie shade by beetroot, and in which chunks of cauliflower, onion and turnip zing with acidity. That jasmine rice pudding comes ethereally dusted in matcha, like a pixie swimming pool. Yes, it is a big bowl of rice pudding at 11am, but I’m not complaining, not least because of its beautiful notes of gooseberry and lime leaf. I’ve started the day with carbs, carbs and more carbs, and a pot of good earl grey tea; if only all days could be so wantonly good.Outlier’s sandwiches, meanwhile, are frankly ridiculous. The fried chicken thigh on a house milk bun is a clodhopper, not for the meek, and comes doused in red harissa, lemon mayo and ranch dressing. The beef shin toastie is three inches thick and crammed with meat, smoked cheddar and fennel jam, all pressed between two big slices of tin loaf. It is crisp and damp all at once. Who finishes these sandwiches? Competitive eaters only, at a guess. I stash half of it away in a paper box to save for later, archly aware that down south it would be three times the price.View image in fullscreenOutlier’s chocolate fudge cake comes ‘topped with a giant wave of coffee buttercream’.By this time, we are full to bursting, yet someone is loading that cake counter with fresh chocolate fudge cake topped with a giant wave of coffee buttercream. There are cinnamon buns in brown butter frosting, too, as well as olive oil cake cut into neat slabs. It’s so rare in this day and age to see home-baked cakes that have not been delivered frozen by a van, and that aren’t also going to 17 other shops in the vicinity. Instead, these are bespoke numbers made by people standing all of eight feet away from you.So, stranger on Buchanan Street with your big pen and your TK Maxx receipt tipoff, you were absolutely correct to flag me down. Outlier has a buzz for good reason. You cannot fake fabulous by simply buying in cool crockery and a freezer full of someone else’s pastry. I shall return for the lamb shoulder with green harissa and black cardamom yoghurt, and a poppyseed and raspberry custard bun. Next time, though, I’ll be prepared and wear a loose waistband. This place is not an outlier at all, but centre stage in all the big reasons to love Glasgow.Outlier38 London Road, Glasgow G1 (no phone or website). Open all week, Mon-Thurs 8am-4pm, Fri & Sat 8am-5pm, Sun 9am-5pm (opening for dinner Thurs-Sun in early 2027). From about £25 a head, plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsRestaurantsGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I gave my ex our house and half my savings, but now I feel resentful | Relationships | The Guardian
description: Your feelings are understandable. Exploring and accepting them may help you move on
Author: Annalisa Barbieri
Headline: Your feelings are understandable. Exploring and accepting them may help you move on
Content: Illustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration: Alex Mellon/The GuardianAsk Annalisa BarbieriRelationshipsI gave my ex our house and half my savings, but now I feel resentfulYour feelings are understandable. Exploring and accepting them may help you move onAnnalisa BarbieriSun 25 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 07.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI was with my ex-partner formore than 20 years.We were mostly happy and I expected us to be together for life.For well over half the relationship, I was the sole breadwinner and, at my ex’s request, managed our finances. We were reasonably well off, with savings and without a mortgage. We even had a holiday home, albeit a static caravan.I retired early, and the problems we had in our relationship grew.We had both loved travel, but I was repeatedly told we couldn’t afford it, which I knew was nonsense.Iwent back to workin ademanding new field, but my ex showed no interest.I spent more time away from home and began therapy (my suggestion of couples’ therapy was rejected). After a year of therapy, I saidI was leaving.My exsaid we couldn’t afford to split up. So, I gavethem the house andmore than half the savings, and moved to the caravan. In the last six years I have bought a new house, have awonderful new partner and have travelled. I amsuccessful in my workand doing things I dreamed about for years.But I can’t let go of my resentment of my ex. The many material things I brought to the relationship and left behind. The fact that my ex is living in a house worth twice my own.That I turned myself inside out to provide for someone but never got any credit.These things are petty. I look for a book that I paid for, and realisemy ex took it, and I can’t stop thinking about it. I want to let it go, but how?You didn’t say whose name the assets were in – joint names, their name or only yours. You didn’t mention children either. This would substantially change things. I am working on the assumption that you voluntarily gave all this to them with no legal guidance to do so and no children were involved. If so, then I don’t think how you feel is at all unreasonable and I am astounded.I went to UKCP-registered psychotherapist Hazel Hyslop who also wanted to “acknowledge your courage and resourcefulness. You have shown that you can make difficult decisions and create a different life for yourself.”But it’s understandable, Hyslop said, “that you feel confused by your resentment. From the outside, it appears you’ve moved on. Yet emotionally, part of you may still be living with the unfairness of what happened. Accept and acknowledge your feelings and give yourself permission to feel them. You might find that makes it easier to move forward.”double quotation markI don’t think you realise just how resourceful you are. But isn’t it exhausting having to be that person?It’s not petty to be annoyed that a book, or anything else, is with your ex. Because it’s not just about the book, is it?Hyslop said: “The book may represent everything you feel you contributed and left behind. Your money, possessions, labour, care and responsibility. Your resentful feelings may be saying: ‘What I gave mattered. I mattered. Why was this never recognised?’ These feelings are not petty. They may be signals that an important part of your experience still needs to be acknowledged.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMy friends are spouting conspiracy theories – what should I say? | Ask Annalisa BarbieriRead moreResentment alerts us that a line has been breached. It’s an important emotion, often aligned with anger. Maybe you could put your energies into naming the line that’s been crossed and how it makes you feel. If you can tune into it I really think a lot may lighten.You could also try writing it all down; that may make you furious, but it can really help (you don’t need to do anything with the letter). I don’t think you realise just how resourceful you are. But isn’t it exhausting having to be that person? I hope your new partner can lighten some of this for you going forward and look afteryou.Every week, Annalisa Barbieri addresses a personal problem sent in by a reader. If you would like advice from Annalisa, please send your problem toask.annalisa@theguardian.com. Annalisa regrets she cannot enter into personal correspondence. Submissions are subject toour terms and conditions. The latest series of Annalisa’s podcast is availablehere.Comments on this piece are pre-moderated to ensure the discussion remains on the topics raised by the article.
