title: What is the £100k income ‘cliff-edge’? | Tax | The Guardian
description: The tax-free personal allowance starts to be taken away when you hit six figures, and in England you lose access to childcare subsidies
Author: Zoe Wood
Headline: The tax-free personal allowance starts to be taken away when you hit six figures, and in England you lose access to childcare subsidies
Content: A family with two young children loses roughly £30,000 of financial support that either parent earns, even after earning just £1 more than £100,000 a year, according to AJ Bell.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PAView image in fullscreenA family with two young children loses roughly £30,000 of financial support that either parent earns, even after earning just £1 more than £100,000 a year, according to AJ Bell.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/PATaxWhat is the £100k income ‘cliff-edge’?The tax-free personal allowance starts to be taken away when you hit six figures, and in England you lose access to childcare subsidiesZoe WoodSun 25 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBelieve it or not, there are downsides to earning more than £100,000 a year – particularly if you have small children.“It’s the ambition of many people to reach an income of £100,000, but it does come with an unexpected sting in the tail,” says Sean McCann, a chartered financial planner at NFU Mutual.Those who make it into six figures face a 60% tax bill on some income. That is because the tax-free personal allowance starts to be taken away once you earn more than £100,000.For every £2 of income over that, you lose £1 of the £12,570 annual tax-free personal allowance.“This means that any earnings between £100,000 and £125,140 are effectively taxed at 60%,” says McCann. “When you add on the 2% national insurance payable, that means you only keep £38 of every £100 earned.”An estimated 800,000 people are in this position, according to a freedom of information request by NFU Mutual.InEngland, high earners also lose access to government childcare subsidies once a parent has an adjusted net income of more than £100,000 for a tax year.As a result, a family with two young children loses roughly £30,000 of financial support if either parent earns even £1 more than the threshold, according to the investment platform AJ Bell.There are three components to this: tax-free childcare; free hours’ childcare; and child benefit.AJ Bell’s maths is for a family with a nine-month-old baby and a two-year-old, and puts a value of £4,000, £23,872, and £2,337 on the respective elements.graphicSarah Coles, the platform’s head of personal finance, says parents “lose a big chunk” of support as soon as they hit the earnings limit: “It isn’t tapered away gradually, hence the ‘cliff-edge’ moniker.”All entitlement to tax-free childcare (worth up to £2,000 a child a year) goes, Coles explains.You also forgo the 30 hours funded term-time childcare for children aged nine months old to three years old, and half the 30 hours for children aged between three and four.And at this level, all the family’s child benefit entitlement (currently £27.05 a week for your eldest or only child, and £17.90 for each additional child) is clawed back by the high-income child benefit charge (a tax “penalty” that kicks in when someone’s income exceeds £60,000).So how many missed out on funded childcare because a parent exceeded the income threshold?Official government data suggests that between 50,500 and 99,000 children in 2025-26. That is according to a freedom of information figures obtained by the wealth management firm Quilter. That is up sharply on just two years earlier, when it was estimated at between 15,600 and 30,800.Zoe WoodExplore more on these topicsTaxIncome taxChildcareFamily financesChild benefitsBenefitsChildrenfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Retail leads the way on paternity leave as government urged to improve offer | Business | The Guardian
description: M&S and Tesco are among employers offering six weeks, highlighting gap with construction and agriculture
Author: Joanna Partridge
Headline: M&S and Tesco are among employers offering six weeks, highlighting gap with construction and agriculture
Content: M&S employee Joe Erskine says six weeks’ paid leave ‘made a huge difference’ to him and his family.Photograph: Joe ErskineView image in fullscreenM&S employee Joe Erskine says six weeks’ paid leave ‘made a huge difference’ to him and his family.Photograph: Joe ErskineBusinessRetail leads the way on paternity leave as government urged to improve offerM&S and Tesco are among employers offering six weeks, highlighting gap with construction and agricultureJoanna PartridgeSun 25 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 12.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“Being able to take six weeks’ paid paternity leave, flexibly, made a huge difference to me and my family, giving me the time to support my partner and settle into being a new parent,” said Marks & Spencer employee Joe Erskine.The food and clothing retailerincreased its paternity leave offeringfrom two to six weeks at full pay in 2024, meaning Erskine benefited from the new policy when his second child was born 17 months ago.M&S and Tesco are among the retailers leading the way in offering enhanced paternity leave to their staff, new research has shown, highlighting the widening gap between the more family-friendly policies offered to new fathers working in the retail sector compared with those in construction, manufacturing and agriculture.Both companies offer six weeks at full pay to employees, far outstripping the statutory two-week minimum paternity leave offer and making them among the most generous of UK blue-chip companies listed on the FTSE 100, according to figures compiled by campaign group The Dad Shift and Ian Dinwiddy of Inspiring Dads.Privately owned companies Ikea, Lego and Virgin Media O2 now also offer more weeks of fully paid leave to new fathers.The enhanced paternity leave offered by retailers including Asda, Waitrose and Lidl in recent years means that just five employers are responsible for upgrading parental leave for nearly 650,000 workers.Retail businesses and the shop workers’ union Usdaw held a roundtable discussion in parliament, hosted by Labour MP Connor Rand, to discuss the transformation in working parents’ lives brought in by changes to parental leave.Rand, who was a researcher for Usdaw prior to his election to parliament in 2024, said the entitlement was crucial for his family: “Through the ups and downs, I could bond with my son and support my partner because of paternity leave. Too many dads in our country can’t do this. That’s bad for them, bad for their partner and bad for their children. It must change.”Campaigners have long argued that the UK has one of the least generous paternity leave offers in the world, ranked 40th out of 43 Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development countries. Over two decades after paternity leave rights were introduced in Britain, they argue the country has fallen behind and now has theleast generous entitlement in Europe.Employed fathers in the UK are entitled to two weeks’ statutory paternity leave paid at £194.32 a week, or 90% of their average weekly earnings, whichever amount is lower, totalling less than half the national living wage.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenJoe Erskine benefited from the new M&S policy when his second child was born 17 months ago.Photograph: Joe ErskineMany companies offer enhanced paternity leave by topping up the statutory offer to full salary, in some cases for a longer period of time.However, there is a growing disparity between different sectors of the economy. Analysis by The Dad Shift found that the construction sector employs around one in 10 working men, but only accounts for about one in 15 recipients of statutory paternity pay.This could partly be because some construction workers are self-employed and currently have no entitlement to paid paternity leave, as is also the case for many of Britain’s agricultural workers, the majority of whom are self-employed.Construction company JCB only offers two weeks’ full pay in paternity leave, although this has been increased from the three days it previously offered.Engineering firm Rolls-Royce, which makes jet engines for planes, turbines for ships and small nuclear power plants, has a workforce that is more than 80% male but currently only offers two weeks’ fully paid leave.More than 100 Labour MPs havecalled on Andy Burnhamin recent weeks to commit to improving the UK’s paternity leave in the upcoming budget, warning that lowest-paid fathers arethe hardest hitby inadequate paternity leave provision.They are calling for the introduction of six weeks of paternity leave paid at 90% of earnings, capped at £1,200 a week, with the offer extended to self-employed fathers.An 18-month government reviewof the UK’s parental leave system is expected to report later this year.Explore more on these topicsBusinessMaternity & paternity rightsWork & careersRetail industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Cookie theft: how fraudsters get the digital key to your accounts | Scams | The Guardian
description: ‘Session cookies’ are a primary target for hackers letting them hijack and use your accounts
Author: Hilary Osborne
Headline: ‘Session cookies’ are a primary target for hackers letting them hijack and use your accounts
Content: Cookie warning … one of the best ways to defeat hackers is to get into the habit of always logging out of an account.Photograph: Rawf8/AlamyView image in fullscreenCookie warning … one of the best ways to defeat hackers is to get into the habit of always logging out of an account.Photograph: Rawf8/AlamyScam watchScamsCookie theft: how fraudsters get the digital key to your accounts‘Session cookies’ are a primary target for hackers letting them hijack and use your accountsHilary OsborneSun 25 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’ve had a busy morning of life admin, logging into various accounts to check balances and make payments. At the end of a productive few hours you close your laptop and move on to your next job.What you don’t know is that fraudsters have hijacked your session with the bank and are now able to access your account. You are the victim of cookie theft, which belongs to a type of fraud known as “session hijacking”.“Cookies have become the primary target for hackers,” says Marijus Briedis, chief technology officer at cyber security company NordVPN. In the year to June it identified 52bn cookies in stolen data circulating online.When you log into a website, such as your bank’s, you are given a unique cookie that sits on your device and stores your data temporarily. This means you can move from page to page without repeatedly being asked for your login details. It’s called a “session cookie” – or key – and as soon as you log out, it stops being of use.View image in fullscreenMove passwords out of your browser and into a dedicated password manager.Photograph: Maria Vonotna/AlamyBut while the session is open – and that will last beyond your activity if you choose to be remembered on a website, or if you do not properly close it – you could be vulnerable to cookie theft.Briedis says: “Think of a session cookie as a digital key that’s already turned in the lock. When you stay logged into a site, that cookie is what keeps the door open for you. If a hacker steals that active cookie, they essentially become you.“They don’t need your password, they don’t trigger a login alert, and they can often bypass your multifactor authentication (MFA).”The cookies are stolen from your device. The theft is usually a result of you having inadvertently downloaded malware.“Once that malware is on your device, it goes straight for your browser’s database, grabs all those active session cookies, and sends them back to the hacker,” says Briedis. “They’re essentially reaching into your digital pocket and grabbing your keys while you’re not looking.”What it looks likeIt looks like a regular session on the web. At some point you will have logged in and given your password, and maybe used MFA to prove it’s you.You may not realise that you are a victim until you later find that someone has used the session cookie to hack your account.If it’s a social media or email account you may discover it’s been used byscammers to trick other people. If it’s your bank they could access your account, or they could use details they find to perpetratean impersonation scam.And if you were shopping online, the fraudsters could change and redirect your order and charge it to your saved payment details.You may be alerted by a security alert from a site, for example, a message asking if you have tried to change any details.What to doBe really careful about the extensions and software you download, because that’s whereinfostealermalware will usually be hidden.Look out for signs that your laptop or phone has been infected with malware. Briedis says red flags include your device suddenly struggling with simple tasks, a battery that drains faster than it should, frequent crashes, or a browser that starts behaving oddly with redirects, pop-ups, or a changed homepage.Do not use insecure public wifi for sites that require you to log in. The chance of cookies being stolen through this channel is low, but you should always be cautious.Get into the habit of logging out of accounts. “Just closing a tab doesn’t end the session,” says Briedis. ”You need to manually log out to invalidate that cookie and make it useless to a thief.”He suggests moving passwords out of your browser and into a dedicated password manager.Clearing your cookies regularly will reduce what’s available to be stolen.If you suspect you have been compromised, run an antivirus scan. Also log out of your accounts on every device and change your passwords.Use MFA on accounts, as it does still offer more protection than a simple password.Alert your bank if you notice any suspicious payments.Explore more on these topicsScamsScam watchCookies and web trackingIdentity fraudCybercrimeData and computer securityHackingMalwarefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: From five-fingered trainers to the shoeless shoe: what’s with all the freaky footwear? | Fashion | The Guardian
description: ‘Ugly’ shoes, once the preserve of the catwalk, have gone mainstream. Why are so many people taking a walk on the wild side?
Author: Chloe Mac Donnell
Headline: ‘Ugly’ shoes, once the preserve of the catwalk, have gone mainstream. Why are so many people taking a walk on the wild side?
Content: Schiaparelli’s trompe l’oeil mules, Loewe’s balloon shoes and Curtsy’s toe separator inspired heels.Composite: GuardianView image in fullscreenSchiaparelli’s trompe l’oeil mules, Loewe’s balloon shoes and Curtsy’s toe separator inspired heels.Composite: GuardianGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.FashionFrom five-fingered trainers to the shoeless shoe: what’s with all the freaky footwear?‘Ugly’ shoes, once the preserve of the catwalk, have gone mainstream. Why are so many people taking a walk on the wild side?Chloe Mac DonnellSun 25 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUntil recently, a busy commuter train would be packed with people wearing low-key, unobtrusive shoes. An elegant and inoffensive pump, a sporty trainer or a polite and basic ballet flat, they were the type of shoes that said background extra rather than main character energy.But now change is afoot. Deliberately strange designs are reaching new heights of desirability. Polarising rather than pretty, these shoes tend to be flat, a little bit orthopaedic and, according to the internet, “ugly”.From Vibram’s glove-likeFiveFingers, which punctuate each toe, to barely there mesh shoes that leave the foot looking like a boned and rolled ham at Christmas, fashion’s new favourite shoes are leaning into the ludicrous. Welcome to the new era of freaky footwear.View image in fullscreenVibram’s FiveFingers“We are now at a liberating place where more people can have fun with their shoes,” says Dal Chodha, a writer and lecturer at Central Saint Martins fashion school in London. He finds this trend “thrilling”, saying it “forces someone to embrace the jolt of something that feels ugly or absurd”. While previously these designs were confined to the catwalks, they are becoming more common on the streets.According to the fashion search platform Lyst, demand for cloven hoof-likeTabistyles, designed to split the hallux (big toe) from the rest of the toes, has increased fourfold since 2022. Meanwhile, FiveFingers are up 57% year on year.Shoes that were once reserved for taking out the bins or nipping round the corner for milk are now increasingly being worn to the office – and even weddings. Simone Rocha has created supersizedCrocsand smothered them in pearls and gemstones, whileEtrojoins Dior and Valentino in reimagining Birkenstocks’ “anti‑fashion” cork footbed clogs.View image in fullscreenSimone Rocha x Crocs Soho sandal in chai and …View image in fullscreen… Simone Rocha x Crocs ballerina platform in espressoThis summer, the hype for a pair ofGardanas, £38 earthworm-coloured French gardening clogs, led to lengthy waiting lists (and not only for the green‑fingered).Celinesells a similar mossy-coloured pair for £670.Meanwhile, on the high street everywhere from John Lewis to Zara is championing the “Frankenshoe”, such as sneakerinas, an amalgamation of a sneaker and a ballerina flat. These new cross-breeds include thesnoafer, a marriage between a sneaker and a penny loafer.View image in fullscreenNew Balance 1906 loafers in fairweather blueHeels haven’t completely disappeared, but they have been re-envisioned asdeflated balloonsand even broken eggs. In American designer Tory Burch’s latest lineup, sheinverted the heelitself, creating the illusion of a flat mule while simultaneously elevating the wearer. A stubby “nipple heel” measuring half an inch is now the sought-after height.View image in fullscreenLoewe’s deflated balloon shoe and …View image in fullscreen… Tory Burch’s pierced muleValerie Steele, chief curator of the Museum at the Fashion Institute of Technology in New York and author of Fetish: Fashion, Sex & Power, says society has a long history of strange shoes. She points to medieval poulaines, a shoe with an elongated toe that showed the wearer’s social ranking. Some were so long they had to be fastened to the knee to prevent tripping. Chopines, towering platform shoes worn by women from the 15th century, were also used to denote status, while in ancient Greece sex workers are reputed to have worn sandals with “Follow me” carved into the soles. Steele says today’s purposely strange designs let the wearer “play with elements of ugliness”, allowing someone to make a fashion statement without committing to a whole look. “Shoes are far away from your face, so you can experiment without looking ugly,” she says.Chodha, who as a teenager wore Nike Air Rift trainers featuring a split-toe design, now favours a “potato” shoe. As the name suggests, this style of footwear isn’t dissimilar to a freshly dug maris piper. Even M&S has got behind the spud style. A £45 bulbous,soft suede pairhas become one of its fastest-selling options for autumn.View image in fullscreenM&S Suede toggle cord flat ballet pumpsFor some, provocation is part of the appeal. “Anyone who is resisting standard forms of beauty or propriety or practicality in their choice of footwear is in some way embracing a punk spirit,” Chodha says. They also offer an opportunity to “challenge what and why we think something is ugly”.double quotation markWhen politically there is a big right swing, you have a lot of people that through their clothing want to say, ‘I’m not that’Barbara Janeczek, curator manager at Lyst, says designs are becoming more extreme as “fashion has an incredible ability to normalise the previously unwearable”. She describes today’s iterations as “exposing, dividing or framing the foot in ways we’re not used to seeing”.Tiffany Hsu, chief buying and group fashion venture officer at the luxury e-tailer Mytheresa, prefers the term “talking point shoes” rather than ugly, explaining that the style is “designed to create a reaction and bring something unexpected to a look”. Lars Byrresen Petersen, founder of a popular shoe meme account@ LarsLaLa, favours the word “extreme”. Some of his most liked posts are where he has compared shoes tocondomsand mops.The popularity of the trend can be pegged to the “wrong shoe theory”, a term coined by stylist Allison Bornstein in 2023. This styling trick involves purposely wearing an unexpected shoe (think a kitten heel with tracksuit bottoms, or flip-flops with tailored trousers) to make a look more interesting.Bornstein saysa shoe that is a little “off” works because “it signals that there is some intention and choice, and therefore it gives your look personality”.Some view the trend as a backlash against the uniform pageantry of the Maga aesthetic. Republicans love a nude pointy-toe stiletto almost as much as the presenters of Fox News. “When politically there is a big right swing, you have a lot of people that through their clothing want to say, ‘I’m not that,’” Steele says. A freaky shoe can be like a “secret masonic handshake”, she adds.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hoof-type Tabi shoe was first thrust into the spotlight in the 1980s, when Martin Margiela featured the subversive riff on a 15th-century Japanese sock design in his debut collection. Now the Tabi-ification extends to trainers, ballet flats and Mary Janes across various brands. Byrresen Petersen, who has been wearing the style “every day for the past 10 years”, isn’t thrilled about their new universal appeal. “People who aren’t familiar with the shoe’s history are just wearing them for the shock value,” he says.View image in fullscreenMaison Margiela’s Tabi ballerina (left) and Tabi Mary-Janes (right).Composite: GuardianWhile some freaky shoes conceal the foot, it’s the toe‑bearing styles that are really captivating fashion. Similar to Hollywood’s naked dressing trend, they offer a quick flash of foot or even a full-frontal view of each toe. It’s a trend as divisive asCurtsy’s toe separator inspired heels– where each toe is embraced in its own thong strap.Steele says feet and shoes have long been fetishised, as the outline of a foot can be compared to a miniature version of the human body. Toes can be squeezed together to create “cleavage”, while the round curve of the heel is considered similar to the bum. Steele says it was once thought to be “erotic” to wear a slingback. “You were letting your ‘butt’ hang out!”It’s a trend growing against the backdrop of the mainstreaming of foot fetishes. The photo-sharing site Wikifeet, which ranks celebrities’ feet for their beauty, getsnearly 20m views a month. (Rihanna and Margot Robbie score five stars while Michelle Yeoh currently sits at a one.) Selling foot pics has become a lucrative side hustle for many, including the singer Lily Allen, who shares hers on OnlyFans, a subscription-based site most commonly featuring porn. Allen, who posts under the username FTSE500,has saidshe makes more money from #feetpics than she does from Spotify streaming. On social media, the phrase “No free feet pics” plays into the idea, with users carefully cropping photos so their exposed toes aren’t on display.While “potato shoes” are prevalent in menswear, toe-framing styles are less so.Saint Laurentrecently horrified viewers when it sent male models down the catwalk wearing transparent PVC Oxford brogues. When Alexander Skarsgård wore them on the red carpet, they quickly became clouded with condensed perspiration. “I asked myself, ‘Why torture women with plastic shoes, but not men?’” Anthony Vaccarello, who helmed the brand at the time, remarked on the idea behind them.double quotation markOnce everyone gets comfortable with the weird thing, you have to find something weirderView image in fullscreenSaint Laurent’s see-through dress shoes.Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD via Getty ImagesSteele points out that masculinity has been historically associated with heavy boots: “Men’s fashion generally emphasises sexuality through tightness or padding, not so much through body exposure.” Naked toes suggest vulnerability and, “Men don’t want to look vulnerable. They’d rather look armoured.”Why are shoes getting so freaky right now? Chodha says that, like the miniskirt in the 60s, these styles are rebellious and liberating. They can be viewed as an extension of the writer Leandra Medine’s “man repeller dressing”, where the wearer prioritises their own likes and comfort over the diktats of the traditional male gaze. Others view it as a rejection of millennial “girlboss” culture, a movement that glamorised a relentless work ethic associated with spike heels and polished looks, which is now considered toxic by gen Z.Or could it be connected to the economic moment? A recent report warned that the UK was at risk of“a lost generation”. From a lack of job opportunities to the housing crisis and increasing fears over the use of AI, many young people are deeply anxious about their future. As a result, some are embracing a “soft life”, prioritising comfort and a focus beyond the 9-5. Grounding rather than grinding – a five-finger shoe that connects the wearer with the soil beneath them fits the moment. The writer Liana Satenstein has described that particular shoe as “an orgasmic exhale for the foot”.View image in fullscreenSchiaparelli’s Trompe l’Oeil loafers“There’s a sort of jouissance to the walk young people walk,” says Chodha. “I don’t think young people are marching or stomping, because, of course, they all feel so disengaged with the world.” While their predecessors furiously click-clacked around in skyscraper heels, today’s twentysomethings are more likely to be found padding around slowly with a matcha in hand. Chodha says that the heeled stomp “feels out of step with the time”.View image in fullscreenChanel’s ‘shoeless shoe’.Photograph: Marc Piasecki/Getty ImagesWhere next?“Once everyone gets comfortable with the weird thing, you have to find somethingweirder,” says Janeczek, who credits “fashion’s one-upmanship” for playing a role in fuelling the trend for weird shoes. Chanel has offered a pilot run of what that might look like, challenging the very definition of what constitutes a shoe. Its “shoeless shoe”, first seen during its catwalk show in Biarritz in France in April and laterworn by Margaret Qualleyto a London film premiere,features just a heel cap, bearing its double CC logo, leaving the bare foot to walk without any protection at all.Flex those toes, the time has come to let them loose!Explore more on these topicsFashionWomen's shoesMen's shoesAccessoriesHigh heelsChanelSaint LaurentfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Carving out a greener future: how the Swiss ski resort of Laax is meeting the climate crisis head on | Ski resorts | The Guardian
description: Gondolas on demand, electric piste-grooming and chemical-free snow cannons – how Laax is ‘greenstyling’ its future
Author: Kevin Rushby
Headline: Gondolas on demand, electric piste-grooming and chemical-free snow cannons – how Laax is ‘greenstyling’ its future
Content: A snowboarder freestyling in the Laax snowpark.Photograph: Philipp Ruggli/Flims LaaxView image in fullscreenA snowboarder freestyling in the Laax snowpark.Photograph: Philipp Ruggli/Flims LaaxSki resortsCarving out a greener future: how the Swiss ski resort of Laax is meeting the climate crisis head onGondolas on demand, electric piste-grooming and chemical-free snow cannons – how Laax is ‘greenstyling’ its futureKevin RushbySun 25 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s the worst ski resort nightmare: hillsides of shaggy yellow grass streaked with slush under a leaden sky that’s coughing up sleet. Parts of Europe – places previously accustomed to crisp snow fields and pristine blue skies – are now facing this calamity, something meteorologists might describe as a British winter.Not everywhere, of course. Only lower altitudes are seeing such disasters. Higher up, normal service continues. I’m in the Swiss resort of Laax, where most of the slopes are at about 2,000 metres, lofty enough to be snow-secure, for now. The halfpipe is busy with dudes in baggy trousers and headphones nonchalantly practising their double corks. On the traditional pistes there are four-year-olds who could probably ski before they could walk. And then – Switzerland has its wacky side – three young men in first-world-war greatcoats on antique wooden skis propel themselves with rough-hewn quarter-staves.Is all this destined to disappear, perhaps in our children’s lifetimes? To put it in stark, white and black terms: are ski resorts in the same predicament as oil-dependent desert states, watching their one key source of wealth dwindle and disappear?If so, Laax is not going down without a fight. This unusual Swiss resort, close to the Austrian border, is making a bold attempt to be carbon neutral by 2030, a goal that requires cutting out all oil use, making all energy generation sustainable, and reducing food waste to zero. Stung by climate crisis criticism levelled at the ski industry, this community is now far ahead of most. What I have come to see may turn out to be the future of winter sports.View image in fullscreenLaax is regarded as one of Europe’s most environmentally progressive ski resorts.Photograph: Nicholas Iliano/Flims LaaxDown in Laax, I meet Reto Gurtner, 71, CEO of the Flims Laax resort. His father built the first ski lifts back in 1962. “Although there had been summer visitors since the 19th century, Laax was a poor village back then,” says Gurtner.In the 1970s, something significant changed. Gurtner went to study at UCLA and, under the California sun, discovered skateboarding. Even now the memory makes his eyes light up. “They were inventing new sports and I loved the style: no nationalism or militarism. Skateboards, mountain bikes, snowboards – if you did a good run, everyone applauded. It didn’t matter who you were. There was a freedom about it.”He came home with a degree in economics, but more importantly perhaps, a snowboard and a mountain bike. “We went up on the glacier and built the first halfpipe with shovels.”At first, there was a lot of resistance. Local ski outfitters refused to stock snowboards, while in summer, farmers were outraged at the sight of cyclists pelting down mountain tracks. “We made every cyclist wear a bib,” says Gurtner with a chuckle. “Then the farmers thought it was a race and were fine with that.”Conversation with Gurtner is a wild ride. We cartwheel through Steve Jobs, the German poets and the Wu-Tang Clan, as he describes how his visionary approach evolved into something he calls “greenstyle”, an optimistic and well-designed future.double quotation markThe new gondola system does away with unoccupied ski gondolas going up and down the mountainsideThat vision is found in all the new buildings around the resort, nowhere more so than the ski lift in the neighbouring village of Flims, where I head with local guide Doris Rellstab. “The new gondola system does away with unoccupied ski gondolas going up and down the mountainside,” she says. A complex algorithm allows skiers to choose one of five destinations up the mountain, despatching individual gondolas, which balances energy efficiency with passenger demand. As we are lifted smoothly up over the fir trees, the quiet efficiency of this on-demand system becomes immediately apparent.Rellstab tells me how things have changed in the half century since she began teaching winter sports. “Yesterday, I taught my first Arab group. They were a lot of fun.”Our destination is Segnes, high above the treeline at 2,100 metres. Having left the gondola, we don snow shoes and head into a bowl-like snow-filled valley. A couple of miles ahead, the valley ends in a sheer rock face topped by a jagged range of peaks. “That’s the Tschingelhörner,” says Rellstab. “Can you see the line in the rock below the peaks? That was once a geological mystery.”In 1848, the celebrated geologistRoderick Impey Murchisonarrived here with a local expert,Arnold Escher von der Linth. Older rocks were overlaying younger, a puzzle for which there was no explanation. It took more than a century for scientists to solve the problem: the ancient African tectonic plate was riding up over the younger European one. The world was indeed upside down.In summer, this area is covered in rare Alpine flowers and there’s a mountain hut to stay in. Next to us are the tracks of a snow hare. “Wildlife is doing well here,” says Rellstab. “The wolf and lynx have both returned.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenIn summer, the resort becomes an Alpine mountain biking hotpsot.Photograph: Balz WeberIn fact, climate change appears to be assisting wolves in the Alps. The first Alpine pack was recorded in 1993, and by 2021 there weremore than 250, with an annual growth rate of about 25%. Switzerland, once entirely wolf-free, now has about40 packs. Rellstab shows me a website where sightings are monitored. There are conflicts with farmers and hunters, but the numbers keep growing, an indication that parts of the ecosystem are doing well out of retreating snowlines.Perhaps more surprising is that lack of snow is not a big worry to the resort. As Gurtner points out: “Laax is not snow-dependent. A halfpipe or a snow freestyle playground doesn’t need a lot, and we make it with hydro power. And we’ve got mountain bikes and amazing hikes.”double quotation markLaax is not snow-dependent. A halfpipe or a snow freestyle playground doesn’t need a lot, and we make it with hydro powerLater that day, I am up on the mountain with my skis, wandering around on blue runs. Conditions are a bit icy and I’m playing safe, finding myself on a less frequented route that dips down into the valley. And then I come over a ridge and the snow on either side is gone – only the piste remains, a broad band of white curling down through green pasture dotted with lovely old barns. Cannon snow is more durable, surviving longer when the “real” stuff melts.Most Alpine ski stationsare already reliant on it, but unlike many, Laax does not add any chemical or biological additives to the water in its cannons. With sustainable power sources and electric piste-grooming machinery now becoming available, cannon snow is not as environmentally destructive as it may appear.How to have a sustainable family ski holiday: take the train and head highRead moreAt the foot of the hill, I reach the village of Falera, neighbour to Laax. There is one old chair lift, clanking and squeaking, and as I approach it comes to a halt. “Sorry,” says the attendant, “we are closed now.”I wander into the village, all hand-hewn barns with neat log stacks. I can’t see any cars. If Laax is taking the technological solution, its neighbour appears to have chosen a less frenetic and more traditional route to net zero. After 20 minutes, a bus (electric, naturally) appears. As I ride back to Laax, I check thewildlife websitethat Rellstab recommended. And I get a shock. According to a CCTV report from a few hours earlier, a wolf had walked within a mile of me. Outside my hotel, I jump off the bus. Evening is falling. I wait for a line of silent cars to go by. With electric motors everywhere, the town is hushed. Climate change, I reflect, is nothing if not unpredictable. When the wolves howl, you will hear them.The trip was provided byFlims Laaxand rental equipment byEcoski.Trainsrun from Zurich via Chur and the Rhine Gorge toIlanz, where there’s abus serviceto Laax.Inghamsoffers aseven-nighttrip to Laaxfrom £1,618pp B&B, including flightsExplore more on these topicsSki resortsSkiing holidaysSwitzerland holidaysSnowboardingEurope holidaysGreen travelWinter sports holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘I think of it as anti-brain rot’: how our podcast team creates space for thought  | Podcasting | The Guardian
description: The journalists behind our new show Radical Thinking wanted audiences to experience a guest’s thought processes rather than simply hear their hot takes. But achieving this required a very different approach
Author: Gautam Malkani
Headline: The journalists behind our new show Radical Thinking wanted audiences to experience a guest’s thought processes rather than simply hear their hot takes. But achieving this required a very different approach
Content: In conversation… (left to right) writers Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor, and Guardian columnist Aditya Chakrabortty.Illustration: Natalie Gegan/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIn conversation… (left to right) writers Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor, and Guardian columnist Aditya Chakrabortty.Illustration: Natalie Gegan/The GuardianInside the GuardianPodcasting‘I think of it as anti-brain rot’: how our podcast team creates space for thoughtThe journalists behind our new show Radical Thinking wanted audiences to experience a guest’s thought processes rather than simply hear their hot takes. But achieving this required a very different approachGautam MalkaniSun 25 Oct 2026 10.01 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 10.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt doesn’t often happen during interviews. Something inside the person starts shifting. Fresh ideas get forged in real time.Our new podcast seriesRadical Thinking with Aditya Chakraborttyhas already managed to generate many such moments. Each time it happens, you can almost hear the expression changing on the guest’s face. At one point, I switched from audio to video to witness the change and then watch as they refined their thoughts.The effect is riveting. It’s also by design.“We didn’t want this podcast to be a boxing match,” says Kirsty Major, a Guardian deputy opinion editor and an executive producer of Radical Thinking. “We hold guests to account where needed, but ultimately it’s about giving them the space to really think.”Introducing Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty – podcastRead moreThe series sees Guardian columnist Aditya Chakrabortty sit down with some of today’s major thinkers to discuss the forces that are transforming our world and how we can meet the myriad challenges that are confounding conventional wisdom.Fellow executive producer Maz Ebtehaj likens the approach to focusing on people’s thought processes. “We’re encouraging people to think about why they think a certain thing,” she says. “We’re sort of holding a magnifying glass up to their politics and their values, but in an exploratory way not a confrontational way.”“We’re also trying to get a better understanding of where a guest’s thinking leads them,” says Aditya. “I might not always agree with what they think, but I’m really interested in how they got there and whether we share any premises. And because the interviews are exploratory rather than accusatory, we get those moments when a guest says something they perhaps didn’t expect to say.”Whether you are listening to the podcast or watching it, it’s striking how each episode of Radical Thinking leaves you feeling notably nourished. That owes as much to the podcast’s radical approach as it does the radical ideas discussed on the show. By deliberately letting listeners and viewers experience a guest’s thought processes rather than simply hear their hot takes, the team hopes the podcast will feel distinct.“I expressly think of it as anti-brain rot,” says Aditya. “When people talk about doomscrolling and brain rot, notice that they often slip into the passive voice. What they’re really talking about is how they no longer feel as if they have control over their lives. People want a different way of thinking about what’s going on in their world and that’s what we’re trying to provide.”View image in fullscreenMichael Gove exploring his political views on Radical ThinkingPhotograph: James Tindale/The GuardianThis sense of mission is coupled with an urgency that informs the series as the far right continues to gain power around the world by exploiting people’s grievances. “We’re living through some very precarious moments right now, and that requires us to come up with new ideas urgently, or at least to press the ideas people have into service,” says Aditya.“The systems and the ideas and frameworks that we’re used to don’t work any more, so it does call for radical thinking,” adds Maz. “Some of our guests are inherently radical thinkers. Others have radical thoughts.”The show’s guests are drawn from across the political spectrum, including former Greek finance minister Yanis Varoufakis, Spectator magazine editor and former Conservative deputy prime minister Michael Gove, Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor, the playwright James Graham, and the writer and Guardian columnist Nesrine Malik.View image in fullscreenGuardian columnist Aditya ChakraborttyPhotograph: Linda Nylind/The Guardian“That plurality of voices comes from within the Guardian’s own traditions,” says Aditya. “There’s a fascinating bitin the interview with Govewhen I ask what his abiding principle in politics is and he says, I want to fight inequality. How does someone on the right explain that to the rest of us? Not with me saying to him, ‘but you did austerity, you backed Brexit and now this new nativism’... I want to know what throughline he sees there. And actually, what he tells us is shattering.”Another such moment from the first few episodes iswhen Varoufakis explainshow his experience of power radicalised him. “There is the look of defeat on his face,” says Aditya. “There’s also the genuine look of surpriseon Naomi Klein and Astrid Taylor’s faceswhen we start talking about how the left might respond when the AI bubble bursts.”These sorts of moments are spontaneous, but also the result of the way the whole team carefully plans and structures each episode. “I’ve just come out of an all-day meeting where we were thinking about how to structureour interview with James Graham,” says Aditya. “The really big, guiding question we wanted to discuss was whether stories can heal a divided country. What is it like to be the nation’s playwright at a point when the nation is falling apart?”Those meetings are key to the alchemy of the series. “We plot it through,” says Maz. “What’s the guiding thought? Where and what are we going to get to? For example, with Varoufakis, we started by asking him about his upbringing and how he felt during certain moments of his life – because the personal can be very revealing about a person’s political views. We have time to draw emotional connections to people’s politics because each episode is an hour long. So the conversation should feel like a story and by the end the audience should feel they’ve arrived at some sort of answer to that initial guiding thought.”‘Gaza is a moral tear in the universe’: Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor | Radical Thinking with Aditya Chakrabortty – podcastRead moreFor Kirsty, some aspects of the prep were very different from the kinds of journalism she’s previously done. “I went from editing and writing articles to working with the audio team, and they’ve opened my eyes to how you might structure a conversation and plan it out,” she says. “An incredible amount of work goes into that. We have to know what’s already out there and what a guest might say, but we want to go beyond that. By the end of it, you really feel as if you live in their head.”As well as being familiar with each guest’s body of work, Aditya has also written about some of them before. “Another thing that helps inform some of these discussions is that I’ve known some of our guests for a while during the course of my reporting,” he says. “So there’s a degree of informality. I’m not trying to impose on our guests; I want to draw out the best of them. I know their work, I know where the broader conversation is, so I can think about how it can be taken to a different place or how we can add different perspectives. Journalism to me has always been about adding value like that.”“Culture is stagnant, so politics is stuck” – playwright James Graham | Radical Thinking – podcastRead moreOne regular feature involves asking each guest what they would do if they had a billion pounds. The answers aren’t just instructive, they are often informed by the preceding discussion. Another feature involves Aditya summing up what he has taken from each interview – underscoring how everyone comes away from the encounter feeling fortified.Aditya says he hopes this also extends to listeners and viewers and that Radical Thinking proves empowering for audiences – just as he felt empowered by certain news outlets back when he was growing up. “During my childhood and early youth, newspapers and the media always played that role. It was a tool for the rising classes to make themselves better informed about the world.”The podcast’s combination of informative and informal is also aided by its physical space. “We spent a lot of time thinking about the setting,” says Maz. “It’s very dark. It’s very low-lit. At first, we had two sofas but Aditya said it didn’t feel right because it wasn’t how he’d have a conversation. So we put in a table and chairs.”Even without the sofas, however, the work and thought that goes into each episode means the interviews very quickly morph into a more intimate conversation. “It feels pretty therapeutic,” says Aditya. “A lot of stuff spills out.”Watch every episode of the podcast on the Guardian’s Politics Weekly YouTube channelwww.youtube.com/@politicsweekly, or listen wherever you get your podcasts.This article is taken from the Guardian’s weekly email for supporters, sent on Tuesdays.
