title: ‘A hidden tradition’: Benjamin Moser wants you to know Jewish anti-Zionism is not new | Israel | The Guardian
description: The writer rarely questioned the tenets of liberal Zionism growing up. Now he embraces anti-Zionism with the fervor of a new convert
Author: Aaron Gell
Headline: The writer rarely questioned the tenets of liberal Zionism growing up. Now he embraces anti-Zionism with the fervor of a new convert
Content: Benjamin Moser: ‘I 100% stand by my book. People can criticize me for whatever they want, but they can’t criticize me for not making myself clear.’Photograph: Nan GoldinView image in fullscreenBenjamin Moser: ‘I 100% stand by my book. People can criticize me for whatever they want, but they can’t criticize me for not making myself clear.’Photograph: Nan GoldinIsrael‘A hidden tradition’: Benjamin Moser wants you to know Jewish anti-Zionism is not newThe writer rarely questioned the tenets of liberal Zionism growing up. Now he embraces anti-Zionism with the fervor of a new convertAaron GellSun 25 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 15.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 1987, the Israeli human rights attorney Felicia Langer was paying a visit to the Neve Tirza women’s prison when a client named Siham shared some disturbing news: the prisoners held there had recently been sprayed with a chemical agent that left them writhing on the floor. Langer grabbed a tissue that had been exposed to the substance – a piece of evidence, perhaps, in a future legal case. Then, on impulse, she lifted it to her face and inhaled deeply. Her hope, she wrote later, was that doing so might enable a doctor to identify the toxin.This anecdote appears in Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History,by Benjamin Moser. In it, the Pulitzer prize-winning author profiles a dozen Jews who actively opposed Zionism, before and after the establishment of Israel – from Aaron Samuel Tamares, a Polish rabbi who began inveighing against Jewish nationalism in the late 19th century; to British diplomat Edwin Montagu, who sought to derail the 1917 Balfour declaration promising a Jewish state in Palestine; to Israeli “new historian” Avi Shlaim – figures he sees as part of “a hidden tradition … of people who, though long dismissed and despised, were ultimately proven right”. Along the way, he seeks to dismantle the Zionist “fairytale,” as he puts it, piece by piece.Langer’s heedless act made her ill but failed to provide the evidence she’d hoped for. It serves as a haunting analogy, however, for Moser’s own work of historical inquiry-slash-self-purification. Having been raised on what he considers a false narrative of the Israel-Palestine conflict, and therefore at risk of moral complicity in an apparent genocide, Moser now proposes to expose himself and his readers to a counter-narrative, however uncomfortable – Siham’s tissue as written history.Anti-Zionism: A Jewish History by Benjamin Moser review – the deep roots of a contemporary movementRead moreOf course, Zionism is a complex and multilayered subject, more hotly contested today than ever before. Where some see a movement of liberation and self-preservation, a principled, heroic response to centuries of oppression and near annihilation, others see a ruthless campaign of land theft, violent dispossession and genocide. Moser, having been raised with the former analysis, now embraces the latter with the defiant fervor of a new convert.When asked during a recent interview in Brooklyn what had changed his mind, the author replied with characteristic brashness: “I didn’t understand the settler-colonialist element – that a group of foreigners sponsored by imperialist powers with bayonets had come into this country that was 95% to 97% non-Jewish and just said: ‘Everybody, fuck off.’”View image in fullscreenAnti-Zionism A Jewish History by Benjamin MoserPhotograph: DoubledayThis is not, to be clear, the consensus view (early Zionist immigrants to Palestine were mostly unarmed refugees fleeing pogroms). And anti-Zionismoccasionally indulges in a similarly essentializing style. While the book is,as its subtitle has it, a work of history,it is also an impassioned act of soul-searching and, in places, a blunt polemic. This makes for an awkward combination, one that sometimes sacrifices objectivity on the altar of moral catharsis. Asked by Piers Morgan to respond to a critic who’d faulted his book for being overly simplistic, Moser cheerfully embraced the assessment: “Idothink it’s black and white!” he declared of the Israel-Palestine conflict.Anti-Zionism appears at a difficult juncture for the pro-Palestine movement, in which polarizing rhetoric and recrimination have become increasingly commonplace as Israel’s killing in Gaza continues. (See, for example, thedeclarationby the Green Party of England and Wales that Zionism is racism, thejeeringof New York mayor Zohran Mamdani for attending a 7 October vigil and anincreasingwillingnessto defend the massacre of 1,200 people in southern Israel as a legitimate response to oppression.) For some, even to suggest that not all Zionists favor ethnic cleansing, Jewish supremacy and the obstruction of Palestinian self-determination smacks of equivocation in the face of mass murder.Moser’s book has given rise to considerable pushback for embodying that vehemence. Critics in the New Yorker, the New York Timesand other influential outlets have taken issue with his portrayal of Zionism as fundamentally malevolent – and Palestinians as essentially blameless – and some have made note of factual inaccuracies.The author seems unfazed, chalking up the critical reviews to politics. “A lot of the people who are coming for me now, who are they? They’re liberal Zionists,” he insisted. “Because what I say is: the whole thing from the very beginning was rubbish. It was a terrible idea. Israel is not something with problems. Itisa problem.”The grandson of Holocaust survivors, Moser, a lanky 50-year-old, was raised in the Reform tradition in Houston, Texas, and rarely questioned the basic tenets of liberal Zionism: that the establishment of a Jewish state in Palestine was a meritorious answer to centuries of victimization, that Israel represented a stronghold of democracy surrounded by hostile neighbors and that Arab recalcitrance was the primary obstacle to a peaceful two-state solution. “The idea of rebuilding a persecuted people in the land from which, millennia before, they had been exiled,” he writes in Anti-Zionism, “appealed to my sense of romance, and of justice … And so, though I was disappointed by Israel, Zionism remained, in my mind, something pure.”A turning point occurred in the summer of 2016, when Moser accepted an invitation to speak about his acclaimed biography of the Brazilian novelist Clarice Lispector at the Palestine festival of literature. PalFest, as it’s known, is not simply a literary event; attendees tour the West Bank, meet Palestinian counterparts and absorb the grim brutality of the occupation up close. While walking down an eerily quiet street in Hebron, a West Bank city where Palestinians must contend with severe restrictions on their movement and constant settler abuse, Moser found himself overwhelmed by what seemed to him a terrible injustice. (The writer Ta-Nehisi Coates, in his recent bookThe Message,described a similar awakening in Hebron.) “I’m from Houston,” Moser said, but “I could walk down the street in this city where people whose families have lived there for thousands or hundreds of years were literally not allowed.”View image in fullscreenFestival participants, including Benjamin Moser, center, have their identities checked while walking through an area of the city inhabited by Israeli settlers on 24 May 2016 in Hebron, Palestine.Photograph: Rob Stothard for the Palestine festival of literatureAside from detailing the experience in a 2021 Substackpost, Moser largely kept his growing misgivings about Israel to himself until last year, when he published a fiery personalessayin the inaugural issue of Equator magazine, a bracing attempt to reconcile the Zionism of his youth with the grotesque civilian suffering imposed on Gaza in the wake of Hamas’s 7 October assault. The piece prompted “a huge reaction, probably more than anything I’ve ever written, all positive”, Moser said. It will be anthologized in the forthcoming edition ofThe Best American Essays.“I thought, we have to write about how Jews are not on board with this,” he told me. In the essay Moser reserves special vitriol for American Jewish leaders, who as he puts it, “were happy to sacrifice our civil liberties, our free press, our judiciary, our foreign relations, to sustain the killing” inGaza.To tell the stories of these 12 apostates, and do so with such obvious affection – he calls such figures “the moral aristocracy of Jewish people” – is in some fundamental sense to join their circle, and to thereby knowingly invite the same calumny that rained upon each one in turn.Moser has a lot to lose. He achieved wunderkind status in his early 30s with his Lispector biography, and was then offered the career-making opportunity to become the authorized biographer of intellectual titan Susan Sontag, a project he pursued with great zeal, conducting hundreds of interviews and nabbing the Pulitzer for the resulting 800-plus page monolith. More recently he published The Upside Down World,a collection of essays on Rembrandt, Vermeer and other Dutch masters. He has, to all appearances, won the literary lottery: when not traveling the world to research his books, he lives in the Netherlands and with his partner, Dutch novelist Arthur Japin, occasionally decamping to a charming tumbledown country house in southwestern France.View image in fullscreenBenjamin Moser reads to an audience at the Arab Culture Association on 24 May 2016 in Haifa, Palestine.Photograph: Rob Stothard for the Palestine festival of literatureWhy then take the risk of swatting at the most polarizing of geopolitical hornets nests?“I think that at a time of genocide, you can either sit on the sidelines and exempt yourself from criticism and think that makes you feel safe,” he said, “or you can, as they say in Brazil, give your face to be beaten.”The first blow came from the New Yorker,to which Moser has contributed a handful of pieces. Isaac Chotiner, who plainly shares Moser’s queasiness around Israel’s wanton destruction of Gaza, wrote areviewof the book that was blistering, to say the least, deeming Moser’s “approach to facts … slovenly to the point of reckless”.Chotiner focuses his critique on the book’s treatment of what Moser calls the “third rail” of Holocaust studies – the ways in which Zionist leaders found ways to cooperate with the Third Reich. “Did the Zionist movement benefit from the Holocaust?” Moser asked during our interview. “A lot of historians disagree, and a lot agree. I have my viewpoint, which I make very clear.”Moser introduces this idea by outlining the shockingly anti-Jewish views of several prominent Zionists, including the movement’s founder, Theodor Herzl, who predicted that “The antisemites will become our most dependable friends,” and himself showed a penchant for classic antisemitic tropes, deploying a 17th-century antisemitic slur, “Mauschel,” to describe Jewish anti-Zionists. “We are a nation of hagglers and crooks,” Herzl wrote, “because Mauschel proliferates and plays stock market tricks.”View image in fullscreenMuna Hassan guides festival participants, including Benjamin Moser , around the Jerusalem’s Old City on 21 May 2016.Photograph: Rob Stothard for the Palestine festival of literatureBut Chotiner makes a compelling case that Moser’s attachment to this theme leads him to misrepresent several important facts. In particular, Moser’s book points to several articles in the Zionist press that appear to whitewash Nazi atrocities or advocate Jewish compliance, which Chotiner demonstrates do no such thing when presented with more context.One can grant the validity of such objections, however, while also acknowledging the virtue of Moser’s larger project: a searching, vivid frontal assault on an ideology that is now fueling one of the greatest atrocities of our time. “It’s just like, people are getting killed every day,” Moser said with a long sigh. “And they want to fight with you about your footnotes. Then they want to attack you personally and try to destroy your career. But I 100% stand by my book. People can criticize me for whatever they want, but they can’t criticize me for not making myself clear.”A few months ago, Moser visited Berlin to attend his niece’s batmitzvah. There, he visited the former home of his grandparents and paused to contemplate theStolpersteine,the commemorative brass “stumbling stones”, dedicated to their memory. Before immigrating to the US, his grandfather, Franz Egon Moses, had spent time in Mandatory Palestine. Moses’s volume of Herzl’s Zionist Writings is now in Moser’s library. Had he lived, Moses might well reject his grandson’s turn toward anti-Zionism. But maybe not.“I hope they’d be proud of me,” Moser said of his ancestors, growing somber. “People didn’t stand up for them. People shut up. They took their kids to school and went shopping, just like all these people are doing now. I don’t want to be that kind of person.” Briefly removing his glasses, Moser gave his eyes a quick wipe. “Those aren’t the people I respect.”Explore more on these topicsIsraelPalestineGazaIsrael-Gaza warHistory booksMiddle East and north AfricaJudaismfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Greg Wise on how he and Emma Thompson coped with failed IVF: ‘We hit an existential crisis – she was not a proper woman and I was not a proper man’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Their hopes of having a second child were dashed. Two decades on, the actor remembers the grief and pain of that time
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Their hopes of having a second child were dashed. Two decades on, the actor remembers the grief and pain of that time
Content: Greg Wise, photographed last month.Photograph: Cian Oba-Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGreg Wise, photographed last month.Photograph: Cian Oba-Smith/The GuardianLife and styleGreg Wise on how he and Emma Thompson coped with failed IVF: ‘We hit an existential crisis – she was not a proper woman and I was not a proper man’Their hopes of having a second child were dashed. Two decades on, the actor remembers the grief and pain of that timeGreg WiseSun 25 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“I’m afraid this cycle has not been successful.” Emma and I cannot catch each other’s eye. We sit mute in our grief in the silence of theIVFdoctor’s office. This is a kind of grief that is often not understood even to be grief at all. A grief about the loss of a potential child. An anticipatory grief – a grief for something that hasn’t yet appeared – a mourning for a possibility, of a longed-for future life to welcome, love and nurture. And there are no set grief rituals for this – for a child never present – no space in our society to mark, to grieve an actual physical death. It is a silent, achingly lonely, atomised grief. We had undergone many attempts in the years after the birth of our daughter Gaia. But that did not make this any easier.Each cycle, each time we sat in that office, we had to ignore our grief and concentrate wholeheartedly and positively on our next attempt. We didn’t access any help over this time. We didn’t seek out counselling as a couple. I had no knowledge of how to process my grief – compounded month on month. Further cycles, more drugs, more fertility hormones, more ovarian hyperstimulation, injections, scans, blood tests came and went, all proving unsuccessful. I supported all wholeheartedly, but Emma was devastated by her inability to conceive again. In her mind, she had failed and could not forgive herself for that failure. And nothing I could say would change her point of view.Her deep grief took her away. I had to deny mine. Try to comfort her rather than myself. Such is the lot of the self-appointed saviour.Emma and I had met seven years before on the set of the film Sense and Sensibility. She had adapted Jane Austen’s novel, and was playing Elinor Dashwood; I was John Willoughby, a “caped Adonis” on an enormous white horse, galloping in and scooping up her injured and prone sister Marianne, delivering her back home. As I leave the scene, the hero of the hour, the saviour of potential catastrophe, in a swirl of cape and the heady musk of testosterone: “His manly beauty and more than common gracefulness were instantly the theme of general admiration.” The problem was, this was how I had always seen myself in real life.Emma and I came together in the unreal space that is a film set. They are very seductive spaces, film sets. Protected spaces, as we are all outside our natural, everyday lives. And it was here that my roles as saviour in the film and as saviour in life collided.I galloped in, on my big white horse, scooped her up, andsavedher.View image in fullscreenThe couple in 2001.Photograph: Evan Agostini/Getty ImagesEmma’s husband had moved out of their home just before the filming started. She was in profound grief at the apparent ending of their marriage. But she also held a chronic grief. Her father, Eric Thompson – the writer and narrator of the cult television programme The Magic Roundabout – had suffered his first heart attack when Emma was eight. He had had a severe stroke 10 years later, which left him semi-paralysed, and she took it upon herself to help this extraordinarily skilled lover of language to speak again. He died when she was 23.She had already lost her wonderful uncle – her mother, Phyllida’s, brother James. He had been in a catastrophic car crash in his early life, and had never fully recovered. He suffered a brain haemorrhage when Emma was in her late teens. She was the only family member present to make the decision to turn off his life support, before she walked back home, alone, with a bin bag filled with his clothes. Within a few short years of her father’s death, she also lost the other vital male figure in her life, her godfather.Filming finished, we hid ourselves in my little two-up, two-down house in north London. Both of us bringing along our overstuffed suitcase of grief, bulging with recent and age-old unresolved pains.double quotation markAfter three years together, it was time to settle. It was, we decided, time to start a familyThis was the first shape that was created. We bonded in our grief – Emma’s present grief at the end of her marriage, my anticipatory grief that she might nonetheless try to revivify it, grief at the possibility of the death of this relationship, so soon, with so much recent love and so much future promise.Then everything exploded when the tabloid press found us out and we had to escape. And created a new shape – the fugitives.We went to work in Los Angeles, rented a house there, filmed projects, lived a fun life up in the hills, with a pool, a convertible sports car. Our shape now of a hopeful, creative, unfettered, adventurous, outward-looking, energised couple. But this shape could not last. We had to reshape ourselves to the realities of our lives. And Emma now divorced, we decided it was time to come back home. After three years together, it was time to settle. It was, we decided, time to start a family.Then the next grief hit us.We were unable to conceive. And Emma was fast approaching 40.The simple fact of us not being able to get pregnant was momentous. It is one of those major marking points, the end of one way of looking at life, as it is a death, in a way – a death of a possibility, a death of a new shape that had been expected, and brought both a profound grief and a deep sense of shame in its wake. A shame borne by both me and Emma, as we saw ourselves as unable to fulfil our purest and most natural role in life – to procreate. We hit an existential crisis – it’s a given, all the stories we had read as children, telling us that girls grow up to become mothers; boys, fathers – Emma was, therefore, not a proper woman and I was not a proper man.Even without knowing the root of our problem, I was gnawed at by the sense of being emasculated. The confusion of my fertility somehow being aligned to my manliness, virility and sexual potency. I couldn’t shake the feeling that I had somehow failed as a man, with the simple fact that I had spun in my head – infertility equals impotence.We both undertook tests to see where the problem lay. The problem lay with Emma. We would never be able to conceive naturally. IVF was the only option if we wanted to have a child of our own.double quotation markWe didn’t know that IVF opens up a potential minefield of grief – a constant swinging between hope and despair within each cycle of the treatmentIt is absolutely extraordinary that IVF treatment exists. Extraordinary, but also brutal. And oddly, within a process that hopefully results in the creation of a human, it can feel utterly dehumanising. It is purely a clinical process and easy to become totally overwhelmed with every aspect: decision-making, appointments, injection schedules, scans, where to get the treatment, how many embryos to transfer.We knew we were so fortunate to be able to afford to undertake the process, but we didn’t know that embarking on IVF opens up a potential minefield of grief – a constant swinging between hope and despair within each cycle of the treatment. It was physically gruelling for Emma. She was exhausted, in pain, filled with chemicals, her hormones all over the place, overstimulated while at the same time having to try to remain resolutely calm.And all I could do was support her; within this treatment, all my capacity for any sense of agency was almost nonexistent. My job in its clinical entirety was purely to provide some sperm. That was it. I just had to do a quick sprint; she was on the marathon.And I couldn’t fix this. I couldn’t make things better or make this work. This was so hard for me to confront – I couldn’t be the saviour now. I just had to try to be strong, protecting Emma as best I could, trying to lighten the load as much as I could. But this was her gig, not mine.Our very first attempt at IVF resulted in a positive pregnancy test just days before her 40th birthday. Four weeks before we welcomed in the new millennium, we celebrated the arrival of our beautiful, healthy baby daughter Gaia, whom we’d first seen at four-cells old. Our shape had changed once more: we were now awestruck, doting parents.View image in fullscreenThompson and Wise, with their newborn daughter, Gaia, in 1999.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyIn Gaia’s second year of life, we started another IVF cycle. And failed. Repeatedly.That day in the doctor’s office, we decided to stop. The most difficult decision we had yet had to make. No result, nothing tangible, it just stopped. It had failed. Rationally, it was the only decision we could have come to – emotionally, it was untenable. We were dislocated, isolated in our overwhelming grief. I now know we were slipping into complicated grief.Even though there can be no set timescale for processing, the myriad of feelings within the grief can expand themselves into our void of loss and become a chronic problem. This grief can consume our lives.The precision of the grief, the focus of the loss, muddies and seeps out and, over time, if not addressed, metamorphoses into major depression. This is where it took us, an overbearing blanket of sadness covering the two of us. And we both felt so alone; we couldn’t address it as a couple, we didn’t seek help together.This complicated grief, given the medical moniker prolonged grief disorder, now classed as an official mental health disorder, hits about one in 10 of us powerless to come to terms with our loss half a year on. A helplessness, inability to accept, disbelief, numbness. Grief is natural, grief is healthy, grief is essential in the process of being able to adjust to where we find ourself after a loss, but it can become a clinical problem, it can disrupt our life so fully that we can’t find a way out. And it can be made even more toxic if guilt and shame are in the mix.I had never been a more grief-sodden mess, feeling myself, months after we had finally made the decision, falling into a black depression. I had totally hit the bottom and could not navigate myself out of the darkness I found myself in. There was nothing I could do. Other than to ask for help.Ihave always been a bit of a northern man about getting medical help. I am terrifically accident-prone. From a childhood spent falling out of trees to being a grownup with a collection of madly dangerous power tools, I have often wandered back to the house with blood streaming, large bone-showing holes, but refusing to seek out a medical professional. I have a certain amount of shame attached to my self-inflicted injuries; that the medics would view me as they would a child with a saucepan wedged on their head – humorous, a bit pathetic, but mainly just idiotic.double quotation markI knew I was in pain. I knew that I needed professional helpI viewed therapy in the same way. A neurotic American fixation, an ego-fuelled unnecessary waste of time and money, and something to be sneered at. Our lot in life was to deny, obfuscate and just bloody well get on with it. This was my belief.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThen I moved in with Emma. She had started her therapy before we got together, and would wander off down the street to see her Jungian therapist weekly. After a while, I started to perceive this as a threat. I’d heard stories of a partner getting therapy and then breaking up the relationship – that it involved laying the blame for the couple’s ills on the other partner. The fact that I thought this illustrates the fear and pain that were my constant companions.I was told many years later that you finally go into therapy when you realise that the pain you are carrying is greater than the pain of exploring it. And therapy is painful, without doubt. It is painful because you are exposing things that have been living in the very core of your being for perhaps your entire lifetime, and often these things don’t give themselves up without a fight.But I knew I was in pain. I knew that I needed professional help. Starting it was the best decision I have ever made.Ibegan my journey in a little upstairs room in central London. The first thing that confused me was that I wasn’t lying down – the pose adopted in all the films I’d watched. The second thing was that, six sessions in, the only one seeming to be doing any talking was me. I couldn’t see any therapy happening whatsoever. It was gently pointed out to me that nothing could be discussed until my story had unfolded enough to be looked at.I brought shame with me into the room. It wrapped around me, muffled me. Shame brings muteness. I needed to articulate what had up till now never been articulated. That was one of the most difficult aspects of this, telling my history, as honestly and personally as possible.But a large part of my shame was that I didn’t seem to be doing this properly. I would start to try to unpack with, “I think …” and be told, “I would really like to know what youfeel…”I didn’t know what I felt. Apart from feeling I wanted to stop coming to therapy. That I was being made to feel ashamed by the process.Even though everyone’s grief is unique to them, there are clear patterns to where it sits, whether in feeling or thought. I approached my grief in a cerebral way, as I had been brought up to do: think my way through.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Cian Oba-Smith/The GuardianI was grieving the way the majority of men grieve. I  had my dad as my original guide to what being a man looked like; I had my single-sex school, bringing along with it how boys should behave and what kinds of men they should become; I ventured out into my adult life as Man the Saviour – the protector, the provider of safety and security, setting aside my wants for the sake of the other, emotionally restrained, self-controlled.This is what I brought into the therapy. What it is to be a man – independent, not showing vulnerability, strong, stoic. All these traits, given to me to wear like an ill-fitting jacket, made this type of therapy almost impossible for me. I was thoughtful, active, a problem-solver, but I was being asked to be open, expressive, available emotionally.It took me a while to see that this type of therapy was not for me. That this style required an expression of feeling. That here, grief meant emotion. That my being different from the model that was being expounded meant I was failing. I had to go and see what else was on offer.And there is an almost limitless amount of therapy available – animal-assisted, humanistic, psychosynthesis, existential, Jungian, Freudian, gestalt … The psychoanalytic side – about the unconscious, dream analysis, free association – all emotion-driven. But alongside this is an action-oriented approach – behavioural therapy – identifying patterns, working out solutions, using a pen and paper. Being cognitive. This was the one for me.There are two main strands of cognitive therapy – analytic (CAT) and behavioural (CBT). The analytic looks at our past to try to understand our present-day thoughts and actions. Questionnaires are filled out, problem patterns are written down, ways of navigating found. The behavioural focuses on our present-day problems, helps change the way that life is looked on, replacing negative thoughts, encouraging a more positive outlook.I found myself working with a CAT therapist. I felt, for the first time within a therapeutic setting, that I was using my natural strengths – I had always needed to draw a problem on paper: create a diagram, a flow chart, a design. This was the way my mind worked; that’s what led me to study architecture. Here, I was doing the same thing – seeing myself from different angles, where the constructional stresses lay and how the shape of my present form was dictated by the layers of design and building over my lifetime. Over the next few months, we got to work rebuilding.We can think that we are utterly unique, and our situation has never been viewed before, that we are totally alone in our personal struggle, that nobody would be able to understand our plight, our grief, but we are all just like every other human being – trying to navigate our way through the difficulties of life, with what we were bequeathed, what we have experienced since and with what hits us on a seemingly daily basis. This is all therapy is – telling our story to somebody who will help us make connections, make us feel we are seen, we are heard, know that we are not alone. A therapist is just somebody who has been told many, many stories and – just as there are only eight notes in a scale but they give us plainchant, Purcell and Pink Floyd – it’s the same in this: our melody is unique, but is made up of only eight notes. Therapists help us to retune, rescore and play our melody to its fullest beautiful potential.Ihave a large collection of power tools which I use in my various woodwork and building projects – I am pretty handy with them. I never start by reading the manual. I learn by doing. My two university degrees were chosen with this in mind. I wanted to attack my studies in a tangible way, with pen and paper in architecture, with my body and imagination in acting. I had done the same thing with my grief. Now I was being shown that a manual actually exists. It was time to work through it.The CAT was the start of my grief work, the most important work I’ve ever done. Realising that my attempts over my life to deny, ignore or run away from my grief had just made the struggle harder. Beginning to find it, see it, give it a shape and a presence in me, and then facing into it and seeing how it can be dealt with, gave me a peace I don’t think I’d known until that point. Working through it was painful, but my avoidance of the work had caused me so much suffering.It’s exhausting being a saviour. There is no rest. No peace. Endlessly scanning the skies for the damsel-in-distress bat signal. Endlessly jumping on my steed and charging off to the rescue of said damsel. Being helped to unpack this and let this saviour figure gallop off was a welcome relief. Finding that he was just the response to childhood griefs, to my bequeathed fractured family dynamic, it wasn’t me, although it had shaped my being thus far. I was helped to tell the story of me as the grieving child and build out from there. And there was nothing else I could do but square up to it at this time – this place I found myself of such deep grief at the failure to have another child, alongside my already being a father. My small child now my physical responsibility, knowing that looking back at myself as the small child was now my emotional responsibility.double quotation markWe had our beautiful, extraordinary daughter … we were a family. I came to appreciate that the present wildly outweighed any sense of lossMy grief at the fracturing of the shape that Emma and I had so lovingly created, my grief at the impossibility of a family shape that we had so desperately yearned for, my grief at my past, all now starting to be articulated.And we had our beautiful, extraordinary daughter. Feeling our hearts would explode with the love we felt for her. This tiny person, this ball of emotion, this  intrigue, this joy. Her exploration of a wholly new world, with its excitement, its confusion, its wonder, its fascination, wobbling alongside my new explorations.Such gratitude. Whatever shape we had battled with, we were a family. I came to appreciate that the present wildly outweighed any sense of loss.My therapeutic work brought another bit of clarity along with it – that Emma and I were grieving differently. Her grief deeply emotional, mine thoughtful. We were suffering from what life had thrown at us, but also, we were suffering because we were each bemused by the other’s response to their suffering. But we were just doing grief our own way.Grief can make us feel so utterly lonely. Feeling not understood, or misunderstood, finding others’ expression of grief incomprehensible. Unable to prise apart our own present, future and past pains. Feeling muddied and overwhelmed by all these different griefs. For me, therapy helped me to learn that by acknowledging and understanding my own grief, I could acknowledge and understand another’s. That if I could truly see my own pain, I could see someone else’s. Not try to hide it or ignore it, but see it, accept it, work with it.Above all, not to minimise it. That my pain, my grief, had to be recognised, however small or insignificant it seemed within the great griefs of the world.This is an edited extract from Grief Talking by Greg Wise, published by Bluebird on 5 November at £18.99. title: Exiled opposition leader María Corina Machado returns to Venezuela | Venezuela | The Guardian
description: Nobel peace prize winner’s return after almost a year in exile is unlikely to please interim president Delcy Rodríguez
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Nobel peace prize winner’s return after almost a year in exile is unlikely to please interim president Delcy Rodríguez
Content: Upon her return after almost a year in exile, María Corina Machado attended mass in Barquisimeto.Photograph: Vente Venezuela Press/ReutersView image in fullscreenUpon her return after almost a year in exile, María Corina Machado attended mass in Barquisimeto.Photograph: Vente Venezuela Press/ReutersVenezuelaExiled opposition leader María Corina Machado returns to VenezuelaNobel peace prize winner’s return after almost a year in exile is unlikely to please interim president Delcy RodríguezTom Phillipsin Rio de JaneiroSun 25 Oct 2026 15.56 EDTFirst published on Sun 25 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Venezuelan opposition leader,María Corina Machado, has announced she has returned to Venezuela almost a year after she left the country to receive the Nobel peace prize.“I’m here. With you,” she wrote on X on Sunday lunchtime.Her close ally Edmundo González, who is in exile, confirmed her arrival. “Venezuela! I am thrilled to announce to you that our leader, my dear María Corina, is on Venezuelan soil,” he posted on social media.“Today is a very important day for Venezuelans. Our sovereign voice returns with her to lead and guide this process!” he said, adding that he too would soon return.It was not immediately clear how Machado, 59, had managed to return to Venezuela but footage on social media showed she was in Barquisimeto, the capital of Lara state, which is about 220 miles west of the capital, Caracas.Images showed her surrounded by supporters holding mobile phones in the Sanctuary of the Divine Shepherdess church.View image in fullscreenMachado at the Sanctuary of the Divine Shepherdess in Barquisimeto.Photograph: Jose Miguel Alarcon/EPAFootage posted on social mediaby her close ally Pedro Urruchurtu showed hundreds of supporters gathered outside the church to greet her, shouting: “Freedom! Freedom! Freedom!”TheTrump administrationhad reportedly opposed Machado’s return, believing her presence would complicate the cosy relationship it has struck up with the interim president, Delcy Rodríguez, since abducting her former boss, Nicolás Maduro, in January.Nicolás Maduro tells New York court new torture allegations are ‘false’Read moreMachado and Rodríguez are political arch-rivals.Machado slipped out of Venezuela last December – a few weeks before Maduro’s capture – and in recent months has reportedly made more than half a dozen failed attempts to return home, including after the devastating earthquake that hit the northern coast in June.View image in fullscreenMachado is surrounded by supporters in Barquisimeto on Sunday.Photograph: Jesus Hernandez/APAfter Maduro was seized, many had expected Donald Trump to give Machado his blessing to take power. Her movement is widely believed to have beaten Maduro in the 2024 presidential election, but he refused to hand over power.Instead the US president embraced Rodríguez, Maduro’s vice-president, who now governs a country widely seen as a US protectorate.Machado has repeatedly heaped praise on Trump for launching the operation to remove Maduro, and gave him her 2025 Nobel peace prize medal, which she had been awarded for her peaceful challenge to Venezuela’s authoritarian government.‘It’s utter surrealism’: Venezuela’s Chavistas lament government’s embrace of TrumpRead moreAsked by reporters on Sunday about her return, Trump said: “I don’t know anything about it, but I think she’s a very nice woman. She gave me her Nobel prize, so how can I say anything else?“I hope she’s safe. She’s a very nice woman. But we’re doing very well in Venezuela.”The US secretary of state​, Marco Rubio, claimed credit for creating the conditions that allowed Machado’s safe return after 10 months in exile.Her return “is the direct result of the U​S​-supported reconciliation talks which has already seen hundreds of political prisoners freed and hundreds of political opposition figures return from exile”, he said.From Barquisimeto, Machado headed east through the ​state of Yaracuy towards Caracas in a convoy of vehicles.Images released by aidesshow her reaching out from a car’s sunroof towards dozens of supporters who had gathered at the roadside to see her.Members of Venezuela’s government have long hinted that Machado would be arrested if she tried to return as a result of her years-long struggle for political change. But there was no sign of the security services bothering her on Sunday as she moved towards the capital, perhaps suggesting Washington had sanctioned her return and instructed Rodríguez’s government not to react.Machado has called for fresh presidential elections to be held by July 2027, but it is unclear whether the Trump administration supports that timeline given the lucrative partnership it has struck up with Rodríguez.Trump announced what he called “the biggest oil deal in world history” with Venezuela in August, subsequently describing the agreement as the spoils of January’s brief “war”.Explore more on these topicsVenezuelaMaría Corina MachadoAmericasDelcy RodríguezUS foreign policyNicolás MaduroTrump administrationnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brazilians vote in presidential election runoff pitting leftist Lula against far-right Bolsonaro | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Incumbent president lost in first round to senator and son of convicted ex-president
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Incumbent president lost in first round to senator and son of convicted ex-president
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro and Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva debate on 18 October 2026 in São Paulo, Brazil.Photograph: Tuane Fernandes/NurPhoto/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro and Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva debate on 18 October 2026 in São Paulo, Brazil.Photograph: Tuane Fernandes/NurPhoto/ShutterstockBrazilBrazilians vote in presidential election runoff pitting leftist Lula against far-right BolsonaroIncumbent president lost in first round to senator and son of convicted ex-presidentTiago Rogeroin Rio de JaneiroSun 25 Oct 2026 10.41 EDTFirst published on Sun 25 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBrazilians are going to the polls on Sunday in a highly unpredictable runoff in which the leftist president,Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, is attempting an unprecedented comeback against the far-right senatorFlávio Bolsonaro, who won the first-round vote.Bolsonaro’s surprise victory despite not leading most polls made him the favourite three weeks ago, but since then Lula’s campaign has gained ground, and the two go into the contest virtually tied.The gap between them was the narrowest ever recorded in a first round, at less than 2% of the vote, and the 80-year-old president has spent much of the runoff campaign focused on turnout – abstention reached a record high in the first round and disproportionately affects his voters – and on stoking fears over what a return to power by a member of the Bolsonaro family could mean.Battle over Meta’s alleged Bolsonaro bias intensifies days before Brazil presidential runoffRead moreA congressman for more than 20 years with few bills passed, the 45-year-old Bolsonaro is the eldest son of the former presidentJair Bolsonaro, who is under house arrest serving a 27-year sentence for attempting a coup to overturn his 2022 defeat to Lula.“I think the time has come for real change,” said Bolsonaro after voting on Sunday morning at a school in Rio de Janeiro’s north zone. “Brazil can’t take another four years the way things are ... Everyone’s life has got worse.”Lula voted in São Bernardo do Campo, the industrial city where hispolitical career begannearly half a century ago, and said he had “never seen anything like” the leftist demonstrations – many emerging organically among young people – that swept the country in support of him during the runoff.“What the people have done for me in these past few days is something I can never repay. It is so much generosity, so much affection, so much love. I will be eternally grateful,” said Lula, adding that he was “confident” the people would not choose Bolsonaro.The senator has promised that if elected he will pardon his father, and with an even more conservative congress taking office next year, he has vowed to “change the constitution and re-democratise this country”, sending chills through those who fear he could follow in his father’s authoritarian footsteps.View image in fullscreenLula attending a closing campaign rally in São Paulo on Saturday.Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/Reuters“We’re facing two completely different projects for the country,” said voter Nuno Rau, 63, an architect and writer. “One points towards the end of social rights and the end of democracy itself; on the other side is someone who fought for income distribution and free public education. I may have criticisms of Lula, but there is no way to choose Bolsonaro,” he added.Aparecida Moreira, a 62-year-old lawyer, will vote for Bolsonaro mainly because of the “iron fist” security policy he proposes, including building five “mega-prisons” inspired by those of El Salvador’s populist autocrat Nayib Bukele.“I agree with Bolsonaro’s idea of chemical castration for rapists, because there is no crime worse than rape,” said Moreira, adding that voting for Lula would be the same as voting for the“dictator” Alexandre de Moraes, the justice who, despite not having been appointed by Lula, is widely associated with him by Bolsonaro supporters because he oversaw the former president’s conviction.Both Flávio Bolsonaro and Lula drewlarge crowdsto their final campaign rallies on Saturday in Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo and Belo Horizonte.In northern Minas Gerais state, Iara Pimentel, a councillor from Lula’s party, sufferedfacial injuriesand had to be taken to hospital after the motorcade in which she was travelling was hit by glass bottles and bricks thrown by Bolsonaro supporters. “It is unacceptable for people to be attacked for expressing their political views,” Pimentelpostedafter leaving hospital.View image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro dancing at a rally in São Paulo on 18 October.Photograph: Alexandre Meneghini/ReutersWith each side of supporters virtually “crystallised”, the election will be decided by the small number of voters who identify with neither candidate.Bolsonaro began the runoff campaign with a lead and the support of most other defeated candidates, but instead of growing, he stagnated in the polls.Many analysts saw this as the result of part of the population suddenly waking up to the “fear” of a Bolsonaro returning to power, as well as controversies including the fact that the senator is under investigation in two federal police inquiries over alleged corruption and money laundering.Lula, by contrast, radically changed his digital strategy and benefited from student-led protests across the country, most of which did not even involve the president.“In the first round, Lula’s campaign failed to connect with the population, but now it has been civil society movements that have driven his growth,” said the political scientist Helcimara de Souza Telles.View image in fullscreenLula attending a closing campaign rally on Saturday.Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/ReutersThe final polls published on Saturday showed Bolsonaro stillslightly ahead.The result is expected late Sunday evening, and whatever the outcome, the race is expected to be decided by a narrow margin in Latin America’s largest country, with an electorate of 159 million.Many analysts believe that if Lula overturns his first-round defeat, Bolsonaro could follow his father’s example from four years ago and refuse to concede, and that Donald Trump, a longstanding ally of the Bolsonaro clan, could refuse to recognise the result.“Trump wants to ‘colonise’ all of Latin America in pursuit of its own interests,” said Telles, adding that, with rightwing candidates having won all seven presidential elections held in Latin America since Trump began his second term,Brazilis one of the few countries in the region still offering any resistance to the US president.“So a Bolsonaro victory would mean losing Brazil to a model of autocracy backed by the US,” she added.Explore more on these topicsBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaFlávio BolsonaroJair BolsonaroUS foreign policyAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Signs suggest Thomas Markle Sr may be ‘sex offender of the grossest kind’, says Philippine minister | Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Forensic analysis of found images continues as Meghan’s father denies possessing child sexual abuse images
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: Exclusive: Forensic analysis of found images continues as Meghan’s father denies possessing child sexual abuse images
Content: Thomas Markle Sr, pictured in an ITV interview in 2018, has denied possessing child sexual abuse images.Photograph: ReutersView image in fullscreenThomas Markle Sr, pictured in an ITV interview in 2018, has denied possessing child sexual abuse images.Photograph: ReutersMeghan, the Duchess of SussexSigns suggest Thomas Markle Sr may be ‘sex offender of the grossest kind’, says Philippine ministerExclusive: Forensic analysis of found images continues as Meghan’s father denies possessing child sexual abuse imagesOliver HolmesandCaroline DaviesSun 25 Oct 2026 07.52 EDTFirst published on Sun 25 Oct 2026 05.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAll signs point to Thomas Markle Sr being a “possible sex offender of the grossest kind” although a full forensic investigation will give a “definitive picture”, the Philippine interior minister has told the Guardian.Authorities in the south-east Asian country are analysing digital images allegedly belonging to the estranged father of the Duchess of Sussex that were said to have been found at his former home in Cebu. Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, reported to authorities last week that he had apparently discovered a stash of child sexual abuse images.The duchess, already estranged from her father, broke off all contact with him last year, reportedly telling him she and the authorities were aware of allegations he had abused young girls, it is understood.In a final letter to her father first reported by the Sun on Sunday, sent while he was in a hospital in thePhilippineshaving had a leg amputated, Meghan made clear he would never see his grandchildren Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, and that she would never contact him again, it is understood.Jonvic Remulla, the Philippine interior minister, told the Guardian: “In these cases where family disputes are mixed up, we have to consider all the angles. Right now all signs point to a possible sex offender of the grossest kind. We want to be sure before we release the findings. The forensics data will be complete in a week.”Remulla said a statement would be released once the data had been analysed, without giving a specific date. “Please give us a week to determine the contents and to come up with a definitive picture,” he said. “We will release a statement then.”Markle Sr has denied possessing child sexual abuse images, telling the Daily Mail the accusations were “sick lies”. Philippine police are also investigating a laptop found at the home in Cebu where Markle Sr had been living until he returned to the US earlier this year.In a statement given to Agence France-Presse, Remulla said the Philippine national police inspected Markle’s former home and found a “trove of child pornography materials as well as a laptop”.“The PNP will coordinate with their counterparts to locate and take appropriate legal actions against Mr Markle if found that there is sufficient evidence to charge him,” he said.Markle Sr has told the Mail the computers had not been in his possession since he left Mexico with his son in 2025 and moved to the Philippines “for a fresh start”. He said: “This is bullshit. It’s just a bunch of lies. It’s sick. I have no idea why Tom is trying to destroy me with these lies.”The Sun reported on Friday that Meghan’s half-brother, Thomas Markle Jr, told detectives in the Philippines he had discovered “hundreds, if not thousands” of child sexual abuse images on computers and mobile phones stored in four large boxes at the home in Cebu. Markle Jr, 60, said he had also contacted the FBI in the US, the newspaper said.Meghan has revealed she learned of allegations against her father in 2019, having been told by the Metropolitan police, and said she was given assurances these claims were being investigated. Sources said she had been advised that speaking publicly about the claims could have jeopardised any potential legal case and also put her at risk of legal action.On Saturday the Met confirmed it had passed a letter “containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom” to Meghan and the Duke of Sussex in 2019 but did not share details with other law enforcement agencies. Scotland Yard is considering whether to refer itself to the Independent Office for Police Conduct to review its actions.The duchess was “upset and really frustrated” that the Met had not acted on allegations made in that letter, sources said.In a new interview with the Mail on Sunday, Markle Sr said he had “never had sex with anyone under the age of 18”, telling the paper that when he was single he travelled to the Philippines at least twice and paid for sex.He is reportedly in a Florida rehabilitation centre after his leg amputation.In a statement on Friday, Meghan said she was “deeply distressed at the news that has come to light in the last 24 hours, and my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed”.She said: “In 2018, a letter was sent to the Metropolitan police and Royalty and Specialist Protection. That letter was subsequently shared with me. It made troubling and disturbing allegations against my father and I was given assurances that these were being investigated.“I hope it can now be understood that, despite certain media publications’ distortion over the years, any distance from my father, and my choice to not allow him to have contact with our children, was for one reason: to protect them. I trusted that the authorities were doing the same for other families.“Although the breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine, my sincerest hope is that justice will be fully served and that the priority remains the safety and protection of innocent children.”Sources later clarified she had misremembered the year in which the Met had contacted her, and confirmed it had been 2019, not 2018 as she said on Friday.The FBI said in a statement on Friday that it was “aware of the allegations and will provide support, as appropriate, to the Philippine authorities. We will also investigate any related allegations of federal violations of US law.”Explore more on these topicsMeghan, the Duchess of SussexMonarchyPhilippinesAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Extremely disappointed’: WA government seeks reimbursement from Deloitte over flawed university report  | Western Australian politics | The Guardian
description: State paid consultancy firm $166,000 for feasibility study on merging the three tertiary institutions
Author: Krishani Dhanji
Headline: State paid consultancy firm $166,000 for feasibility study on merging the three tertiary institutions
Content: Deloitte is under pressure after a report into the potential merger of three WA universities contained AI-hallucinated references and incorrect figures.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPView image in fullscreenDeloitte is under pressure after a report into the potential merger of three WA universities contained AI-hallucinated references and incorrect figures.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPWestern Australian politics‘Extremely disappointed’: WA government seeks reimbursement from Deloitte over flawed university reportState paid consultancy firm $166,000 for feasibility study on merging the three tertiary institutionsGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastKrishani DhanjiandJosh TaylorSun 25 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 19.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Western Australian government has said it is “extremely disappointed” and is seeking an “expedited” cost recovery from Deloitte after errors were discovered in a report about a potential university merger, including AI-hallucinated references and hundreds of millions of dollars in cost discrepancies.The government paidDeloitte$166,000 for a feasibility study on merging the University of Western Australia, Curtin University and Murdoch University.Deloitte considered three merger options between the three universities, with “low”, “mid” and “high” cost scenarios, and broke down the calculations of those costs in the report’s appendix.Under the “high” cost scenario of a merger between Curtin and UWA, the report calculates the “total costs to day 1” as $514m, and “post day 1” over five years at $145m. The total cost of those two payments is $659m but the report wrote $399m – a $260m discrepancy.Prof Stephen Bartos, an expert in public sector governance at the University of Canberra, said the errors discredited the report. “In my view, they’re so extensive that you probably need a new report, or at the very least someone to go through that material from the ground up and rework it manually without the use of AI,” he said.“Any errors in a report like this, especially on something controversial like a university merger, discredits the report, and Deloitte shouldn’t have had these errors.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailUnder a “low” cost merger scenario between Curtin, UWA and Murdoch, the total costs to day one are $396m and total post day one over five years are $116m. That total would be $512m but the report calculates the two numbers to $823m – a $311m discrepancy.Deloitte is already under pressure after it was revealed in the media this month that the same report contained hallucinated AI references, leading the state opposition to label it “AI slop”.The consultancy firm admits in its report it used generative AI to “support the collation of research, synthesis of information and editorial proofing” and had earlier dismissed the errors as “minor”.Deloitte to pay money back to Albanese government after using AI in $440,000 reportRead moreA spokesperson for the WA government told Guardian Australia that the Department of Energy and Economic Diversification had written to Deloitte to expedite the cost recovery process for the report.“We are extremely disappointed these errors are being found now,” the spokesperson said.“We are advised they do not affect the modelling in the report or its findings, but any errors will be corrected as part of a review by Deloitte which will re-issue the report.“All available data, along with new information, will be interrogated by the university reform business case.”The WA tertiary education minister, Tony Buti, described them as “typos”, though a day later said he was angry and disappointed with Deloitte.Guardian Australia has found that one of the references to a World Health Organization report has a ChatGPT metadata tag on the URL, indicating that the link was directly sourced from the chatbot.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the report, Curtin University is referred to repeatedly as the Curtin University of Technology – a name the institution has not used since 2010, and that was changed under an act of state parliament in 2017.Bartos said the numbers diverging so significantly was cause for concern. “Unless the numbers add up, a government might not want to do it,” he said.Prof Christian Downie, from the Australian National University’s school of regulation and global governance, who has previously examined submissions to government that contained AI hallucinations, said human errors happened and mistakes in reports could be expected and, although Deloitte outlined broadly its use of AI in the report, there was a lack of transparency.“We need much more detail about how [AI is] being used and for what parts of the report writing process,” he said. “If they’re going to use it for data collection and if there’s concerns about the data, then that needs to be detailed in the report.”Downie said without transparency it was hard to have confidence in the report. He said broadly as AI use increases, governments need to reassess their contracts with consultancy firms.“All levels of government, both state and federal, need to be recalibrating their contractual relationship arrangements when they outsource work to consulting firms to ensure that the proper incentives and penalties are in place in those contracts,” he said.The WA government has that argued the merger is a “once-in-a-generation” opportunity. Buti told the ABC on Tuesday: “I want to commit to it if the business case stacks up, and then it’s a government decision.”It was not supported by Murdoch University, whose vice-chancellor, Prof Andrew Deeks, criticised the report and penned an op-ed on the university’s website arguing that “all that a university merger will do for WA is cost a lot of time, money and energy, while reducing choices for students and alienating alumni”.“That the Western Australian government continues to be taken in by this nonsense is extraordinary,” he wrote. “Another fail for Deloitte.”Deloitte did not respond to questions from Guardian Australia.Explore more on these topicsWestern Australian politicsWestern AustraliaDeloitteAustralian universitiesAustralian educationAI (artificial intelligence)Consulting (Australia)newsShareReuse this content

title: Serbian leader Aleksandar Vučić ousted by student movement in seismic election | Serbia | The Guardian
description: Vučić’s 12-year reign looks to have been ended by record turnout of voters in election provoked by student-led protests
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: Vučić’s 12-year reign looks to have been ended by record turnout of voters in election provoked by student-led protests
Content: Celebrations break out in Belgrade as Student List win elections by a landslideSerbiaSerbian leader Aleksandar Vučić ousted by student movement in seismic electionVučić’s 12-year reign looks to have been ended by record turnout of voters in election provoked by student-led protestsAshifa Kassam, and Ana Milosavljević in BelgradeSun 25 Oct 2026 19.42 EDTFirst published on Sun 25 Oct 2026 16.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe long-serving leader ofSerbia, Aleksandar Vučić, has conceded defeat, ushering in a seismic political shift after a historic election that saw ​the increasingly authoritarian leader pitted against a student-led movement that had spent two years protesting against his government.Vučić pointed to preliminary results that suggested voters had overwhelmingly backed the students, potentially giving them a majority in the country’s 250-seat parliament.“We still do not have final ⁠results,” Vučić told supporters at his party headquarters in Belgrade. “On the basis of a sample … it is clear ⁠that we have lost these ​elections, the Student ‌List has ‌won, they will have between 135 ‌and 140 seats and we will have 105.”View image in fullscreenIlija Srdanović, first on the electoral list ‘Student List – Students Win’, celebrates after the first results of the parliamentary election in Belgrade.Photograph: Đorđe Kojadinović/ReutersA representative sample by the ​CeSID-IPSPS pollsters suggested that the ​Student List’s candidate list will have ​138 deputies, while Vučić’s rightwing Serbian Progressive party (SNS) garnered 104 seats. The remaining seats ‌were likely to be shared ​between ethnic ​national minority parties, said the pollsters.As news broke that Vučić’s 12 years in power had come to an end, celebrations erupted on the streets of Belgrade and other cities.In the capital, Ivana, 43, was ecstatic. “This feels like New Year’s Eve to me, like three New Year’s Eves all at once, really,” she said. “We can finally breathe again.” She added that she was hoping for swift accountability for top members of the ousted regime, a key campaign pledge from the Student List.View image in fullscreenA person celebrating the election results hugs a police officer as the result of the Serbian election prompts street celebrations in Belgrade, Serbia.Photograph: Ana Milosavljevic/The GuardianOthers offered handshakes, high fives and hugs to police officers in the streets, while a chorus of honking horns rang out from passing cars.At the headquarters of the Student List, supporters chanted “Victory, victory!” as they applauded, cried and traded hugs. “Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard,” said Radomir Saičić, a professor at Belgrade University, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters. “Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future.”The scenes of joy came hours after arecord number of voters turned up to cast their ballot on Sunday. Across the country, long lines snaked out of polling stations, with some reporting wait times of up to two hours. By 7pm local time pollsters and monitors CeSID and Ipsos put the turnout at 67.6%, the highest since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992.The high turnout, along with the estimated 150,000 peoplewho flockedto the students’ final pre-election rally last week in Belgrade, fuelled early speculation that the students may have rallied enough support to launch a new political era in the Balkan country.Serbian voters around the world queue to cast ballots in snap parliamentary electionIn the lead-up to the vote, opinion polls had varied wildly, with analysts pointing to the high degree of uncertainty at play as the candidates representing the grassroots student movement went up against Vučić’s SNS.The results were watched across the world as part of10 pivotal days of electionsacross the globe in which the authoritarian right is facing off against pro-democracy forces. The victory for the student-led movement in Serbia is also likely to reverberate across Europe, adding momentumto the youth and student proteststhat have rocked cities across the continent.View image in fullscreenA man, carrying his dog, leaves a polling station after casting his vote as people queue to vote during the parliamentary election in Belgrade.Photograph: Marko Đurica/ReutersAs people waited for the election results to come in, speculation had begun to swirl online about whether Vučić would seek to hold on to power regardless. His swift admission of defeat, however, was reminiscent of his ally,Viktor Orbán, in neighbouring Hungary six months ago, fuelling hopes of a democratic resurgence to central Europe.The high-stakes election in the EU-candidate country traces back to November 2024, when a concrete canopycollapsed at the Novi Sadrailway station, killing 16 people. The tragedy set off protests among students, snowballing into a broad anti-government movement as evidence suggested that slipshod construction, fraud and corruption were to blame for the roof collapse.As Vučić, theincreasingly authoritarian leaderwho has dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade, grappled with mounting pressure from the students, he resigned the presidency last month to gamble on snap elections.View image in fullscreenPeople in Belgrade celebrate Aleksandar Vučić’s defeat at the polls.Photograph: Armin Durgut/APThe students seized on the chance to transform the movement into political power. They announced a slate of 250 candidates for the 250-seat parliament, ranging from academics to athletes and farmers, as they called on voters to back their push to rebuild Serbia’s economy and restore its democracy.The campaign pitted them against the political monolith of Vučić’s SNS party, leaving them in an uphill battle against a ruling party that had taken over almost all of the broadcast channels and which wielded ministries and other state institutions as political tools.Vučić had repeatedly sought to undermine the students by accusing them of being stooges of foreign powers, a charge that the students have dismissed. As he pledged to increase pensions and public sector salaries, Vučić sought to present himself as a leader capable of walking the diplomatic tightrope between the country’s ties with the west, and Russia and China to steer Serbia through global uncertainties.Undaunted, the students took to the streets, staging rallies, turning up in the rural areas that had long been Vučić strongholds and going door-to-dooras they sought to pitch themselvesas the anti-establishment candidates and to rally voters behind their slogan of “Serbia or Mafia?”View image in fullscreenFormer Serbian basketball player Dejan Bodiroga, a candidate for the Student List, celebrates after Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat in Belgrade, Serbia.Photograph: Petr David Josek/APThe message was reiterated on Sunday as Dejan Bodiroga, a candidate on the Student List and the Euroleague Basketball president, cast his ballot in Belgrade.“Today, above all, Serbia is fighting for freedom and for the return of a country that has been hijacked,” Bodiroga told reporters. “Serbia is voting today to decide which direction it will take – towards the future or the past.”In the lead-up to Sunday’s vote, both international and local election monitors expressed concerns about detentions and reports of surveillance and cyber-attacks against activists.On Sunday, independent monitoring groups warned of recorded cases of photographing of ballots that suggested pressure on voters, attempted vote-buying and carousel voting.Among them was Raša Nedeljkov of the election monitory CRTA, who said that “a large number of irregularities continue to be recorded, while violent incidents outside polling stations are also becoming increasingly frequent”.Explore more on these topicsSerbiaEuropeProtestActivismnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Door to EU is open’ new Serbian government told after Vučić concedes election – Europe live as it happened | Serbia | The Guardian

Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Student List movement projected to have 141 seats in the new parliament, well clear of the 126 required for majority
Content: 19.37 EDTUpdated projection: Student List wins with 52.9% vote, 141 seats in new parliamentThe latest version of the Ipsos/CeSID poll, updated with the partial results, gives the Student List 141 out of 250 seats in the new parliament with 52.9% of the vote share.That’swellclear of the 126 required for majority.Vučić’s list will have 103 seats in the new parliament,with 38.8% of the vote share.Four minority parties will take the remaining six seats in the new assembly.Share

title: Macron accused of putting France’s right to protest at risk with ‘vandal’s law’ | France | The Guardian
description: Making innocent protesters liable for damage would be bad for rule of law and play into far-right hands, say opponents
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Making innocent protesters liable for damage would be bad for rule of law and play into far-right hands, say opponents
Content: A protester throws a projectile towards police after a demonstration against rising living costs in Paris on Saturday.Photograph: Thibault Camus/APView image in fullscreenA protester throws a projectile towards police after a demonstration against rising living costs in Paris on Saturday.Photograph: Thibault Camus/APFranceMacron accused of putting France’s right to protest at risk with ‘vandal’s law’Making innocent protesters liable for damage would be bad for rule of law and play into far-right hands, say opponentsAngelique Chrisafisin ParisSun 25 Oct 2026 15.57 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 16.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmmanuel Macronhas been accused by trade unions of trying to curb the fundamental French right to protest as the government fast-tracks a bill to make protesters pay for damage caused by vandalism at street demonstrations even if they did not directly cause it themselves.The French president, who leaves office next spring, has faced more than a month ofprotestsin which high-school students haveblockaded schoolsdemanding a response to teacher absences, repairs to decrepit buildings and changes to the university applications platform.Trade unions andgilets jaunes(yellow vest) anti-government protesters are now joiningsustained street demonstrationsin a growing social crisis over schools, as well as the cost of living and public services. Authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrating after France saw one of itsworst days of violence in yearsearlier this month when largely peaceful demonstrations were marred by looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings.The senate will this week debate the government’s proposed “vandals pay” law. The legislation would mean that a person protesting could be held liable to pay up to €10,000 for damage and vandalism even if they did not directly cause it themselves, if they were continuing to demonstrate nearby or as part of the same group as perpetrators. The bill also provides for greater use of drones over protests.Hundreds of thousands march across France in protests over schools and policingRead moreThe prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, said the bill, which was originally prepared in the wake ofviolent clashesafter Paris Saint-Germain’s victory over Arsenal in the football Champions League in May, was “absolutely essential” after looting and burning during recent demonstrations across France.The bill comes as the government struggles to contain the current crisis.Marine Le Pen, of the far-right, anti-immigration National Rally (RN), has seen her frontrunner status in next spring’s presidential election boosted as she seeks to reinforce her law-and-order credentials and back police.Le Pen, who has lodged an appeal to France’s highest court over herconviction for embezzlement of European parliament funds, launched her presidential campaign on Sunday at a rally in Orléans, promising to “bring back order to France”.The RN has claimed the “vandals pay” bill was originally its idea and Le Pen said she would ensure damage to property was paid for by rioters. Le Pen told a cheering crowd of more than 8,000 people at the rally: “Vandals will pay and if it takes their whole life to pay, then they will spend their whole life paying.”She said: “We are going to restore the rule of law. Who can claim that there is rule of law when hordes come to ransack and burn our buildings?”Éric Coquerel, fromJean-Luc Mélenchon’s radical left La France Insoumise, said on Sunday that the “vandals pay” law “would mean the end of street demonstrations” in France because people would not want to take the risk of being held responsible and made to pay up to €10,000 for vandalism they had not committed. The Communist senator Fabien Gay told the parliamentary TV channel Public Sénat: “No demonstration could take place again in our country.”In an open letter toLe Monde, leftwing trade unions and France’s Human Rights League wrote: “This unfair law, which is a serious attack on the freedom to demonstrate, should be abandoned, or risk a major step back for the rule of law.”At this weekend’s protests there was widespread anger at Macron forbanning non-union demonstrationsthat his government deemed “illegitimate” and for keeping all protesters away from city centres.Although Macron has not put in place a state of emergency, the government and local authorities have introduced limits on demonstrating, including bans on gatherings in front of schools and demonstrating in city centres, as well as curfews in some places and extended periods of police custody for the record number of people arrested.NFL shutters Paris fan experience as protests overshadow first France gameRead moreAt demonstrations this weekend, many said they had come out to defend the French right to protest in the street. Street protests in France, which are seen as a fundamental way for people to make themselves heard by a centralised state, have regularly been used to express criticism of changes to the law, frompension changestosame-sex marriage.Serge Slama, a professor of public law at Université Grenoble Alpes, told Telerama magazine: “Although a state of emergency has been ruled out [by Emmanuel Macron] at this point, we have seen a number of decrees bringing a wide restriction on public liberties.”He said this was “unprecedented” and would benefit the far right if they won elections next year, allowing them to put in place further crackdowns without changing the law.Lecornu will meet representatives of protesting high-schoolers on Monday as the government comes under pressure to respond to their demands with funding and school repairs in order to avoid further school blockades.Explore more on these topicsFranceProtestEmmanuel MacronMarine Le PenEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Portuguese police with dogs and batons dismantle housing protest camps | Portugal | The Guardian
description: More than 30 people arrested as officers clear at least 100 tents in central Lisbon and about 50 in Porto
Author: Ashifa Kassam
Headline: More than 30 people arrested as officers clear at least 100 tents in central Lisbon and about 50 in Porto
Content: A police officer in riot gear removes a tent from the protest camp in Lisbon’s Rossio Square.Photograph: José Sena Goulão/EPAView image in fullscreenA police officer in riot gear removes a tent from the protest camp in Lisbon’s Rossio Square.Photograph: José Sena Goulão/EPAPortugalPortuguese police with dogs and batons dismantle housing protest campsMore than 30 people arrested as officers clear at least 100 tents in central Lisbon and about 50 in PortoAshifa Kassamand agenciesSun 25 Oct 2026 11.32 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 11.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GooglePolice inPortugalhave dismantled housing protest camps in Lisbon and Porto, baton-charging campaigners in the early hours of Sunday and arresting more than 30 people.The raids were the latest incident in days of clashes between police and campaigners who – inspired bysimilar campsin Spain – had sought to pitch tents in central squares to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis.Dozens of officers, some with dogs, moved shortly after 2am on Sunday to clear out the more than 100 tents that had sprung up in Lisbon’s Rossio Square. Police said they had also taken down a smaller camp of about 50 tents in Porto’s Dom João I Square.The camp in the heart of Lisbon had been set up after thousands of people marched along one of the Portuguese capital’s main thoroughfares to rail against housing prices that have soared past average incomes in the country.Police described their actions on Sunday as proportionate and said they had earlier urged people to leave the camps of their own accord. The operations in the two cities led to the arrests of 31 people for disobedience and 171 structures were removed, police said on social media. Eleven people were injured, including three police officers.View image in fullscreenRiot police arrest a woman in Lisbon.Photograph: José Sena Goulão/EPAReuters reported that 25 people detained in Lisbon had been released with orders to appear in court on Monday.The group Casa Para Viver (A Home to Live In) contested the police figures, saying the raids had left more than 20 people injured as police moved into the camps with batons, dogs and rubber bullets.“Choosing the early morning to deploy police dogs and fire rubber bullets at people who were sleeping or peacefully protesting is a political decision,” the group said in a statement as it called for further protests on Wednesday. “It shows that this government would rather crack down on those who speak out against the housing crisis than solve the crisis itself.”Fabian Figueiredo, an MP with the Left Bloc, described the police action as a “wound that had been inflicted” on the country’s democracy. “Fighting for a home is a right.
