So is peaceful protest. The constitution guarantees both,” he said on social media. “Let’s keep going – for the sake of our future.”The housing protest camps in Portugal trace back to early October when campaigners began pitching tents in Porto, prompting police toclearthem out. Similar actions soon began sprouting up in Lisbon, leading todozens of arrestsand reports of injuries as police repeatedly clashed with campaigners.As European citiesgrapple with a waveof discontent, much of the focus in Spain and Portugal has been on housing costs that have priced many local people out of the market.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionHouse prices in Portugal havemore than doubledsince 2017, while those seeking to rent have struggled with prices that have nearly doubled, fuelling one of Europe’smost acute home affordability crises.Residents have long told ofbearing the bruntof a market that has surged as a result of liberalisation, the issuing of so-called golden visas, digital nomad schemes and the proliferation of short-term rentals.Campaigners have called on the centre-right government to scrap proposed legislation that would make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases. The legislation recently passed a first parliamentary reading.In Spain, the sprawling housing camp in the centre of Madridmarked its fourth week on Saturday, becoming one of the most tangible symbols of a widespread protest movement that hasled to early general electionson 29 November.With contributions from Reuters and Agence France-PresseExplore more on these topicsPortugalProtestEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Volkswagen to build $4bn Audi SUV factory in US despite job cuts at home | Volkswagen (VW) | The Guardian
description: VW investment, creating 4,500 jobs in Georgia, comes amid Trump’s damaging tariffs, intense Chinese competition and costly shift towards EVs
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: VW investment, creating 4,500 jobs in Georgia, comes amid Trump’s damaging tariffs, intense Chinese competition and costly shift towards EVs
Content: Audi’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a rally on Saturday to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia.Photograph: Friso Gentsch/EPAView image in fullscreenAudi’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a rally on Saturday to announce the factory in Macon, Georgia.Photograph: Friso Gentsch/EPAVolkswagen (VW)Volkswagen to build $4bn Audi SUV factory in US despite job cuts at homeVW investment, creating 4,500 jobs in Georgia, comes amid Trump’s damaging tariffs, intense Chinese competition and costly shift towards EVsJasper Jollyand agenciesSun 25 Oct 2026 09.43 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 11.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAudi has said it will spend $4bn (£3bn) to build its first factory in the US, as its parent company, Volkswagen, struggles with the impact of steep tariffs imposed by Donald Trump.The German brand’s chief executive, Gernot Döllner, joined Trump on stage at a campaign rally on Saturday night to announce the factory in Macon,Georgia, in an unusual move by a big European brand just days before the US midterm elections.The Republican party under Trump is trying to retain control of both houses of Congress, butit is polling poorlyas it struggles withhigher fuel prices caused by Trump’s war on Iran, as well as his trade war against some of the US’s biggest trading partners.Volkswagen to cut further 50,000 jobs as it ends row with union over revival planRead moreTrump has long tried to convince voters that his tariffs are helping to increase the number of manufacturing jobs in the US, and has seized on any new factory investments. However, US vehicle and parts employment has fallen since Trump took office last year.Audi, Volkswagen’s most important premium brand, hassuffered from Trump’s 15% tariffs on importsfrom the EU as well as the president’s efforts to cut sales of battery electric vehicles in favour of petrol cars.It said it aims to build 200,000 SUVs at the new US factory, creating 4,500 jobs. The factory will build the Q7, Q8 and Q9 SUVs, shifting some production from Bratislava in Slovakia.Volkswagen has said Trump’s tariffs cost it up to €5bn(£4.2bn)a year, before the impact of lower sales. The German manufacturer this month said it was still struggling with “continued high pressure from import tariffs”. The carmaker was also forced to shift some production of its cheapest cars, such as the Jetta saloon and Taos SUV, from Mexico to the US.The new factory may add to tensions in Germany, where Volkswagen has started tocut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the job losses on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as the tariffs and a need to invest heavily in the shift to EVs for markets other than the US.Döllner said he accepted the invitation to speak at Trump’s rally out of respect for the US.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“We are planning to bring our ⁠biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon, Georgia,” he said at the event. “This is a long-term investment because we believe in the American market.”Volkswagen’s chief executive, Oliver Blume, told investors in July that “US tariffs create a significant burden and restrict international trade”.However, the group has said there is still demand in the US for Audi’s large petrol SUVs, and it is planning its largest-ever SUV, the Q9, with the American market in mind. Large petrol-powered SUVs have played abig role in global carbon emissions.Explore more on these topicsVolkswagen (VW)Automotive industryGermanyUS economyTrump administrationTrump tariffsEconomicsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Emirati diplomat who helped deliver aid to Gaza enters UN secretary general race  | United Nations | The Guardian
description: Lana Nusseibeh has Palestine’s endorsement but faces criticism over UAE’s human rights record and alleged funding of the RSF in Sudan
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Lana Nusseibeh has Palestine’s endorsement but faces criticism over UAE’s human rights record and alleged funding of the RSF in Sudan
Content: The UAE ambassador to the UN, Lana Nusseibeh, who has entered the race to succeed the current secretary general, António Guterres.Photograph: Amr Alfiky/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe UAE ambassador to the UN, Lana Nusseibeh, who has entered the race to succeed the current secretary general, António Guterres.Photograph: Amr Alfiky/ReutersUnited NationsEmirati diplomat who helped deliver aid to Gaza enters UN secretary general raceLana Nusseibeh has Palestine’s endorsement but faces criticism over UAE’s record on human rights and SudanPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorSun 25 Oct 2026 15.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 15.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn Emirati diplomat who as UAE ambassador to the UN helped secure the delivery of humanitarian aid to Gaza has entered the race as a late contender to succeedAntónio Guterresas the world body’s secretary general.Lana Nusseibeh, who is of Palestinian heritage, is widely noted for her advocacy of the Palestinian cause and the two-state solution and has won the endorsement of the state ofPalestine.She is however facing criticism over the UAE’s contested role in arming the Rapid Support Forces in Sudan, a group that has been accused of genocide by two successive US administrations.Nusseibeh, 48, has been one of the leading UAE diplomats denying reports that the UAE supplied weapons to RSF leader Mohamed Hamdan “Hemedti” Dagalo in defiance of a UN arms sales ban.A grouping of Latin American and Caribbean states, CELAC, has also sent a letter of objection to the security council, claiming her late entry came just as a consensus was emerging behind their region holding the UN top job.Fears mount that next UN chief will downgrade climate actionRead moreNusseibeh, who was educated at Cambridge University, was born in 1978 in Abu Dhabi, where her father, Zaki, had emigrated after the Arab-Israeli 1967 war made it difficult for him to return to his birthplace, Jerusalem.She is the niece of Sari Nusseibeh, a distinguished Palestinian intellectual and author of a widely admired book on Palestine, Once Upon a Country.She has justified her late – but widely predicted – entry into the race on the grounds that the UN security council appears to be close to deadlock on the six remaining candidates in the race, with no one as yet able to establish a clear lead after six rounds of voting, the latest on 16 October.The latest straw poll – the first in which it was revealed whether any of the five permanent members of the 15-strong UN security council objected to a candidate – ended with Rebeca Grynspan of Costa Rica holding the lead spot.But Grynspan faced objections from two unidentified permanent security council members, making it harder for her to claim she is a breakaway consensus candidate. She has support from nine security council members and objections from five. Guterres is due to stand down at the end of the yearOther candidates include: the Argentine diplomat Rafael Grossi; the UN envoy from Guyana, Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett; Olara Otunnu, a distinguished veteran Ugandan diplomat; and Ecuador’s former foreign minister María Fernanda Espinosa. Two previously declared candidates have pulled out.In her vision statement, Nusseibeh said: “At the heart of the UN sits a wager: that states will give up a little today to gain a great deal together over time.“States have not stopped needing to partner with one another, but they no longer trust that cooperation will yield sufficient returns. Rebuilding that trust, with faster, more certain, and more realistic results, is the work of the UN.”Brett McGurk, who served in the Biden administration as a top national security adviser, backed Nusseibeh for her work onGaza.“How did UAE become the largest global provider of humanitarian aid to Gaza, according to UN data? Because of Lana Nussaibeh – a diplomat who knows everyone and works with them … she would be an inspired choice for this impossible job,” he said.Cuts force World Food Programme to end support for half a million Palestinians in GazaRead moreNickolay Mladenov, the Bulgarian diplomat who heads Donald Trump’s Gaza Board of Peace, said Nusseibeh “has always understood that the UN works when someone is willing to systematically build the bridges nobody else wants to build”.He added: “In the Security Council [as UAE representative] she did that quietly and consistently and with great professionalism. She now has the chance to take that same spirit and ethos to the UN secretariat.”But there is a fierce backlash from human rights activists who point to the UAE’s domestic human rights record and its alleged funding of the RSF in Sudan, the group responsible for killing thousands, including in the capture of El Fasher in October last year.A January 2024 report by the UN panel of experts described allegations from sources in Chad and Darfur – including those of arms being smuggled into the RSF from the UAE – as credible.One of the strongest attacks on Nusseibeh’s candidacy has been mounted by Kenneth Roth, the former executive director of Human Rights Watch, over her denials of UAE provision of any “military, logistical, financial or political support to any faction in Sudan”. The UAE says it supports the formation of a civilian-led government in Sudan.Explore more on these topicsUnited NationsAntónio GuterresUnited Arab EmiratesMiddle East and north AfricaGazaPalestinenewsShareReuse this content

title: Israeli soldiers raze neighbourhood in Hebron, driving families from homes | West Bank | The Guardian
description: PM Benjamin Netanyahu vows ‘to destroy this place’ in retaliation for militant attack on army checkpoint
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: PM Benjamin Netanyahu vows ‘to destroy this place’ in retaliation for militant attack on army checkpoint
Content: Israeli troops destroy Hebron neighbourhood following attack on military checkpointWest BankIsraeli soldiers raze neighbourhood in Hebron, driving families from homesPM Benjamin Netanyahu vows ‘to destroy this place’ in retaliation for militant attack on army checkpointJulian Borgerin JerusalemSun 25 Oct 2026 02.24 EDTFirst published on Sat 24 Oct 2026 08.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIsraeli troops have levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron, driving out hundreds of families incollective punishment for a militant attackon an army checkpoint outside the West Bank city, local Palestinian authorities said.The Hebron municipality estimated that 35 hectares (86 acres) had been destroyed or marked for destruction and about 1,500 people had been evicted from their homes by Saturday afternoon in the district of Ein Deir Baha. The whole city of 250,000 people was sealed off by checkpoints on every point of entry.Videos sent by a Hebron resident showed a substantial area of devastation with every house over several blocks flattened in an urban area. One video showed soldiers marking Palestinian houses with a sprayed black cross, another showed a bulldozer tearing down a stone wall on a hillside and another showed a large residential building festooned with Israeli flags.View image in fullscreenSoldiers patrol the northern checkpoint in Hebron after Israeli forces levelled a neighbourhood in Hebron.Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/GettyPeople said the building was the home of a prominent Hebron family that had been commandeered as a temporary military headquarters.The large-scale demolitions followan attack on Fridayon an Israeli military checkpoint outside Hebron by two gunmen. After a 20-minute gunfight, two Israeli soldiers were killed, three injured and the two gunmen were also killed.Israeli elections will take place in four days and the prime minister,Benjamin Netanyahu, and the extreme-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, travelled to the site of the attack to promise an immediate and ferocious response.mapHeidi Levine recounts how Palestinian youths helped save her in settler attackRead moreNetanyahu said Israel would “act to destroy this place”. Smotrich who is standing for election in a smaller coalition party, had himself filmed wearing body armour in front of a Palestinian building being demolished. He said he had ordered “the immediate demolition of a wide row of illegal Arab structures adjacent to the attack site”.Smotrich also called for “a comprehensive military campaign … exactly like in Gaza and Lebanon”. Ein Deir Baha, the focus of the demolitions, was alleged to be the home district of the two gunmen.A spokesperson for the Hebron municipality said that about 300 families had been evicted. Some had taken refuge in the homes of friends and relatives, while the municipality said it had opened community halls and children’s play areas to shelter others.View image in fullscreenIsrael’s finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, filmed himself wearing body armour in front of a Palestinian building being demolished.Photograph: Ammar Awad/ReutersA Palestinian news agency, Wafa, reported Israeli plans to displace a further 2,500 people. “We are being collectively punished for something we neither did nor supported,” a Hebron civil rights activist, Issa Amro, said. “Our suffering is being turned into political material for Israel’s elections, while innocent families pay the price.”Amro said his sister’s family was one of the hundreds driven out of their homes.“We are talking about hundreds of families who left their homes because of this, and they are not at all connected to what happened yesterday [Friday],” Amro said in a telephone interview. “It’s a very big area and we don’t know what’s going on, whether it is only election propaganda or if it’s a serious plan from decisions on what to do after the election.”View image in fullscreenA Palestinian man clears debris outside a business demolished by Israeli forces in Hebron.Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/GettyThe Israeli Defense Forces (IDF) said in a written statement that approximately 2,000 residents of the target area belonged to a clan which the IDF said was “associated with Hamas and from which the terrorists who carried out yesterday’s attack originated”.“As part of the operation, civilians who wished to evacuate were permitted to temporarily leave the area through designated screening points staffed by the ISA and IDF soldiers,” the statement said.Separately, the IDF said, it was carrying out demolitions near the site of Friday’s attack, saying it was tearing down “infrastructure and structures built in violation of the law, in order to enforce law and order and remove potential security risks posed by these structures”.Explore more on these topicsWest BankBenjamin NetanyahuMiddle East and north AfricaIsraelPalestineInternally displaced peoplenewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘That’s the way the city works’: how the UAE changed the face of Andy Burnham’s Manchester | Manchester | The Guardian
description: The story of the emirates’ presence in Manchester winds from the Arab Spring to some of the most deprived places in England – with complicated results
Author: Josh Halliday
Headline: The story of the emirates’ presence in Manchester winds from the Arab Spring to some of the most deprived places in England – with complicated results
Content: Sheikh Mansour has built an extensive portfolio, while growth in the city helped power Andy Burnham (top) to No 10.Illustration: Anaïs Mims/GettyView image in fullscreenSheikh Mansour has built an extensive portfolio, while growth in the city helped power Andy Burnham (top) to No 10.Illustration: Anaïs Mims/GettyThe Sunday readManchester‘That’s the way the city works’: how the UAE changed the face of Andy Burnham’s ManchesterThe story of the emirates’ presence in Manchester winds from the Arab Spring to some of the most deprived places in England – with complicated resultsEmirati-linked firms’ ownership of Manchester land ‘up 39%’ in 10 yearsJosh HallidaySun 25 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 07.40 EDTShareWhen Hosni Mubarak, Egypt’s long-ruling dictator, was toppled from power in the Arab spring protests of 2011, his downfall sent shock waves across the Middle East. It also helped change the face of modernManchester.Mubarak’s successor, the Muslim Brotherhood leader Mohamed Morsi, was a sworn enemy of theUnited Arab Emirates, whose rulers feared the advance of Morsi’s Islamism.The UAE, a key western ally, was concerned that David Cameron’s UK government was not strong enough on the Muslim Brotherhood and warned ministers it couldpull billion-pound arms dealsif Britain did not act.A secret Whitehall unit was hastily established to keep the oil-rich emirates on side. Lucrative investment deals were offered in private meetings laterrevealedby the Guardian.One of these would turn Abu Dhabi’s nowcrisis-stricken ownership of Manchester City football clubinto a much deeper stake in the city itself.View image in fullscreenAn aerial view of the Etihad Stadium, the home of Manchester City, with the Ancoats and New Islington neighbourhoods in the background.Photograph: Dominic Lipinski/Bloomberg/Getty ImagesFifteen years after the Egyptian revolution, a Guardian analysis can reveal a stark rise in the amount of land and property owned by the UAE government or Emirati developers in Manchester over the past decade – extending to the size of 260 football pitches at its peak in 2023.Manchester City’s owner, Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan, has built an extensive portfolio outside the club, including the UK’s biggest indoor arena, an “upper-upscale hotel” that opened last month, a suite of apartment blocks and investment in world-leading university research through a firm run by Khaldoon al-Mubarak, the City chief executive.Thecheating scandalat Manchester City has put the spotlight on the wider influence of Abu Dhabi in the city, the growth of which helped power Andy Burnham to Downing Street.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham, then mayor of Manchester, speaking to Manchester City’s chair, Khaldoon al-Mubarak, at the Etihad Stadium in September 2019.Photograph: Martin Rickett/PAThrough interviews with key past and present local politicians and officials, new data analysis and an examination of public records spanning more than a decade, the Guardian can now tell the story of how the oil-rich state’s influence has grown, what it has meant for Manchester, and how it has fuelled concerns about the city becoming “a northern version of London”.‘We were seeking a very significant investment’Ten years ago, the sight of the murky-green Rochdale canal was a sign you had strayed too far out of Manchester’s lively Northern Quarter and should turn back. Now drinkers and diners gravitate to the area, pulled in by trendy waterside bars serving up £6.90 pints and an artisanal bakery where a single croissant costs £7.50.View image in fullscreenNew Islington marina, part of the new, modern Ancoats.Photograph: Mark Waugh/The GuardianThat transformation began in summer 2013, when David Cameron’s government sought to defuse tensions with the UAE and asked Manchester city council to draw up three investment proposals for the super-rich emirates.One of these resulted in a £1bn deal called Manchester Life, under which the council sold a prime slice of city centre land to Abu Dhabi for £5m to build 6,000 homes, along with a right of first refusal on other projects.Richard Leese, the leader of Manchester city council at the time, told the Guardian: “That was a UK government-brokered deal and we were obviously seeking a very significant investment for what would in total have been a £1bn scheme.“Housing development in and around the city centre and Ancoats in particular had stopped and been stopped for several years. At that time there were no [other] developers who were either willing or able to do it.”View image in fullscreenRichard Leese wearing a City scarf in Manchester town hall in May 2010 when he was the leader of the city council.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianIn apress release, Leese hailed the partnership as a “world-class exemplar of regeneration” and “a platform for the delivery of more than 6,000 new homes”.However, only 2,039 homes have been delivered by Manchester Life – a third of the total promised – with a further 2,839 homes being built by other developers. The total of 4,878 new properties is nearly 20% short of the 6,000 envisaged.Despite the council’s longstanding policy of at least 20% of new developments being for social and affordable housing, only 8% of these 4,878 properties fell into that category – and none were provided by Manchester Life.View image in fullscreenHomes-to-rent adverts in New Islington.Photograph: Mark Waugh/The GuardianFood banks and luxury flatsA five-minute walk from the new Abu Dhabi-funded apartments, which are home to the city’s first Michelin-starred restaurant, the nave of a former Methodist church is stacked high with emergency food for those living on surrounding streets.The short walk to the Etihad Stadium includes some of the poorest areas in the secondmost deprivedlocal authority in England. Within only half a mile, there are four charity food banks or distribution sites, one of which has a plaque marking its opening by Burnham in 2021.“It’s bound to cause resentment,” said Mark Blake, the chief executive of Manchester Central Foodbank, of the sudden influx of shiny apartments, expensive eateries and well-paid tenants.“When it’s in your face and is during a cost of living crisis it potentially could lead to some unrest. I think it should be a real concern.”View image in fullscreenThe food bank at Trinity Ancoats.Photograph: Mark Waugh/The GuardianParking has become a flashpoint, with reports of cars being vandalised after being left on council estate streets by those living or dining at the Abu Dhabi-funded properties. Tenants of the swanky apartments are encouraged to leave food to local food banks in donation boxes in each of the luxury blocks.“People are feeling all these cultural divides that are played out through the proxy of housing and everyday issues around parking,” said Alan Good, a Lib Dem councillor for Ancoats and Beswick. “Residents tell me they look at the shiny new towers and there’s a resentment – a feeling that they’re not benefiting from what Manchester is benefiting from.”Good said he felt Manchester was becoming a “northern version of London” as an “insane” property crisis compounded the misery for the city’s 20,000 people on the social housing register.Dr Matthew Stallard, a University College London researcher and chair of trustees at Manchester Central Foodbank, said there was an uncomfortable disconnect between the city’s reputation nationally – with “Manchesterism” becoming a byword for a thriving metropolis with an eye on broader social benefits – and the reality for many in the city.View image in fullscreenMatthew Stallard, the chair of trustees at Manchester Central Foodbank, in Ancoats.Photograph: Mark Waugh/The Guardian“If you look at central Manchester and all the skyscrapers and you go out in every direction by a mile and a half or two miles, you’re then in some of the most deprived neighbourhoods in the country. In Ancoats, it’s a very clear line where the money is and where the money’s not.”Awkward questionsIn summer 2016, Burnham was keenly aware of Greater Manchester’s housing crisis. He told theSalford Starthat if elected, he would stop large property firms benefiting from multimillion-pound taxpayer-funded loans from the mayoral authority.There were concerns, he said, that theGreater Manchestercombined authority (GMCA) fund had “been used to provide loans to large companies, which should have used their own finance instead, and that is too focused on city centre and luxury schemes”.Barely a year later, Burnham signed off a £55m loan to Jersey-registered property firms owned bySheikh Mansour, scion of one of the world’s wealthiest families with a reported fortune of about £300bn.View image in fullscreenSheikh Mansour speaks with the Manchester City player Pablo Zabaleta and manager Pep Guardiola during a training camp in Abu Dhabi in 2017.Photograph: Victoria Haydn/Manchester City FC/Getty ImagesGMCA said its loans fund was available to all developers who met the lending criteria and that the loans had been repaid in full. But these decisions arenow being investigatedby councillors on GMCA’s scrutiny committee.There are awkward questions for Burnham, too. Weeks before the loans were approved, he enjoyed hospitality from City’s owners in a meeting that came to light only last week after disappearing from public records. The prime minister initially said he had had only one “significant” meeting with the club’s bosses – in 2021 – but a further five have since emerged.Burnham said last week he had asked GMCA to conduct a “manual trawl of everything, as I want everything possible to be out there”. He added: “There’s no question about that – full transparency.”There appeared to be little transparency, however, when it came to the council’s long-term relationship with Manchester City’s owners.In December 2015, it signed a 10-year “collaboration agreement” with Abu Dhabi giving the emirates first refusal on land near the city centre. A specific clause in effect gagged the council’s democratically elected politicians from announcing the deal without written approval from Sheikh Mansour’s firm.View image in fullscreenModern apartments in the New Islington area.Photograph: Mark Waugh/The GuardianOther Manchester developers only discovered this years later. “It’s blatant partiality on a massive scale. It stinks,” said one property consultant. A council spokesperson defended the clause as “a standard agreement between two parties that ensures announcements or information releases are agreed by all parties”.All of the property, now worth an estimated £350m, is ultimately owned by Sheikh Mansour via Jersey-domiciled subsidiaries, with the super-rich Emirati receiving the rent paid by the hundreds of mostly young professionals who live there.The council said it had received nearly £3m as part of an undisclosed profit-sharing agreement and a further £17.6m in council tax. However, the precise return to the taxpayer – and the terms under which the deals were struck – remain unknown.Leese, 75, stepped down as council leader after 25 years in December 2021, becoming honorary president at Manchester City two years later. When approached by the Guardian, he denied the Abu Dhabi deal was shielded from scrutiny and defended his appointment at Manchester City.“This was something that happened after I retired from the council. Whether it would have been appropriate when I was on the council, I would have questioned that,” Leese said.One senior former council officer, who worked in the property and development team, described the culture in this period as “Kremlin-like” or akin to “a medieval court” where officials could show “no dissent” towards the decisions of the Labour leadership.“When you’ve got a council that’s 99% one party, there wasn’t really room for discussion,” they said, adding that they felt some senior leaders got “blinded by schmoozing around” with Abu Dhabi executives and others.Leese denied he got too close to Manchester City, the team he supports, or gave them favourable treatment as council leader. “There are a lot of players in Manchester that the city council is close to,” he said.View image in fullscreenManchester City players lifting the Premier League trophy in 2018.Photograph: Michael Regan/Getty“That’s the way the city works – in partnership.”Manchester city council has strongly denied claims of a “sweetheart deal” with Abu Dhabi after researchers at the University of Sheffieldconcludedit had “sold the family silver too cheaply” by giving the land to Abu Dhabi at a cheaper rate than comparable developments.The future No 10 NorthIn 2017, three years after the first Abu Dhabi deal and the year Burnham became Greater Manchester mayor, council leaders made another huge bet. They paid £42m for a hollowed out retail park next to the £1bn Manchester Life development, described at the time as the biggest ever land purchase in Manchester city centre.Its price was at least six times higher per acre than the adjacent land sold for £5m to Sheikh Mansour – and it would later be identified as the permanent future home of Burnham’s No 10 North.This former retail park was also a partnership with Abu Dhabi. Again, the terms were shielded from scrutiny as members of the public were excluded from council hearings – but inside the town hall, the fallout was significant.View image in fullscreenThe former central retail park being cleared.Photograph: Mark Waugh/The GuardianA senior council property officer, Dominic Hayes, resigned abruptly in March 2018 over concerns about the deals the council was doing with Mansour’s group. He listed a series of complaints in an email to the council chief executive, Joanne Roney, who the previous year had succeeded the all-powerfulHoward Bernsteinwhen he retired after 29 years in charge.In a tense meeting days after the resignation, a senior council figure, Eddie Smith, is said to have told colleagues that Hayes had thrown them “under a bus” and that the leadership was furious. According to contemporaneous notes by a colleague, seen by the Guardian, Smith said Hayes had made “not acceptable [and] possibly dangerous” criticisms of a Manchester City board member who was a key figure in the Manchester Life deal.Smith is then said to have commented: “You don’t criticise the council’s relationship with the football club in this organisation and hope to survive.” Smith, who left the council in 2020, denies making the comment.Yet Hayes’ concerns were serious enough to warrant an internal investigation into governance at the council. It found that anxieties about the council’s deal-making were not limited to just one officer.A second senior employee told auditors they were concerned that the council had “overpaid” for the rundown retail park, according to an official record of the meeting. That officer raised concerns that the Abu Dhabi-led project was “driving the master planning for a site they didn’t own”.When Burnham became prime minister in July, the site was tipped as the permanent home for No 10 North. As scrutiny of the Abu Dhabi link grew in October, these plans were quietly shelved.‘The fragility of the Manchester model’Council sources noticed a change of approach under Leese’s successor, Bev Craig, when she became council leader in December 2021.View image in fullscreenBev Craig in 2021, the year she was appointed leader of Manchester city council.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianCraig ordered a review of the Manchester Life deal to make sure it was “all legal, all above board”, she told BBC Radio Manchester this month, adding: “The answer was yes.”One of the reviews commissioned by Craig, who succeeded Burnham this year as Greater Manchester mayor, waspublished in July. It found that while the deals with developers such as Abu Dhabi had delivered “significant benefits”, there were “weaknesses in documentation, monitoring and assurance”, particularly around the profit-sharing nature of these deals.Prof Jonathan Silver, a University of Sheffield researcher who has analysed the Manchester Life deal, said the growing buy-up of land and property by Emiratis raised “major concerns about the fragility of the ‘Manchester model’ and its reliance on attracting flows of international finance, whatever the cost”.View image in fullscreenA banner thanking the Manchester City owner Sheikh Mansour during a Premier League match last weekend at the Etihad Stadium.Photograph: Simon Stacpoole/Offside/GettySilver said there were “urgent questions” about what would happen to the hundreds of homes in the Manchester Life developments if Sheikh Mansour was forced or decided to sell Manchester City in light of the cheating scandal.Leese remains confident the Abu Dhabi deals were a huge success for the city. Asked whether he would have handled the partnership any differently given the concerns raised by academics and others, he said: “No. Nothing that I can think of. It is a phenomenally good deal for Manchester.”Additional reporting:Carmen Aguilar GarcíaandMichael GoodierExplore more on these topicsManchesterThe Sunday readUnited Arab EmiratesMiddle East and north AfricaGentrificationUrbanisationHousingMayoral electionsShare

title: ‘Gaza’s suffering has become campaign fodder’: Palestinians fear the worst from Israel election | Middle East and north Africa | The Guardian
description: Humanitarian catastrophe largely ignored as rivals Gadi Eisenkot and Benjamin Netanyahu vow to end Hamas rule
Author: Seham Tantesh
Headline: Humanitarian catastrophe largely ignored as rivals Gadi Eisenkot and Benjamin Netanyahu vow to end Hamas rule
Content: Nearly a million Palestinians have been displaced by the Israeli bombardment, which has killed nearly 75,000 people.Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/ReutersView image in fullscreenNearly a million Palestinians have been displaced by the Israeli bombardment, which has killed nearly 75,000 people.Photograph: Mahmoud Issa/ReutersMiddle East and north Africa‘Gaza’s suffering has become campaign fodder’: Palestinians fear the worst from Israel electionHumanitarian catastrophe largely ignored as rivals Gadi Eisenkot and Benjamin Netanyahu vow to end Hamas ruleSeham Tanteshin Gaza andLorenzo TondoSun 25 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 02.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAs Israel preparesto go to the polls, Palestinians in Gaza are bracing for an outcome that could shape their future, knowing their fate rests with the country that has reduced much of the territory to rubble and killed nearly 75,000 people.Gaza, where nearly a million displaced Palestinians face dire sanitary conditions, water shortages and the constant threat of Israeli strikes, has been largely absent fromthe election campaign.Both Benjamin Netanyahu’s far-right coalition and Gadi Eisenkot’s opposition Yashar party have focused instead on the goal of destroying Hamas in the wake of the 7 October attacks and the trauma inflicted on Israeli society. The humanitarian catastrophe unfolding just across the borderhas received little, if any, attention.“We hope a government will come to power that is less inclined towards killing, displacement and our extermination,” said Sami Abu Rumi, 47, from Rafah, who is now displaced in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis. “But, ultimately, we see the thinking of Israeli governments as largely similar.”View image in fullscreenGadi Eisenkot championed the “Dahiya doctrine” in the 2006 war with Hezbollah, which advocated overwhelming force against civilian areas where militants operated.Photograph: Ariel Schalit/APNeither Netanyahu nor Eisenkot has set outa clear plan for Gaza’s future. Both have vowed to end Hamas rule and both support Donald Trump’s controversial peace plan.Eisenkot, the former military chief whose party is leading Netanyahu’s Likud in the polls, has pledged to restore Israel’s international standing after three years of war. Yet he is no dove.A senior commander during Israel’s 2006 war with Hezbollah, Eisenkot, whose son and two nephews were killed fighting in Gaza, later championed the“Dahiya doctrine”, which advocated overwhelming force against civilian areas where militants operated. Critics say the strategy has since been employed in Gaza, causing widespread destruction that, they argue, amounts to war crimes.“Eisenkot talks of defeatingHamas, while Netanyahu boasts about military operations and the killing of Palestinians,” said Abu Rumi. ‘‘Gaza’s suffering has become campaign fodder. Meanwhile, families here struggle to feed their children, keep them in school and access medical care. With homes and infrastructure destroyed, simply surviving has become a daily struggle.”Earlier this week, the Arab-led Joint List party in Israel aired a48-second election videoshowing drone footage of Gaza’s ruins. “[We] behave as if everything that has happened here is completely normal,” the voiceover says. “As if tens of thousands of people weren’t killed here … as if entire cities were not destroyed and turned into wastelands.”The party vows it “will not be silent”, adding: “[The other parties] want more destruction. We offer life.”‘The biggest motivation is fear’: High turnout among Israel’s Palestinians could unseat NetanyahuRead moreThe chances of Arab parties joining an Eisenkot-led coalition are slim to none, although they could offer support from outside government. Yet among Palestinians inGaza, pessimism runs deep: whoever wins, little is expected to change.“I do not believe anyone genuinely cares about Gaza or has its people’s interests at heart,’’ said Haneen Hamdouna, 45, from Beit Lahia, who has also been displaced to al-Mawasi. ‘‘Whether it is Netanyahu, Eisenkot or someone else, attacking Gaza seems to have become part of Israeli election campaigning.“For years, we have said that the incoming government might be better than the one before it, only to be shocked when it turns out to be worse. Perhaps 200 trucks would be allowed into Gaza instead of 100, but that would not mean any real change in our lives.”In Gaza, most people are too preoccupied bythe struggle to find food and waterto follow the election campaign. Fears of renewed hunger are mounting as markets run short of fresh produce and other essentials.Residents say commercial deliveries have been suspended for about a week, driving up prices. Flour now costs more than three times its previous price, while dwindling humanitarian aid has left families increasingly vulnerable to another food crisis.View image in fullscreenCandidates in the upcoming Israeli election include Yair Golan of the Democrats party (left billboard) and the Arab-led Joint List.Photograph: Amir Cohen/ReutersYet, some people in Gaza are following the Israeli elections closely, driven less by hope of change than fear of what the outcome could mean for their future.They fear that Palestinian suffering has become a recurring feature of Israeli election campaigns, with candidates competing over who can take the toughest stance towards Gaza rather than offering any prospect of a better future.“A friend was supposed to hold his son’s wedding in the coming days,” said Karim Mareesh, 43. “But he decided to postpone it until after the Israeli elections. He feared that the far-right government might secure another term, prompting the war to resume and forcing him to flee again. He could lose his tent and the wedding supplies he had struggled to save up for.”Hope is hard to find in Gaza, where three years of war have reduced entire neighbourhoods to wastelands of shattered concrete and bomb craters. It is harder still to imagine a future when Israeli restrictions on food and humanitarian aid have turnedhunger into a weapon of war. And almost impossible to see any light at the end of the tunnel when more than20,000 Palestinian children have been killedsince 7 October 2023.“I feel that everything said about addressing our suffering is nothing more than an attempt to soothe our pain, or simply words and promises that we no longer believe,” says Noor AlMoghanni, 20, from Gaza City.“Whether Netanyahu wins or loses, the reality here will not change. As I see it, their goal is to destroy Gaza and the foundations of life here.”Explore more on these topicsMiddle East and north AfricaIsrael-Gaza warGazaPalestineIsraelBenjamin NetanyahuHamasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi ‘sounds strong’ but is isolated, son says | Myanmar | The Guardian
description: Kim Aris tells the Guardian chance to speak with detained Nobel laureate was ‘public relations’ move from military leaders
Author: Oliver Holmes
Headline: Kim Aris tells the Guardian chance to speak with detained Nobel laureate was ‘public relations’ move from military leaders
Content: Kim Aris, the son of Myanmar's ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi, has long demanded ‘proof of life’ with regards to his mother.Photograph: Tian Macleod Ji/APView image in fullscreenKim Aris, the son of Myanmar's ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi, has long demanded ‘proof of life’ with regards to his mother.Photograph: Tian Macleod Ji/APMyanmarMyanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi ‘sounds strong’ but is isolated, son saysKim Aris tells the Guardian chance to speak with detained Nobel laureate was ‘public relations’ move from military leadersOliver Holmesin BangkokSat 24 Oct 2026 22.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 17.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMyanmar’s former democratic leaderAung San Suu Kyiappears to be in good physical and mental health but is living in near-complete isolation, her son has said after the first call with his 81-year-old mother in more than five years.“She still sounds certainly all there mentally, and physically she sounds strong,” Kim Aris said. “I don’t think she has anybody outside of the military or the police around her, so essentially she’s been held in solitary confinement from what I gather.”After being deposed in a2021 military coup, the Nobel Peace prize laureate has been moved to an unspecified location in the capital. “I’m still not entirely sure where she is,” said Aris. “I think it’s a residence in Naypyidaw, which is fenced off and it has a scrubby bit of land around it.”View image in fullscreenAung San Suu Kyi talks on the phone with her son on Thursday, in a photo released by the Myanmar presidential office.Photograph: Myanmar President Spokesperson Office/APAris, who has lived in the UK most of his life and whose late father was a British historian, was allowedto speak to his mother on Thursday at the Myanmar embassy in London. While he welcomed the chance to talk, he said the invitation was part of a “public relations” campaign by the country’s military leaders.The former junta chief Min Aung Hlaing has sought to rebuild international diplomatic ties, and in April switched his military fatigues for civilian clothes afterelections that were widely condemned as a sham.Activists have long demanded “proof of life” for Aung San Suu Kyi, as well as scores of other political prisoners. In August, shewas finally photographed during a Red Cross visit. Last week, a government spokespersonpublished imagesof her smiling in a wood-panelled room as officials delivered two gardening books given to her as gifts by Britain’s King Charles. A paper calendar on the wall behind her showed the date.Aris said these photo-ops were well-known stunts that the regime had used before to pretend his mother, a national icon, was being treated fairly. The daughter of the assassinated national independence hero Gen Aung San has spent much of her life since the late 1980s in and out of house arrest for leading pro-democracy movements.“She remains completely shut off from the rest of the world. I think she’s unaware of what’s happening outside of where she is because she’s not allowed any newspapers or radio or television,” Aris said. “She’s been locked up for five years on trumped-up, politically motivated charges and she should be free.”Ruled for decades by generals and suffering from western sanctions, Myanmar experienced a brief democratic moment after Aung San Suu Kyi was allowed to run in a2015 election that her party overwhelmingly won. She took up the role of “state counsellor” under a civilian-military power-sharing agreement.View image in fullscreenAung San Suu Kyi shakes hands with Myanmar’s military commander-in-chief Min Aung Hlaing (left) in December 2015.Photograph: Lynn Bo Bo/EPAHer international reputation was soon tarnished after the2016-2017 mass killings and expulsions of Rohingya Muslims. Aung San Suu Kyi flew to the international court of justice in The Hague, where she said she acknowledged military units might have used “disproportionate force”, butdefended the governmentagainst accusations of genocide.Blunder in, abandon allies and court a dictator: it’s the Trump doctrine, now playing out in Myanmar | Steve BloomfieldRead moreAris said that his mother was never “silent” on theRohingyacrisis and what she said on the issue “could fill volumes”. Under her leadership, Myanmar launched a domestic inquiry and appointed the former UN chief Kofi Annan to head a commission.He added that as state counsellor, Aung San Suu Kyi was “always walking on a tightrope”, knowing the military could strip her of her fragile power at any moment.“The very hard-won nascent democracy that she was trying to lead was holding on to things by a thread,” he said. “The military could have taken over at any point, and they were doing their best to make my mother’s situation a lot more difficult and to undermine her position. And I think in that respect they did a pretty good job.”The 2021 power grab by the military triggered a civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to conflict monitors.Aris said the level of public global support for his mother had “dwindled incredibly” since the Rohingya crisis and that the whole country was now suffering from a lack of international attention. While many governments have called for Aung San Suu Kyi’s release, she is not treated as the beloved international figure that she once was.“Never mind my mother, the fact that people ignore what’s happening in Burma shouldn’t be down to what was being done to the Rohingya,” he said, using the country’s former name. “And that seems to be the case sometimes, that people say: ‘Oh, well, look how the Rohingya were treated. We can ignore what’s happening in Burma.’”Explore more on these topicsMyanmarAung San Suu KyiSouth and central AsiaMyanmar coupRohingyanewsShareReuse this content

title: Burnham to double spending on homelessness amid drive to end rough sleeping by Christmas | Homelessness | The Guardian
description: Downing Street will allocate a further £432m in this week’s budget, bringing total funding for finding a ‘lasting solution’ to nearly £900m
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Downing Street will allocate a further £432m in this week’s budget, bringing total funding for finding a ‘lasting solution’ to nearly £900m
Content: ‘Rough sleeping isn’t a fact of life,’ said Andy Burnham before a rough sleeping summit on Monday that will bring together business and charities.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘Rough sleeping isn’t a fact of life,’ said Andy Burnham before a rough sleeping summit on Monday that will bring together business and charities.Photograph: Murdo MacLeod/The GuardianHomelessnessBurnham to double spending on homelessness amid drive to end rough sleeping by ChristmasDowning Street will allocate a further £432m in this week’s budget, bringing total funding for finding a ‘lasting solution’ to nearly £900mRowena MasonWhitehall editorSun 25 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham is to double spending on ending rough sleeping to almost £900m by the end of the current parliament, as he steps up efforts to get people off the streets by Christmas.The prime minister has pledged to offer every rough sleeper in England a safe route off the streets or wider support as a central part of his premiership.As he prepared for a Downing Street summit on ending rough sleeping on Monday, Burnham said the budget would bring a further £432m commitment to helping to tackle homelessness.The sum is on top of an initial £442m from Ministry ofHousing, Communities and Local Government budgets that will be allocated to the problem before March 2027.Speaking ahead of the meeting, which will bring together charities and businesses, Burnham said: “Rough sleeping isn’t a fact of life. It’s a thing governments either choose to accept or don’t.“Well, I don’t accept it. That’s why we’re doubling funding so that people aren’t just offered a safe route off the streets this winter but have that same support right through the rest of this parliament too.“But we can’t do it alone. If we’re going to end rough sleeping, we need every part of society behind us on this. So today we’re bringing together businesses, charities and local leaders in Downing Street to make sure this is a solution that lasts.”Andy Burnham calls on wider society to help end rough sleeping by ChristmasRead moreBurnham’s mission to end rough sleeping is already under way with just two months to go before his deadline. There are specialist outreach teams and new accommodation spaces operating in Coventry, and further provision is being rolled out in places including Plymouth and Camden over the coming weeks.The additional funding is being provided in an attempt to solve the problem of rough sleeping in the longer term. As mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham introduced schemes such as A Bed Every Night to offer emergency accommodation, but while the number of rough sleepers fell, it then began to increase again.Burnham has previously said this was because “we were the only place providing that level of support and, understandably, people then travelled to Greater Manchester to access that support”.He has said ending rough sleeping across the country will only be possible “if all areas are pulling in the same direction, and that’s what this funding is designed to achieve”.11:13Will Andy Burnham get rough sleepers off streets by Christmas? – The LatestThe prime minister’s rough sleeping summit on Monday will bring together businesses, charities, housing providers and local leaders as they attempt to create more lasting changes.Alongside the government, other organisations are making pledges towards solving the problem, with the National Housing Federation working with housing associations to identify at least 2,000 potential homes and bed spaces, including empty properties that could be brought back into use.Virgin Media O2 will provide practical digital support to frontline organisations, while the charities St Mungo’s and Haircuts4Homeless will work with L’Oréal on hair salons and wellbeing provision for those who have been sleeping rough.View image in fullscreenRayner, pictured with Burnham at a homeless accommodation centre in Newcastle this year, said ending rough sleeping was a ‘big ambition’.Photograph: Lauren Hurley/No 10 Downing StreetAngela Rayner, the housing secretary, said it was a “big ambition” and the government would “not back down from making sure everyone has the offer of a route off the streets this Christmas”.She said: “The first step is giving people a roof over their head and freedom from the nightly struggle to find somewhere safe to sleep. But Christmas is only the beginning and that’s why we will keep working together to tackle the root causes of homelessness and end rough sleeping for good.”The homelessness charity Shelter welcomed the announcement. Its acting CEO, Mairi MacRae, said the funding showed “the government understands that a safe home is not a privilege, it is a necessity”.However, the Conservatives dismissed the move, with Katie Lam, the shadow housing secretary, accusing the government of wanting to spend too much money on ending rough sleeping.Why are rough sleepers dying a stone’s throw from luxury waterfront houses in Victoria?Read more“Burnham is throwing another £432m at a problem he failed to solve in Greater Manchester,” she said. “UnderLabour, rough sleeping has hit record highs – yet their answer is always more taxpayers’ money and more empty promises.”Referring to the chancellor, Lam said: “[John] Healey must use his budget this week to cut taxes for working people, get the ballooning benefits bill under control, and stop pushing up energy prices. Instead of piling more costs on to hard-working people, Healey must focus on easing the cost of living and delivering real value for taxpayers’ money.”Explore more on these topicsHomelessnessAndy BurnhamAngela RaynerLabourBudget 2026HousingPovertynewsShareReuse this content

title: Two dead and 160,000 properties without power as Storm Boelo batters UK | UK weather | The Guardian
description: Man aged 60 and another in his 20s killed by falling trees in Scotland and London as Met Office reports gusts of up to 84mph
Author: Hannah Al-Othman
Headline: Man aged 60 and another in his 20s killed by falling trees in Scotland and London as Met Office reports gusts of up to 84mph
Content: Waves crash over the promenade during Storm Boelo on Sunday in Largs, Scotland.Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWaves crash over the promenade during Storm Boelo on Sunday in Largs, Scotland.Photograph: Jeff J Mitchell/Getty ImagesUK weatherTwo dead and 160,000 properties without power as Storm Boelo batters UKMan aged 60 and another in his 20s killed by falling trees in Scotland and London as Met Office reports gusts of up to 84mphHannah Al-OthmanandCharlie MoloneySun 25 Oct 2026 18.19 EDTFirst published on Sun 25 Oct 2026 06.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleTwo people have been killed and more than 160,000 properties have been left without power as Storm Boelo continues to batter the UK.Two men, one aged 60 and the other in his 20s, were killed by falling trees on Sunday, police said. The 60-year-old died in south-westScotlandwhile the man in his 20s was killed in London.A spokesperson for Police Scotland said: “We were made aware of a 60-year-old man having been struck by a falling tree on a minor road at Mid Kelton at about 10.30am on Sunday, 25 October 2026.“The man was pronounced dead at the scene. There are no suspicious circumstances and a report will be submitted to the procurator fiscal in due course.”In London, the man was killed when a tree fell on to his car at 12.40pm as he drove through Mill Hill in the north of the city.Ch Insp Guy Ellwood said: “Our thoughts are with the loved ones of the young man who lost his life.”The adverse weather that arrived in northern parts of the UK on Saturday evening wasthe second named storm in as many days, afterStorm Austen brought strong windsto south-west England on Friday.The Met Office said wind speeds widely reached 60-70mph, affecting areas in an amber warning zone that came into force at 9pm on Saturday.The warning covered Scotland, parts ofNorthern Irelandand the far north of England, with gusts reaching more than 80mph in exposed coastal spots.The island of Tiree in the Inner Hebrides was hit by 82mph winds, according to the forecaster, while wind speeds reached 84mph in Argyll and Bute and 83mph in Snowdonia (Eryri).Approximately 53,000 homes in Scotland were still without power by 5pm on Sunday, according to updates from SP Energy Networks and Scottish and Southern Electricity Networks.Across Great Britain, 161,400 customers were without power, according to the Energy Networks Association (ENA).The Scottish government’s “resilience room” met to discuss the impact of the storm on Sunday afternoon, with ministers focusing on the outages and how they were being restored.Scotland’s first minister, John Swinney, met senior politicians, emergency agencies and forecasters to discuss the government’s response, amid warnings that similar conditions would return early next week.Storm Boelo causes severe flooding in town centre of Largs, ScotlandEngineers had restored power to 344,900 customers but 82,600 remained disconnected, the ENA said on Sunday morning. The figure included more than 30,000 homes across Scotland.The ENA said: “The networks have been focused on reconnecting customers this morning, though the continuing severe weather in some regions is limiting network engineers’ opportunities to safely start the work of restoring customers’ power today and access to certain areas remains difficult. Engineers are working around the clock to identify and fix faults.”Train travel was disrupted on Sunday. Network Rail Scotland shared an image of flooding from the tracks to the platform at one Glasgow station, and fallen trees above the lines near another. Speed restrictions were in place across Scotland and several sections of its railways were closed, the operator added.Network Rail shared images of a trampoline beneath a train and a shed by the tracks, and it reminded people living near rail lines to firmly secure objects in their gardens.Some flights were diverted from landing at Leeds Bradford airport and others were cancelled.The Met Office advised people in affected areas to secure loose items in gardens and to stay indoors as the storm posed a danger to life from flying debris and crashing waves.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Met Office chief forecaster, Jason Kelly, said: “Storm Boelo will be felt across the UK this weekend, with the strongest winds and greatest potential for disruption in the north.“Amber warnings are in place across mainland Scotland, parts of Northern Ireland and the far north ofEngland, where gusts of 60-70mph are expected widely, with the potential for 80mph in exposed coastal locations.View image in fullscreenWaves at Gourock in western Scotland on Sunday.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PA“Strong winds will also affect other parts of the UK, with gusts of 50-60mph possible in places. Heavy rain will provide an additional hazard, particularly in the north, bringing the potential for further impacts. People should prepare for the potential for disruption, particularly to travel and power supplies.”Several events have been cancelled this weekend due to the inclement weather. Visit Liverpool said the River of Light event, featuring illuminated artworks, had been cancelled “in the interests of safety”, while London’s annual Diwali on the Square celebrations on Sunday were cancelled on the advice of independent health and safety experts.Edinburgh Castle was closed on Sunday because of the high winds and adverse weather, while the Fountains Abbey estate in North Yorkshire was also closed for the day, after its Fountains by Floodlight event on Saturday evening was cancelled.View image in fullscreenA road closure on the A78 near Skelmorlie in North Ayrshire after Storm Boelo passed through the area.Photograph: Jane Barlow/PAThe Environment Agency had issued six warnings as of 1.45pm that flooding was expected for spots in northern parts of England, as well as 50 alerts stating flooding was possible. The Scottish Environment Protection Agency said 17 flood warnings and 11 flooding alerts were active as of the same time.Cumbria police said they had received a number of calls overnight to localised flooding and fallen trees blocking roads across the county, and urged motorists to drive with care while emergency services worked to clear the obstructions.The amber warning sits within wider yellow wind warnings, which cover parts of England farther south, as well as north Wales and the whole of Northern Ireland.Hundreds of homes were still without power in south-west England after Storm Austen hit the region on Friday, bringing 76mph winds to St Mary’s airport in the Isles of Scilly, with 74mph recorded at Aberporth in south Wales and 71mph at Culdrose in Cornwall.Stuart Wilson, from Transport Scotland, said “significant recovery work” was required before the network returned to normal.The Scottish social justice and housing secretary, Shirley-Anne Somerville, said on Sunday: “Disruption to travel is likely to continue into tomorrow and I strongly recommend people check official sources such as the Met Office, Traffic Scotland, transport operators and local authority channels before setting out.“While we expect some respite from the adverse weather during the day on Monday, there is a possibility of more severe weather conditions early on in the week and we urge everyone to continue to follow advice and heed any warnings.”Explore more on these topicsUK weatherScotlandNorthern IrelandNorth of EnglandEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: Cabinet split emerges over controversial Rosebank oilfield decision | Oil | The Guardian
description: Chancellor is in favour of North Sea project, but energy secretary has said she is leaning towards rejecting it
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Chancellor is in favour of North Sea project, but energy secretary has said she is leaning towards rejecting it
Content: The chancellor John Healey, and the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, visit a gas plant in Aberdeen on 21 October.Photograph: Kirsty O’Connor/TreasuryView image in fullscreenThe chancellor John Healey, and the energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, visit a gas plant in Aberdeen on 21 October.Photograph: Kirsty O’Connor/TreasuryOilCabinet split emerges over controversial Rosebank oilfield decisionChancellor is in favour of North Sea project, but energy secretary has said she is leaning towards rejecting itRowena MasonWhitehall editorSun 25 Oct 2026 16.29 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 17.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA cabinet split has emerged over whether to approve drilling at the Rosebank oilfield, with the chancellor,John Healey, in favour of the controversial North Sea project.The energy secretary, Miatta Fahnbulleh, is ultimately in charge of the decision, and the Guardian reported last week thatshe was leaning towards rejecting itaftergranting permissionfor the smaller Jackdaw gasfield.It is understood, however, that Healey backs approving the licence, which is on hold over concerns about the project’s environmental impact.The chancellor hinted at his support last week when he told ITV he expected oil and gas revenues to contribute to a new energy wealth fund, suggesting he was anticipating income from Rosebank. The prime minister would be expected to make the final call if there is conflict on the decision.No 10 declined to comment on Sunday after the Mail on Sunday reported that Andy Burnham and Healey had agreed to try to push the project through, saying it was a matter for the energy secretary.map of producing hydrocarbon fields in UK watersFahnbulleh is responsible, but the views of Burnham and Healey will hold weight in the choice over whether or not to go ahead.She told the Guardian the rationale behind Jackdaw did not apply to Rosebank, saying the UK would rely on gas as it made the transition to net zero and that it would be better to take it from relatively low-carbon sources in the North Sea than importing it.“One is a gasfield that caters for the domestic market, while the other is an oilfield that is mainly for export,” she said. “It is right that we judge each application in its own right, and it is absolutely critical that the decision is consistent with our climate obligations, our carbon budgets and the end destination we need to get to with the energy transition.”If the Rosebank field is rejected, it would be a blow for the North Sea energy industry and a major victory for climate campaigners. A final decision is expected before the end of the year.Labour MPs said on Wednesday that there would be a big pushback in the party if Rosebank was approved, though most are prepared to accept the arguments that Jackdaw was a necessary part of the transition to net zero.MPs are understood to have discussed ways of forcing or encouraging a parliamentary vote on Rosebank should it be approved, as a way of expressing dissent.Officials say Fahnbulleh has not yet made her decision. Rosebank would produce emissions about seven times greater than Jackdaw, and Fahnbulleh is understood to believe it would do less for UK energy security, given that most of the oil would be exported.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA spokesperson for the Department forEnergySecurity and Net Zero said: “We do not comment on speculation. The North Sea remains a vital national asset, and oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come – alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis.“Any decision will take into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received during the consultation process.”Fahnbulleh has promised that future revenues from the North Sea will be spent on green energy projects through an energy wealth fund. She said last week that the fund would be given £2bn in the budget.“When we have tax revenues that are coming from the oil and gas industry, it is right that we invest that in the transition we need to make in energy,” she said, adding that the money would be spent on renewables, nuclear and other clean energy schemes.She could not, however, say exactly which tax revenues would be given to the fund, or how much that may generate. “The chancellor will make those details clear in the budget,” she said.Explore more on these topicsOilFossil fuelsEnergy industryEnvironment policyMiatta FahnbullehJohn HealeyLabournewsShareReuse this content

title: Cabinet ministers back Burnham’s call for debate on return to free movement with EU  | Labour | The Guardian
description: PM’s plea supported by Angela Rayner, Ed Miliband and business leaders, while some ‘red wall’ MPs voice concern
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: PM’s plea supported by Angela Rayner, Ed Miliband and business leaders, while some ‘red wall’ MPs voice concern
Content: Angela Rayner and Andy Burham in August. She has said his comments on the EU relationship are ‘just pragmatism’.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Pool AFP/APView image in fullscreenAngela Rayner and Andy Burham in August. She has said his comments on the EU relationship are ‘just pragmatism’.Photograph: Toby Shepheard/Pool AFP/APLabourCabinet ministers back Burnham’s call for debate on return to free movement with EUPM’s plea supported by Angela Rayner, Ed Miliband and business leaders, while some ‘red wall’ MPs voice concernRowena MasonandJasper JollySun 25 Oct 2026 15.57 EDTFirst published on Sun 25 Oct 2026 09.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAndy Burnham’s call for the UK to consider a return to free movement with Europe has been backed by senior cabinet ministers but risked a rift with “red wall” Labour MPs, who say it could jeopardise Brexit-voting seats.The prime minister made his plea for an“honest discussion” about freedom of movementin an interview with the Sunday Times, making clear that staying out of it would no longer be a red line in talks with the EU.Burnham also revealed his belief that rejoining the single market and accepting free movement could be done without the need for another referendum, ifLabourput it in their manifesto. In contrast, he said fully rejoining would need another in-out poll.The prime minister said: “Freedom of movement had very significant challenges associated with it and I spoke about them in my previous time in parliament. But, at the same time, it was a type of immigration that perhaps wasn’t as difficult [as now].“Revolving-door migration where people would come and then go back is different. The balance of migration has changed, hasn’t it, since then? I think we’ve just got to have an honest discussion about those things.”His remarks were supported by Angela Rayner, the housing secretary, as well as Stella Creasy, the chair of the Labour Movement for Europe. However,Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, is among those Labour MPs who have previously been more cautious about closer ties with Europe, while a number of backbenchers with heavily pro-Brexit seats in the north and Midlands are wary about reopening the arguments for free movement or rejoining the EU.Rayner told the BBC’s Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg she would “like to have an honest conversation about what the trade-offs could be, and then put that to the people at a general election”, and Creasy, the Labour MP for Walthamstow, said Burnham was right that the UK was “long overdue for a grownup conversation about what EU freedom of movement actually means”.View image in fullscreenStella Creasy said the UK was ‘long overdue for a grownup conversation about what EU freedom of movement means’.Photograph: Milo Chandler/AlamyA number of senior cabinet ministers are keen for the UK to form a much closer relationship with the EU to help boost growth, potentially involving a return to the single market and accepting free movement as a result. Those in favour of reopening the discussion includeEd Miliband, the foreign secretary.At a New Statesman event during the Labour party conference in September, however, Mahmood said rejoining the EU would not be a “simple, straightforward thing” and there were “quite hard trade-offs”, such as eliminating trade friction without “some of the burdens that also brings”.One senior minister under Keir Starmer said the reopening of the debate on free movement was “brave” given how divisive it had been in theBrexityears. “It’s a question of timing. Public opinion is of a place where you can start to have this debate,” he said. “Theresa May, Rishi Sunak, Keir Starmer: what they were all trying to do was get as close as possible without freedom of movement. There is now the a possibility of being brave and making the case on single market and free movement without going for rejoin.”Labour MPs with pro-Brexit seats have expressed scepticism about rejoining the bloc, including Jonathan Hinder, the MP for Pendle, who recently pressed the prime minister in parliament to rule out a return to free movement.One red wall MP said they thought debating free movement was the right thing to do but many colleagues in the north-east, especially in coastal areas, had begun to raise serious concerns. “These MPs are definitely raising the alarm,” they said. “Andy may have to work out if he can win without them, which is brutal but true.” Another Labour MP from a Brexit-voting area said it would “undoubtedly put seats at risk to Reform” but that Burnham was making an argument from a position of strength, having taken the party to higher poll ratings in recent weeks.Worries were brought up publicly on Sunday by Richard Walker, the Labour peer and executive chair of Iceland, who told Times Radio that restarting the debate would be a “dangerous precedent” and that opening the borders would not help the “1 million young people that are out of work”.In his party conference speech last month, Burnham fired the starting gun on the argument about rejoining the EU as one potential route, but his latest comments suggest he appears to be favouring the option that would avoid a referendum.Although Labour’s manifesto pledges no return to free movement and the single market, Burnham signalled it could still be up for discussion at next month’s EU summit.Burnham’s comments at the weekend drew an immediate response from the right of politics, with the Conservatives and Reform UK criticising the idea of reopening the debate. Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said the idea of reopening free movement was “another example of Burnham’s foot-in-mouth syndrome”.View image in fullscreenKemi Badenoch said Burnham ‘hasn’t thought this through or the implications’.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPANigel Farage, the Reform UK leader, called it a “total betrayal of Brexit Britain and his Makerfield pitch”.“He is also deluded to say immigration was different when we were members of the EU. We will fight this dishonesty,” he added.Polling suggests voters in the UK are increasingly open to rejoining the EU or a single market arrangement involving free movement. The concept of free movement was that British and EU citizens could move more freely for jobs within the bloc, which also shared a single market for goods and services.Luke Tryl, a polling and focus groups expert at the More in Common thinktank, said on Sunday that people tended to be less concerned about free movement given years of high non-EU migration but would be more exercised about EU budget contributions or joining the euro.During the Brexit referendum, the topic was hotly debated, with the leave campaign arguing that the UK would be able to take control of its borders if it voted to exit the EU. However, in the years that followed, net migration rose to a peak of944,000 in the year ending March 2023under a new points-based system, up from330,000 before the Brexit vote.Burnham’s decision to open the debate on free movement was welcomed by some businesses, which have grown frustrated at the lack of progress on the issue, and on reducing the extra paperwork required to do business with EU customers since Brexit – both seen asobstacles to faster economic growth.The British Chambers of Commerce lobby group called for the Treasury to analyse the various economic options for different forms of EU-UK relationships. Most economic studies have concluded that a closer EU relationship would benefit the UK economy.William Bain, head of trade policy at the BCC, said the common understanding strategy agreed by Keir Starmer in May 2025 was “approaching the ceiling of what can be achieved”.This week’s budget is expected to underscore the damage to the economy from Brexit, including from a drop in net migration. The Resolution Foundation, a thinktank, said that if migration falls by 300,000 over the next five years it would translate to a hit to government tax revenues of £4.7bn in 2029-30, reducing chancellor John Healey’s room for manoeuvre.The Institute for Fiscal Studies, another thinktank, estimated that lower net migration estimates would reduce the chancellor’s “headroom” by between £1bn and £5bn by 2031-32, depending on how the government’s Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR) chooses to model the expected reductions in population.The OBR has previously estimated that Brexit barriers to trade and free movement have caused a long-term hit of about 4% of UK output.Explore more on these topicsLabourAndy BurnhamAngela RaynerStella CreasyShabana MahmoodForeign policyBrexitnewsShareReuse this content

title: Has Healey’s military-style budget secrecy really played out so differently to past budgets? | Budget 2026 | The Guardian
description: Chancellor was said to be worried about market-sensitive leaks, yet significant policies have been heavily trailed in the media
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Chancellor was said to be worried about market-sensitive leaks, yet significant policies have been heavily trailed in the media
Content: The chancellor, John Healey – photographed here meeting British personnel in Estonia while he was defence secretary – is said to have deployed ‘military-style protocols’ to prevent leaks of his budget.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.View image in fullscreenThe chancellor, John Healey – photographed here meeting British personnel in Estonia while he was defence secretary – is said to have deployed ‘military-style protocols’ to prevent leaks of his budget.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.Budget 2026AnalysisHas Healey’s military-style budget secrecy really played out so differently to past budgets?Rowena MasonWhitehall editorChancellor was said to be worried about market-sensitive leaks, yet significant policies have been heavily trailed in the mediaSun 25 Oct 2026 15.35 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 16.14 EDTShareThe public has been told repeatedly thatJohn Healeyis so concerned about budget leaks that he has set up defence-style “compartmentalisation” to prevent the Treasury’s financial secrets escaping.The macho military analogies began in mid-August when Healey was said by the Telegraph to be “on a war footing” to stop the drip of information that he believed had beleaguered Rachel Reeves.The Financial Times added that “military-style protocols” were being deployed, while the Spectator was excited about the use of “classified computer systems” and the i newspaper described a process where officials could sign in to only their parts of the document and could not access the sections they were not working on.This weekend, the Observer reported that Healey was “flabbergasted” by the lack of security around financial information when he became chancellor and “it was so different to how we did things in the MoD”.The chancellor is known to have been worried that market-sensitive leaks cost Britain billions in the run-up to the last government’s budgets. But has this time around been so different after all?Despite the heightened “security” around Wednesday’sbudget, many of its announcements have been leaked already from a clear mixture of authorised and unauthorised sources.It emerged well in advance that there will be ahigher tax on banks– a deeply market-sensitive policy – and apackage of energy supportfor the most vulnerable.View image in fullscreenIt has already emerged that the budget will include an energy support package for the most vulnerable.Photograph: Libby Welch/AlamyThere will also be billions of pounds in extra defence spending, directed towards the British Business Bank and National Wealth Fund, as well as a £1bn crackdown on online VAT sales, with big retailers such as Amazon, eBay and Temu to be responsible for
