title: NFL today: How to watch Chiefs v Seahawks, TV channels & live stream Sunday 25 October | Seattle Seahawks | The Guardian
description: How will the Kansas City and Seattle fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Author: Alex Kirshner
Headline: How will the Kansas City and Seattle fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Content: Sam Darnold’s form has slumped this season.Photograph: Geneva Heffernan/APView image in fullscreenSam Darnold’s form has slumped this season.Photograph: Geneva Heffernan/APNFL watching and streaming guideSeattle SeahawksNFL today: How to watch Chiefs v Seahawks, TV channels & live stream Sunday 25 OctoberHow will the Kansas City and Seattle fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream optionsAlex KirshnerSun 25 Oct 2026 15.45 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 15.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSunday Night Footballthis week is a blockbuster. The Chiefs take their undefeated record to Seattle, where the defending-champ Seahawks should have an early sense of urgency. Mike Macdonald’s team enter at 3-3, already a full three games (plus, for now, a tiebreaker) behind the gangbusters 49ers. To have any real shot at a home playoff game — a critical edge in last year’s Super Bowl run — the Seahawks need to get a win against a resurgent Chiefs squad who nothing like the husk they appeared to be down the stretch last season.In addition to a clash between two marquee franchises, the evening is a homecoming for one of the most important players of the young season: Kenneth Walker III. The Seahawks-turned-Chiefs running back has been key to KC’s offensive revitalization after signing as a free agent following his Super Bowl MVP nod with Seattle. The Chiefs were in the bottom half of the league in rushing yards per carry last year but this season hold a whopping lead over the second-place team, averaging 5.5 yards to the Bills’ 5.1. The 26-year-old Walker is having a career year and has worked his way from “good player” to “maybe the Offensive Player of the Year.”Date:Sunday 25 October 2026Time:8.20pm ET/5.20pm PT/12.20am GMT (Monday 26 October)Stadium:Lumen Field (Seattle, Washington)How to watchUnited States:Watch onNBC, or stream onFubo.Canada:Stream onFubo Sports Pro.United Kingdom:Watch onSky Sports NFL or Sky Sports Main Event, or stream withNOWorNFL Game Pass on DAZN.What to watch forThe Seahawks need to get Sam Darnold on track. Sure, leading the club to a Super Bowl win has bought the veteran some goodwill, but Darnold has been bad enough that the Seahawks fan in your life has probably texted you at least once to call for the elevation of backup Drew Lock. Darnold, who was hurt earlier in the year, is throwing interceptions on a career-worst 4.7% of his throws. His passing success rate reacheda career high 50% last yearbut has dipped to 40% in the early going here, one of the lowest marks he’s posted.Meanwhile, the Chiefs don’t have big problems right now, but they do have little ones that they should address in the near term. One of them is that Patrick Mahomes has had pedestrian numbers in three of the team’s five games, onlyreallylighting it up in a Week 3 win over the dreadful Dolphins. This hasn’t been a big issue with Walker setting the world on fire, but as Mahomes gets deeper into the season and further from the ACL and LCL tears that ended his season last year, you’d hope to see some growth. The bad news here: Seattle is giving up 4.3 adjusted net yards per attempt,by far the best mark in football. One might expect that for the Chiefs to stay unbeaten, Walker will need to keep doing the heavy lifting.Explore more on these topicsSeattle SeahawksNFL watching and streaming guideKansas City ChiefsNFLUS sportsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthropic sued for allegedly using 274 Elvis Presley songs to train AI models | US news | The Guardian
description: Authentic Brands Group says AI company infringed on rights of songs by the King such as Can’t Help Falling in Love
Author: Marina Dunbar
Headline: Authentic Brands Group says AI company infringed on rights of songs by the King such as Can’t Help Falling in Love
Content: ‘The defendant … has built its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before,’ the lawsuit says.Photograph: Universal Pictures. All Rights Reserved./PAView image in fullscreen‘The defendant … has built its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before,’ the lawsuit says.Photograph: Universal Pictures. All Rights Reserved./PAUS newsAnthropic sued for allegedly using 274 Elvis Presley songs to train AI modelsAuthentic Brands Group says AI company infringed on rights of songs by the King such as Can’t Help Falling in LoveMarina DunbarSun 25 Oct 2026 14.25 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 14.41 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe owners ofElvis Presley’s music catalogue are suing artificial intelligence (AI) companyAnthropicfor allegedly using Presley’s songs to train their models without permission.Authentic Brands Group, the licensing organization that has ownership of both Presley’s music and likeness, is accusing Anthropic of infringing on the rights of 274 songs by Presley. The lawsuit, first reported byBillboard, was filed on Friday.While AI firms have already facedcopyright infringement claimsfrom the Recording Industry Association of America (RIAA) andmusic labelssuch as Sony,Universaland Warner Records, this case represents one of the first major legal challenges brought directly by an artist’s estate against an AI developer. The result could set a broader precedent for how AI companies are allowed to use existing music catalogues.“The Elvis plaintiffs bring this action to enforce these exclusive rights against the defendant that has built its entire business model based on copyright infringement at a scale never seen before,” lead attorney Richard Busch wrote in the lawsuit.The lawsuit claims that “from its inception, Anthropic’s AI model, ‘Claude,’ has created infringing output of copyrighted material of virtually every song from every catalog available on the internet”.It further accuses Anthropic of utilizing 274 of Presley’s songs to train its AI model. These works include Can’t Help Falling in Love, All Shook Up and A Little Less Conversation. The plaintiffs are seeking $150,000 per infringed track, or about $41m (about £31m).skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines USGet the most important US headlines and highlights emailed direct to you every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnthropic sued over alleged theft of ‘tens of thousands’ of songsRead more“Even Anthropic’s institution of guardrails (albeit ineffectively) to purportedly limit outputs which infringe upon music copyrights, after being caught, along with its knowledge that its guardrails were ineffective to stop creating outputs which infringed music copyrights, demonstrates that Anthropic knowingly engaged and continues to willfully engage in copyright infringement of others’ musical works,” the lawsuit states.AI music platforms work by analyzing large amounts of recorded music in order to learn the sounds, structures and expressions of songs, and then allows users to create their own AI-generated music via text or speech prompts.Musicians haverepeatedlyexpressed concernsthat their music and voices are being used without their permission by AI models, as well asfears thatAI-generated “slop” musiccould replacehuman-made songs.Some AI bots have even begunimpersonatingreal living artists on music streaming platforms. Last week, music streaming giantSpotifyannounced it hadremovedabout 50m songs considered AI slop from its recommendations to users over the past year.Explore more on these topicsUS newsElvis PresleyAnthropicLaw (US)AI (artificial intelligence)Pop and rockComputingnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Extremely disappointed’: WA government seeks reimbursement from Deloitte over flawed university report  | Western Australian politics | The Guardian
description: State paid consultancy firm $166,000 for feasibility study on merging the three tertiary institutions
Author: Krishani Dhanji
Headline: State paid consultancy firm $166,000 for feasibility study on merging the three tertiary institutions
Content: Deloitte is under pressure after a report into the potential merger of three WA universities contained AI-hallucinated references and incorrect figures.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPView image in fullscreenDeloitte is under pressure after a report into the potential merger of three WA universities contained AI-hallucinated references and incorrect figures.Photograph: Dan Himbrechts/AAPWestern Australian politics‘Extremely disappointed’: WA government seeks reimbursement from Deloitte over flawed university reportState paid consultancy firm $166,000 for feasibility study on merging the three tertiary institutionsGet ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastKrishani DhanjiandJosh TaylorSun 25 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 19.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Western Australian government has said it is “extremely disappointed” and is seeking an “expedited” cost recovery from Deloitte after errors were discovered in a report about a potential university merger, including AI-hallucinated references and hundreds of millions of dollars in cost discrepancies.The government paidDeloitte$166,000 for a feasibility study on merging the University of Western Australia, Curtin University and Murdoch University.Deloitte considered three merger options between the three universities, with “low”, “mid” and “high” cost scenarios, and broke down the calculations of those costs in the report’s appendix.Under the “high” cost scenario of a merger between Curtin and UWA, the report calculates the “total costs to day 1” as $514m, and “post day 1” over five years at $145m. The total cost of those two payments is $659m but the report wrote $399m – a $260m discrepancy.Prof Stephen Bartos, an expert in public sector governance at the University of Canberra, said the errors discredited the report. “In my view, they’re so extensive that you probably need a new report, or at the very least someone to go through that material from the ground up and rework it manually without the use of AI,” he said.“Any errors in a report like this, especially on something controversial like a university merger, discredits the report, and Deloitte shouldn’t have had these errors.”Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailUnder a “low” cost merger scenario between Curtin, UWA and Murdoch, the total costs to day one are $396m and total post day one over five years are $116m. That total would be $512m but the report calculates the two numbers to $823m – a $311m discrepancy.Deloitte is already under pressure after it was revealed in the media this month that the same report contained hallucinated AI references, leading the state opposition to label it “AI slop”.The consultancy firm admits in its report it used generative AI to “support the collation of research, synthesis of information and editorial proofing” and had earlier dismissed the errors as “minor”.Deloitte to pay money back to Albanese government after using AI in $440,000 reportRead moreA spokesperson for the WA government told Guardian Australia that the Department of Energy and Economic Diversification had written to Deloitte to expedite the cost recovery process for the report.“We are extremely disappointed these errors are being found now,” the spokesperson said.“We are advised they do not affect the modelling in the report or its findings, but any errors will be corrected as part of a review by Deloitte which will re-issue the report.“All available data, along with new information, will be interrogated by the university reform business case.”The WA tertiary education minister, Tony Buti, described them as “typos”, though a day later said he was angry and disappointed with Deloitte.Guardian Australia has found that one of the references to a World Health Organization report has a ChatGPT metadata tag on the URL, indicating that the link was directly sourced from the chatbot.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn the report, Curtin University is referred to repeatedly as the Curtin University of Technology – a name the institution has not used since 2010, and that was changed under an act of state parliament in 2017.Bartos said the numbers diverging so significantly was cause for concern. “Unless the numbers add up, a government might not want to do it,” he said.Prof Christian Downie, from the Australian National University’s school of regulation and global governance, who has previously examined submissions to government that contained AI hallucinations, said human errors happened and mistakes in reports could be expected and, although Deloitte outlined broadly its use of AI in the report, there was a lack of transparency.“We need much more detail about how [AI is] being used and for what parts of the report writing process,” he said. “If they’re going to use it for data collection and if there’s concerns about the data, then that needs to be detailed in the report.”Downie said without transparency it was hard to have confidence in the report. He said broadly as AI use increases, governments need to reassess their contracts with consultancy firms.“All levels of government, both state and federal, need to be recalibrating their contractual relationship arrangements when they outsource work to consulting firms to ensure that the proper incentives and penalties are in place in those contracts,” he said.The WA government has that argued the merger is a “once-in-a-generation” opportunity. Buti told the ABC on Tuesday: “I want to commit to it if the business case stacks up, and then it’s a government decision.”It was not supported by Murdoch University, whose vice-chancellor, Prof Andrew Deeks, criticised the report and penned an op-ed on the university’s website arguing that “all that a university merger will do for WA is cost a lot of time, money and energy, while reducing choices for students and alienating alumni”.“That the Western Australian government continues to be taken in by this nonsense is extraordinary,” he wrote. “Another fail for Deloitte.”Deloitte did not respond to questions from Guardian Australia.Explore more on these topicsWestern Australian politicsWestern AustraliaDeloitteAustralian universitiesAustralian educationAI (artificial intelligence)Consulting (Australia)newsShareReuse this content

title: Neighbours is being recut into a microdrama focused on Margot Robbie – and her co-stars aren’t happy | Neighbours | The Guardian
description: Actor’s storylines in the famous soap will be recut into vertical micro-episodes to be watched on phones – but her fellow cast members say they haven’t been consulted
Author: Ima Caldwell
Headline: Actor’s storylines in the famous soap will be recut into vertical micro-episodes to be watched on phones – but her fellow cast members say they haven’t been consulted
Content: Margot Robbie as Donna Freedman with Jackie Woodburne as Susan Kennedy in Neighbours. Fremantle, the soap’s producer, is working with RoseBerry Media to repurpose Robbie’s old episodes to make a vertical drama designed for phones.Photograph: FremantleMedia/REXView image in fullscreenMargot Robbie as Donna Freedman with Jackie Woodburne as Susan Kennedy in Neighbours. Fremantle, the soap’s producer, is working with RoseBerry Media to repurpose Robbie’s old episodes to make a vertical drama designed for phones.Photograph: FremantleMedia/REXNeighboursNeighbours is being recut into a microdrama focused on Margot Robbie – and her co-stars aren’t happyActor’s storylines in the famous soap will be recut into vertical micro-episodes to be watched on phones – but her fellow cast members say they haven’t been consultedIma CaldwellSun 25 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 20.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe long-running Australian soap operaNeighboursis being recut with AI into a microdrama designed to be watched on phones, sparking a debate among the show’s actors and the industry over the wider implications of television archives being mined for new content.RoseBerry Media, which specialises in making “vertical television” for phones, has repurposed original episodes of Neighbours for distribution on its Epis platform, using an AI-assisted production tool called RedSnapper.The microdrama made from the footage will initially focus on Margot Robbie’s character, Donna Freedman, whom she played from 2008 to 2011. Two of Robbie’s storylines will be recut into vertical micro-episodes, creating about 150 minutes of content.The Neighbours star Stefan Dennis has voiced concerns over the project, telling the Herald Sun it was “unbelievably invasive, morally and legally wrong and somehow it appears we can’t do anything about it”.“I’ve got my agent [on it],” he said. “I imagine everyone else on Neighbours is doing the same thing, as well as the MEAA [Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance] and Australian Writers’ Guild. Whether they can stop it is another thing. We’re dealing with a very big machine.”Dennis’s agent told Guardian Australia he would not be commenting further.‘Money grab’A former Neighbours cast member, Matthew Werkmeister, who played Zeke Kinski from 2005 to 2011 and appeared alongside Robbie in a love-triangle storyline, told Guardian Australia that he only learned about the deal when he was approached for comment.“I find it extremely concerning,” Werkmeister said. “Not from any money-making point of view, but from my image being used through AI and a platform I did not consent to.”View image in fullscreenEloise Mignon as Bridget Parker, Margot Robbie as Donna Freedman and Matthew Werkmeister as Zeke Kinski in Neighbours.Photograph: FremantleMedia/RexWerkmeister said he had received no notification from the Neighbours producer, Fremantle, or RoseBerry Media regarding whether residuals would be paid to actors in the vertical series. Guardian Australia understands that any residuals will be paid to writers and actors based on their agreements for the series, as per normal process.“When I signed my original contracts, I was 13,” he said. “In all honestly I can’t remember exactly every line point, but AI and streaming platforms, let alone vertical streaming platforms, didn’t exist and was not a consideration.”Werkmeister dismissed claims that the vertical format would introduce the classic soap to younger audiences and called the venture a “money grab for Fremantle”.“They’re just trying to dump their existing library to make a quick buck,” he said. “I’d be intrigued to know if they reached out to the wonderful Margot Robbie, since her star power is likely a main motivator for this venture.”Guardian Australia has contacted Robbie for comment.Mattie Webb, the agent for the actor Sam Clark – who played Donna’s partner, Ringo Brown – said Clark was waiting to hear from US actors’ union Sag-Aftra before commenting.But Webb, an LA-based manager with 27 years’ experience, said AI was rapidly disrupting the entire industry. “All week I’ve been dealing with deepfake videos and AI,” he said. “It’s a whole new world.”The birth of a $15bn industryThe Neighbours microdrama arrives amid a boom in vertical serials, which are usually made up of episodes around just one-minute long and tailored for mobile phone viewing. The microdrama market, which originated inChina, was estimated to be worth up to $15bn (A$21.4bn) globally last year.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionTelevision in titbits: the rise of the billion-dollar microdrama industryRead moreSome verticals areentirely original and shot for the format, while others are cut from existing material; in 2023, Paramount Pictures released Mean Girls on TikTok as 23 episodes. Others are entirely unofficial, with fans recutting their favourite shows into snippets for millions of viewers on social media.In this era, Neighbours is a goldmine, having broadcast more than 9,300 episodes between its launch in 1985 and end in 2025. The soap also served as a launchpad for several international stars, including Robbie, Guy Pearce, Kylie Minogue, Jason Donovan, Dichen Lachman, Natalie Imbruglia, Liam Hemsworth and Jesse Spencer.In commentsreported by Varietylast month, Fremantle’s commercial and international chief executive, Jens Richter, described the project as “an exciting example of how technology and creative thinking can unlock new value from our diverse catalog and content library”.Fremantle defended the microdrama when contacted by Guardian Australia, saying that it will only use “original, previously broadcast footage, dialogue and performances”.RedSnapper, the AI technology, “does not generate new scenes or performances, alter actors’ faces or likenesses, or use synthetic voices”, a spokesperson told Guardian Australia.RedSnapper was used to help with “catalogue analysis, editing and vertical reframing, with a human editor reviewing and approving every stage of the editing process”.A RoseBerry Media spokesperson said the company was aligned with Fremantle’s response and had “nothing further to add”.Push for regulationAustralia’s largest union for actors, the Media, Entertainment and Arts Alliance, confirmed it was assisting Neighbours cast members and their representatives after the announcement.The MEAA acting chief executive, Adam Portelli, said anyone involved in Neighbours could contact the union “to ensure their work is not exploited without their knowledge, consent or fair compensation”.Portelli called on the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, and parliament to legislate to protect the creative sector by ensuring workers “are fairly and directly compensated when their work is exploited by AI”.A spokesperson for the Australian Writers’ Guild told Guardian Australia it was “in discussions with Fremantle and hopes to reach a fair resolution soon”.Werkmeister also backed legislative intervention, warning that the project would set a precedent that would reach far beyond Ramsay Street.“Converting existing work via AI without proper consultation or fair compensation sets a concerning precedent,” he said.“We urgently need way more robust AI regulations, guardrails and proper consent mechanisms in place.”Explore more on these topicsNeighboursAI (artificial intelligence)Margot RobbieDramaSoap operaTelevisionAustralian trade unionsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Cookie theft: how fraudsters get the digital key to your accounts | Scams | The Guardian
description: ‘Session cookies’ are a primary target for hackers letting them hijack and use your accounts
Author: Hilary Osborne
Headline: ‘Session cookies’ are a primary target for hackers letting them hijack and use your accounts
Content: Cookie warning … one of the best ways to defeat hackers is to get into the habit of always logging out of an account.Photograph: Rawf8/AlamyView image in fullscreenCookie warning … one of the best ways to defeat hackers is to get into the habit of always logging out of an account.Photograph: Rawf8/AlamyScam watchScamsCookie theft: how fraudsters get the digital key to your accounts‘Session cookies’ are a primary target for hackers letting them hijack and use your accountsHilary OsborneSun 25 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYou’ve had a busy morning of life admin, logging into various accounts to check balances and make payments. At the end of a productive few hours you close your laptop and move on to your next job.What you don’t know is that fraudsters have hijacked your session with the bank and are now able to access your account. You are the victim of cookie theft, which belongs to a type of fraud known as “session hijacking”.“Cookies have become the primary target for hackers,” says Marijus Briedis, chief technology officer at cyber security company NordVPN. In the year to June it identified 52bn cookies in stolen data circulating online.When you log into a website, such as your bank’s, you are given a unique cookie that sits on your device and stores your data temporarily. This means you can move from page to page without repeatedly being asked for your login details. It’s called a “session cookie” – or key – and as soon as you log out, it stops being of use.View image in fullscreenMove passwords out of your browser and into a dedicated password manager.Photograph: Maria Vonotna/AlamyBut while the session is open – and that will last beyond your activity if you choose to be remembered on a website, or if you do not properly close it – you could be vulnerable to cookie theft.Briedis says: “Think of a session cookie as a digital key that’s already turned in the lock. When you stay logged into a site, that cookie is what keeps the door open for you. If a hacker steals that active cookie, they essentially become you.“They don’t need your password, they don’t trigger a login alert, and they can often bypass your multifactor authentication (MFA).”The cookies are stolen from your device. The theft is usually a result of you having inadvertently downloaded malware.“Once that malware is on your device, it goes straight for your browser’s database, grabs all those active session cookies, and sends them back to the hacker,” says Briedis. “They’re essentially reaching into your digital pocket and grabbing your keys while you’re not looking.”What it looks likeIt looks like a regular session on the web. At some point you will have logged in and given your password, and maybe used MFA to prove it’s you.You may not realise that you are a victim until you later find that someone has used the session cookie to hack your account.If it’s a social media or email account you may discover it’s been used byscammers to trick other people. If it’s your bank they could access your account, or they could use details they find to perpetratean impersonation scam.And if you were shopping online, the fraudsters could change and redirect your order and charge it to your saved payment details.You may be alerted by a security alert from a site, for example, a message asking if you have tried to change any details.What to doBe really careful about the extensions and software you download, because that’s whereinfostealermalware will usually be hidden.Look out for signs that your laptop or phone has been infected with malware. Briedis says red flags include your device suddenly struggling with simple tasks, a battery that drains faster than it should, frequent crashes, or a browser that starts behaving oddly with redirects, pop-ups, or a changed homepage.Do not use insecure public wifi for sites that require you to log in. The chance of cookies being stolen through this channel is low, but you should always be cautious.Get into the habit of logging out of accounts. “Just closing a tab doesn’t end the session,” says Briedis. ”You need to manually log out to invalidate that cookie and make it useless to a thief.”He suggests moving passwords out of your browser and into a dedicated password manager.Clearing your cookies regularly will reduce what’s available to be stolen.If you suspect you have been compromised, run an antivirus scan. Also log out of your accounts on every device and change your passwords.Use MFA on accounts, as it does still offer more protection than a simple password.Alert your bank if you notice any suspicious payments.Explore more on these topicsScamsScam watchCookies and web trackingIdentity fraudCybercrimeData and computer securityHackingMalwarefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lara Croft is 30! We look at the video game icon’s biggest blunders | Games | The Guardian
description: We all know the highlights of the tomb raider’s storied career – but what about the lowlights? We dig deep to unearth the archaeologist’s less glorious moments
Author: Ellie Gibson
Headline: We all know the highlights of the tomb raider’s storied career – but what about the lowlights? We dig deep to unearth the archaeologist’s less glorious moments
Content: Thirty years of kicking ass … Lara Croft in Tomb Raider IV-VI Remastered, 2025.Photograph: AspyrView image in fullscreenThirty years of kicking ass … Lara Croft in Tomb Raider IV-VI Remastered, 2025.Photograph: AspyrGamesLara Croft is 30! We look at the video game icon’s biggest blundersWe all know the highlights of the tomb raider’s storied career – but what about the lowlights? We dig deep to unearth the archaeologist’s less glorious momentsEllie GibsonSun 25 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 06.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHappy birthday, Lara! This month marks 30 years since Ms Croft first swan-dived into our lives with her unique blend of athletic prowess, archaeological expertise and giant knockers. More than 100 million Tomb Raider games have been sold since. We all remember the good times: the bold design and sheer playability of the original titles; the establishment of Lara as a 90s icon, embodying both lads’ mag culture and girl power; the way she made games cool, even appearing on the cover of the Face. We’ve had blockbuster movies, big budget reboots, andshiny reissues. And who could forget the time we got topowerwash her house?But no one gets to 30 without a few skeletons in the closet – or in Lara’s case, butlers in the freezer. So here’s a look at the darker parts of her past.Lara Croft, corporate shillView image in fullscreenLara Croft sells Lucozade in 1999.Photograph: Core DesignLara’s image has been used to hawk a multitude of products over the years, from cereal and soft drinks to reasonably priced Spanish hatchbacks. Low points include the 1999 promo for a German women’s magazine in which Lara tells us what she really, really wants isn’t the Dagger of Xian or the MacGuffin of Atlantis, but abig meringuey wedding dress.See also the weirdDreamcast advertwhere Lara talks about the console as if it’s a jar of anti-ageing moisturiser. This led an entire generation of women to try reducing the appearance of fine lines by rubbing Sega hardware on their faces. Because she’s worth it? Let’s hope the money was.Murdered by her makersView image in fullscreenOne last adventure … Tomb Raider: Chronicles.Photograph: Eidos InteractiveBack in 1996, no one predicted how successful this quiet game about a posh archaeologist made by a small team in Derby would be. But once publisher Eidos realised it was in possession of a goose that laid golden eggs, it launched an intensive battery farming operation. Core Design was forced to churn out a newTomb Raidertitle every year.Four games in, the developers had had enough. In 1999 they decided to bury Lara under a collapsing pyramid at the end of The Last Revelation. News of her demise was tucked away towards the end of the design document, the Core team having taken a punt that their publisher overlords wouldn’t bother reading that far.They were correct. The Eidos execs were furious when they learned of Lara’s fate, but it was too late to change the game’s ending. Instead they put pressure on Core to find a narrative workaround so they could squeeze out one last PS1 adventure. The result was Tomb Raider: Chronicles, which begins with a memorial service for Lara and continues in a series of flashbacks. It isrubbish.Lara’s emo periodView image in fullscreenEmo Lara Croft with the reviled Kurtis Trent... Tomb Raider: Angel of DarknessPhotograph: Core DesignLara’s first PS2 outing, The Angel of Darkness, was released in 2003. It was aiming for mature and edgy, but landed slap bang in the middle of dull and depressing.The game missed the point of what players loved about Tomb Raider – the thrill of exploring exotic locations and abandoned temples. No one asked to wander around a gloomy version of Paris that could pass for Croydon, talking to sex workers and pawn shop owners while dressed in double denim.It didn’t help that the game was full of bugs and had awful controls. A terrible new strength mechanic forced the player to build up Lara’s muscle before she could perform previously simple tasks, like moving a crate.To top it all off, a secondary protagonist was introduced: tiresome edgelord Kurtis Trent, whose toxic masculinity ruined the party for everyone. Which brings us to…Terrible sidekicksView image in fullscreenAbsolute liability … Jonah Maiava and Lara Croft in the TV series Tomb Raider: The Legend of Lara Croft, 2024.Photograph: COURTESY OF NETFLIXAnother key appeal of the original Tomb Raiders was the feeling of being a solo adventurer exploring a strange world, never knowing when the eerie silence would be shattered by the snarl of a hungry wolf. No one ever wished Lara was accompanied by a bloke in a padded gilet saying: “Hey, I wonder if that rusty key we found will fit in this rusty lock?”But when Crystal Dynamics took over from Core in the 00s, they decided Lara needed some annoying sidekicks. The worst offender is Jonah, who makes his debut in the 2013 reboot. Not only is he feckless and mansplainy, he actively creates work for Lara by being an absolute liability. Over the course of their adventures he gets trapped, tortured, stabbed, kidnapped, knocked unconscious, shipwrecked, buried in an avalanche, caught in a tsunami, falsely declared dead, and almost killed in a plane crash. Ironically, the only calamity that doesn’t befall Jonah is being swallowed by a whale. A shame.Big screen blundersNone of the Tomb Raider films are stellar – although many middle-aged women have a soft spot for the first Angelina Jolie outing, in which our hero dispatches an army of goons without having to leave the house, or even get out of her pyjamas.The follow-up, The Cradle of Life, is absolute twaddle.Philip Frenchcalled it “repetitive and curiously inert”. The BBC’sNev Piercewent further: “Incoherent, dumb and stupefyingly bland … It’s as though theywantedto make a terrible film.”Pierce went on to describe Lara as a “pumped-up Judith Chalmers”, which points to a missed casting opportunity – who wouldn’t want to watch the affable host of Wish You Were Here…? scale Angkor Wat with a grappling hook?View image in fullscreenAbsolute twaddle … Angelina Jolie in Lara Croft: Tomb Raider – The Cradle of Life, 2003.Photograph: REUTERSPlayboy problemAlthough Chalmers never got the chance, plenty of other women were cast in the role of real-life Lara over the years. They included model Nell McAndrew, who donned the turquoise tank top to promote Tomb Raider III.Things went tits up when she also appeared in Playboy magazine, the game’s logo proudly displayed on the cover alongside the words: “LARA CROFT NUDE.”Core Design sued, unhappy that the video game character they had endowed with comically enormous breasts was being sexualised. They won – a judge orderedstickers be applied to 20,000 copies of the magazine, covering up the offending logo. It is not known how badly this affected sales among the Playboy readers eager to catch an illicit glimpse of unlicensed intellectual property.Reboot controversyView image in fullscreenLara Croft having a bad time in 2013’s Tomb Raider reboot.Photograph: Crystal Dynamics/Square-EnixThe 2013 Tomb Raider reboot was solid and polished. However, its creators failed to understand Lara’s appeal as a strong, enigmatic main character, particularly for female gamers.Art director Brian Horton talked about wanting to make players “care for” Lara. He said her torturous experiences and ripped clothing would show “beauty and vulnerability”, suggesting this was “sexy in its own way”.The controversy really kicked off after a trailer was released showing a man pinning Lara against a wall and groping her. Executive producer Ron Rosenberg said the sexual assault would make players want to “protect” the game’s protagonist, and “root for her in a way you wouldn’t root for a male character”. This focus on the male gaze and demotion of Lara to damsel in distress represented a staggering failure to read the room, and to notice there were women in it.Thirty years of hurt?There’s no doubt that Lara has endured some dark times over the last three decades. In fact, she’s had it harder than any other veteran video game character. No one ever suggested Solid Snake would have more appeal if he sported a gigantic pair of testicles, or insisted on giving Mario daddy issues. (Although, as annoying sidekicks go, Sonic the Hedgehog’s mate Tails gives Jonah a run for his gold rings.)Yet here she is, still standing, withanother adventure arriving next year. Perhaps this one will tell Lara’s true origin story: how she rose to prominence not because of her prominent chest, or past traumas, but because she was the cool, enigmatic star of a bloody great game.Lara Croft remains a leading icon of gaming culture, despite the repeated failure of sexist developers and unimaginative marketing teams to understand her power. As someone born after she was created might say, that’s why Lara Croft is the GOAT – not just the greatest of all tomb raiders, but the greatest of all time.Explore more on these topicsGamesLara Croft: Tomb RaiderTomb RaiderfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Influencers have taken over my city. If you can’t beat ’em, join ’em | Dave Schilling | The Guardian
description: I can’t say I’m enjoying my new gig as a would-be creator. But these days, I don’t have much choice
Author: Dave Schilling
Headline: I can’t say I’m enjoying my new gig as a would-be creator. But these days, I don’t have much choice
Content: ‘I miss the days when making a thing and sharing it with the world was hard.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I miss the days when making a thing and sharing it with the world was hard.’Illustration: Fortunate Joaquin/The GuardianOpinionSocial mediaInfluencers have taken over my city. If you can’t beat ’em, join ’emDave SchillingI can’t say I’m enjoying my new gig as a would-be creator. But these days, I don’t have much choiceSun 25 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 07.01 EDTShareI recently started posting videos onInstagram. Like, actual videos.Reels, as they call them. Where I say things, with one of those obnoxiously tiny microphones with the fuzzy head on top. I remember when microphones were gigantic tubular monstrosities that you couldn’t accidentally swallow without a pretty substantial effort and a handful of God-given talent.Why am I making Reels? Because if I don’t, I’ll die in obscurity, penniless and alone. The global creative industry revolves around video content on social media, forcing even a mildly attractive middle-aged divorced parent to try to be a star just to pay the bills.If I can turn into a well-compensated influencer by peddling mycomplaints about the new Burbank airport terminal, I will. I can either try to swim in the fetid pool of the attention economy or get eaten by a shark who posts TikToks about carb-conscious dieting.Are my gen X peers the influencers the world has been waiting for? | Emma BeddingtonRead moreOf course, that doesn’t mean I have to like it.In fact, I really, really don’t. I feel what gen Z might refer to as cringe whenever I open up CapCut and try to cobble together a coherent thesis while my head floats in front of a green screen.It’s so easy to squirt a Reel out, and the medium so thoroughly demands the aesthetic feel rough, that it’s almost like a mockery of the idea of creation. My Uber Eats order didn’t include the Diet Coke I ordered? Let me do a Reel about how mad I am. Too much air in my bag of potato chips? Better make a Reel. The Dodgers lost? Reel time.I miss the days when making a thing and sharing it with the world was hard. It doesn’t even have to be good. Just tasty enough for the Pac-Man monster that is the algorithm.It being so simple to make a Reel is why thousands of people are doing it, and getting rich in the process. Influencers are everywhere, especially in big cities such asLos Angeles.They wander around, consumed with a thirst for “hidden gem” restaurants to film in front of, or elaborate cocktails to try. They film explainer videos about your laundromat because it used to be owned by a mob boss or has a ghost living there. Since I started trying to be an influencer, I’ve filmed contentwhile next to someone else also filming content a few yards away.This is what I imagine the California Gold Rush was like – starving maniacs with greed in their eyes sifting around for something to change their lives. But swap out Levi’s jeans and a floppy hat for Alo workout gear and On Running sneakers.Food influencing alone has become a massive industrythat can make or break the success of a restaurant, or worse,make it so insufferable to try to eat therethat normal people stay home so as not to end up an unpaid extra in someone’s vlog.Some places, such as the fancy-pantsHotel du Cap-Eden-Roc in Antibes, are fighting back against the Night of the Living Dead invasion of content prospectors. The hotel has banned photoshoots to combat guests who have allegedly booked lunch reservations, then skipped the meal to take pictures in expensive clothes. Instead of functioning businesses tasked with serving paying customers, some places have devolved into mere backdrops for someone’sRobin Leach fantasy.Look, I’ve on more than one occasion gone to the Sunset Tower hotel in West Hollywood with the explicit purpose of taking a bunch of photos for Instagram. I’ll do it again, too.But what I will not do is not have the decency to sit down for a burger and a martini first. The Tower Bar is one of the most popular influencer traps in the city. The last time I was there, there were no cameras around, but it felt like there were. The Tower Barhas tried to limit photographyfor years, but no amount of begging has stopped patrons from snapping and ’gramming when they can.Maybe a part of me wishes there were cameras around at the Sunset Tower. I wouldn’t be making Reels if part of me didn’t have the same thirst as the rest of the would-be influencers that haunt our major metropolitan areas.That need is inside of me, even if I’m partially repulsed by it. My sense of modesty is a voice in my head, but it’s actually a quiet one that gets drowned out whenever I get a dopamine hit from a like on IG. If it feels good, why stop?But it’s not just that it feels good. It is, as I said earlier, a way to make ends meet. It is a career path that, unlike almost every other one, isn’t shrinking faster thanLizzo’s album sales.As social media video platforms such as Instagram Reels and YouTube gain more and more ubiquitousness in our lives, and as ad dollars migrate to those platforms from places that emphasize the written word, ignoring these opportunities starts to seem like a losing fight.Restaurants can litigate and scribble rules on menus. Hotels can ban photoshoots. But this is the equivalent of banning breathing. I fear that society is now built for influencers, or more modestly, the entertainment industry is.I might be too late to make money from influencer posting. I’m also probably too old for it. But if I didn’t, I would just be sitting around in a rapidly contracting room full of old writers typing away while the walls of their professional lives close in on them.We used tomake movies in this town. You’d see a film crew or two in every neighborhood. Studio backlots would be buzzing with activity.The lunch spots where Hollywood movers and shakers used to dine are now the real backlots. The cameras are in our pockets. The sets are the mundane slop of everyday life. And the cast of characters is staring back at you in the mirror.Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humoristExplore more on these topicsSocial mediaOpinionInstagramLos AngelesTikTokcommentShareReuse this content

title: The trouble with ‘kids these days’: are we giving young workers a fair go? | Gaynor Parkin and Dave Winsborough | The Guardian
description: George had spent decades building his firm and was looking for someone with ‘common sense’. Over time, he learned the importance of being explicit about his expectations
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: George had spent decades building his firm and was looking for someone with ‘common sense’. Over time, he learned the importance of being explicit about his expectations
Content: A survey of employers described many young people leaving education with a perceived lack of ‘work readiness’, poor resilience, and lacking work experience.Photograph: Carol Yepes/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA survey of employers described many young people leaving education with a perceived lack of ‘work readiness’, poor resilience, and lacking work experience.Photograph: Carol Yepes/Getty ImagesThe modern mindPsychologyThe trouble with ‘kids these days’: are we giving young workers a fair go?Gaynor Parkin and Dave WinsboroughGeorge had spent decades building his firm and was looking for someone with ‘common sense’. Over time, he learned the importance of being explicit about his expectationsThe modern mindis a column where experts discuss mental health issues they are seeing in their workSun 25 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 19.13 EDTShare“I want to be able to retire and leave it in good hands, it’s a great little business for someone.”George* was almost wringing his hands as he spoke, exasperation evident on his face, recalling an attempt to hire someone for his window-cleaning business.“He didn’t even bring a pack-up [lunch from home] so we had to waste time driving to find a shop he could get food from. Then the next day he brought a tub of yoghurt, which by mid-morning had turned sour sitting on the dashboard of the van. The lad had no common sense!”George was trying to develop a succession plan. He loved his business, providing a high standard of care for his customers, many of whom had been with him for years and some for decades. He especially enjoyed the banter with the older clients. Hiring “new blood” had become more pressing with his long-term employee leaving and his wife putting pressure on him to retire “while we can still enjoy ourselves, George”. He had tried out a few young people but no one “made the grade”.The most successful people I meet are often the ones struggling most | Darren LeeRead moreAn apparent lack of work ethic in the younger generation was particularly difficult for George to understand.He was finding out from customers that they were unhappy with the cleaning work done by his worker. “No one told me at the time because they didn’t want to upset me, but after he moved on, they all said he’d done a terrible job”.George’s orientation to work 50 years ago was radically different. “My old boss would literally kick me in the arse if I didn’t do something right. One time he chased me around a house telling me he’d kick me because I answered him back. When I started, he sent me round the hardware shop to get a left-handed screwdriver. Then he sent me back there to ask for a long weight. I felt so embarrassed when I figured it out, standing there for half an hour”.George’s wife asked for help because of how stressed he was, and to help him sort through his succession worries.“I don’t have time or frankly the energy to get some kid ready or teach them a work ethic. Surely that’s what parents and schools should be doing.”For millennia,people have been commenting that “kids these days” are less industrious, smart, respectful and disciplined. Asurvey of employersdescribed many young people leaving education with a perceived lack of “work readiness”, poor resilience and lacking work experience. Other commentatorshave agreedthat gen Z “aren’t work ready”.But organisational psychology finds that so-called generational differences shrink or vanish once controlled for age and life stage. Generational fragility doesn’t hold up well inrobust data; actually, it’s memory bias (projecting one’s own valued qualities on to the youth of the past).While gen Z is unlikely to have different, intrinsically fragile personalities, something did change in their developmental environment, meaning some young people are having greater difficulty making the transition into adult work.Importantly, the labour market is weaker. Additionally, virtual learning and Covid lockdowns contributed to asocialisation gap for gen Z– many of these young people missed out on years of in-person education, work experience, work readiness and life skills.This gap was important information for George. While he is entitled to expect punctuality, effort and acceptable work, he was holding a fixed belief that because he learned those things before he entered work, they must be prerequisites rather than skills that can also be learned through work.Chatbots can exploit our most basic human drive for attachment. Here’s how to have healthier relationship with AI | Gaynor Parkin and Dave WinsboroughRead moreThe yoghurt on the dashboard is funny because it suggests no common sense. But common sense is knowledge that we’ve forgotten learning. George packs his lunch every day because he’s done it for 50 years. And he was taught (inappropriately) that a customer shouldn’t have to point out a dirty window, that being ready to start at eight means arriving before eight, and that finishing a job means checking your own work.In gently encouraging George to reflect that work has always socialised young people into work, as it did for him too, he welled up.“Bugger. I think I just wanted the lad to be the one to take over, and to be perfect. I was a terror to begin with too.”So we worked out a plan for his next apprentice, with three guidelines:Be explicit about what you expect.Teach what can be taught.Watch carefully to see whether they learn.George worked the formula in his next hire. On day one, he explained his rules: “We start at 7.30am; bring your lunch; we take two breaks; phones stay away while we’re working.” And he adopted a clear method – “I’ll demonstrate, then we do it together. Then you do it while I watch. Lastly, you do it alone and I’ll inspect it. If you make a mistake, tell me rather than hide it.”We don’t know yet if he’ll be able to pass the business on. We do know he’s stopped thinking gen Z are all snowflakes.* George’s name, and some details, have been changed for privacyGaynor Parkin is a clinical psychologist at ButtonPsychology. Dave Winsborough is an organisational psychologistExplore more on these topicsPsychologyThe modern mindYoung peoplecommentShareReuse this content

title: As a young man, magazines were my window to the world. That wonder will be lost when all the shops have gone | John Harris | The Guardian
description: The closure of former WH Smith stores around the UK is sobering on many levels. The publications they sold were there to be perused, to broaden horizons, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Author: John Harris
Headline: The closure of former WH Smith stores around the UK is sobering on many levels. The publications they sold were there to be perused, to broaden horizons, says Guardian columnist John Harris
Content: Browsing magazines inside a WH Smith store in Bristol, 2007.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyView image in fullscreenBrowsing magazines inside a WH Smith store in Bristol, 2007.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyOpinionMagazinesAs a young man, magazines were my window to the world. That wonder will be lost when all the shops have goneJohn HarrisThe closure of former WH Smith stores around the UK is sobering on many levels. The publications they sold were there to be perused, to broaden horizonsSun 25 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 09.35 EDTShareTowards the end of the 1970s, the brief but spectacular career of those punk rockers and folk devils the Sex Pistols was followed by The Great Rock’n’Roll Swindle, a rather tawdry drama-documentary. It recast their rise and fall as a huge scam, summed up bya slogan on a T-shirtworn by their former manager Malcolm McLaren: “Cash from Chaos”.Back then, that motto was a neat representation of his personal brand of cultural mischief. But the culture always takes unexpected twists and turns – and 50 years on, an almost-identical maxim seems to be defining the fate of an increasing chunk of the British retail economy. While Andy Burnham pledgesto restore life to town centres, a private equity outfit is busy buying up national retail chains and then shutting down scores of their outlets, while seemingly operating in line with its boss’s most celebratedquotation: “Where there’s chaos, there’s opportunity.”Those words came from Jamie Constable, the owner of a set of businesses thatincludes Modella Capital, which specialises in“distressed investing”and“aggressive restructuring”. In 2024, Modella bought the craft supplies chain Hobbycraft – insisting on its“real commitment to bricks-and-mortar retail”, but thenshutting 18 shops and triggering 600 job losses, whileleaving redundancy costs to the taxpayer. Months later, it acquired the discount outlets branded as The Original Factory Shop, only for the entire chainto collapse. But its most ambitious move wasits recent purchaseof the 480 high-street shops that previously traded as WH Smith, rebranded by Modella as TG Jones (a completely made-up name, which it said would “keep that sense of afamily business”), and the rapidly announcedclosure of up to 150 of them.In September, 19 branchesbreathed their last, in such varied locations as Bath, Southend, Cardigan, Redhill and the Essex new town of Basildon. This month, the shuttersare permanently fallingin – among 23 places – Pinner, Truro, Inverness and Leek in Staffordshire. Thanks to their shortsighted folding into previous WH Smith premises, the closure plan will inevitably mean theloss of many local post offices: by early 2027, 70 will have gone. It will inevitably accelerate the decline of printed newspapers. But for me and many others, the key tragedy in this story is all about magazines, those gloriously tactile creations that played a crucial role in making many of us who we are.I say that as someone who fell in love with this form of publishing as a child, via a weekly educational magazine calledLook and Learn– stuffed, as I recall, with comic-strip versions of Dickens stories, and stuff about space exploration. By my early teens, I was an avid reader of Sounds, the Melody Maker and NME, the so-called weekly music papers that were really magazines whose ink came off on your fingers. Much to my amazement, between my 19th and 26th birthdays, I ended up successively working for all three – until, in 1995, I joined the now defunct company Emap Metro, which set enormous store by its mastery of glossy fortnightlies and monthlies.Some of these names may mean precious little to younger readers, but spark a Proustian rush among older ones: Q, Smash Hits,Select(which I edited for three years), Sky, the metal and hard rock title Kerrang!, Big,Neon, FHM. Most have now closed, but three of the old stable are still standing, under different ownership:Kerrang!, which mostly lives online; the film bible Empire; andMojo, the lovingly produced music magazine that I am thrilled to still write for.Thirty years ago, we all knew that there was no better medium for in-depth interviews, or high-end photography. The management constantly asked us who our intended reader was, and what the future was likely to entail. Even the smallest cover-lines were pored over, as if the mere mention of Placebo or DJ Shadow might attract scores of newbies. And though a lot of us didn’t listen, we were told to never, ever put our magazines in sealed plastic bags (which, in line with a longstanding convention, would contain “free gifts”), for fear of losing the kind of punter who liked to browse before they bought.And therein lies the TG Jones tragedy. The business has rightly acquired an utterly grim reputation, but is – or was – one reliable place to still find shelves full of printed content worthy of endless curiosity. And now? The culturally omnivorous twentysomething in Rickmansworth will no longer chance upon the latest edition of the cutting-edge music monthlythe Wire, and thereby be inducted into a world of esoteric electronica and contemporary avant-garde jazz. The student-age customer in Ormskirk tiring of production-line pop may know nothing of the more substantial music covered by Mojo’s excellent competitorUncut.Would-be radicals will be unable to browse the printed iteration ofTribune; film freaks may be completely unaware of the in-depth, art-house wonders ofSight and Sound. Publishers will fall over themselves to alert us to subscription offers, but for a lot of people, they will be prohibitively expensive.As George Orwell once put it, the UK is “a nation of stamp-collectors, pigeon-fanciers, amateur carpenters, coupon-snippers, darts-players, crossword-puzzle fans”. Products that reflect that enduring aspect of our national character are still at the core of magazine publishing, and why some titles still sell enviably: at the last count, for example,BBC Gardeners’ Worldsold a monthly average of 164,807 copies, while Country Living shifted 107,596. The broad women’s and fashion sector is also still here. It isn’t all over, by any means.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionStill, one can easily imagine a Mark Zuckerberg-esque voice scoffing at all this as so much stone-age nonsense, and claiming that what printed magazines deliver can easily be either replicated or superseded on the internet. Experience often suggests otherwise: witness the fate of the once-independent online music magazine Pitchfork, bought out by the corporate publisher Condé Nast in 2015 andbizarrely foldedinto the workings of the men’s title GQ nine years later: a classic case of what we now know as enshittification. But there is an even bigger point here about how we now engage with the things we like and love, summarised in a forthcoming book titled Circulation: How Culture Moves in the Age of Algorithm by the Nashville-based US music insiderDavid Macias, with a foreword written byDan Clancy, the CEO of the livestreaming platform Twitch.His argument is about music, but its logic applies across the cultural, recreational and sporting board. “The algorithm is great at finding me new music in the limited style I listen to,” he writes. “But it is really bad at showing me something new and different. My listening has become homogeneous, even though I can pick any album ever created.” This is the tedious prospect that the demise of the magazine will only accelerate – so after the high-street chaos has died down, we could be faced with an awful silence, broken only by the leakage from headphones playing the same things over and over again. And to speak the language of the insatiable capitalist, where will anyone find money in that?John Harris is a Guardian columnistExplore more on these topicsMagazinesOpinionConsumer magazinesNewspapers & magazinesWH SmithRetail industryMedia businesscommentShareReuse this content

title: The hill I will die on: The email sign-off is archaic – it needs to go. No regards, Tom | Tom Gill | The Guardian
description: The torture of the inbox is made insufferably worse by the dated cliches at the beginning and end, says journalist Tom Gill
Author: Tom Gill
Headline: The torture of the inbox is made insufferably worse by the dated cliches at the beginning and end, says journalist Tom Gill
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/GettyView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/GettyThe hill I will die onEmailThe hill I will die on: The email sign-off is archaic – it needs to go. No regards, TomTom GillThe torture of the inbox is made insufferably worse by the dated cliches at the beginning and end. Enough!Sun 25 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 11.42 EDTShareIf email were a person, it would be an adult dressed in a teenager’s clothes, desperately trying to stay relevant. Despitebeing 55 years oldand having been surpassed by numerous developments in communication technologies, its functionality remains largely the same as when it was first widely adopted. Unfortunately, so does the etiquette surrounding it.Whereas other forms of communication have long since dispensed with unnecessary textual tassels, email communication styles still lean closer to telegram than a text. Since I last checked, almost no one relishes receiving a new email – unless it’s informing you of a significant cash windfall that means you can, in fact, now quit your job and stop using it altogether. Yet, for some reason, many people start their responses with “Thank you for your email!” I would put this forward as one of the least convincing sentences in the English language.At the other end of the page is one of the most common yet totally unnecessary habits of the digital age: the email signoff. For those who haven’t yet realised, I’m here to tell you that you don’t need to sign your name at the end of an email – I can already see it’s from you. I know your name. Outlook has gone to extraordinary lengths to tell me your name. It’s in my inbox, the “from” field and the thread, and I probably begrudgingly addressed my last email directly to you.And then there is whatever form of final flourish you see fit to precede that with. To me, the whole concept of “regards” – kind, best or otherwise – is archaic and overly formal, not far from sealing the whole thing with a wax stamp and dispatching it via horse. But worse are the new ways of signing things off. “In solidarity”, “Keep dreaming” and the ultimate Covid-era classic: “hope you’re staying positive and testing negative”. This reaches its logical conclusion with the use of “KR” as a signoff. We have begun to admit that we don’t actually feel enough “kind regards” to type the words any more – and yet, the convention rolls on.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe hill I will die on: Forget potholes – the true indicator of societal decline is the ropey shoelace | Coco KhanRead moreThat’s to say nothing of email signatures, which now routinely exceed the length of the emails they are attached to. Name, job title, mobile number, office number, LinkedIn profile, logo, environmental disclaimer, confidentiality notice, statement about working hours and a quote from Maya Angelou. All appended to an email saying: “Running 5 mins late!”However, I appreciate that we must retain some means of expressing digital distaste, such is the harsh reality of the world of work. Therefore, the only use of the word “regards” I will permit is the one placed at the end of an email to communicate blunt and absolute hostility towards the recipient.With absolutely no regards,TomTom Gill is a freelance journalist and consultant from London, based in MelbourneExplore more on these topicsEmailThe hill I will die onSocial etiquetteComputingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Don’t call me ‘mumsy’ – the contempt behind that word makes me livid | Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett | The Guardian
description: It means to be drab, homely or old-fashioned – ‘motherly’, essentially. Why can’t we have some respect for mothers, instead of deriding them, asks Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Author: Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Headline: It means to be drab, homely or old-fashioned – ‘motherly’, essentially. Why can’t we have some respect for mothers, instead of deriding them, asks Guardian columnist Rhiannon Lucy Cosslett
Content: ‘Mumsy’ is essentially saying mums can never be stylish again.Photograph: Juice Images/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Mumsy’ is essentially saying mums can never be stylish again.Photograph: Juice Images/AlamyOpinionParents and parentingDon’t call me ‘mumsy’ – the contempt behind that word makes me lividRhiannon Lucy CosslettIt means to be drab, homely or old-fashioned – ‘motherly’, essentially. Why can’t we have some respect for mothers, instead of deriding them?Sun 25 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 07.15 EDTShareArecentnewspaper headline– “Sorry Radley! These dated handbag brands will make you look mumsy – here’s where stylish A-listers and Royals are shopping instead” – reminded me of a word I despise: “mumsy”.My list of words that make me want to throw things is varied and long, but “mumsy” is near the top. The quality of being mumsy means to be drab, homely or old-fashioned, essentially “motherly”. Something about the casual misogynistic contempt it carries makes me livid. So livid I might even use “that voice”. You know. The scary mum voice that turns misbehaving children in supermarkets into stone.“Mumsy” crops up in fashion coverage, which in autumn is unduly focused on the new school-run “style rules”.Articlesabout how to look chic at theschool gateand short-form videos about “what the cool mums are wearing” add to this feeling that the last thing you, as a mother, would want to appear as is what you actually are: someone’s mum.Of course, it’s understandable, and totally normal, to not want to be entirely defined by your reproductive status. Few of us want our entire identities to be “mother”. I still remember the shock I felt when a health professional first referred to me as “Mum” instead of by my name. It can feel as though you have ceased to be a person in society’s eyes. Add to that the fact your body’s changed because you’ve made and birthed a whole human being, and that you are now responsible for that other human being’s every want and need, drastically limiting the time you have to attend to personal style and grooming, and it can feel hard to know who you are now.These conflicting feelings are never a reason to deride mothers in general, though, or to act like “I’m not a regular mom, I’m a cool mom”. There’s a reason Amy Poehler’scomic Mean Girls catchphrasehas proved so legendary. There’s something inherently ridiculous about working to deny something that you so irrevocably are and will always be. The harsh reality that dawns on you as you transition from not-mother to mother is that you are for ever changed. You can try to dress it up all you want, but the fact is that you’re someone’s mum now.View image in fullscreenAmy Poehler in Mean Girls (2015).New theories ofmatrescencetell us that this change is a lot more complicated than suddenly wearing really naff jeans, although you might be doing that too (or be simply too sleep-deprived to give a toss that you’re wearing really naff jeans. Or using the word “naff”, which is probably also mumsy). The concept of mumsy changes according to the era you are living in. In the 1990s, all the mums wore high-waisted Levi’s 501s, which we even came to call “mum jeans”. This came to be co-opted by fashion brands, albeit using the slightly less mumsy sounding “mom”. I wouldn’t have been caught dead in mum jeans. What am I wearing now, as I type this? That’s right, a pair of vintage 501s. It all comes back round eventually. The teenagers I pass on the school run every morning would never.I look at how their baggy jeans are soaking up the puddles and pigeon piss all the way up to their knees and am not nostalgic. This must have been the sort of zen that my own mum felt; I feel confident in my personal style. That doesn’t mean that fear of mumsiness doesn’t try to stalk us all regardless. The anxiety around this question is palpable on forums such as Mumsnet: what shape of jeans should we be wearing now? Are coloured trainers fashionable?I’m not going to pretend that I don’t care at all, but I would think less of someone who uses the word “mumsy” about other women. I will never forget, long before I had a child myself, one writer I know saying of another that her work was “a bit mumsy”. The writer in question wrote brilliantly and hilariously about parenthood, and also about a lot of other things. I found the way that “mumsy” was used to reduce and deride her intelligence and the quality of her work deeply unpalatable. I also recall an editor saying that she hated seeing the word “mum” in print. I suppose she preferred the more literary sounding “my mother”, which has its place but, let’s be honest, it’s not how most of us speak.It made me realise that it isn’t just fashion, then, that is resistant to mumsiness but culture more generally, and that’s only going to change when mothers and the work they do are afforded the respect they deserve. As it stands, to become a mother is to not only be confronted with biological reality and structural sexism, but to somehow navigate this without dressing, writing or sounding too much like a mother. Perhaps, like the fashion writer Frankie Graddon, whoseSubstack’s strap lineis: “I’ve had a baby, not a style crisis”, the solution is to simply be “Mum-ish”. Whatever. You can prise my 501s from my cold, dead hands.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionRhiannon Lucy Cosslett is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
