You can’t run in that’This article contains spoilers for Ali G: Who Iz I?Catherine ShoardSun 25 Oct 2026 12.13 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 12.38 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJoshua Loudermilk, one of two men apparently discredited by the new Ali G movieAli G: Who Iz I?, has said that he was in on the joke, but that the film-makers didn’t realise this.Loudermilk, a 54-year-old aspiring actor from North Carolina, has told the Guardian he recognised starSacha Baron Cohenearly in the shoot but continued pretending to be a hard-right Maga sympathiser prepared to defend the US border at all costs.The movie involves Loudermilk being recruited by another Cohen character, the ex-Mossad terrorist expert Col Erran Morad, to help form a citizens’ warrior force to protect US borders, making use of his top-secret new weapon: a gun disguised as buttocks.Along with fellow recruit Michael Aboud, the chair of the El Paso county Republican party, Loudermilk joins Morad on a mission to stop the birth on US soil of the baby of a fictional South American drugs kinpin. This involves abducting a woman apparently in labour, abandoning her in a deserted medical facility, kidnapping her newborn child (a lifelike prosthetic) and driving it in a zipped bag to the border in order to deliver it by drone to Mexico.Republican leader embarrassed by Ali G film says he plans to sue Sacha Baron Cohen: ‘A liar and a pervert’Read moreAboud is shown taking the decision to drop the child from a great height into Mexico rather than have it touch US soil. He has since called Cohen a “liar” and a “pervert” and expressed his intention to sue. The film repeatedly stresses that both men were “not in on it”.Loudermilk has told the Guardian he was surprised the production company did not notice social media updates he posted shortly after the shoot in which he named Cohen and expressed his excitement about the project.But rather than being upset about his involvement, Loudermilk – who recently appeared as Squire Dap in the North Carolina Town of Hudson Fall Dinner Theatre’s production of Camelot – says he welcomes the publicity boost.“I want to use this to my benefit,” he says. “I would hope Sacha would read this and laugh, like: ‘Hey, you got me!’ I had so much fun creating that character. I was trying to see if I was any good at acting in comedy. And I realised: ‘Oh, I think I’m good at this.’ And that’s what I wanna do for the rest of my life.”View image in fullscreenJoshua Loudermilk.Photograph: Joshua LoudermilkHis experience began in September 2025 when Loudermilk spotted apost on Craigslistby a body called the American Citizen Initiative (whose website is no longer active) recruiting “patriotic legal Americans” “concerned about the border crisis” who “believe that illegal immigration is out of control”.The ad, one of dozens posted across US states simultaneously, invited “real American citizens” to “attend an exclusive, hands-on event experience where you’ll learn the truth about what’s happening on the border and how you can make a difference”. Attendees were promised $300 as well as travel expenses.“I was like: this seems kind of weird,” says Loudermilk, who describes himself as broadly apolitical. “I don’t really care much about our borders. My mom’s from Ireland.”Recently made redundant, his motivation for responding was primarily financial. “I know rightwing and leftwing organisations have money and will pay people to just hold a sign up. I remember thinking: I wanna get on that gravy train. I want some George Soros money. I’ll pretend to be whatever. Just let me feed my family. It could have been save the whales and I would have done it.”In his application, Loudermilk fabricated hard-right views, mentioned that he had been a preacher and neglected to declare his ambitions to become a comedy actor – in part, he says, out of embarrassment. He then filled in a “silly questionnaire – very obvious, very slanted to the right”.Loudermilk was then called for a video interview, which involved the identification of left-leaning celebrities, as well as figures including Borat, Cohen’s bumbling Kazakh reporter, who Loudermilk duly named.He was also asked if he was a Trump supporter. “The funny thing is: not really. He’s just a leader. But I was like: I’m going to be an improv actor so I said: ‘Yeah, I support Trump!’ Next thing I know they’re like, ‘We want you to come out to be a part of this.’The company flew him to Ontario, California, with an initial offer of $1,000, plus food and expenses, on top of which Loudermilk received a further $700. “It was all real secretive. They frisked me down and I got in a truck to go to a karate studio.”Once he arrived, Loudermilk was greeted by security and informed an Israeli commander wanted to meet him. “That was a red flag. Why would Israeli commander be in America? I go in there and immediately I see this really tall guy with this horrible plastic surgery. My first thought was: that looks like Sacha Cohen. But I was like: nah, that can’t be him.”View image in fullscreenSacha Baron Cohen as ex-Mossad terrorist expert Col Erran Morad in the 2018 show Who is America?Photograph: ShowtimeLoudermilk’s suspicions were further raised, he says, when he met his fellow recruits. “They were old, old, old white guys who were really out of shape. Everyone’s wearing these Trump shirts. They didn’t seem like warriors. I thought: they could probably get better people for this.”Morad then produced the top-secret new gun in the shape of large, strap-on bottom, out of which bullets are fired from the anus. Initially, Loudermilk was baffled by its logistics. “I kept thinking: no-one’s gonna wear that thing because your butt’s gonna be abnormally large. No one has a butt like that. Are you gonna put a butt on top of a butt? You can’t run in that. And you’d have to wear some really big khaki pants.”He volunteered to be first to try the weapon out, whereupon Morad demonstrated the trigger system, which involves the pumping of an attached rubber penis. “And he kept calling it ‘shmeckel’. I’m like: that’s Sacha Cohen. At that moment I knew it.“And I was like: oh no, I can’t break character. I’ve got to go along with it. So what I decided [was] that whatever he did, I was going to take it another step further. He’s not going to punk me; I’m going to trick him. So I decided to get into character and just have a good time because they’re paying me.”As the plot became more “ridiculous”, says Loudermilk, so his enjoyment increased. During a scene in which he, Morad and Aboud help deliver the (prosthetic) baby, the three men become covered with fake excrement. “This big blast of pooping pap,” recalls Loudermilk – but he was reassured after inadvertently sampling some of the fluids. “I thought: ‘This doesn’t taste bad.’ So I just kind of hung in there. It was disgusting, but I was having fun.”View image in fullscreenLoudermilk and Aboud in Ali G: Who Iz I?Photograph: Ali G: Who Iz I?At the climax at the Mexican border, says Loudermilk, he handed the remote control to the drone to Aboud, “because that was boring. It was ridiculous – they’re not flying a real baby”. Instead, he “wanted to have fun with Sacha,” so he grabbed the “butt-gun”, yelling about the need to defend themselves, and eventually discharged fire, aided by Morad, who helps pump the penis trigger.Loudermilk declines to defend Aboud’s decision to then endanger the life of the baby by dropping it from the drone, but expresses some sympathy for his unwitting co-star.“I felt sorry for the poor fella. Because I’m all-in and he’s just kind of following me around like in a daze, like: what’s happening? He was scared to death, and obviously very uncomfortable, bless his heart.“I’d never met the guy before, but [at times] it felt he was totally freaking out on me. So I had to make him believe that I believed all this. So I would tell him, ‘You’re being a wimp, man. Our freedom is on the line.’ I kept trying to keep him from quitting.“But I’m surprised he didn’t figure it out. Like, come on, Michael – why would they recruit you to defend our border? Think about it.”Loudermilk concedes his decision to maintain the pretence of being far-right once he had worked out the true nature of the project was in part because he “was a little offended. Like: really? You’re picking on these Americans that aren’t the brightest. You’re gonna make fun of them and they’re not gonna know any better. So I decided I needed to be their ally, even though I’m not that way.”View image in fullscreenBaron Cohen at the film’s Los Angeles premiere.Photograph: Mario Anzuoni/ReutersAt the end of filming, Loudermilk signed a non-disclosure agreement at the request of the production company, which he says he was not given a copy of, and which mostly related to the top-secret weapons. “They came up to me after I was done and said, ‘Oh, you did so well!’ I said, ‘You get what you need? Can I talk about it?’ They said, ‘Oh no, not yet. Especially the butt-gun.’”Loudermilk considers any such terms breached now the film is out and mentions him by name: “It’s fair game.” He adds that, after shooting, he had some qualms about not coming clean to them that he had twigged. “I felt a little bad. And that’s why I thought: I should make a little post.”In December last year, Loudermilk posted three times on his public Facebook page about “eight hours of intense filming one on one with Sasha [sic] Cohen”, as well as twice on his Instagram, which is also public.“But they never saw it. And the fact they missed that makes it even better to me. So I guess it’s on them.”Last week, representatives for the film confirmed again to the Guardian that Loudermilk was not in on the joke. They have not yet responded to a further followup question on this.The film was released nationwide in the UK on Friday, as well as in a limited run in the US. Loudermilk, who has not yet watched it, says he is unconcerned about the prospect of recriminations from anyone upset by his apparent actions.“That people would be disgusted is a compliment. Oh, I really did a good job, huh! I pulled it off and I was so proud of myself.”Explore more on these topicsFilmAli G: Who Iz IRepublicansSacha Baron CohenFilm industryComedy filmsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Stephen Fry: ‘Sherlock Holmes altered the course of my whole life’ | Arthur Conan Doyle | The Guardian
description: Nearly a hundred years after Arthur Conan Doyle’s last Sherlock Holmes story, the writer and broadcaster unravels the mystery of the detective’s enduring appeal
Author: Stephen Fry
Headline: Nearly a hundred years after Arthur Conan Doyle’s last Sherlock Holmes story, the writer and broadcaster unravels the mystery of the detective’s enduring appeal
Content: Stephen Fry in Sherlock Holmes: A Game of Shadows.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyView image in fullscreenStephen Fry in Sherlock Holmes: A Game of Shadows.Photograph: Collection Christophel/AlamyArthur Conan DoyleStephen Fry: ‘Sherlock Holmes altered the course of my whole life’Nearly a hundred years after Arthur Conan Doyle’s last Sherlock Holmes story, the writer and broadcaster unravels the mystery of the detective’s enduring appealStephen FrySun 25 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 14.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt has become quite the fashion for contemporary writers to have a go at reinventing past classics. We’ve seen it done with imperishable literary heroes like Bond, Jeeves, Poirot and Winnie-the-Pooh. This is a relatively new phenomenon. But not in the case ofSherlock Holmes, where the practice is almost as old as the man himself.Sherlock Holmes was the conception ofArthur Conan Doyle, a Scottish doctor down on his luck who had turned his hand to fiction to make up for a worrying lack of success in attracting patients to his surgery. Conan Doyle could never have guessed that the first Sherlock Holmes story he wrote, A Study in Scarlet, published in the 1887 issue of Beeton’s Christmas Annual, would in a few years propel him and the characters he created to literary fame. The personalities and characteristics of Holmes and Watson became as familiar to late Victorians as their own friends and families. The readership was worldwide and spread across all ages and classes.Conan Doyle himself – frustrated by the burdensome discomfort of what he felt had become something of a millstone around his neck – killed off his creation by having Holmes apparently plummet to his death in Switzerland’s Reichenbach Falls, pulling his arch-enemy Moriarty down with him into the roaring cataract. The public outcry was swift and over­whelming. Grown men and women wept openly, black armbands were adopted, and a host of angry readers wrote abusive letters to Conan Doyle’s publishers, to the Strand magazine and to Conan Doyle himself. He grudgingly bowed to public pressure and unearthed a story set before Holmes’s plunge into the abyss – The Hound of the Baskervilles. But only after the clamour still refused to subside did he at last bring his hero back to life in The Return ofSherlockHolmes, presaging a new stream of short stories and a full-length novel, The Valley of Fear. He was to continue writing Sherlock Holmes adventures right up until 1927, although he never set a story later than the eve of the first world war.During his lifetime, stage productions (he collaborated on the first himself) and silent films were produced, and after his death in 1930 the great post-Conan Doyle Holmesian caravan began to rumble into full life.View image in fullscreenJeremy Brett as the famed detective in the ITV series Sherlock Holmes.Photograph: Landmark Media/AlamyNow, you should know that the Sherlock Holmes body of work written by Arthur Conan Doyle himself is called by Sherlockians “the Canon” (coincidentally and happily an anagram of Conan). The Canon comprises four full-length novels and five collections of short stories.In all, 60 canonical stories. How many have been written since? I don’t believe it is possible to count. I know I have written one myself. Conan Doyle’s son Adrian Conan Doyle, along with the great Golden Age mystery writer John Dickson Carr, wrote a collection of new stories under the title The Exploits of Sherlock Holmes. After that, the stampede was on, in all media, of course. The Hollywood films starring Basil Rathbone as Holmes and Nigel Bruce as Watson began in 1939 with the canonical The Hound of the Baskervilles, but soon began to move the pair into all kinds of modern settings. By the 1940s, they were doing their bit for the homeland by pitting themselves against the Nazis. The Conan Doyle Estate was open to allowing and authorising such variations, which soon became an established and legitimised part of the whole Sherlock Holmes enterprise. Between 2014 and 2023 Holmes emerged from copyright and entered the public domain.Most Sherlockians I have come across will, like me, cite Jeremy Brett as their favourite Holmes, but one feels there will always be a new kind of Sherlock for every age. I had the honour of playing Sherlock’s brother Mycroft in Guy Ritchie’s Sherlock Holmes: A Game of Shadows, with Robert Downey Jr and Jude Law as Holmes and Watson, and the pleasure of reading the entire Canon for Audible. Along with the publication of my own Holmes pastiche, these were the completion of some kind of a lifelong dream. The closing of a very strange circle.I can say without the slightest fear of exaggeration that Sherlock Holmes altered and determined the whole course of my life. Let me explain.I had been entranced by the Sherlock Holmes stories from the earliest age. I read and reread the entire corpus of stories avidly and before long I had joined, as their youngest member to date, the august Sherlock Holmes Society of London. This eccentrically aristocratic institution had Lord Gore-Booth as chair and the Marquess of Donegal as editor of its magazine, the Sherlock Holmes Journal. I managed to get permission from my housemaster to leave school one weekend, travel by train to London and attend a society meeting, at which I was scheduled to read a paper. The subject of my disquisition? Well, I had noticed with excitement one day the parallels between Sherlock Holmes’s description of Professor James Moriarty (“He is extremely tall and thin, his forehead domes out in a white curve, and his two eyes are deeply sunken in his head”) and TS Eliot’s description of Macavity the Mystery Cat (“his eyes are sunken in. His brow is deeply lined with thought, his head is highly domed”). The society was being very kind in letting me address them on this topic: any fool could see that Eliot had based his Macavity entirely on Moriarty, it was hardly news. I thought I had discovered a great literary secret. At any rate, the event went well, but the sequel did not.double quotation markHe was surely the first caped crusader, for all that his cape was constructed of good tweedI stayed in London, sitting in cinemas from dawn till midnight and watching any number of films. By the time I came to and hopped on a train back to school, a full three days later than had been agreed and sanctioned, I found that I had been officially declared missing. My parents and the police were informed, and the hunt was on. The fat was truly in the fire, my number finally up. The school expelled me. That expulsion led to other expulsions and disasters, which culminated in my landing in prison; I shan’t go into too much detail: Moab Is My Washpot, the first volume of my autobiography, is also happily still in print, and the full story can be read there.View image in fullscreenA poster for the 1939 film of The Hound of the Baskervilles, starring Basil Rathbone and Nigel Bruce.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyAnyway, all these ructions finally got me thinking straight and determining to change my ways and try for Cambridge, the university on which I had always set my heart. I did get there, where I met my friend Hugh Laurie and found myself set on the course of writing and performing which has filled my life ever since. None of which could have happened without that Sherlock Holmes Society evening and its cascade of consequences back in the early 70s.But I still haven’t quite addressed the most pertinent question.Why? Why do these characters – Holmes, Watson, Mrs Hudson and Mycroft (along with that hapless cast of professional bunglers, sceptics and sincere admirers from Scotland Yard) – seem to attract reinvention and retelling so much more than any other fictional creations? And why the Game? How did that arise? The Game, I should explain, is what Sherlockians call the tradition of Holmesian scholarship that makes the very serious and straight-faced assumption that Holmes and Watson were real and that they actually did live at 221B Baker Street and that everything Watson writes about (although he makes plenty of mistakes in consistency and continuity) truly did historically happen.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenMartin Freeman as Doctor John Watson, left, with Benedict Cumberbatch in the eponymous role of BBC TV’s Sherlock.Photograph: Robert Viglasky/BBC/HartswoodBut I repeat:why? This doesn’t happen with Poirot, Father Brown or Lord Peter Wimsey. What’s so special about the denizens of Baker Street?Well, one can begin by making the surely undeniable statement that Sherlock Holmes is one of the most fully realised and enduring fictional characters ever created. Very quickly, his complex and rounded personality, the details of his intellect, his manners, his dress, his habits, his appetites, techniques and methods combined to create a place for him in the public consciousness of a kind that had never before been experienced in literature.Holmes’s world is also vivid and tangible. Everyone who has read even a handful of stories will have their own clear picture of the Baker Street rooms, the fireplace, the test tubes, the violin case, the pipe rack, the fog at the window … we all have our images, reaffirmed or modified by countless films and television adaptations certainly, but unmistakably real. So real, indeed, that even as the stories were still being written and published, tens of thousands around the world behaved as if Holmes and Watson truly lived and breathed. From as far as Japan and South America came letters addressed to 221B Baker Street begging for Holmes’s assistance. Some even wrote to Buckingham Palace and Downing Street to urge the king and prime minister to award Sherlock Holmes a knighthood.But there is, I think, another reason for the astonishing connection that Holmes made with the public on his arrival and that he continues to make in all the multiplicity of his incarnations today. And that is need. The world needed him in 1887 and the world needs him now.View image in fullscreenDónal Finn as Moriarty (left) and Hero Fiennes Tiffin as Holmes in Young Sherlock.Photograph: Daniel Smith/PrimeWith the great rise in literacy from the middle of the 19th century onwards, it perhaps seems inevitable that a new kind of fiction should arise that tried to solve the puzzle of the lately arrived Big City – most especially the biggest by far in the world, London. The daunting size of the metropolis was something quite new in human history. Society was transforming itself from a knowable hierarchy into a bewildering network. It could be seen structurally as like a great web, interlinked and complex, mastered only by those sensitive enough to understand, touch, feel and identify every node and every twitch on the filament. In fact, by a Sherlock Holmes.And after Holmes, of course, ten thousand more detectives sprang up, all with their own USPs, their own special ways of clearing up mystery and caging the monsters. But so, too, did a strange breed of 20th-century heroes who offered a similar promise of bringing light and order to the darkness and chaos of modernity, but in their case without bothering to think much. I mean, of course, the comic book and film superheroes. Our infantile side (and there was never an age in our history that so encouraged and coddled our inner child as the present) seems to have embraced magic, flying, invisibility, X-ray vision and all kinds of impossible superpowers. It seems to me fair to suggest that Superman and Batman, unlikely as it may seem, follow in the great detective’s footsteps and owe him their being. He was surely the first caped crusader, for all that his cape was constructed of good tweed. They, like him, answered a need.‘If you try to fix Holmes, you’ll get your arse handed to you’: do we really need another Sherlock remake?Read moreWhy so many have moved from valuing the real and achievable powers that Holmes exhibits – achieved through his own self-training, study and practice – to valuing imaginary, unearned, randomly achieved magical superpowers is another question. But fortunately the appetite for Holmes and real deductive talent is undiminished, too. We can have both kinds of hero, after all. On television alone, for every Superman and Deadpool, there has always been – as well as a new Sherlock for each new generation – a Columbo, a Monk or a Ludwig reaffirming the power of the Sherlockian method and re‑establishing the primacy of mind over mayhem. Holmes’s cigar ash, footprints and almost invisible telltale particles are the forerunners of the crime lab’s mitochondrial DNA, epithelial particles and microfibres, and his magnifying glass gives way to today’s scanning electron microscope. But the principles are quite unchanged. Which is why he is the presiding spirit behind every CSI operative and why the modern Scotland Yard criminal database (the Home Office Large Major Enquiry System) has initials that spell out the name HOLMES.Like London and the wider human world, the world of Holmes and Watson is a work in progress, capable of being modernised and made over in countless ways, but always, underneath it all, entirely its noble and magnificent self.Sherlock, a collection of new stories with an introduction by Stephen Fry, is published by Simon & Schuster. title: ‘I’d rather live through something publicly than escape it privately’: Jack Antonoff on survivor’s guilt and still singing love songs after his breakup | Jack Antonoff | The Guardian
description: Whether he’s playing the role of soul-baring artist or starry producer, the Bleachers frontman strives to keep his integrity intact. He weighs in on Ed Sheeran, his love of working on ‘high-stakes’ albums and why he’s standing by the songs about his marriage
Author: Alexis Petridis
Headline: Whether he’s playing the role of soul-baring artist or starry producer, the Bleachers frontman strives to keep his integrity intact. He weighs in on Ed Sheeran, his love of working on ‘high-stakes’ albums and why he’s standing by the songs about his marriage
Content: I’m with the band … Antonoff (second from right) with his band Bleachers.Photograph: Alex LockettView image in fullscreenI’m with the band … Antonoff (second from right) with his band Bleachers.Photograph: Alex LockettJack AntonoffInterview‘I’d rather live through something publicly than escape it privately’: Jack Antonoff on survivor’s guilt and still singing love songs after his breakupAlexis PetridisWhether he’s playing the role of soul-baring artist or starry producer, the Bleachers frontman strives to keep his integrity intact. He weighs in on Ed Sheeran, his love of working on ‘high-stakes’ albums and why he’s standing by the songs about his marriageSun 25 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 08.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSitting in the restaurant of a Denver hotel, in the middle of a US tour with his band Bleachers,Jack Antonoffshrugs. “There’s this intense need to figure me out,” he frowns, “and I don’t really know where it comes from, because I keepexplaining all of it.”He has a point. For the last 12 years, Bleachers have released a succession of albums packed with Antonoff’s strikingly personal and frank songs. Being strikingly personal and frank was the whole point. Antonoff had previously been guitarist in Fun, a pop-rock band who went supernova with their 2011 single We Are Young. Despite co-writing a song that sold 10m copies in the US alone, Antonoff says he “hated” the experience “because I wasn’t the leader, they weren’t my words, and I needed to write a song that if I fucking died tomorrow would be my life story”.He says he insisted his then-record label release said song I Wanna Get Better as Bleachers’ debut single “to let people know what they were in for”. It depicted Antonoff literally screaming in anguish, “losing my mind” with grief in the wake of his younger sister’s death, aged 13, from a brain tumour. You can tell it set the confessional tone of Bleachers’ oeuvre just by looking at some of their other song titles: I’m Ready to Move On, Everybody Lost Somebody, Stop Making This Hurt, Self-Respect, I Can’t Believe You’re Gone, We Should Talk.Their latest album, Everyone for Ten Minutes, offers his audience what you might call the Jack Antonoff origin story: there are songs about his teenage years spent traversing the US in his parents’ minivan, touring down-at-heel punk venues with an emo band called Outline, which by his own account was a pretty hair-raising experience (“Teenagers, in a van, drinking a lot, smoking pot, taking psychedelics, smoking what we thought was hash but turned out to be black opium,” he laughs, “I’m amazed we survived”), to which his parents only agreed because his sister’s illness meant “they could not give a fuck about anything that didn’t really matter. When something serious, existential is going on in your life, you get a little less stressed about a parking ticket or grades, you know?”double quotation markThere’s a difference between joyfully seizing the moment and something that’s predicated on anxietyIf Bleachers were the only thing that Jack Antonoff did, then it would all seem terribly straightforward. But, of course, they aren’t the whole story. Around the same time he started the band, he metTaylor Swiftat an awards ceremony, bonded over a mutual love of 80s synth duo Yazoo and embarked on a creative collaboration that ultimately led Antonoff to become perhaps the most in-demand pop producer on Earth: he’s worked not just on 11 Taylor Swift albums, but with Sabrina Carpenter, Lorde, Lana Del Rey, St Vincent, Kendrick Lamar and Gracie Abrams, among a host of others. He is in the vaunted position of being a blue-chip pop mega-producer who also makes soul-baring, Bruce Springsteen-influenced angst-rock, and insists neither activity takes precedence over the other in his career.“I’m in a very narrow group of people who truly do both, probably,” he nods. “Usually someone’s slumming it on one side: songwriters or performers who think they can produce a record but then have to really care about someone else’s work in a deep way, or producers who think: ‘Now it’s my turn!’ but don’t have that thing you can’t even describe that drew you to write your own songs and fucking sing them in front of people since you were a kid.”Indeed, for all his protestations that he’s really terribly straightforward, Jack Antonoff seems anything but. Rather, he seems like such a mass of complexities and contradictions that you sometimes get the impression he might be trying to puzzle them out himself, in front of you. He’s clearly very driven, but he worries his drive is bound up with “survivor’s guilt” over his sister’s death, “about not going for things or using my time when someone you love didn’t get time, which is not the best way to live – there’s a difference between joyfully seizing the moment and something that’s predicated on anxiety”.View image in fullscreenJack of all trades … Antonoff with (from left) Phoebe Bridgers, Julien Baker and Lucy Dacus of boygenius and Taylor Swift at the 2024 Grammy Awards.Photograph: Michael Buckner/Billboard/Getty ImagesHe decries the constant chatter of opinion on the internet: “I don’t give a fuck any more, it’s like, the very act of engaging negatively on the internet is inarguably such a fucking low-vibrational joke, and I think artists for too long over the past decade have read into it and there’s less than nothing there.” But equally he says he enjoys making “super high-stakes albums … helping to architect and guide something that everyone is going to have an opinion on, that people love to have the hottest opinions on”.He thinks his role in making some of the biggest records of the century so far is widely misconstrued as shadowy and machiavellian (“He’s annoyingly, inescapably, maddeningly everywhere…the designated steward of Tasteful Pop,” protested one piece on music website Pitchfork, which went on to accuse him of “musical manspreading” and suggest he had “extreme Main Character Energy”). “One of the great misconceptions of how it works in my world is that I write songs and hand them to, like, a pop star, which I’ve never done once in my life,” he says, but declines to discuss how it actually works because “it doesn’t really matter”. Besides he’s sick of people constantly trying to explain everything online. “You’re on your phone all the time beingexplainedsomething,” he says. “You’re being explained what’s happening in this country, you’re being explained how a train works, it’s like an information dump and it’s killing people’s imaginations. ‘Do you want to sound like Jack Antonoff? Here’s how he did it!’ It’s made me want to allow people to imagine the magic of it all.”Certainly, in the context of 21st-century pop, he’s a very odd fish. He is obviously someone who moves with enviable ease among the pop aristocracy: he apparently ended up working on Kendrick Lamar’s multiple Grammy-winning 2024 album GNX when he popped into the studio to visit a friend and “didn’t leave for three years”; Bruce Springsteen isn’t just an influence but a friend, collaborator with Bleachers and mentor (best advice thus delivered by The Boss: “Don’t live in the dream, let the dream live in you”). But Antonoff both looks noticeably more like someone who might have spent his teens playing gigs in anarchist book stores on drugs than someone who co-wrote, say, Sabrina Carpenter’s Please Please Please – close-cropped hair, tattered skate pants, Sonic Youth T-shirt – and often sounds more like a chippy indie outsider than someone who recently enjoyed chicken nuggets with caviar at Taylor Swift’s wedding.Certainly, he is more free with his opinions than you might expect from someone who operates at the top table of pop, a world where artists tend to have any capacity for controversy media-trained out of them. He’s currently engaged in a war of words with Live Nation over gig ticket prices (he is proud that Bleachers’ tickets are “as low as they can physically possibly be”). “Live Nation keep missing the point, because every time I say something, they’ll call my people and say: “Let’s have a meeting.’ You don’t get it, I don’t want to fucking talk to you people, I want to make it clear that I’m not fucking OK with you turning the most sacred thing into the world into some weird free-market piece of shit … the idea that if you’re rich, any ticket you want is yours at any time and if you’re not, you have to go through this demoralising online experience where you get whacked and kicked and fucked around.”View image in fullscreenWhen the Fun stops, stop … Antonoff (left) with Nate Ruess and Andrew Dost in his first major band.Photograph: Dave Hogan/Getty ImagesWhen I meet him, his social media channels are filled with abuse from commenters angry that a Jewish artist has made a point of saying “free Palestine” onstage at Bleachers shows: he points out that he was saying it long before the recent Ed Sheeran/Macklemore controversy blew up but says he has “felt way more emboldened to say it now, because it’s not in any way a strange, uncomfortable or controversial thing to say, it’s a deeply human thing to say. If you think it is [controversial] you’re lost in some other sauce that is so crazy. They’re going to let some fucking promoter tell me what I can say? Don’t book me. I’ll play for free outside. [Ed Sheeran] missed a massive, beautiful opportunity there: just cancel the whole fucking tour, then play for free outside each venue, raise a bunch of money, rather than let a fucking billionaire tell you what to do. The reason it’s not an anomaly or niche issue is because we all live in a world where billionaires are constantly telling us what to do. So stand the fuck up.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionOf course you could argue that Antonoff has more freedom to be unguarded than the artists he works with. Bleachers enjoy a curious kind of success – their albums sell respectably rather than astronomically and they’ve never come “even close”, Antonoff points out, to having a huge crossover hit. Yet they are capable of filling out Madison Square Garden with an audience that Antonoff says aren’t there to see “that producer’s band”. His own celebrity is largely by proxy, thanks to the company he keeps in the recording studio – his 2023 wedding to actorMargaret Qualleytook place amid a scrum of fans and paparazzi, but that seemed to have less to do with the bride and groom than the fact that Taylor Swift was in attendance.Recently, the gossip pages have been alive, first with his former partnerLena Dunham’s memoir Famesick, which suggested that one of the reasons their romance floundered was because Antonoff was more invested in shepherding Lorde through her Difficult Second Album than their relationship, and latterly with news of his marriage’s collapse. That came as a surprise given that Bleachers had released an album thick with loving peans to Qualley and to marriage a matter of weeks before their split was announced: one of them, You and Forever, even came with a video starring the couple together.double quotation markThe deal I’ve made with my audience is I’m going to tell you honestly how I feel and I’m going to risk  standing behind itAntonoff thus currently finds himself on tour, singing songs about a relationship that’s now over. When I mention it, he first interrupts me – “Oh, I can imagine what you’re going to say: it’s bizarre” – then clarifies my point: “Songs which I wrote recently,” he nods. “I obviously was really worried about this specific thing, I sat long and hard with it and thought: ‘If I change the setlist …’ and in my gut there was a unanimous jury that said, ‘No, this is the deal. The deal I’ve made with my audience is that I’m going to tell you honestly how I feel and I’m going to risk at any moment having to stand behind it for fucking ever.’Fans and A-list stars gather for the wedding of Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce in New York – in picturesRead more“Anyone could relate to the terrible sadness and pain, but there’s a great power to it also,” he says. “It’s actually been really beautiful. I mean, for people to come together, to know what I write a song about, to know how that must feel for me now, to know what that song means to you as an audience member, to just hold it all and sort of celebrate. I don’t rewrite the past, I have no shame about the things I’ve said. My life has been dedicated to making it impossible for me to rewrite the past, because I’m standing there, singing about how I felt during the good times, so when the bad times hit I can’t look myself in the mirror and pretend that those times didn’t exist. I would rather live through something publicly than even escape it privately.”After we speak, on stage at Colorado’s Red Rocks Amphitheatre, there is indeed a fraught emotional charge to Bleachers’ performances of Dirty Wedding Dress and You and Forever. Antonoff follows the latter by playing I Wanna Get Better alone on acoustic guitar. The audience – who, as he promised, are an odd combination of twentysomething women, middle-aged couples and a smattering of grizzled Deadheads in tie-dye T-shirts, none of whom look as if they’re there to see Taylor Swift’s producer in the flesh – bellow along, so loudly that they’re in danger of drowning him out entirely. For a moment, in the spotlight, Jack Antonoff does not need figuring out.Bleachers aretouring the UK and Ireland, 23 November to 4 December; tour starts Kingston upon Thames. Their album Everyone for Ten Minutes is out now.Explore more on these topicsJack AntonoffPop and rockMargaret QualleyTaylor SwiftinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I’m not someone who has sex to music. I like uncomfortable silence’: Katherine Ryan’s honest playlist | Katherine Ryan | The Guardian
description: The comedian unashamedly loves the Spice Girls’ Wannabe and cries to Boyz II Men, but which novelty song changed her life?
Author: Rich Pelley
Headline: The comedian unashamedly loves the Spice Girls’ Wannabe and cries to Boyz II Men, but which novelty song changed her life?
Content: Katherine Ryan … ‘If I like a song, I just like it. I have no shame’Photograph: Suki Dhanda/The GuardianView image in fullscreenKatherine Ryan … ‘If I like a song, I just like it. I have no shame’Photograph: Suki Dhanda/The GuardianHonest playlistKatherine Ryan‘I’m not someone who has sex to music. I like uncomfortable silence’: Katherine Ryan’s honest playlistThe comedian unashamedly loves the Spice Girls’ Wannabe and cries to Boyz II Men, but which novelty song changed her life?As told toRich PelleySun 25 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe first song I fell in love withMy mother would sing and dance and cook and clean in the kitchen, as many 80s moms did, to divas like Madonna and Paula Abdul. Material Girl made me think: “This is who I want to be.”The first single I boughtI bought three records at the same time – Jagged Little Pill by Alanis Morissette, a Sheryl Crow single and Waterfalls by TLC – from Sam the Record Man in Sarnia, Ontario, with money I’d saved up from doing chores around the house. My uncle was always trying to influence me with Canadian music, and he wasn’t wrong for doing so.The song I do at karaokeProbably Son of a Preacher Man. Although I think karaoke is the best way to let many people know straight away that you are an attention-seeking alcoholic, so I do try to stay away from it.The song I inexplicably know every lyric toGive me a wine, and somehow I know all the words to the entire score of Hamilton, even though I’ve only seen it twice. [Sings Satisfied] “I’m a girl in a world in which my only job is to marry rich. My father has no sons, so I’m the one who has to social climb for one. I’m the oldest and the wittiest and the gossip in New York City is insidious.”The best song to play at a partyAnything early-2000s hip-hop or R&B, like Gasolina by Daddy Yankee.The song I can no longer listen toWhat I Am by Will.i.am with Sesame Street. It makes me cry because he’s giving positive affirmations to young kids about being strong and being the best version of yourself. I can’t even get through it because it makes me so sad. I start worrying that these kids need Sesame Street and Will.i.am to tell them that they’re special.The song I secretly like, but tell everyone I hateIf I like a song, I just like it. Every Spice Girls song – I have no shame. I don’t need to be a music snob. I would crank up Wannabe any time, anywhere.The best song to have sex toI’m not someone who has sex to music. I like uncomfortable silence. But if I had to choose, Let Me Love You by Mario.The song that changed my lifeThe Chanukah Song and Ode to My Car by Adam Sandler. I would have been about 11 or 12, and it was the first time I thought: “Oh, wait a minute. These can be funny and make music. You can make trauma a little bit funny, or at least be trauma-adjacent. You can make darker subjects funny.” I listened to his album over and over.The song that gets me up in the morningCurrently, I’m So Happy by Ms Rachel because we have so many small children. It has a really great message. I really love what’s available for kids now.The song that makes me cryWater Runs Dry by Boyz II Men. I wanted to use it in The Duchess. It’s meant to be about a romantic partner, but whenever I heard it I thought of my daughter growing up. It’s about two people not communicating properly any more and wanting to get back to where they started, and I thought about that relationship changing as she got older.The song I want played at my funeralThong Song by Sisqó.Katherine Ryan has partnered with meal-subscription service Gousto. title: Greg Wise on how he and Emma Thompson coped with failed IVF: ‘We hit an existential crisis – she was not a proper woman and I was not a proper man’ | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Their hopes of having a second child were dashed. Two decades on, the actor remembers the grief and pain of that time
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Their hopes of having a second child were dashed. Two decades on, the actor remembers the grief and pain of that time
Content: Greg Wise, photographed last month.Photograph: Cian Oba-Smith/The GuardianView image in fullscreenGreg Wise, photographed last month.Photograph: Cian Oba-Smith/The GuardianLife and styleGreg Wise on how he and Emma Thompson coped with failed IVF: ‘We hit an existential crisis – she was not a proper woman and I was not a proper man’Their hopes of having a second child were dashed. Two decades on, the actor remembers the grief and pain of that timeGreg WiseSun 25 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“I’m afraid this cycle has not been successful.” Emma and I cannot catch each other’s eye. We sit mute in our grief in the silence of theIVFdoctor’s office. This is a kind of grief that is often not understood even to be grief at all. A grief about the loss of a potential child. An anticipatory grief – a grief for something that hasn’t yet appeared – a mourning for a possibility, of a longed-for future life to welcome, love and nurture. And there are no set grief rituals for this – for a child never present – no space in our society to mark, to grieve an actual physical death. It is a silent, achingly lonely, atomised grief. We had undergone many attempts in the years after the birth of our daughter Gaia. But that did not make this any easier.Each cycle, each time we sat in that office, we had to ignore our grief and concentrate wholeheartedly and positively on our next attempt. We didn’t access any help over this time. We didn’t seek out counselling as a couple. I had no knowledge of how to process my grief – compounded month on month. Further cycles, more drugs, more fertility hormones, more ovarian hyperstimulation, injections, scans, blood tests came and went, all proving unsuccessful. I supported all wholeheartedly, but Emma was devastated by her inability to conceive again. In her mind, she had failed and could not forgive herself for that failure. And nothing I could say would change her point of view.Her deep grief took her away. I had to deny mine. Try to comfort her rather than myself. Such is the lot of the self-appointed saviour.Emma and I had met seven years before on the set of the film Sense and Sensibility. She had adapted Jane Austen’s novel, and was playing Elinor Dashwood; I was John Willoughby, a “caped Adonis” on an enormous white horse, galloping in and scooping up her injured and prone sister Marianne, delivering her back home. As I leave the scene, the hero of the hour, the saviour of potential catastrophe, in a swirl of cape and the heady musk of testosterone: “His manly beauty and more than common gracefulness were instantly the theme of general admiration.” The problem was, this was how I had always seen myself in real life.Emma and I came together in the unreal space that is a film set. They are very seductive spaces, film sets. Protected spaces, as we are all outside our natural, everyday lives. And it was here that my roles as saviour in the film and as saviour in life collided.I galloped in, on my big white horse, scooped her up, andsavedher.View image in fullscreenThe couple in 2001.Photograph: Evan Agostini/Getty ImagesEmma’s husband had moved out of their home just before the filming started. She was in profound grief at the apparent ending of their marriage. But she also held a chronic grief. Her father, Eric Thompson – the writer and narrator of the cult television programme The Magic Roundabout – had suffered his first heart attack when Emma was eight. He had had a severe stroke 10 years later, which left him semi-paralysed, and she took it upon herself to help this extraordinarily skilled lover of language to speak again. He died when she was 23.She had already lost her wonderful uncle – her mother, Phyllida’s, brother James. He had been in a catastrophic car crash in his early life, and had never fully recovered. He suffered a brain haemorrhage when Emma was in her late teens. She was the only family member present to make the decision to turn off his life support, before she walked back home, alone, with a bin bag filled with his clothes. Within a few short years of her father’s death, she also lost the other vital male figure in her life, her godfather.Filming finished, we hid ourselves in my little two-up, two-down house in north London. Both of us bringing along our overstuffed suitcase of grief, bulging with recent and age-old unresolved pains.double quotation markAfter three years together, it was time to settle. It was, we decided, time to start a familyThis was the first shape that was created. We bonded in our grief – Emma’s present grief at the end of her marriage, my anticipatory grief that she might nonetheless try to revivify it, grief at the possibility of the death of this relationship, so soon, with so much recent love and so much future promise.Then everything exploded when the tabloid press found us out and we had to escape. And created a new shape – the fugitives.We went to work in Los Angeles, rented a house there, filmed projects, lived a fun life up in the hills, with a pool, a convertible sports car. Our shape now of a hopeful, creative, unfettered, adventurous, outward-looking, energised couple. But this shape could not last. We had to reshape ourselves to the realities of our lives. And Emma now divorced, we decided it was time to come back home. After three years together, it was time to settle. It was, we decided, time to start a family.Then the next grief hit us.We were unable to conceive. And Emma was fast approaching 40.The simple fact of us not being able to get pregnant was momentous. It is one of those major marking points, the end of one way of looking at life, as it is a death, in a way – a death of a possibility, a death of a new shape that had been expected, and brought both a profound grief and a deep sense of shame in its wake. A shame borne by both me and Emma, as we saw ourselves as unable to fulfil our purest and most natural role in life – to procreate. We hit an existential crisis – it’s a given, all the stories we had read as children, telling us that girls grow up to become mothers; boys, fathers – Emma was, therefore, not a proper woman and I was not a proper man.Even without knowing the root of our problem, I was gnawed at by the sense of being emasculated. The confusion of my fertility somehow being aligned to my manliness, virility and sexual potency. I couldn’t shake the feeling that I had somehow failed as a man, with the simple fact that I had spun in my head – infertility equals impotence.We both undertook tests to see where the problem lay. The problem lay with Emma. We would never be able to conceive naturally. IVF was the only option if we wanted to have a child of our own.double quotation markWe didn’t know that IVF opens up a potential minefield of grief – a constant swinging between hope and despair within each cycle of the treatmentIt is absolutely extraordinary that IVF treatment exists. Extraordinary, but also brutal. And oddly, within a process that hopefully results in the creation of a human, it can feel utterly dehumanising. It is purely a clinical process and easy to become totally overwhelmed with every aspect: decision-making, appointments, injection schedules, scans, where to get the treatment, how many embryos to transfer.We knew we were so fortunate to be able to afford to undertake the process, but we didn’t know that embarking on IVF opens up a potential minefield of grief – a constant swinging between hope and despair within each cycle of the treatment. It was physically gruelling for Emma. She was exhausted, in pain, filled with chemicals, her hormones all over the place, overstimulated while at the same time having to try to remain resolutely calm.And all I could do was support her; within this treatment, all my capacity for any sense of agency was almost nonexistent. My job in its clinical entirety was purely to provide some sperm. That was it. I just had to do a quick sprint; she was on the marathon.And I couldn’t fix this. I couldn’t make things better or make this work. This was so hard for me to confront – I couldn’t be the saviour now. I just had to try to be strong, protecting Emma as best I could, trying to lighten the load as much as I could. But this was her gig, not mine.Our very first attempt at IVF resulted in a positive pregnancy test just days before her 40th birthday. Four weeks before we welcomed in the new millennium, we celebrated the arrival of our beautiful, healthy baby daughter Gaia, whom we’d first seen at four-cells old. Our shape had changed once more: we were now awestruck, doting parents.View image in fullscreenThompson and Wise, with their newborn daughter, Gaia, in 1999.Photograph: PA Images/AlamyIn Gaia’s second year of life, we started another IVF cycle. And failed. Repeatedly.That day in the doctor’s office, we decided to stop. The most difficult decision we had yet had to make. No result, nothing tangible, it just stopped. It had failed. Rationally, it was the only decision we could have come to – emotionally, it was untenable. We were dislocated, isolated in our overwhelming grief. I now know we were slipping into complicated grief.Even though there can be no set timescale for processing, the myriad of feelings within the grief can expand themselves into our void of loss and become a chronic problem. This grief can consume our lives.The precision of the grief, the focus of the loss, muddies and seeps out and, over time, if not addressed, metamorphoses into major depression. This is where it took us, an overbearing blanket of sadness covering the two of us. And we both felt so alone; we couldn’t address it as a couple, we didn’t seek help together.This complicated grief, given the medical moniker prolonged grief disorder, now classed as an official mental health disorder, hits about one in 10 of us powerless to come to terms with our loss half a year on. A helplessness, inability to accept, disbelief, numbness. Grief is natural, grief is healthy, grief is essential in the process of being able to adjust to where we find ourself after a loss, but it can become a clinical problem, it can disrupt our life so fully that we can’t find a way out. And it can be made even more toxic if guilt and shame are in the mix.I had never been a more grief-sodden mess, feeling myself, months after we had finally made the decision, falling into a black depression. I had totally hit the bottom and could not navigate myself out of the darkness I found myself in. There was nothing I could do. Other than to ask for help.Ihave always been a bit of a northern man about getting medical help. I am terrifically accident-prone. From a childhood spent falling out of trees to being a grownup with a collection of madly dangerous power tools, I have often wandered back to the house with blood streaming, large bone-showing holes, but refusing to seek out a medical professional. I have a certain amount of shame attached to my self-inflicted injuries; that the medics would view me as they would a child with a saucepan wedged on their head – humorous, a bit pathetic, but mainly just idiotic.double quotation markI knew I was in pain. I knew that I needed professional helpI viewed therapy in the same way. A neurotic American fixation, an ego-fuelled unnecessary waste of time and money, and something to be sneered at. Our lot in life was to deny, obfuscate and just bloody well get on with it. This was my belief.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThen I moved in with Emma. She had started her therapy before we got together, and would wander off down the street to see her Jungian therapist weekly. After a while, I started to perceive this as a threat. I’d heard stories of a partner getting therapy and then breaking up the relationship – that it involved laying the blame for the couple’s ills on the other partner. The fact that I thought this illustrates the fear and pain that were my constant companions.I was told many years later that you finally go into therapy when you realise that the pain you are carrying is greater than the pain of exploring it. And therapy is painful, without doubt. It is painful because you are exposing things that have been living in the very core of your being for perhaps your entire lifetime, and often these things don’t give themselves up without a fight.But I knew I was in pain. I knew that I needed professional help. Starting it was the best decision I have ever made.Ibegan my journey in a little upstairs room in central London. The first thing that confused me was that I wasn’t lying down – the pose adopted in all the films I’d watched. The second thing was that, six sessions in, the only one seeming to be doing any talking was me. I couldn’t see any therapy happening whatsoever. It was gently pointed out to me that nothing could be discussed until my story had unfolded enough to be looked at.I brought shame with me into the room. It wrapped around me, muffled me. Shame brings muteness. I needed to articulate what had up till now never been articulated. That was one of the most difficult aspects of this, telling my history, as honestly and personally as possible.But a large part of my shame was that I didn’t seem to be doing this properly. I would start to try to unpack with, “I think …” and be told, “I would really like to know what youfeel…”I didn’t know what I felt. Apart from feeling I wanted to stop coming to therapy. That I was being made to feel ashamed by the process.Even though everyone’s grief is unique to them, there are clear patterns to where it sits, whether in feeling or thought. I approached my grief in a cerebral way, as I had been brought up to do: think my way through.View image in fullscreenPhotograph: Cian Oba-Smith/The GuardianI was grieving the way the majority of men grieve. I  had my dad as my original guide to what being a man looked like; I had my single-sex school, bringing along with it how boys should behave and what kinds of men they should become; I ventured out into my adult life as Man the Saviour – the protector, the provider of safety and security, setting aside my wants for the sake of the other, emotionally restrained, self-controlled.This is what I brought into the therapy. What it is to be a man – independent, not showing vulnerability, strong, stoic. All these traits, given to me to wear like an ill-fitting jacket, made this type of therapy almost impossible for me. I was thoughtful, active, a problem-solver, but I was being asked to be open, expressive, available emotionally.It took me a while to see that this type of therapy was not for me. That this style required an expression of feeling. That here, grief meant emotion. That my being different from the model that was being expounded meant I was failing. I had to go and see what else was on offer.And there is an almost limitless amount of therapy available – animal-assisted, humanistic, psychosynthesis, existential, Jungian, Freudian, gestalt … The psychoanalytic side – about the unconscious, dream analysis, free association – all emotion-driven. But alongside this is an action-oriented approach – behavioural therapy – identifying patterns, working out solutions, using a pen and paper. Being cognitive. This was the one for me.There are two main strands of cognitive therapy – analytic (CAT) and behavioural (CBT). The analytic looks at our past to try to understand our present-day thoughts and actions. Questionnaires are filled out, problem patterns are written down, ways of navigating found. The behavioural focuses on our present-day problems, helps change the way that life is looked on, replacing negative thoughts, encouraging a more positive outlook.I found myself working with a CAT therapist. I felt, for the first time within a therapeutic setting, that I was using my natural strengths – I had always needed to draw a problem on paper: create a diagram, a flow chart, a design. This was the way my mind worked; that’s what led me to study architecture. Here, I was doing the same thing – seeing myself from different angles, where the constructional stresses lay and how the shape of my present form was dictated by the layers of design and building over my lifetime. Over the next few months, we got to work rebuilding.We can think that we are utterly unique, and our situation has never been viewed before, that we are totally alone in our personal struggle, that nobody would be able to understand our plight, our grief, but we are all just like every other human being – trying to navigate our way through the difficulties of life, with what we were bequeathed, what we have experienced since and with what hits us on a seemingly daily basis. This is all therapy is – telling our story to somebody who will help us make connections, make us feel we are seen, we are heard, know that we are not alone. A therapist is just somebody who has been told many, many stories and – just as there are only eight notes in a scale but they give us plainchant, Purcell and Pink Floyd – it’s the same in this: our melody is unique, but is made up of only eight notes. Therapists help us to retune, rescore and play our melody to its fullest beautiful potential.Ihave a large collection of power tools which I use in my various woodwork and building projects – I am pretty handy with them. I never start by reading the manual. I learn by doing. My two university degrees were chosen with this in mind. I wanted to attack my studies in a tangible way, with pen and paper in architecture, with my body and imagination in acting. I had done the same thing with my grief. Now I was being shown that a manual actually exists. It was time to work through it.The CAT was the start of my grief work, the most important work I’ve ever done. Realising that my attempts over my life to deny, ignore or run away from my grief had just made the struggle harder. Beginning to find it, see it, give it a shape and a presence in me, and then facing into it and seeing how it can be dealt with, gave me a peace I don’t think I’d known until that point. Working through it was painful, but my avoidance of the work had caused me so much suffering.It’s exhausting being a saviour. There is no rest. No peace. Endlessly scanning the skies for the damsel-in-distress bat signal. Endlessly jumping on my steed and charging off to the rescue of said damsel. Being helped to unpack this and let this saviour figure gallop off was a welcome relief. Finding that he was just the response to childhood griefs, to my bequeathed fractured family dynamic, it wasn’t me, although it had shaped my being thus far. I was helped to tell the story of me as the grieving child and build out from there. And there was nothing else I could do but square up to it at this time – this place I found myself of such deep grief at the failure to have another child, alongside my already being a father. My small child now my physical responsibility, knowing that looking back at myself as the small child was now my emotional responsibility.double quotation markWe had our beautiful, extraordinary daughter … we were a family. I came to appreciate that the present wildly outweighed any sense of lossMy grief at the fracturing of the shape that Emma and I had so lovingly created, my grief at the impossibility of a family shape that we had so desperately yearned for, my grief at my past, all now starting to be articulated.And we had our beautiful, extraordinary daughter. Feeling our hearts would explode with the love we felt for her. This tiny person, this ball of emotion, this  intrigue, this joy. Her exploration of a wholly new world, with its excitement, its confusion, its wonder, its fascination, wobbling alongside my new explorations.Such gratitude. Whatever shape we had battled with, we were a family. I came to appreciate that the present wildly outweighed any sense of loss.My therapeutic work brought another bit of clarity along with it – that Emma and I were grieving differently. Her grief deeply emotional, mine thoughtful. We were suffering from what life had thrown at us, but also, we were suffering because we were each bemused by the other’s response to their suffering. But we were just doing grief our own way.Grief can make us feel so utterly lonely. Feeling not understood, or misunderstood, finding others’ expression of grief incomprehensible. Unable to prise apart our own present, future and past pains. Feeling muddied and overwhelmed by all these different griefs. For me, therapy helped me to learn that by acknowledging and understanding my own grief, I could acknowledge and understand another’s. That if I could truly see my own pain, I could see someone else’s. Not try to hide it or ignore it, but see it, accept it, work with it.Above all, not to minimise it. That my pain, my grief, had to be recognised, however small or insignificant it seemed within the great griefs of the world.This is an edited extract from Grief Talking by Greg Wise, published by Bluebird on 5 November at £18.99.
