title: ‘I can’t believe I get to see that’: One Born Every Minute is back for a 12th series | Television | The Guardian
description: Reality TV show returns to focus on childbirth, diversity and the sharing of stories in a social media age
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Reality TV show returns to focus on childbirth, diversity and the sharing of stories in a social media age
Content: The new series of One Born Every Minute features more complicated pregnancies and surgical procedures.Photograph: Dragonfly/Channel 4View image in fullscreenThe new series of One Born Every Minute features more complicated pregnancies and surgical procedures.Photograph: Dragonfly/Channel 4Television‘I can’t believe I get to see that’: One Born Every Minute is back for a 12th seriesReality TV show returns to focus on childbirth, diversity and the sharing of stories in a social media ageRachel HallSun 25 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 06.36 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen One Born Every Minute first aired in 2010, viewers loved its fly-on-the-wall take on life in a maternity unit, from midwives idly chatting about unusual pregnancy cravings to parents squabbling over whether to call their child Zeus.Almost two decades later, as the show is rebooted for a generation who spend their lives on social media, much has changed. Parents now share far more about their struggles with miscarriages, infertility and mental health; audiences have to be lured away from watching reels on their phones with more rigorous storytelling.“Quite a bit is different about the way that people have children,” said Will Rowson, executive producer at Dragonfly, which makes the show forChannel 4. “People are so used to sharing. They expect to share, there is a willingness to share, and that is a generational thing.”View image in fullscreenPeace, who will be featured with her twin newborns, wants viewers to understand the importance of ‘not letting things out of your control get to you’.Photograph: Dragonfly/Channel 4The first episode of the show, which airs on Sunday night, tackles topics that have come to the foreground in the years since the Bafta-winning first run ended in 2018. These include caesarean births – it notes that these have doubled over the past decade – as well as health anxiety and pregnancy loss.The series focuses on parents – a shift from medical staff being the prominent characters in the previous 11 series. Rowson said it would delve into an “enormously diverse range of stories” thanks to a wider approach to casting and a move away on TV from “eclectic, whimsical” scenes. A tighter budget was also a factor.He said: “We’re recognising that people will get their miscellany and gentle anthropology elsewhere, so we make sure we’re giving the narratives, the backstories of the families, and understanding what the birth means to them. That’s the sort of context and richness you don’t get in a 30-second clip.”Like its predecessor, the show takes a visceral, no-holds-barred approach to what’s shown, from bellies being sliced open to a baby being pulled out smeared in faeces. Set in St Mary’s hospital inManchester, which specialises in maternity care, the series will feature more complicated pregnancies and surgical procedures. “It’s an extraordinary thing to witness, you go ‘oh my goodness, I can’t believe I get to see that’,” said Rowson.Faye, who is shown giving birth by C-section, said the show had given her a way to experience the birth of her son differently. “I remember shaking, and feeling this overwhelming feeling of being cold and quite scared. And actually, when I’ve seen it back, I’m in really safe hands, and I got to see my little boy being born.”‘I felt something was wrong with me’: Faye shares the heartbreak of multiple miscarriages – videoShe was also motivated to take part because – as anNHSclinical lead – she wanted viewers to see “what’s going on in the background, and how much hard work people do”. She added: “You always hear the bad stuff and not the good stuff.”In the first episode, Faye shares the heartbreak of multiple miscarriages, leading her to believe she would not have children until a surprise pregnancy at the age of 38. She said she wanted to help people understand “how many women it happens to, and how difficult it is to experience”.“I just felt something was wrong with me. I felt this lack of being a woman, and it fed into my [former] marriage, and everything broke down further from that,” she said. When she finally became pregnant, her earlier losses intensified her anxiety: “I said to [my partner] Will ‘if I experience it again, I think I’ll be broken’.”View image in fullscreenFaye and Will hug in One Born Every Minute. She will share with Channel 4 viewers the heartbreak of multiple miscarriages.Photograph: Dragonfly/Channel 4Peace, who also features on the show, wanted to showcase the experience of having twins, from concerns over their growth, to the decision to have a C-section. “I would love to watch that,” she said, adding that she started watching the show as a child: “I love seeing normal women with normal bodies having normal pregnancies.”Through sharing her experience of miscarriage, the unexpectedness of having twins, and the health complications her daughter was born with, Peace wanted viewers to understand the importance of “not letting things out of your control get to you”.She added: “I didn’t want to do it at first, because I didn’t want to open up about [miscarriage], and because I feel it seems like a taboo topic to talk about, and you blame yourself. There is this perception of having a perfect pregnancy.”Like many other parents who took part, her partner, Kwamdeen, felt the episode would be “a great memento” to show their children.The casting director, Nsofwa Nwannadi, said she was surprised by how open people were and was moved by the desire among those who experienced challenges for “people to understand that they are not alone, it’s not stigmatised, it’s not your fault”.Some participants applied to be on the show, with many responding to communications sent out by the hospital, Nwannadi said. Her team sought out a diverse range of participants and experiences by engaging with minority ethnic, LGBT and disability communities.Unlike reality TV, in which participants are cast for their personalities, “this is real life, we’re reflecting what’s actually there at the hospital”, she said.This included fathers ruminating on fatherhood and modern masculinity, mothers expressing fears about sublimating their identities to motherhood, and birthing partners discussing their decision to remain child-free.“It’s been lovely to have been privy to a myriad of different stories, backgrounds and journeys. It’s not a one-size-fits-all situation, and that’s great, actually,” Nwannadi said.One Born Every Minute airs on E4 from Sunday at 9pm.Explore more on these topicsTelevisionChannel 4Reality TVHealthNHSPregnancyChildbirthnewsShareReuse this content

title: Two children’s laureates to give royalties to Sally Rooney after her UK sales halted | Sally Rooney | The Guardian
description: Irish and Welsh authors Chris Haughton and Nicola Davies show solidarity after Rooney’s support for Palestine Action
Author: Haroon Siddique
Headline: Irish and Welsh authors Chris Haughton and Nicola Davies show solidarity after Rooney’s support for Palestine Action
Content: The bestselling author is unable to receive royalties from UK sales because of her public support for the direct action group.Photograph: Martina Bocchio/Awakening/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe bestselling author is unable to receive royalties from UK sales because of her public support for the direct action group.Photograph: Martina Bocchio/Awakening/AlamySally RooneyTwo children’s laureates to give royalties to Sally Rooney after her UK sales haltedIrish and Welsh authors Chris Haughton and Nicola Davies show solidarity after Rooney’s support for Palestine ActionHaroon SiddiqueLegal affairs correspondentSun 25 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 11.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe children’s laureates for Ireland and Wales are donating royalties from their works to Sally Rooney in a show of solidarity after she wasforced to stop selling booksin the UK because of her support for Palestine Action.Chris Haughton, Ireland’s children’s literature laureate, said he also wanted to demonstrate the “absurdity” of the bestselling author being unable to receive royalties from her own UK sales because of her public support for the direct action group.Haughton, whose books have sold millions worldwide, said: “I really want to express my full support for Sally Rooney. As someone who is in the UK a lot of the time, I can’t do what she has done, but I can support her instead of supportingPalestine Action.View image in fullscreenChris Haughton.Photograph: Kirstine Bowen“As authors, we need to be focused on freedom of expression, this is everything we’re about, and this is just showing solidarity with an author who has bravely spoken out.“The entire situation is just a farce. SendingSally Rooneythe money adds another level of absurdity to this absurd situation, it’s making a mockery of the law.”Haughton said he has twice been arrested for holding placards allegedly supporting Palestine Action, which became the first direct action group to beproscribed under the UK Terrorism Actin July last year, placing it in the same category as the likes of al-Qaida and Boko Haram. His alleged offence carries a maximum sentence of six months in prison.After the ban was introduced, Rooney, whose books include Normal People and Conversations with Friends, said she woulduse proceeds from her sales to support Palestine Action. Providing money one knows or has reasonable cause to suspect will or may be used for terrorism carries a maximum jail term of 14 years.Nicola Davies, the children’s laureate forWalesand author of The Day War Came, about a child refugee from war, said: “I can’t say that I am standing up for the children of Wales if I allow the children of Gaza to be murdered and mutilated without comment.“Gaza is smaller than the Welsh county of Flintshire, and it’s as if all Wales’s children were concentrated there and being bombed. So I support Sally Rooney in the stand she’s taken, and when my half-year royalties arrive shortly, I will donate to her the royalties from my book The Day War Came, whose sales have been boosted by the conflicts in Ukraine and Palestine.”View image in fullscreenNicola Davies.Photograph: Bronac McNeill/BronacMcNeillHaughton, who will be donating royalties from his UK book sales, said: “Palestine Action are the only organisation – or the most effective organisation – in the UK that that has had some success in stopping arms going to a genocide. I’m very sure that I will be on the right side of history.”Asked at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday whether he would review the ban on Palestine Action in light of Rooney’s situation, Andy Burnham said proscription “followed a rigorous and evidence-based process that came before this house, endorsed by parliament”.He said he would not comment further given that the supreme court is due to hear alegal challenge to the banon 4 and 5 November. The challenge is on the basis that the ban interferes disproportionately with the rights to freedom of expression and protest.Explore more on these topicsSally RooneyPalestine ActionIrelandWalesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Martina Arroyo obituary | Opera | The Guardian
description: US soprano known for her rich, opulent tone and her acclaimed performances as Aida and other Verdi heroines
Author: Barry Millington
Headline: US soprano known for her rich, opulent tone and her acclaimed performances as Aida and other Verdi heroines
Content: Martina Arroyo in costume as Aida at the Metropolitan Opera in New York in 1965.Photograph: Metropolitan Opera ArchivesView image in fullscreenMartina Arroyo in costume as Aida at the Metropolitan Opera in New York in 1965.Photograph: Metropolitan Opera ArchivesOperaObituaryMartina Arroyo obituaryUS soprano known for her rich, opulent tone and her acclaimed performances as Aida and other Verdi heroinesBarry MillingtonSun 25 Oct 2026 07.11 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 07.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe soprano Martina Arroyo, who has died aged 90, was one of the generation of black American opera singers – others were Marian Anderson, Leontyne Price,Shirley VerrettandGrace Bumbry– who in their early careers faced institutionalised racial prejudice before achieving international recognition. Having proved herself to be one of the finest exponents of the leading Verdi roles, Arroyo was finally able to establish herself in the US, as well as worldwide, and went on to become, after her retirement from the stage, a distinguished teacher and ambassador for the art form.Although her vocal talent had been noticed at an early age, she was advised, in view of the paucity of opportunities for black singers, to develop a back-up career – she was engaged for a year as a high-school classroom teacher and for two further years as a social worker – before achieving a measure of recognition from two events in 1958, when she was 22.In March that year she won theMetropolitan OperaAuditions of the Air, an annual singing competition sponsored by the Met, performing Aida’s O Patria Mia, and in September she made her debut at Carnegie Hall as the First Coryphée in the American premiere of Ildebrando Pizzetti’s Assassinio nella Cattedrale (based on TS Eliot’s Murder in the Cathedral).She made her official Met debut the following year in the small role of the Celestial Voice in Don Carlo, but then for three seasons sang only supporting roles. Advised to make her career in Europe, where skin colour was a less prohibitive issue, she was given prominent roles at major houses including Vienna, Deutsche Oper Berlin, Hamburg, Frankfurt and Stuttgart. This was a period of intense activity, requiring her in one year to perform in 45 different European cities over a span of 48 days.View image in fullscreenArroyo performing at a gala concert in the congress hall at the Deutsches Museum in Munich, Germany, 1978.Photograph: Fred Lindinger/United Archives/Getty ImagesShe also had a residency at this time with Zurich Opera (1963-65) and it was while visiting her family in New York in 1965 that she received a telephone call fromRudolf Bing, general manager of the Met, inviting her to cover forBirgit Nilssonas Aida in two days’ time. Assuming it was a practical joke, Arroyo replied that she usually went to a matinee film that day with her mother, but thought she could make it to the opera in time for the evening performance. Bing assured her it was no hoax and went on, in view of the standing ovation she received that night, to offer her a contract, as a result of which she won acclaim in Don Carlo, Madama Butterfly and Il Trovatore. She was still not offered new productions there, but did open three seasons in Verdi roles, which were to become her staples.In these roles, notably Leonora in both Il Trovatore and La Forza del Destino, Amelia in Un Ballo in Maschera, Lady Macbeth, Elvira in Ernani and Elisabetta di Valois in Don Carlo, but also in the title roles of Madama Butterfly and Ponchielli’s La Gioconda, she displayed an alluringly voluptuous voice, yet with a steely core. She also had an ability to soar at climaxes but to fine down the tone in more intimate passages. One critic spoke for many when he described Arroyo’s as “the most dramatic and genuine Verdian voice to be heard these days” in 1970, though she was occasionally criticised in later years for a less developed ability to inhabit roles.Born in Harlem, New York, to Demetrio Arroyo, a mechanical engineer, and Lucille Washington, an amateur pianist, Martina was taught the piano by her mother, sang in local choirs and was encouraged in her enthusiasm to learn ballet. After attending Hunter College high school, affiliated with the prestigious Hunter College, she was in due course admitted to the latter, deciding to read Romance languages, the better to advance a career in opera. She had already been taking lessons, from the age of 14, from the voice coach Marinka Gurewich, teacher of Bumbry, among many others, and stayed with her for the next 40 years, until her own retirement and Gurewich’s death.View image in fullscreenLeonard Bernstein conducting Martina Arroyo in a dress rehearsal for Verdi’s Requiem, with the London Symphony Orchestra, in St Paul's Cathedral, 1970, filmed for the Aquarius arts television series.Photograph: ITV/ShutterstockShe made her UK debut in 1968 as Valentine in a concert performance of Meyerbeer’s Les Huguenots at the Royal Albert Hall, alongsideJoan SutherlandandGabriel Bacquier, conducted byRichard Bonynge. In the same month she was back at the Met appearing as the first black Elsa in Wagner’s Lohengrin there, oppositeSándor Kónya. She returned to London two months later to make her Covent Garden debut, as Aida, impressing the critic of Opera magazine with her “rich, opulent” tone and drawing a comparison with Price as an equally “moving and proud Aida”. Her voice was frequently to be compared with that of Price, the latter’s being judged as more smoky and sensual, Arroyo’s as warmer and more evenly balanced. She was to return to Covent Garden on repeated occasions in the roles of Aida and her other signature Verdi heroines.Her most notable recordings include her Elena in I Vespri Siciliani under Levine, Amelia in Un Ballo in Maschera under Riccardo Muti (judged the finest of available recordings byLord Harewoodin the 1993 Met Guide to Recorded Opera), Leonora in La Forza del Destino under Gardelli and an Aida recorded live at La Scala in 1972 under Abbado. Arroyo also proved herself a fine Mozartian, recording the roles of both Donna Anna (underColin Davis) and Donna Elvira (under Karl Böhm) in Don Giovanni. Also impressive is the well-schooled technique and sensitive phrasing she brought to a recording including Schubert and Brahms songs in the Liederabend disc of 1967.Arroyo’s interest in a wide repertory beyond opera was exemplified by her participation in the world premiere ofKarlheinz Stockhausen’s Momente – both the original version in Cologne (1962) and the first enlarged version at the Donaueschingen festival in 1965 – and in that of Samuel Barber’s Andromache’s Farewell, with the New York Philharmonic under Thomas Schippers, commissioned to celebrate the orchestra’s inaugural season at Lincoln Center in 1963.Her teaching was distinguished by its focus on the complete preparation of operatic roles, and after her retirement she established in 2003 the non-profitMartina Arroyo Foundation, providing immersive tuition for emerging young artists. In recognition of this work she received an Opera Honors award from the National Endowment for the Arts (2010) and the Kennedy Center Honors (2013).Her marriage to the viola player Emilio Poggioni in 1961 ended in divorce, and she subsequently married the French banker Michel Maurel. He died in 2011.Martina Arroyo, opera singer, born 2 February 1936; died 13 October 2026Explore more on these topicsOperaMetropolitan OperaGiuseppe VerdiobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Zadie Smith tells Dua Lipa inequality has made culture clashes feel ‘existential’ | Books | The Guardian
description: Novelist says demise of Britain’s ‘incredible’ welfare system and housing struggles have led to deeper divisions
Author: Ella Creamer
Headline: Novelist says demise of Britain’s ‘incredible’ welfare system and housing struggles have led to deeper divisions
Content: Dua Lipa interviews Zadie Smith during the London literature festival at the Southbank Centre, London.Photograph: Pete Woodhead/PAView image in fullscreenDua Lipa interviews Zadie Smith during the London literature festival at the Southbank Centre, London.Photograph: Pete Woodhead/PABooksZadie Smith tells Dua Lipa inequality has made culture clashes feel ‘existential’Novelist says demise of Britain’s ‘incredible’ welfare system and housing struggles have led to deeper divisionsElla CreamerSun 25 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 14.47 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe novelistZadie Smithhas said that inequality has made culture clashes feel “existential”, adding that it has become “natural to look to your left and think ‘who the fuck are you?’”In an interview withDua Lipaas part of the Southbank Centre’s London literature festival, Smith argued that the demise of Britain’s “incredible, historic” welfare system has led to greater divisions.The pair discussed Smith’s debut novel,White Teeth, which was published in 2000 and primarily set in the last three decades of the 20th century.Asked by Lipa about how attitudes towards multiculturalism have changed since the 80s and 90s, and the current “dividing line” on immigration in UK politics, Smith pointed to increased inequality and unemployment.“When you’re living in basically decent housing, when you hurt yourself you know you can go to hospital and be treated just like the rich kid down the road – then the differences [with others] become interesting, sometimes annoying, but not existential,” said the novelist.“Now, they’re existential. When you can’t get a job, when there’s no housing, when your schools are falling apart, when the hospitals are falling apart – now it feels existential.”White Teeth traces the stories of three families – the Joneses, the Iqbals and the Chalfens – and is set in Kilburn and Willesden in north-west London, where Smith grew up. The writer praised her state education, saying it has stood her “in incredibly good stead” throughout her life. “I can talk to anyone. The posh kids up the hill? Not so much.“Now, when you look at my neighbourhood, the same schools, the same situations – everything is harder, everybody is poorer, everybody is struggling more,” she continued. “It becomes very, very natural to look to your left and think ‘who the fuck are you?’ That is an economic and structural question.”Smith encouraged developing “a nostalgia for the left”. While “you don’t want the LGBTQ+ politics of the 80s, you don’t want the racial prejudice” depicted in White Teeth, “do you want the healthcare and the schools and the education? I think you do. So it’s about looking back and seeing what was of value – and what was [of] value to me was a social democracy that basically functioned, and might function again if people cared about it, wanted it, believed it could happen again.”On the writing process for White Teeth – which she began when she was 21 and was published when she was 24 – Smith said that she finished the acclaimed novel in the aftermath of being broken up with and moving back in with her mum.“Everybody else was out clubbing, I was like, ‘I’m fucking stuck in this room, finishing a novel,’” she said. But Valentine’s Day was approaching, and “all my girlfriends were like ‘we gotta go out, go on the pull’.” She ended up finishing it on 14 February and then “literally ran straight out to the club” – so the ending of the novel is “a chaos”, she said, adding that this is “why young people shouldn’t write novels”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSince White Teeth, Smith has written five novels – The Autograph Man, On Beauty, NW, Swing Time and The Fraud – along with short stories and nonfiction. Her most recent book was the essay collection Dead and Alive.Lipa and Smith also discussed facing criticism for their works, with Lipa saying that “learning to live with reviews – bad reviews, good reviews” was “one of the hardest things for me to learn to deal with”. Smith said that literary criticism is “absolutely essential” because it “helps develop taste”.“I’m very interested in criticism,” added Smith. “Even if it’s a bad review of me, if it’s well written, if it’s intelligent … I quite love ‘takedowns’.”London literature festival runs until 1 November, with speakers selected by Lipa including Patti Smith, Malorie Blackman and Hisham Matar. Lipa runs a book club, Service95, through which she interviews authors on a monthly basis.Explore more on these topicsBooksZadie SmithDua LipaSouthbank CentreWhite TeethLiterary festivalsClass issuesnewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: a horny drama stuffed with sex in a car, toilet and … city farm  | Television & radio | The Guardian
description: Adultery is a moreish series starring Romola Garai and Dominic Cooper. Plus, hit gang thriller This City Is Ours is back. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: Adultery is a moreish series starring Romola Garai and Dominic Cooper. Plus, hit gang thriller This City Is Ours is back. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Risky Business … Romola Garai and Dominic Cooper in Adultery on ITV1.Photograph: Thomas Wood/ITVView image in fullscreenRisky Business … Romola Garai and Dominic Cooper in Adultery on ITV1.Photograph: Thomas Wood/ITVTV tonightTelevision & radioTV tonight: a horny drama stuffed with sex in a car, toilet and … city farmAdultery is a moreish series starring Romola Garai and Dominic Cooper. Plus, hit gang thriller This City Is Ours is back. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Phil Harrison,Graeme Virtue,Jack SealeandEllen E JonesSun 25 Oct 2026 02.15 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 02.17 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAdultery9pm, ITV1“Attraction plus obstacle equals excitement.” This is the risky life motto that bored, put-upon personal trainer Beth (Romola Garai) takes to heart after her best mate unexpectedly dies. Wife to a useless husband and mother to an ungrateful son, it doesn’t take much for handsome doctor Tom (Dominic Cooper) to catch her eye. But Tom also happens to be the married father of Beth’s son’s new girlfriend. Created and written by Bafta winner Danny Brocklehurst (Shameless, Brassic), the addictive drama follows a steamy, sex-packed affair over six episodes – and the fallout from it. While the opener remains pretty PG, we’re promised trysts in cars, toilets … and a city farm.Hollie RichardsonKevin McCloud’s Listed Britain7pm, Channel 4This exploration of Britain’s listed buildings acts as a polemic, too: why do the buildings we choose to preserve nod towards power and grandeur? Kevin McCloud visits a few (including the Palace of Westminster, Hereford Cathedral and Chatsworth House) but also wonders why many apparently humbler buildings, including pubs, aren’t protected.Phil HarrisonThis City Is Ours9pm, BBC OneView image in fullscreenHoliday from hell … This City Is Ours on BBC One.Photograph: BBC/Left Bank Pictures/James StackThe hit Liverpool gang drama remains on top form in its second series. Picking up where it left off, Michael (the brilliant James Nelson-Joyce) and Diana (Hannah Onslow) are enjoying the quiet life in Spain, when a Colombian cartel member intrudes with questions about his brother Ricardo. Back in Liverpool, a tense dinner party, an even more tense car wash and an unexpected face from the past stir trouble among the gang.HRMortimer & Whitehouse: Gone Fishing9pm, BBC TwoSeries nine of the laid-back angling odyssey gets off to a bittersweet start as it features the final appearance of loyal terrier Ted, who passed away earlier this year. As ever, he threatens to steal the show, frolicking around Paul on the banks of the Ribble in Lancashire and nosing his way into Bob’s hotpot.Graeme VirtueApocalypse9pm, Channel 4The doomy but silly reality experiment concludes, with its two rival groups of survivors having reached some sort of accord. While that’s jeopardised by someone running their mouth during a shared feast, the exploration of new territory offers a big clue about how to end the experiment by securing evacuation.Jack SealeA Course Called Ireland9.30pm, BBC TwoBill Murray is buying sweets in Cork when Margaret stops to ask for his autograph: “Do you still do the acting now or anything?” She narrates this rather lovely series following the Hollywood star around Ireland as he reconnects to his ancestors on a golf tour with journalist and friend Tom Coyne. After being mistaken for another Hollywood actor, he plays his first golf in Kinsale.HRFilm choiceThe Boston Strangler,10.10pm, Talking Pictures TVView image in fullscreenCreepy and kooky … Tony Curtis with Henry Fonda in The Boston Strangler.Photograph: RONALD GRANTTony Curtis turns up halfway through, playing against type as the now DNA-linked killer, Albert DeSalvo. The real stars, though, are the dogged detectives of Boston PD, featuring a host of reassuringly craggy-faced character actors such as George Kennedy and Murray Hamilton, and headed up by John S Bottomly (Henry Fonda). They run down seemingly every creep and kook in eastern Massachusetts before eventually landing on their man. Director Richard Fleischer’s use of split-screen adds to both the pacing and the period feel.Ellen E JonesLive sportInternational One-Day Cricket: Pakistan v England, 7.30am, Sky Sports Main EventHarry Brook captains England in their third Tri-Series match in Lahore. England v Sri Lanka is on Thu at 8am.Premier League Football: Man United v BournemouthSun, 12.30pm, Sky Sports Main EventSunderland v Leeds is at 4.25pm.Explore more on these topicsTelevision & radioTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Carving out a greener future: how the Swiss ski resort of Laax is meeting the climate crisis head on | Ski resorts | The Guardian
description: Gondolas on demand, electric piste-grooming and chemical-free snow cannons – how Laax is ‘greenstyling’ its future
Author: Kevin Rushby
Headline: Gondolas on demand, electric piste-grooming and chemical-free snow cannons – how Laax is ‘greenstyling’ its future
Content: A snowboarder freestyling in the Laax snowpark.Photograph: Philipp Ruggli/Flims LaaxView image in fullscreenA snowboarder freestyling in the Laax snowpark.Photograph: Philipp Ruggli/Flims LaaxSki resortsCarving out a greener future: how the Swiss ski resort of Laax is meeting the climate crisis head onGondolas on demand, electric piste-grooming and chemical-free snow cannons – how Laax is ‘greenstyling’ its futureKevin RushbySun 25 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt’s the worst ski resort nightmare: hillsides of shaggy yellow grass streaked with slush under a leaden sky that’s coughing up sleet. Parts of Europe – places previously accustomed to crisp snow fields and pristine blue skies – are now facing this calamity, something meteorologists might describe as a British winter.Not everywhere, of course. Only lower altitudes are seeing such disasters. Higher up, normal service continues. I’m in the Swiss resort of Laax, where most of the slopes are at about 2,000 metres, lofty enough to be snow-secure, for now. The halfpipe is busy with dudes in baggy trousers and headphones nonchalantly practising their double corks. On the traditional pistes there are four-year-olds who could probably ski before they could walk. And then – Switzerland has its wacky side – three young men in first-world-war greatcoats on antique wooden skis propel themselves with rough-hewn quarter-staves.Is all this destined to disappear, perhaps in our children’s lifetimes? To put it in stark, white and black terms: are ski resorts in the same predicament as oil-dependent desert states, watching their one key source of wealth dwindle and disappear?If so, Laax is not going down without a fight. This unusual Swiss resort, close to the Austrian border, is making a bold attempt to be carbon neutral by 2030, a goal that requires cutting out all oil use, making all energy generation sustainable, and reducing food waste to zero. Stung by climate crisis criticism levelled at the ski industry, this community is now far ahead of most. What I have come to see may turn out to be the future of winter sports.View image in fullscreenLaax is regarded as one of Europe’s most environmentally progressive ski resorts.Photograph: Nicholas Iliano/Flims LaaxDown in Laax, I meet Reto Gurtner, 71, CEO of the Flims Laax resort. His father built the first ski lifts back in 1962. “Although there had been summer visitors since the 19th century, Laax was a poor village back then,” says Gurtner.In the 1970s, something significant changed. Gurtner went to study at UCLA and, under the California sun, discovered skateboarding. Even now the memory makes his eyes light up. “They were inventing new sports and I loved the style: no nationalism or militarism. Skateboards, mountain bikes, snowboards – if you did a good run, everyone applauded. It didn’t matter who you were. There was a freedom about it.”He came home with a degree in economics, but more importantly perhaps, a snowboard and a mountain bike. “We went up on the glacier and built the first halfpipe with shovels.”At first, there was a lot of resistance. Local ski outfitters refused to stock snowboards, while in summer, farmers were outraged at the sight of cyclists pelting down mountain tracks. “We made every cyclist wear a bib,” says Gurtner with a chuckle. “Then the farmers thought it was a race and were fine with that.”Conversation with Gurtner is a wild ride. We cartwheel through Steve Jobs, the German poets and the Wu-Tang Clan, as he describes how his visionary approach evolved into something he calls “greenstyle”, an optimistic and well-designed future.double quotation markThe new gondola system does away with unoccupied ski gondolas going up and down the mountainsideThat vision is found in all the new buildings around the resort, nowhere more so than the ski lift in the neighbouring village of Flims, where I head with local guide Doris Rellstab. “The new gondola system does away with unoccupied ski gondolas going up and down the mountainside,” she says. A complex algorithm allows skiers to choose one of five destinations up the mountain, despatching individual gondolas, which balances energy efficiency with passenger demand. As we are lifted smoothly up over the fir trees, the quiet efficiency of this on-demand system becomes immediately apparent.Rellstab tells me how things have changed in the half century since she began teaching winter sports. “Yesterday, I taught my first Arab group. They were a lot of fun.”Our destination is Segnes, high above the treeline at 2,100 metres. Having left the gondola, we don snow shoes and head into a bowl-like snow-filled valley. A couple of miles ahead, the valley ends in a sheer rock face topped by a jagged range of peaks. “That’s the Tschingelhörner,” says Rellstab. “Can you see the line in the rock below the peaks? That was once a geological mystery.”In 1848, the celebrated geologistRoderick Impey Murchisonarrived here with a local expert,Arnold Escher von der Linth. Older rocks were overlaying younger, a puzzle for which there was no explanation. It took more than a century for scientists to solve the problem: the ancient African tectonic plate was riding up over the younger European one. The world was indeed upside down.In summer, this area is covered in rare Alpine flowers and there’s a mountain hut to stay in. Next to us are the tracks of a snow hare. “Wildlife is doing well here,” says Rellstab. “The wolf and lynx have both returned.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenIn summer, the resort becomes an Alpine mountain biking hotpsot.Photograph: Balz WeberIn fact, climate change appears to be assisting wolves in the Alps. The first Alpine pack was recorded in 1993, and by 2021 there weremore than 250, with an annual growth rate of about 25%. Switzerland, once entirely wolf-free, now has about40 packs. Rellstab shows me a website where sightings are monitored. There are conflicts with farmers and hunters, but the numbers keep growing, an indication that parts of the ecosystem are doing well out of retreating snowlines.Perhaps more surprising is that lack of snow is not a big worry to the resort. As Gurtner points out: “Laax is not snow-dependent. A halfpipe or a snow freestyle playground doesn’t need a lot, and we make it with hydro power. And we’ve got mountain bikes and amazing hikes.”double quotation markLaax is not snow-dependent. A halfpipe or a snow freestyle playground doesn’t need a lot, and we make it with hydro powerLater that day, I am up on the mountain with my skis, wandering around on blue runs. Conditions are a bit icy and I’m playing safe, finding myself on a less frequented route that dips down into the valley. And then I come over a ridge and the snow on either side is gone – only the piste remains, a broad band of white curling down through green pasture dotted with lovely old barns. Cannon snow is more durable, surviving longer when the “real” stuff melts.Most Alpine ski stationsare already reliant on it, but unlike many, Laax does not add any chemical or biological additives to the water in its cannons. With sustainable power sources and electric piste-grooming machinery now becoming available, cannon snow is not as environmentally destructive as it may appear.How to have a sustainable family ski holiday: take the train and head highRead moreAt the foot of the hill, I reach the village of Falera, neighbour to Laax. There is one old chair lift, clanking and squeaking, and as I approach it comes to a halt. “Sorry,” says the attendant, “we are closed now.”I wander into the village, all hand-hewn barns with neat log stacks. I can’t see any cars. If Laax is taking the technological solution, its neighbour appears to have chosen a less frenetic and more traditional route to net zero. After 20 minutes, a bus (electric, naturally) appears. As I ride back to Laax, I check thewildlife websitethat Rellstab recommended. And I get a shock. According to a CCTV report from a few hours earlier, a wolf had walked within a mile of me. Outside my hotel, I jump off the bus. Evening is falling. I wait for a line of silent cars to go by. With electric motors everywhere, the town is hushed. Climate change, I reflect, is nothing if not unpredictable. When the wolves howl, you will hear them.The trip was provided byFlims Laaxand rental equipment byEcoski.Trainsrun from Zurich via Chur and the Rhine Gorge toIlanz, where there’s abus serviceto Laax.Inghamsoffers aseven-nighttrip to Laaxfrom £1,618pp B&B, including flightsExplore more on these topicsSki resortsSkiing holidaysSwitzerland holidaysSnowboardingEurope holidaysGreen travelWinter sports holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: How to make mushroom stroganoff – recipe | Food | The Guardian
description: An age-old Russian favourite, rich and full of flavour, in nine easy steps
Author: Felicity Cloake
Headline: An age-old Russian favourite, rich and full of flavour, in nine easy steps
Content: Who needs meat? Felicity Cloake’s mushroom stroganoff.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food Styling: Flossy McAslanView image in fullscreenWho needs meat? Felicity Cloake’s mushroom stroganoff.Photograph: Robert Billington/The Guardian. Food Styling: Flossy McAslanFelicity Cloake's masterclassFoodHow to make mushroom stroganoff – recipeAn age-old Russian favourite, rich and full of flavour, in nine easy stepsFelicity CloakeSun 25 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleStroganoff is a richly savoury dish of sautéed beef in soured cream named after a 19th-century count (though no one seems quite sure exactly which one). But it was only as recently as the 20th century that this age-old Russian favourite was gussied up with onions and mushrooms. Here, it has evolved again to eschew the meat altogether – and you may be surprised how little you miss it.Prep15 minCook40 minServes415g dried porcini2 large onions50g butterSalt and black pepperFreshly grated nutmeg, or ground allspice300g white or chestnut button mushrooms4 field mushrooms250ml soured cream, preferablyśmietana(see step 7)1 tbsp Polishsarepska, or English mustardA squeeze of lemon(optional)Chopped chives or dill, to finish1 A note on the fatDon’t be tempted to reduce the amount of butter in this dish – stroganoff shouldneverbe low-fat – but do feel free to substitute a plant-based alternative, or a good rapeseed or olive oil and a plant-based creme fraiche, though you may also need to add a spritz of lemon juice to taste at the end.2 Prep the vegView image in fullscreenPut the dried porcini in a heatproof bowl, pour over 200ml just-boiled water and leave to soak while you get everything else ready. Peel and thinly slice the onions. Put a wide frying pan on a medium-low heat, add half (25g) the butter and leave to melt.3 Fry the onionsView image in fullscreenFry the onions, along with a pinch of salt and a good grating of nutmeg or allspice, in the melted butter, stirring regularly to ensure they don’t burn, until soft, golden and sweet. Meanwhile, briefly rinse the button mushrooms, if necessary, or brush any dirt off them. If they’re small, leave them whole, and cut into halves or quarters if large.4 Fry the button mushroomsView image in fullscreenScoop the softened onions into a bowl, leaving as much butter as possible behind in the pan. Turn up the heat to medium-high, then saute the button mushrooms in the residual butter until softened and well browned. Scrape the cooked mushrooms into the fried onion bowl.5 Dry-fry the field mushroomsBrush the field mushrooms, then trim and cut into roughly 1½cm-thick slices. Put the pan back on a medium-high heat and, once it’s hot, add the sliced mushrooms and give them a very light sprinkling of salt. Cook, turning occasionally, for eight to 10 minutes, until their liquid has evaporated and the sound from the pan is a sizzle rather than a hiss.View image in fullscreen6 Add butter and fry againAdd the remaining 25g butter to the now dry mushroom pan, then keep frying, turning so the mushroom slices cook evenly on both sides, for roughly seven to 10 minutes, until they’re a glossy, rich and golden brown. Scoop the sliced mushrooms into a second bowl. (The dish can be prepared ahead up to this point.)7 Finish the sauce baseView image in fullscreenAdd the porcini soaking liquid (fine-strained, if need be, to remove any grit) to the pan, scrape the base to deglaze, then gradually whisk in the soured cream – ideally, go for Polishśmietana, which often has a slightly higher fat content than much UK soured cream and is thus less likely to curdle. Stir in the mustard (again, Polish brands are ideal) and heat very gently.8 Add the fried onion mixView image in fullscreenReturn the fried onions and button mushrooms to the pan. Finely chop the drained soaked porcini and stir them in, too. Leave to simmer very gently for 10 minutes (if the mix curdles, it will look less than appetising, but rest assured it will still be perfectly safe to eat), then stir in the fried field mushrooms towards the end.9 Season and serveSeason to taste with salt, black pepper and some more nutmeg or allspice, if you like, and add a spritz of lemon juice if it needs it. Serve hot, but not bubbling, topped with finely chopped chives or dill and paired with steamed rice or mashed or sauteed potatoes, or even wide egg noodles, as stroganoff is commonly enjoyed in the US.Explore more on these topicsFoodFelicity Cloake's masterclassVegetablesVegetarian food and drinkStewEastern European food and drinkMain coursefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Outlier, Glasgow G1: ‘This kind of carefully orchestrated can’t-be-arsedness is really quite magical’ – restaurant review | Restaurants | The Guardian
description: You cannot fake fabulous by simply buying in cool crockery and a freezer full of someone else’s pastry
Author: Grace Dent
Headline: You cannot fake fabulous by simply buying in cool crockery and a freezer full of someone else’s pastry
Content: Outlier, Glasgow: ‘Intensely likeable.’Photograph: Stephen Lister/The GuardianView image in fullscreenOutlier, Glasgow: ‘Intensely likeable.’Photograph: Stephen Lister/The GuardianGrace Dent on restaurantsRestaurantsReviewOutlier, Glasgow G1: ‘This kind of carefully orchestrated can’t-be-arsedness is really quite magical’ – restaurant reviewYou cannot fake fabulous by simply buying in cool crockery and a freezer full of someone else’s pastryGrace DentSun 25 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Sun 25 Oct 2026 07.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn my misspent youth, I’d head to Glasgow to watch the likes ofFields of the NephilimandHawkwindat theBarrowland Boardroom, drink snakebite and buy posters from the touts on Gallowgate to Blu-Tack to my bedroom wall and tear holes in my mother’s woodchip wallpaper. Today, however, I’m here to visitOutlier, a bakery/restaurant/art space that serves warm bread, sticky treats and porchetta with beetroot and plum caponata. It’s on London Road just minutes from the Barrowland, and I’ve wound up here thanks only to a complete stranger on Buchanan Street who wrote down its name on the back of an old receipt and pressed it into my hand. She implored me to try the green jasmine rice pudding, the fresh sourdough and the chocolate and hazelnut babka. We used to do this type of inter-human face-to-face contact thing a lot back in the 1980s, before the internet ruined life.View image in fullscreenOutlier’s ‘clodhopping’ fried chicken thigh in a milk bun.Outlier originally opened back in 2022, after Steven Turner, who had previously run various arts venues, applied to turn the building into a space for artists with a kitchen attached. What we have now is a fairly sparse but charming space, tiled a bit like an old swimming baths in places, in mustards and dark, glossy browns. There are pale, unvarnished wooden tables, speckled stoneware plates, green, pressed-glass tumblers and prices handwritten on scraps of coloured card. When it all comes together, this kind of carefully orchestrated can’t-be-arsedness is really quite magical, and from the outset I found Outlier intensely likable.We perch in a window seat, perusing an actively dreamy brunch menu: blood peach panzanella with Isle of Wight tomatoes, Toulouse sausage with braised Umbrian lentils, or celery soup with Highland blue cheese. Even so, it is the cake counter that has proper main-character energy here. Just after opening at 11am, it is piled high with those babka buns, apple crumble and custard cakes, and bright, jubilant strawberry pastries. The bakers work behind that counter on long tables, and a queue snakes through the space and back out of the door. Outlier’s playlist is cheery and knowing – classic ska, Squeeze’s back catalogue – and it just can’t fail to keep things buoyant. Thirty-five years may have passed since I last hung out meaningfully in this postcode, but the place still feels vibrantly alive.View image in fullscreen‘Like a pixie swimming pool’: Outlier’s green jasmine rice pudding.A plate of warm house sourdough comes with a generously large serving of cured sea trout with bronze fennel, sharp horseradish creme fraiche and summer pickles dyed into a hot-pink, Barbie shade by beetroot, and in which chunks of cauliflower, onion and turnip zing with acidity. That jasmine rice pudding comes ethereally dusted in matcha, like a pixie swimming pool. Yes, it is a big bowl of rice pudding at 11am, but I’m not complaining, not least because of its beautiful notes of gooseberry and lime leaf. I’ve started the day with carbs, carbs and more carbs, and a pot of good earl grey tea; if only all days could be so wantonly good.Outlier’s sandwiches, meanwhile, are frankly ridiculous. The fried chicken thigh on a house milk bun is a clodhopper, not for the meek, and comes doused in red harissa, lemon mayo and ranch dressing. The beef shin toastie is three inches thick and crammed with meat, smoked cheddar and fennel jam, all pressed between two big slices of tin loaf. It is crisp and damp all at once. Who finishes these sandwiches? Competitive eaters only, at a guess. I stash half of it away in a paper box to save for later, archly aware that down south it would be three times the price.View image in fullscreenOutlier’s chocolate fudge cake comes ‘topped with a giant wave of coffee buttercream’.By this time, we are full to bursting, yet someone is loading that cake counter with fresh chocolate fudge cake topped with a giant wave of coffee buttercream. There are cinnamon buns in brown butter frosting, too, as well as olive oil cake cut into neat slabs. It’s so rare in this day and age to see home-baked cakes that have not been delivered frozen by a van, and that aren’t also going to 17 other shops in the vicinity. Instead, these are bespoke numbers made by people standing all of eight feet away from you.So, stranger on Buchanan Street with your big pen and your TK Maxx receipt tipoff, you were absolutely correct to flag me down. Outlier has a buzz for good reason. You cannot fake fabulous by simply buying in cool crockery and a freezer full of someone else’s pastry. I shall return for the lamb shoulder with green harissa and black cardamom yoghurt, and a poppyseed and raspberry custard bun. Next time, though, I’ll be prepared and wear a loose waistband. This place is not an outlier at all, but centre stage in all the big reasons to love Glasgow.Outlier38 London Road, Glasgow G1 (no phone or website). Open all week, Mon-Thurs 8am-4pm, Fri & Sat 8am-5pm, Sun 9am-5pm (opening for dinner Thurs-Sun in early 2027). From about £25 a head, plus drinks and serviceExplore more on these topicsRestaurantsGrace Dent on restaurantsFoodBritish food and drinkfeaturesShareReuse this content
